PPT + Resume Shortlisting - 3rd September 2025

Aptitude test - 4th September 2025 Coding test - 19th September 2025 GD + PI - 3rd October 2025

NOTE: This was a pool campus opportunity along with VJTI so the entire process lasted a month. Be mentally prepared for such situations and set your priorities straight. Before this I participated in KPMG hiring process for the Tech Enablement role and it turns out I got selected, but due to a delay in their results I finally ended up with this opportunity.

Placement Process:
journey.prep:
1. Placements are one of the most trying yet important phases of life and you will definitely come out on the other side, a stronger and more confident person. This was my 6th process (OAs excluded!), so learn to take setbacks in a positive way and just keep preparing for your destined company.

2. ATS score checker : http://resumeworded.com/ (try to get >80)

3. Python essentials : Neetcode YT playlist , Blind 75 , Python for Everybody by University of Michigan (Coursera certification). Keep revising CS fundamentals (OS, CCN, DBMS, OOPs) as they are asked in a lot of tests and interviews both.

4. Aptitude : IndiaBix Start aptitude practice early on! Do not underestimate it or think "yeh toh easy hai ho hi jayega". Speed and accuracy only comes through consistent practice and you can't go from 0-100 in aptitude just in one night before your test.

5. For GDs, build your communication skills and quick thinking as they look for people who add value to the discussion by stating relevant points in a concise and articulate manner. The frequency honestly does not matter much, if you speak only 2 times but in a confident and agreeable manner then that would be better than hijacking the whole discussion and arguing with people.

6. On your interview day, remain calm and composed and meditate/listen to songs/think of God (whatever works for you).Try to focus more on the process rather than the outcome to stop overthinking and believe in yourself!!! Stop worrying about the result and just give your best and if it still does not turn out the way you wanted, there is something better in store for you.

7. Luck is a huge factor in every step of the process, so don't take failures personally and just keep trying and improving yourself every day. Trust in God's plan, it will all work out well in the end.

For any queries, feel free to reach out to me through LinkedIn

1. Pre-placement Talk

If you're seriously interested in a company, it's really important to attend the PPT and moreover, really pay attention to what exactly they are looking for, information about the role (location, CTC, I+P or not, etc.), company values and what they do. In this case, the role is that of Corporate Trainee and it has further categories like Developer and Data Scientist that they would decide based on our profiles.

- You can take note of things you find important and want to remember for interview rounds.

- In case of virtual PPTs, keep screenshots of slides with company values, their achievements, skills required etc.

2. Resume Shortlisting

This is a very crucial step and many deserving people sometimes fail to get their resume shortlisted (happened with me in certain initial companies) due to ignoring these basic points:-

● CGPA! Even though it cannot compensate for your lack of skills, maintaining a decent CGPA can definitely save you from being eliminated if the company has internal criteria for filtering out candidates. As far as I have seen, having a CGPA of >7.5 is good enough and will make you eligible for all companies. However if you want to guarantee that they don't eliminate you from their side, stay above 8 just in case. (Mine bordered around 7 which was a mistake on my part but I kinda made up for it through my resume and other areas, so luck is a big factor and if you don't have a good CGPA don't get demotivated because many companies look at your overall profile as well).

● ATS! Since it is unclear what the resume shortlisting criteria is for each company, do not think ATS score does not play a role. There may be times when HRs do not want to look through the resumes of 200-300 candidates so they simply filter on the basis of ATS score. So focus on increasing your resume's ATS score as much as you can (>80 on Resume Worded is great), and there are many techniques to do that by including stats, action words, at least 1 work experience and 2-3 good projects that actually add value, leadership roles, etc.)

● JD! Tailoring your resume according to the role and company you are applying for is really important, so please have a good look at the JD provided (things like skills required, role of intern, what the company does) and strategically include things that will give you an advantage when you talk about them during your interview. In my case, the role wasn't very specific like an SDE or DA or a non-tech role so what worked for me was showing versatility through projects and courses/certifications by adding 2 ML/Data Science related projects and 1 deployed fullstack project. Also, I researched a bit about what the company's main business is and accordingly included an AI-based loan underwriting agent project for brownie points.

You can get a better idea through my resume that I used for Mahindra Finance: Akshata_Mahindra_Resume.pdf

3. Aptitude Test [~150 candidates got resume shortlisted and attempted this round]

This round was conducted on the YUGMA platform and consisted of 100 questions (covering quants, aptitude, logical reasoning, verbal aptitude and behavioral/situation based questions) to be solved in 1 hour. The challenge here was not in the difficulty of the questions but rather effective time management, and also the fact that each question had negative marking as well. I started from the beginning and had solved about 15-20 questions when I realised that there were so many questions to be done in a limited time. I then started solving the behavioral and verbal questions first as they were pretty easy and obvious to answer so they would secure marks, and after covering all those I moved on to the remaining quant questions which revolved around topics like speed distance and time, percentage, profit loss, discounts, etc. which were very doable. Practicing from IndiaBix is more than enough to prepare for aptitude based questions and I also think quick strategising and presence of mind really played a role here. Keeping in mind the negative marking, I left out 10 questions which I was very unsure of. They had purposely included some very indecipherable questions where it wasn't clear what exactly needed to be done. All I can say is just trust your gut and if you really don't know what to do in a question, simply leave it (ofc only in OAs with negative marking). I think ppl who got >70 questions correct were selected after this round.

4. Coding Test [70 candidates shortlisted from previous round]

This was conducted on Assesshub and had 2 sections :-

- The first section had around 20 MCQs on basic python input/output questions which are very doable if you know Python basics like loops, variables, conditional operators, etc.

- The second section had 3 DSA questions (Leetcode easy level) to be solved in Python only. I was able to do these quickly, having been coding in Python since 1st year, but if you are a beginner you can practice with Blind 75 sheet on Neetcode as they have really good solution tutorials in Python. It was a relatively easy coding round as compared to other OAs I had given before, but attention to detail was really important here since for output questions some options were very similar to each other so we

needed to read the code and each option properly. Also, the IDE for DSA questions was quite different to usual ones so we had to adapt our code according to the given main function. I was able to solve all 3 DSA questions and almost all MCQs correctly, and I submitted way before the test ended so maybe both speed and accuracy could have been a factor behind shortlisting for next round.

5. Group Discussion (GD) [29 candidates shortlisted from previous round]

We were divided into panels of 6 and I was in the first one. Before starting the GD, we were briefed about general rules to be followed and time guidelines (9 mins for discussion + 1 min for concluding). The topic given to us was "Technology : Boon or Bane" and we were strictly told to be either for or against but not both. After getting the topic, we had a minute to gather and jot down our thoughts. Here, I prepared my points according to technology being a great boon since that is what I believe. However once the GD started, I was the 3rd person to speak up and everyone before me had spoken for the motion so I spontaneously decided to speak about technology being a bane and wrote down 2-3 points that came to my mind while others were speaking. While this could have been a mistake, I thought in the moment that if everyone speaks for the motion then it would be a very dull discussion with all of just saying "I agree with you…" , and I trusted in myself to speak on the spot without a lot of preparation so my communication skills helped me here. I presented a different viewpoint and was the only one who spoke against the motion (that possibly caught the interviewers' attention).

6. Personal Interview (PI) [11 candidates shortlisted from previous round]

After getting shortlisted from GD, all of us had 2 interviews : technical and HR, neither being eliminatory. They said they would take into account all our scores (aptitude, coding, GD, PI) and accordingly come up with a result in the end. Both the interviews were in no particular order and I had my HR round first:

a) HR : This was a 45-minute long, rigorous HR interview where the Head of HR basically wanted to assess our inner personalities and culture fit rather than technical prowess. She started with my family background, upbringing, what all places I have been to, etc. and also asked about which project taught me the most valuable life lessons and which one made me encounter the most challenges and self-doubts, with simultaneous follow-up questions for each. One important thing here was that I remembered their DE&I (Diversity, Equity & Inclusion) framework from the PPT and subtly included these values in my answers. She asked me a lot of questions about my life experiences and lessons I had learnt along the way to know what kind of a person I am. Towards the end I was also asked if I had come across any unethical practices around me and how I had reacted to them. As far as I could make out from her response to my answers, they look for people who know how and when to speak against something so it's always good to have some answer for these questions. Even if you haven't experienced something, have a presence of mind and think of the most suitable response rather than just saying "No" or "I don't know". Towards the end, she asked me if I had anything to ask her and since I had not really prepared for an HR-specific question I just asked "What are the company's expectations from me in terms of beliefs and values if I get selected?" Again I reiterate, it is always better to have some decent response rather than saying "Nothing".

b) Technical : This interview also lasted around 40 minutes and revolved around technical and resume based questions in depth. The interviewer was friendly and polite, starting with asking me for a brief introduction and then moving on to my projects and work experience. He focused more on

my 'Smart Returns' project and wanted to know how we decided on the problem statement and how exactly we were solving the problem at hand, what the end results are, detailed explanation of the project workflow and how different technologies are integrated together. He then went on to ask me about a case study along similar lines, it was regarding a demand-based shipping feature for orders on Amazon. I explained about a solution through data driven demand forecasting models to predict order volumes for a particular location depending on various factors like age group, economic capacity, geography, etc. He seemed satisfied with my response and asked me how accurate an ML model would be in such a case. I estimated a >80% accuracy since Amazon is a big company operating since long ago so they would have a large customer database hence we would get good accuracy through data analytics. He then asked me how we would handle the 20% inaccurate demand forecasting done by the ML model, and for this I suggested another feature so that the company's customer satisfaction rating and profitability do not get largely affected. He constantly tried to check if I was confident in my responses and finally seemed satisfied with my answer.

5 students got the final offer, and I was extremely grateful to be one of them.

Placement Process:

journey.prep:
Focus on your CGPA. During our time, many compa nies had a minimum CGPA criteria of 7.5, which led to a large number of students being filtered out even before getting the opportunity to sit for the company. It really hurts when you don't even get the chance to appear despite having the skills.

Placements are a tiring yet humbling process. I had reached the HR rounds of InCred and Quantiphi before this opportunity, and both interviews went really well, but I couldn't make it to the final shortlist. That's when I truly realised how important factors like CGPA and luck can be in the placement journey. Sometimes, even after giving your best, things don't work out --but they prepare you for the opportunity that's meant for you.

My personal suggestion would be during your 6th semester, shut out the noise around you and just believe in your hard work . When your day finally comes, everything will start to make sense ,you'll realise why you weren't selected earlier and how it was all just a testing phase before something bigger. Having your family and supportive friends around you trule encourag es you to not get carried away by rejections and prepare for upcoming companies.

Study everything that's commonly asked in interviews. In placements, being a jack of all trades often works better than excelling in just one domain. Practicing DSA is important, of course, but relying only on it won't help much--only 4-5 companies are heavily DSA-focused and I realized it much much later. The rest mostly have doable coding questions in their online assessments and give high importance to aptitude, which most students tend to ignore.

For interviews, know your resume inside out--every project, every line. SQL is the underdog in placements, so make sure to practice it thoroughly beforehand.

When it comes to projects, having a simple project that you understand deeply is far better than having an overly complex one that you can't explain properly. Lastly, know your OS, CN, and DBMS concepts really well--many companies ask questions from these subjects. End-moment preparation won't help much here, so start early. I'd recommend watching CodeHelp's OS playlist, which is around 30 hours long--it's a time investment that's truly worth it.

All the very best for your placements! Give your best, trust the process, and have faith in your hard work. Everything will fall into place when it's meant to.God does have a plan for all

The eligibility criteria required a minimum of 6.0 CGPA in college and 60% marks in both 10th and 12th

1. [Aptitude Round] [All students from Comps,AIML,DS and having minor in computers from EXTC were eligible for the process]

The Aptitude Round consisted of 100 questions covering Quantitative Aptitude, Geometry, Verbal Ability, and Logical Reasoning to be solved in 1 hour. The quantitative section in cluded problems on percentages, ratios, time and work, and geometry -based questions. The verbal section tested grammar, reading comprehension, and vocabulary, while the reasoning section focused on analytical thinking. In addition to these, there were a few behavioral and situational questions such as "If your team member isn't contributing effectively, what would you do?" to assess decision-making and teamwork skills. Overall, the round focused on both technical and behavorial assessment.

This round followed a +4 -1 marking scheme so make sure to attempt the questions you are fully sure about, I managed to solve 94 questions. Since navigation was allowed,I quickly solved logical verbal and behavorial questions in the first 20 minutes and then proceeded to do the aptitude questions.

I practiced Quantitative, Logical, and Verbal Aptitude questions from IndiaBix, and most importantly taking their timed tests greatly helped me improve my speed and time management skills, which play a crucial role in performing well in aptitude exams.

2. [Coding Round] [ 72 candidates were shortlisted for this round]

Round 2 consisted of two sections - the first focused on basic Python MCQs, while the second included easy-level coding questions similar to those found on LeetCode. The only programming language allowed was Python. I was able to solve all the coding questions and pa ss all the test cases, along with answering almost all the MCQs correctly. This round was quite doable, and the key differentiator turned out to be time . Candidates who managed to solve almost all questions accurately and submitted their test about 15 minutes early were the ones who proceeded to the next round .

but since only allowed programming language was python and my primary language was Java,I practiced some basic questions from this youtube channel. https://youtu.be/78FsbjYSWIU?si=ehBIXHc3uNnGOLEF This has around 100 coding questions which will give you a strong grasp of the basics For other DSA rounds,Practice Striver's sheet being well versed with it will help you clear DSA coding rounds of almost all the companies. I practiced python mcqs from Sanfoundry(It has 1000 mcqs but to be able to be quick with mcqs that much of practice will really be worth it as you would have seen or solved all the questions in the past).

3. [Group Discussion Roud] [25 candidates were shortlisted for this round]

The topic given to us was "Technology: Boon or Bane." Candidates who expressed their points in a clear, concise, and professional manner, speaking confidently and with good articulation, were the ones selected for the next round.

4. [Technical Interveiw] [11 students were selected for this round]

The interview was primarily focused on Python and Machine Lea rning. The interviewer was very particular about the answers and often went into detailed discussions. He began by asking me to introduce myself. Since I had researched Mahindra Finance beforehand, I knew that one of its key sectors deals with loan approva l, which aligned well with my credit risk modelling project. I mentioned this connection during my introduction, which led him to ask several project -related questions.

He asked which algorithm I had used, and since I had applied SMOTE during preprocessing , he asked me to explain SMOTE along with its advantages and disadvantages. He then asked me to draw and explain the working of Random Forest and justify why it performed better than XGBoost in my case.

Next, he moved on to questions about my dataset. My p roject involved two datasets that I had merged, so he asked me to write the pandas query for merging them using the ID column as the key. He further asked detailed questions about the types of columns in my dataset and their relevance.

The discussion then shifted to model evaluation metrics, where he asked me to explain precision, recall, and accuracy, and to justify which metric mattered the most in my project context.

After that, he presented a case study scenario: "If Uber ride prices suddenly increase f rom ₹400 to ₹800 within 10 minutes in the same location, how would you identify and fix the bug in your ML model?" He asked me to describe the parameters and features I would use in such a model. He then gave another scenario: "If all drivers in a certain area stop accepting Uber rides and instead take private trips, how would your model detect such behavior?" I explained my approach, mentioning that one of the parameters would be peak -hour timings. He further asked how I would determine peak hours without having an existing dataset.

The interview concluded with me asking him three questions about Mahindra Finance's advancements in Machine Learning and how the company is integrating AI into its operations. Overall, it was a highly engaging and technical discussion that tested both conceptual understanding and practical problem -solving.

5.[HR Round] The HR round surprisingly lasted for around 45 minutes, during which the HR was noting down my answers carefully. The discussion mainly revolved around situational and behavioral questions. I was given several case-based scenarios such as how I would handle a situation where a team member is not contributing effectively, or how I would respond if I witnessed something wrong happening around me. The HR wanted to understand my thought process, decision-making, and ability to handle real-life workplace challenges. Overall, it was a situational round focused on assessing attitude, ethics, and teamwork rather than technical knowledge.

Finally 5 students were selected :)

journey.howSecured:
1. Online Assessment [ Students with >=7 CGPA ]

The first stage was an online assessment consisting of a single DSA question + 4 logic/Aptitude questions. The DSA question was mainly based on mathematical reasoning rather than complex data structures.

After this round, 24 students were shortlisted .

2. Predictive Index Assessment [ 24 students ]

The shortlisted candidates were asked to complete a Predictive Index assessment the following day. This assessment was focused more on behavioural and personality evaluation rather than technical skills.

After this stage, 13 candidates were shortlisted for the interview process .

3. Technical Interview Round 1 (Online) [ 13 students ]

The first technical round was conducted online on a coding platform called Meetl.

The interview focused on:

• Core Java fundamentals

• Java Collections Framework

• Object-Oriented Programming concepts

• DBMS basics

• Data Structures and Algorithms I was given two DSA problems:

• One was Leetcode easy level.

• The second problem was of medium difficulty (roughly LeetCode medium level) .

I had to write the code for both problems and explain the logic clearly . After this round, 3 out of the 13 candidates were shortlisted for the next round.

4. Technical Interview Round 2 (Onsite) [3 students]

This round was conducted onsite at the company office and was a pen-and-paper coding round.

This interview again focused heavily on OOP concepts and Java fundamentals.

Some of the questions included:

• Explanation of Parent p = new Child() and Child c = new Parent() along with reasoning.

• Typecasting in objects.

• Lambda functions in Java.

• Streams in Java.

• Serializable interface.

• Questions about my hackathon experiences and projects.

After this , the interviewer asked 4 DSA questions

1. Linked List

Delete a node in a singly linked list in constant time.

2. Array Problem

Find the second maximum element in an array using one pass and constant space.

3. Integer Stream Problem

The interviewer described a scenario where a large stream of integers flows into a queue throughout the day, with the constraint that the difference between consecutive numbers is always 1.

At the end of the day, we need to answer q queries asking whether a specific number x appeared in the stream, and the requirement was to answer queries in constant time and constant space.

4. Array Partition

Given an array, divide the elements into two arrays such that the difference between their sums is minimum . ( time complexity of order 1 )

The problems themselves were not difficult but were slightly tricky and required reasoning/proof .

I wrote code for all four problems and explained the logic clearly. The interviewer seemed satisfied with both my OOP explanations and DSA solutions.

The next day I received a call from HR saying that the feedback was positive, and I was invited for the next round.

5. Technical Interview Round 3 (Senior Engineering Manager) [ 2 students ]

This round was again conducted onsite and a pen-and-paper round .

The interviewer was an Engineering Manager who had been with the company for around 11 years.

The round began with questions on the Java Collections Framework, after which the discussion went deep into HashMap internals.

I had to explain:

• How key-value pairs are stored

• Load factor

• Rehashing

• Collision handling

• How collision handling worked before Java 8 and after Java 8

After this discussion, I was asked to write a Student class with attributes:

• name

• id

• marks

I wrote the class and implemented the constructor.

Then the interviewer asked whether we could directly use this class as a key in a HashMap.

This question was meant to check my understanding of equals() and hashCode().

I explained:

• The default implementations provided by the Object class

• How they compare memory references

• Why overriding them is necessary for logical equality

I then implemented:

• equals() using student id

• hashCode() accordingly

I also explained what would happen if we did not override these methods.

Next we discussed:

• Comparable vs Comparator

• Writing a Comparable implementation

• Writing a Comparator for a different custom sorting strategy

• What the return values -1, 0, and 1 represent

The interviewer then moved to JDBC, which I had not worked with before, so I honestly mentioned that I had not used JDBC.

We then discussed SQL concepts, including:

• Different types of joins

• Database indexing

• Data structures used in indexing (B-Trees)

Finally, the interviewer asked two logical puzzles:

Puzzle 1: 25 Horses and 5 Tracks

Find the top three fastest horses.

Puzzle 2: 2 Eggs and 100 Floors

Determine the highest floor from which an egg can be dropped without breaking.

The interviewer was mainly evaluating how I approached the problems and broke them down logically, rather than expecting an immediate answer.

I struggled a bit with the horses puzzle, but with some hints I eventually arrived at the solution.

I had mixed feelings after this round because the puzzle part did not go perfectly.

6. Technical Interview Round 4 ( Online ) [ 2 students ]

After about a week, HR informed us that there would be one final technical round.

This round was conducted virtually and had two interviewers:

• One senior engineering leader from the US

• One engineer from the Mumbai office ( if selected , he/she will be your manager )

This round was more conversational compared to previous rounds.

We started with a discussion about my projects and hackathon experiences. I was asked about the most challenging aspects of my projects and how I approached solving them.

One interesting question was about a product in the market that I admire or would like to work on , and I spoke about a technology product I had seen on Shark Tank India.

The discussion then moved into database concepts, including:

• Relational vs Non-relational databases

• MongoDB

• Redis ( Since I had used in my project )

• Why Redis, despite being very fast, is usually not used as a primary database for large systems

I was also given a probability puzzle involving 50 black balls and 50 white balls distributed across two bags , where the goal was to maximize the probability of drawing a black ball.

I initially took some time to reason about the problem, and with a hint from the interviewer I arrived at the correct solution. Towards the end of the interview, the discussion became more open -ended. I asked about a concept the interviewer mentioned called the S2 geometry data structure , which is used for geospatial indexing in systems like Google Maps.

I also asked what areas a new engineer should focus on during the first few months after joining .

Overall I was able to answer all questions in this round , but again felt dumb because I took a lot more time than required on that simple probability puzzle , brain felt saturated at that moment and stopped thinking, but with one hint from interviewer , arrived at the ans .

After this round, there was a long silence from the company for around 14-17 days. During this time, another candidate who was interviewing along with me received a call from HR for the HR discussion round, while I did not receive any update.

Naturally, I felt that my process might have ended there. However, after around two weeks, I unexpectedly received a call from HR informing me that my profile had been moved to a different team internally, and because of that, I would have to go through two additional technical &/ team rounds which were scheduled immediately on the next day .

7. Technical Interview Round 5 ( Online )

The fifth round was conducted by a manager from the Mumbai office with around 7 years of experience. The interview was relatively short and focused mainly on Java fundamentals and problem solving.

He first asked me about the internal working of HashMap, where I explained buckets, key-value storage, hashCode(), equals() , collisions, collision handling, etc.

Then he moved to a DSA problem similar to the "Search Suggestions System" problem on LeetCode.

Similar to : Leetcode Search Suggestions

I came up with a sorting + string prefix matching based solution. O(n^2) and coded the approach and output was correct.

Although the problem had a more optimized binary search based approach possible, he did not ask me to optimize further once the logic and output were correct . The round ended after he asked whether I had any questions for him.

8. Technical Interview Round 6 ( Online )

The sixth and final technical round was with a senior engineer from the US team who had around 15 years of experience. This round was very different from the previous ones.

It was not focused on coding or rapid-fire technical questions. Instead, it was more of a deep two-way discussion about the team, their domains, systems, and the type of work they do. He spent a significant amount of time explaining the team structure and the backend systems they work on.

I asked a few thoughtful questions regarding the domain and one specific question that he appreciated a lot during the discussion. I also asked him what I should focus on learning before joining so that I could reduce the amount of training effort required from the team side once I joined. He seemed to like that question as well, and the overall interaction was very positive and engaging. The conversation lasted for around one hour.

After these rounds, I received a call from HR stating that all interviewer feedback was positive and that the final HR discussion round was scheduled.

The HR round mainly covered resume overview, family background, relocation, future plans, joining timeline, and compensation discussion.

Toward the end of the HR round, I was also introduced to the manager(same person who took my second last interview) of the team I would potentially join, and we discussed the team goals and what I should focus on before joining.

After the HR round, there was another waiting period because the profile had to go through final approval from the US side. Around a month later, I finally received the official confirmation and offer from the company for the role of Junior Software Engineer.

My Experience and Key Lessons:

Placements are honestly all about luck, timing, and having faith in yourself. My experience was nothing less than a rollercoaster ride. I got shortlisted for almost every company in resume screening, cleared several online assessments, and reached multiple interviews -- but I also made silly mistakes that cost me offers early on.

Then came 14th August -- the day everything changed. This morning, I was giving interviews for Baker Hughes. My technical round went really well, and within 10 minutes, I was called for the HR round which also surprisingly went smooth. By noon, I was told my chances of getting selected were very high.

In the middle, I got the message: I was the only student shortlisted for the final round with Hyperverge from their entire Mumbai drive. I was happy, but also very confused -- which one to choose?

Around 3.30 pm I had been selected by Baker Hughes ,but with great support from TPO, especially Zeeshan Sir, the company agreed to let me decide after the results.

So, while everyone else was celebrating after Baker Hughes, I was baffled and busy preparing for my Hyperverge interview.

By evening, I had offers from both companies. It was a tough choice -- one was a core tech role, the other was an APM role that aligned with my passion. I listened to my heart and finally chose Hyperverge.

● Believe in timing. Even after multiple rejections, the right role will come at the right time.

● Keep your LinkedIn profile updated -- companies really do check it.

● Be thoroughly familiar with your resume -- every point should be something you can explain confidently.

● For puzzles and brainteasers, practicing from GeeksforGeeks puzzles is more than enough Top 100 Puzzles Asked In Interviews - GeeksforGeeks

1. Case Study Round [86 candidates appeared from SPIT. The process was conducted simultaneously at both SPIT and KJ Somaiya, the total number of candidates was approx 200+]

We were provided with a Notion file containing two problem statements. The final deliverables for both were:

● A presentation deck (PDF format)

● A short video presentation (max 5 mins) that shows both you and the deck. In the video explain your approach to problem framing and how you developed the solution

We had to choose one among the following two problem statements:

Problem Statement 1:

Design a Lightweight KYC App for Bharat

Context:

You are the Associate Product Manager at a tech startup building digital onboarding solutions. Your company is launching a mobile app targeting rural and semi-urban India, where smartphone specs are low-end, bandwidth is limited and users may not be digitally literate.

The app must support:

● Digilocker-based KYC

● Document-based KYC (Aadhaar, PAN, DL, VoterID)

● Face authentication (liveness, facematch checks)

● Integration with other client apps (SDK integration, web-redirection, etc.)

● Offline & retry-friendly mode

Your Task: Design the KYC solution end-to-end, keeping in mind the following:

1. Product Design & UX:

● How will the app work for users with low digital literacy?

● What will the user flow look like (screens, guidance, fail-safes)? Create wireframes.

● What offline/low-network support will you offer?

2. Features:

● Suggest and implement 2-3 innovative features to improve trust or ease of use using LLMs.

● How will you prioritise which features to build? Create a Prioritisation Matrix

3. Technical Architecture:

● How will you optimize SDK size?

● What trade-offs will you make between on-device vs server-side processing (e.g., facematch, liveness)?

● How will you handle low bandwidth and retry/resume flows?

4. Miscellaneous:

● How would you measure the success of the app?

● Any security concerns and how you'll solve them?

Problem Statement 2:

AI‑Enabled Loan Underwriting Agent for Rural and Semi‑Urban India

Context:

You are an Associate Product Manager at a tech startup developing lending solutions. Your company is launching a mobile app designed for rural and semi‑urban India. The app must work reliably on low‑spec smartphones, work with limited bandwidth, and be user‑friendly for individuals with low digital literacy.

The app must support:

● Instant Personal Loans

● AI enabled underwriting and lending

● Low customer default rates

Your Task: Design an end‑to‑end Loan Underwriting solution taking into account the following key areas:

● Features:

● What specific problems will your solution address? How will you prioritise the most important problems?

● Create two to three innovative features powered by LLMs( Eg: AI agents, Dynamic orchestrators) that can improve underwriting accuracy or ease of use

● How will you decide which features should be built first? Provide a clear prioritisation matrix

● Product Design and User Experience:

● How will the app accommodate users with low digital literacy?

● Describe the user flow for every step of the journey (To be created for every feature)

● Create Wireframes showcasing this solution (To be created for every feature)

● Technical Architecture:

○ Present a high level system design architecture that supports your AI enabled underwriting feature

○ Explain how you will handle low bandwidth environments, especially retry and resume logic to ensure a seamless experience

● Additional Considerations:

○ How will you define and measure success for the app (including key performance indicators)?

○ What security concerns must you address, and how will you mitigate them?

NOTE: For both of the ps, we were allowed to use LLMs or AI tools such as Lovable for ideation. But the final submission must be fully original.

My approach for this round:

● Selecting the problem statement:

○ During the presentation, it was evident that the company emphasized KYC, since that aligns with their core use case.

○ Based on this, I chose Problem Statement 1 - Design a Lightweight KYC App for Bharat.

● Initial research and documentation:

○ Before jumping into deck preparation, I conducted thorough research.

○ Explored articles, government research reports, and examined existing government KYC apps in detail.

○ Captured all useful insights and points in a structured document.

● Preparing the deck:

○ Once the research and documentation were complete, I began working on the presentation deck.

○ There was no page limit specified, so I created a comprehensive 15-page deck.

○ I structured the flow using the CUPS-PDM framework for clarity and coherence.

Deck structure using CUPS-PDM:

○ Context: Included all research findings, statistics, and key numbers to set the stage.

○ User Personas: Defined different user types, highlighting their characteristics and specific problems.

○ Problems: Listed all issues, clearly showing their cause and effect relationships.

○ Solution: ■ Designed solutions feature-wise, ensuring each one addressed previously identified problems as well as the pain points in the problem statement. ■ Included LLM-powered features to demonstrate how these can make the KYC process more efficient and convenient.

○ Wireframes: ■ Since AI tools were allowed, I used v0 by Vercel to create wireframes. ■ Prepared a detailed document specifying app design guidelines - from colors, buttons, and icons to text and overall flow to give it as a prompt. ■ Added all generated screens into the deck to visualize the user journey.

○ Technical Architecture: ■ Built a very detailed architecture slide, focusing on what, why, and how each approach would solve the problem. ■ Covered all pain points mentioned in the problem statement.

○ Metrics: Concluded with success metrics to measure the impact of the solution.

● Key principle followed:

○ I ensured every single detail in the deck had a clear justification.

○ Avoided adding features blindly -- everything was backed by reasoning, research, and alignment with user needs.

Key Takeaways for Preparing the PPT:

● Avoid long paragraphs; use bullet points for clarity.

● Choose neat, professional fonts that are easy to read.

● Use icons and images wherever possible to make slides lively and colorful.

● Add light-colored background boxes behind text to differentiate sections on a page.

● Maintain a consistent heading style on every slide.

● Stick to a uniform color palette throughout to give a cohesive look.

● Start with a minimalist Canva template to save time.

● Avoid wasting time on animations -- since the final submission is PDF, animations won't be visible and take extra effort to set up.

● Use varied slide layouts for different sections to keep it engaging.

● Include as many icons as possible for better visibility and quick understanding.

5-Minute Presentation Video : My Advice and Experience

● Record in a proper environment:

○ Wear a formal shirt and present in a quiet place with no disturbance.

○ Do not leave this task for the last minute - it looks short but can take multiple takes to get right.

● Be prepared for technical issues:

○ You may face network problems, mic glitches, or recording errors, so keep buffer time.

○ In my early attempts, I froze on camera and lost track of what to say -- this is normal, but plan for it.

● Keep your delivery natural:

○ Don't write or read a script - it's obvious and makes you sound robotic.

○ If needed, keep a small note of points to maintain flow instead of memorizing word-for-word.

○ Speak calmly, explain your thought process, and pitch the product naturally.

● Focus on the flow of content:

○ In 5 minutes, highlight why you chose this approach and how it impacts the problem statement.

○ Do not just read from the PPT - explain rather than narrate slides.

○ Keep it conversational but structured so it feels confident and authentic.

● Watch your timing carefully:

○ In my initial recordings, I overshot to 12-15 minutes, which forced multiple retakes.

○ Practice summarizing to stay within 5 minutes.

● Tools I used:

○ I used Zoom to record, presenting the PPT side-by-side with me visible.

2. Domain Knowledge Interviews (Online) [ 5 candidates appeared for this round ]

Preparation:

○ Having justification for every word in my case study.

○ Anticipating all types of questions related to my case study.

○ Revisiting core product management concepts (since this round was domain-focused).

○ Practicing redesigns and new feature ideas for commonly used apps (WhatsApp, Instagram, food delivery apps, Google Drive).

○ Learning how to answer trade-off questions in a structured manner.

○ Reviewing every project and internship on my resume.

○ Preparing approaches for puzzle questions and guesstimates.

Interview Experience:

● Duration: 1 Hour

● Mode: Online (Google Meet)

The interviewer began by introducing himself and then asked me to introduce myself. One of the first questions was:

Being a computer science student with so many hackathon experiences, why product management?

I had prepared for this. I explained that I was always more interested in user-centric thinking, fascinated by how apps are designed and tailored for different users, and that I enjoy working on Figma designs. In hackathons, my approach was always to present solutions not just as projects, but as complete products with thorough research, wireframes, and business models, which gave my teams an edge.

Case Study Discussion:

The interviewer shared his screen with my PPT and asked me to present it. I followed the same calm, natural approach I used in my video presentation but went deeper into the reasoning behind each decision.

● He asked how I gathered the information and why I chose this approach.

● I realized that every word I used could become a question, so I spoke very carefully.

He asked: What is an SDK, and why would a company use it instead of building one themselves?

● I first explained what an SDK is.

● Then I justified with examples: E-commerce apps use PhonePe or Razorpay SDKs because payments aren't their primary focus. Similarly, apps integrate Google Sign-In to save time and resources.

● This reasoning with examples impressed him.

Prioritization and Metrics Question:

He then asked: If you had to choose between two features : photo verification vs offline-first, which would you prioritize as a PM, and on what basis?

I explained using the impact vs effort framework:

1. First discuss feasibility and required resources with the tech team.

2. Conduct user research to gauge impact and need.

3. Align the decision with company goals.

4. Choose the feature that balances user needs and business objectives.

Business & Market Thinking:

Next, he asked: If you had to take a ride, would you choose Ola or Uber? State three metrics.

I answered:

● Ratings/reviews

● Time to reach

● Pricing (including coupons/deals)

Puzzle Question:

The puzzle: 101 coins, one counterfeit, identify in two weighings if it's lighter or heavier.

● I began by noting down key points and clarifying constraints.

● I divided the coins into three groups of 33, with 2 coins left aside, and explained different cases step by step.

● He was satisfied with my systematic approach.

Guesstimate Question:

The guesstimate: How many fine dining restaurants are there in Mumbai?

● I first asked clarifying questions (big restaurants only or small ones too?).

● He said only fine dining restaurants, so I based my estimate on Mumbai's 600 sq km area.

● I used my local knowledge: In a 1 km area near my home, there are about 12 restaurants. In some areas, maybe 4-5, and in upscale areas like Powai, around 15.

● I took an average of 10 per sq km → ~6000 restaurants.

● Initially, I wrongly assumed distance as the unit (thinking from my house as center), then corrected it to area-based reasoning, which I explained clearly.

● He appreciated how I self-corrected and justified the change in approach.

Closing the Interview:

At the end, I was asked if I had any questions. Always prepare 2-3 thoughtful questions beforehand , never say "no," as it shows lack of interest.

I asked:

Product managers are often called the CEO of a product, but what do they actually own? What are their responsibilities?

The interviewer gave a detailed explanation in response.

3. Culture Fit Round [ 1 candidate appeared for this round ]

I was the only candidate selected for this final round.

The interview was online on Google Meet, lasting around 45 minutes. Compared to the earlier rounds, this was much more chill and relaxed. The interviewer emphasized that he wanted honest answers, so don't take much time and say whatever comes to you naturally.

The interviewer asked me to describe my journey from the start.

● I began with my passion for design, and how tough it was initially to adjust in an environment where I felt lost.

● Over time, my interest grew towards UI/UX, leading me to take freelance projects, internships, and hackathon experiences.

● I also spoke about being Head of Events at WIE-IEEE, which involved strategic thinking, event planning, budgeting, and making events engaging to attract people.

● I shared how pitching to stalls for the Women's Week event helped me better understand stakeholder needs.

● Taking hackathon projects beyond just code and bugs, and presenting them as complete products with design and business aspects, deepened my passion for product management.

Key Questions and My Responses:

● You've done 5 internships in 6 months , why so many? Wasn't one enough?How did you prioritize tasks? Wasn't it overburdening? I explained that I never treated internships as just tasks to meet deadlines. Design is something I love, so it never felt like a burden. I can spend hours on Figma, presentations, and product design and that enthusiasm drives me. The interviewer appreciated this perspective. I clarified that my focus was on learning and impact rather than just ticking off tasks, which kept me motivated and balanced.

● Tell me about your best friend in college, what would they say about your strengths and weaknesses? I gave an honest answer about how my friends perceive me, highlighting collaboration, creativity, and persistence as strengths, and mentioning areas I actively work to improve.

● As a product manager, what would you like to spend most of your time doing? I explained that I would love to focus on user research, product strategy, and translating insights into design decisions, because that's where I feel I add the most value.

● If you had abundant money, would you still want to work? If yes, what would you do? I said I'm a creative person who can't sit idle.

○ I would probably teach Figma or create a product management roadmap on YouTube.

○ I would take a world tour to explore ideas and experiences.

○ If I had significant resources, I would start my own startup, which the interviewer liked.

● Looking at our website, what would you improve in its UI? I suggested keeping the color palette and tone as it is but adding a subtle AI-inspired design touch such as a glowing element in the logo or subtle interactive visuals to make it look distinctly AI-driven. The interviewer appreciated this as a unique idea.

● With so many skills and achievements, why is your CGPA 8 and not higher? I explained that I believe real learning happens outside the classroom. I chose to invest my time and prioritized building practical skills, taking internships, participating in hackathons, and gaining real experience over chasing high marks in subjects that were less relevant to my career path.

● Which is your least and most favorite subject? I answered honestly: Computer Communication Networks (CCN) as my least favorite and Design Thinking as my most favorite because of its user-centric problem-solving approach.

At the end, he asked if I had any questions. I prepared in advance and asked:

1. What would my typical day look like as a product manager?

2. What are the top three skills required to contribute effectively as a product manager? This wrapped up the interview on a positive note.

Finally, I was the only one getting the offer (including both SPIT and Somaiya).

What Worked in My Favor

● I had a clear understanding of my past experiences and was able to explain my learnings confidently.

● I demonstrated genuine interest in the business and sales domain, backed by relevant internship and committee experience.

● I researched the company and product beforehand, which helped me pitch the product effectively.

Areas Where I Could Have Performed Better

● I could have shown more energy and enthusiasm, especially during the offline interview.

● Being slightly more expressive in my tone and body language could have made the interaction even stronger.

Preparation Tips for Future Candidates

● Prepare a strong explanation of why you are choosing the role/domain, especially if it is non-technical.

● Research the company, product, and target market thoroughly.

● Always prepare at least one suggestion or improvement idea related to the product.

● Practice a basic sales or product pitch before the interview.

● Be ready to discuss how you manage pressure and prioritize tasks.

Interview-Day Tips

● Stay calm and confident during the interview.

● Listen carefully to the questions before answering.

● Be honest about challenges and explain how you handled them.

● Ask at least one meaningful question at the end of the interview.

● Maintain positive body language and clear communication.

Resume Shortlisting

Interview Online(20th)

Interview Offline(21st)

1. Resume Shortlisting

The resume shortlisting round was conducted through a Google Form in which candidates were required to fill in details about their previous experiences, including committee involvement, internships, and key learnings. Shortlisting was done based on the relevance of these experiences to the role, clarity of interest, and overall consistency in the candidate's profile. This round focused more on understanding practical exposure and motivation rather than just academic performance, and the selected candidates were invited for the interview rounds.

2. Online Interview

The second round was an online interview conducted by Adhik, the founder himself. This round was more conversational in nature and aimed at understanding my background, motivation, and alignment with the company and the role. The interview began with my self-introduction, after which the founder explained the product in detail along with its target market. This helped set the context for the discussion and allowed me to understand the business side of the company better.

Following this, I was asked why I was opting for a non-technical role and what I had learned from my previous internship experience, which I had mentioned in the resume shortlisting form. Since my internship was in the marketing domain, I explained how it sparked my interest in business development and sales, and how I enjoyed working closer to customers and strategy. The founder seemed satisfied with my clarity and reasoning. Towards the end of the interview, I was asked about my place of stay and when I would be able to join if selected. The entire interview lasted around 20-25 minutes. A few minutes after the interview concluded, I received a message informing me that there would be another round scheduled offline the following day.

3. Offline Interview [ No of candidates who appeared for this round - 2 ]

The third round was an offline interview and was more in-depth and practical compared to the previous rounds. It focused on understanding how I handle pressure, manage multiple responsibilities, and perform in a sales-oriented role. The discussion initially revolved around my previous experiences, especially how I balanced my internship alongside committee work. I answered honestly, mentioning that managing both did disturb my schedule initially, but over time I learned to prioritize tasks better and stay focused despite pressure.

Since the role involved business and sales, I was asked to pitch the company's product to the founder as if I were convincing a potential client. I approached the pitch from a day-to-day usage perspective, explaining how the product could be seamlessly integrated into everyday life while being both beneficial and time-saving for users. I focused on practical use cases rather than just features, which helped demonstrate the product's real-world value. The founder appreciated this approach and was satisfied with how I positioned the product. Towards the end of the interview, I was asked if I had any questions. I used this opportunity to ask about his thoughts on expanding the product into a B2C model, especially targeting students as potential long-term users. He appreciated this forward-thinking approach and showed interest in my perspective. After the interview, I asked for feedback and received a very positive response overall, with one suggestion that I could have shown slightly more energy during the interaction. The interview lasted around 25-30 minutes.

The most important thing about placement season you need to understand is that there is a large amount of luck involved. You can increase your chances by practicing as much as possible, but in the end, you really need good luck (only once).

● Be mindful of time management, especially during the aptitude section.

● Stay calm and maintain focus, as the ability to navigate freely in technical sections can be both a benefit and a distraction.

● Be confident when explaining your projects and concepts.

● Review common questions related to your resume and skills.

● Keep giving mock interviews, either online or with friends, to build confidence and improve your performance.

● Maintain a positive attitude, smile, and stay composed throughout.

● If you're unsure about something, it's okay to pause and collect your thoughts before answering.

This was the second time Lombard visited the campus.

There were 4 rounds for this process. It was announced that the recruitment process would include:

1. Online Assessment (OA).

2. 2 Technical Interviews.

3. HR Interview

1. Aptitude and Technical Test [90 mins]:

The first round was a comprehensive test that included aptitude, technical multiple-choice questions (MCQs), and coding. It was divided into 7 sections, and the total duration was 90 minutes. The first section was a coding question (DP) which was to be completed in 30 minutes. The other 6 sections were MCQ questions. The aptitude section was timed and non-navigable, meaning you can navigate between questions but once you exited this section, you couldn't return to it.

The remaining 6 sections covered topics like Database Management Systems (DBMS), Data Structures (DS), Computer Networks (CN), Object Oriented Programming (OOPS), Operating System (OS) and Aptitude.

2. Technical Interview 1 [50-60 mins]:

This round was one of the main rounds of the interview process, lasting approximately 40-45 minutes. It primarily focused on my resume, core technical knowledge, and problem-solving approach.

a. Introduction & Resume Discussion

The interview began with a brief self-introduction, followed by an in-depth discussion of my resume. The interviewers focused on a project where I had implemented multi AI-agents. I was asked questions related to:

● What AI agents are

● Their implementation

● Their working mechanism

● The overall architecture and design decisions

b. System Architecture, AWS, Docker & Kafka

Since AWS, Kafka, and Docker were mentioned in one of my projects, the interviewers explored these topics in detail.

● I was asked to explain the complete architecture of the project.

● One of the interviewers then asked me to list and explain the AWS S3 and Docker commands I was familiar with.

● I was asked about the working of AWS Glue and AWS Athena, including how they are used for data crawling and querying.

● I was asked whether MongoDB can be set up using Docker, to which I answered yes.

● Following this, I was asked to explain all the commands required to set up MongoDB from scratch inside a Docker container, including container creation and configuration.

c. Authentication & Security (JWT)

The discussion then moved to authentication concepts, specifically:

● What is JWT?

● Access Tokens and Refresh Token

● Edge cases related to access and refresh token handling

● Differences between JWT-based authentication and session-based authentication

d. Object-Oriented Programming (OOPS)

Next, I was asked questions related to OOPS fundamentals, including:

● The four pillars of OOPS

● SOLID principles

● Inheritance and its different types

e. SQL & Database Concepts

The interviewers then covered basic SQL concepts, which included:

● Types of joins in SQL

● ACID properties

● Order of execution in SQL queries

● Writing a SQL query to filter duplicate rows from a table

f. Overall Experience

Overall, this was a relatively easy and well-structured round. The key takeaway is to:

● Be confident while explaining your projects and technical concepts

● Stay calm during problem-solving

● Clearly communicate your thought process, as the interviewers were more interested in understanding how I approach problems rather than just the final answer

3. Technical Round 2 [15-20 mins]:

a. Project Discussion

This was the easiest interview. The interviewer asked me to choose any one project that would impress him with my skills and explain it thoroughly. Then he asked follow-up questions on that, which also included a few questions on the tech stack mentioned for each project.

b. Internship & Achievements

He then moved on to the Internship section and Achievements. He asked about hackathons, including which project I made in which hackathon, what problems I faced, and how I tackled them.

For this round, you must have to know each and every feature of the project that you have mentioned, along with the tech stack you have mentioned.

4. HR Round [10-15 mins]:

The final round was a 10-15 minute interview. Make sure you are well prepared for generic HR questions.

The interviewer started with questions such as:

● Where do I belong from

● Where do I currently stay

● How many family members I have and what they do

● Why I am interested in an insurance firm

He then picked one of my projects and asked me to consider a scenario where users are ghosting the platform and how I would expand the business across geographies.

It was more of a conversation-based round aimed at assessing my mindset, thought process, and long-term goals.

5 students were offered the role and I was one of them !!!

Process Date: 11th Sept 2025 (OA), 12th Sept 2025 (Interviews)

1. Resume Shortlisting (~100 students appeared)

So the process started with resume shortlisting. I'm not entirely sure about the exact numbers, but I think around 100 people applied for this role. The company shortlisted around 50 students based on our resumes.

My advice to you guys would be to align your resume with the job description. If they're asking for ML skills, show ML projects. Don't just randomly put projects that don't relate to the role.

Results: 50 students moved forward to the Online Assessment.

2. Online Assessment (~50 students appeared)

The OA lasted 60 minutes. There were 20 MCQs and 4 coding questions. The catch was once you submit a question, you can't revisit it -- this put some pressure on me.

Coding Questions:

Q1. Check if the previous element is smaller than the current element; if yes return true, else false. (This one was straightforward)

Q2. Previous Greater Element problem (Standard stack question)

Q3. Some DSA question related to gradient descent - honestly, I couldn't understand this one properly. It was confusing.

Q4. Rotate array by 2, then you get a string, and if you find any element from that string in your array, replace it with the given element. (Took me some time to understand what they were asking)

I solved 2 coding questions completely. The MCQs were easy to medium, but because I spent time on coding, I couldn't solve all MCQs. Java wasn't available as a language, but since I usually code in C++, it wasn't a problem for me.

When the results came out, only 10 students were shortlisted, and I was one of them.

3. Technical Interview Round 1 (10 students appeared)

I started by introducing myself. They immediately dived deep into my projects, which I had prepared for. Then they gave me the Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock II problem. I already knew it from Striver's DP sheet, so I explained the DP approach confidently. They then asked for the O(n) linear approach -- I explained but made a small mistake. They kindly corrected me and said, "You're on the right track." That encouragement boosted my confidence mid-interview.

They also asked me about the difference between React and normal HTML/CSS and some questions related to my resume .

Then came a rapid-fire round: factorial (loop & recursion), recursion issues (I said TLE), which DS recursion uses (Stack), why use DP, assigning priority to objects (I said priority queue). I liked this part because it felt like a fun quiz rather than grilling.

Some other candidates were asked to open Google Colab do some visualizations/operations on dataset; I wasn't asked that.

Overall, my interview went well.

Shortlist: 5 students.

4. Technical Interview Round 2 (5 students appeared)

We started again with a quick intro and discussion of one of my hackathon projects. Then they gave me a case study:

"You're a Senior Data Analyst at AuxoAI. Microsoft needs 1000 applicants for a job. You have job seeker data from your client. How would you select 1000 candidates for that job role?"

I gave some thought then I said I'd parse resumes using pyresparser and extract features like skills, education, location, and experience, and a few more features that I don't clearly remember now.. My output would be "Eligible/Not Eligible." I initially said Naive Bayes for the model.

Then they asked how I'd handle candidates backing out at the last moment. At first, I overcomplicated it -- I said I would check factors like college tier (if someone is from a top college, they might get better offers), location preferences, salary expectations, and experience level. I thought of approaching it with regression, reasoning that more experienced candidates usually want better opportunities.

But they immediately pointed out that this is actually a classification problem. At that moment, I realized my mistake, smiled, and corrected myself: "In that case, I will use Logistic Regression to classify whether a candidate is likely to back out or not."

I felt like I redeemed myself here by being honest and flexible.

Other candidates were asked guesstimates -- so be ready for that too.

Shortlist: 3 students.

5. HR Round (3 students appeared)

This was just a casual chat. They asked about my family, where I stay, etc. It lasted 5-10 minutes. After such heavy technical rounds, this felt like a breather.

Selected as AI Engineer Intern at AuxoAI with PPO opportunity.

Useful Tips

● For aptitude, use Indiabix and Career Ride YouTube channel.

● For coding, Striver's sheet (especially DP) + LeetCode.

● For SQL, do 50 questions on LeetCode and 50 general SQL problems.

● For ML, Krish Naik's channel is excellent.

● Be ready for case studies -- think aloud, they like your approach even if it's not perfect.

● Don't panic if your language isn't available -- have C++ or Python as backup.

● Be honest if you make mistakes -- it's better than faking an answer.

All the very best! Feel free to reach out if you have any questions. Always happy to help!

The superset application for AuxoAI was opened for us on 4th September 2025. The eligibility criteria for applying was CGPA>=7. There were 5 rounds in total:

1. Resume shortlisting .
journey.prep:
1.Try to have C++ or Python as your primary language and then study OOPS in Java for a well- rounded knowledge base. Even though I knew to solve the coding questions and would have solved all of them collectively in less than 10 minutes(but in Java), my rigidity with Java would have resulted in a costly fumble. 2.The aptitude section for AuxoAI was of a moderate to high difficulty level .I personally used my strong intuition of mathematics to solve the questions.While I had all the time in the world to solve the questions , it won't always be the same .I solved 18-19 questions .

Resources: This video is a goldmine for probability. PROBABILITY in 1 Shot | From Zero to Hero | JEE Main & Advanced

Overall 10 students were selected for the interviews and I was glad to be among them.

3. [Technical Round 1]: ( 10 Students appeared for this round)

The results for the OA were declared around 12 in the night and the interviews were scheduled from 11 in the morning.There were 2 interviewers in each panel.I introduced myself to the panel and then they asked me to select a project on which a deep dive could be possible . I chose the first project on my resume(It was a LSTM+ XGBOOST hybrid model ) , where I explained in detail the methodology of the project .They proceeded by asking the information about the columns used and why only those were selected, the source of the data , the number of rows present , and related questions. They then asked me to tell the metrics of the model (R2_SCORE and the MSE error) and inquired about the mathematical formulas of the metrics

and the intuition behind them.(Some questions such as "explain R2_score to a layman" were also asked. Then I was asked in detail (bohot depth me gaye) about XGBOOST and LSTM and the mathematical intuition behind them .I answered almost all the questions correctly and they were pleased with my fundamentals.They asked me about the gradient descent algorithm and how it works and its mathematical intricacies(fundamental understanding of coordinate geometry and curves is needed). Finally I was asked a bit about GEN-AI . To wrap up the interview , I was asked a simple DSA question. ( Sieve of Eratosthenes) . The expectation was to write a working code . I explained the brute force solution and then explained in detail the optimal approach . I coded the solution (easy tha) and they were pleased by it(it seemed) .Next I was asked about the TC and the SC of the solution ,and I correctly answered it. The interview concluded with me asking a question to the panel . The round lasted around 40 minutes.

Tips: 1. Have strong fundamentals of machine learning and mathematics.

2. Be calm.

4.Technical Round 2 : (5 students appeared for this round) The interview started with my introduction to the panel and another discussion on my projects ensued. They asked many questions on the projects , the technical difficulties and the non technical difficulties which I faced (This was a group project). I was asked about gradient descent and was able to answer almost all the follow up questions on it . Following this, I was asked to design a chatbot for some application (I think this was to check the understanding of the software development cycle ). While I initially stumbled , I was able to rectify and refine my approach iteratively . Finally I was asked a guesstimate on the number of pizzas eaten on a Saturday night in India. The round lasted around 30 minutes.

Tips: 1. In the guesstimate, I did all the calculations mentally , rather than on paper. This can help you . Also it is important to break the problem statement into smaller parts and then find the solution. 2.Be calm.

Round 5: HR ROUND (3 students appeared for this round): This was an informal round conducted by the MD of the company. It lasted around 10 minutes for me .It was just an informal chat wherein he asked me about my day , how do I feel about the situation and just some information on the company .

Tips:

1. A calm mind is the need of the hour .You might be put in unknown and extreme high pressure situations throughout the whole placement process and it is important to not lose your sense of reasoning .

2. Prepare answers for standard HR questions beforehand (jot down the main points) and then try to relate all these points to weave a story .

The interviews concluded by 7 pm on 12/09/25. After that, I departed for my home .But the results were not announced that night and also the following night .It was a really long wait and finally the results were announced on 15/09/25. I was selected finally.

Resources: 1.For Machine Learning and Deep Learning ,CampusX has the best playlist on YT.

1. Playlist name: 100 Days of Machine Learning

2. Playlist name:100 Days of Deep Learning 3.He is making some new playlists on advanced topics as well , do check it out .

2. 3BLUE1BROWN (YT channel ) has some playlists on mathematics. Do check it out . 3.For Puzzles: Since this is a machine learning role , puzzles would be asked mostly on probability(like coins and cards), also you can refer to GFG for top 100 puzzles. 4.DSA: Follow Striver's sheet and then specifically pick some questions from a topic which can help you revise the entire topic. Just do those questions before the OA.(just a suggestion).

General Tips and a small peek into my journey:

1. My placement journey would not have been possible without the constant support of my parents and friends. Have a strong group of people around you who genuinely wish for your success. I feel blessed and lucky to have so many good people in my life. Also , be genuinely happy about others' achievements.

2. Believe in God's plan.

3. My placement journey lasted 78 days.I cleared the online assessments of General Mills (summer intern ) , PhonePE , ZETA , IDFC , BrowserStack , BlackRock , Mahindra and then finally AuxoAI. I was rejected in the initial rounds in General Mills ( was asked a NP hard problem) , PhonePE( I was not confident enough and thus underperformed ), IDFC (was asked about cloud, Springboot ( topics which I did not study) ), Browserstack. I reached the last round in ZETA but was rejected. In BlackRock , I was not given a chance to give an interview even after clearing the OA (was waitlisted ). Throughout this process , I was not asked about any of the projects in even 1 of the interviews and then in AuxoAI , I was asked in detail about my projects(I honestly built the projects) . So , it was a bad streak of luck(for about 2 months) .The thing to note here is that it is fine to take a break of 1- 2 days after a rejection and then have a fresh start leaving everything behind .

4. Patience is something which is quite underrated in this journey. While people around you might be in a hurry to get placed, it is important to keep calm, think rationally, and then take any decision.

5. Luck and the importance of timing cannot be understated in this journey. While consistently getting the toughest questions in OAs (randomized questions in OA) broke me , I was really lucky that AuxoAI came for hiring. Luck evens out in the end (law of averages) but for luck to be on your side, you should be ready to work really hard even in adversity.

I sincerely hope that each one of you achieves more than what you dream of, finds great success, and be satisfied. May your batch perform even better than our batch.

All the very best !!

Feel free to contact me on WhatsApp : 8976801000 and LinkedIn: (19) Dhruv Deshpande | LinkedIn
