Before you read further, I want to inform you that this experience is focused on a Machine Learning (ML) role, not a SDE role. For SDE-specific experiences, I recommend referring to the experiences shared by my peers who were placed in SDE roles.

1.Resuming Shortlisting : ( I think around 90-100 students appeared )

In the resume shortlisting round, we were evaluated on our resumes based on the job description provided by the company. Around 50 students were selected after this round .While I cannot exactly pinpoint the formula to succeed, a good way to increase your probability of succeeding would be to include the skills and languages mentioned in the JD in your resume.

Resume Tips: 1.Since this is an AIML role, I would suggest that you should have all the projects in the field of AIML. Please try not to include development projects (if possible). All the 3 projects mentioned on my resume were based on machine learning.

2. I would recommend including 1-2 projects on your resume where you have developed machine learning models from scratch . These projects highlight your ability to code from scratch and demonstrate a strong fundamental understanding of concepts.

3. Work experience is always appreciated . Try to have an internship before the placement season starts. I did not have any experience and thus was a bit tensed about my chances for this round .

2. Online Assessment ( Around 50 students appeared for the test):

The test was conducted on campus in the afternoon ( around 4pm). The duration of the test was 60 minutes,and there were 2 sections : 1. Aptitude section (20 questions) ,2. Coding section ( 4 questions). Navigation was strict(once you visited a question , you could not visit it again). The aptitude section consisted mainly of topics like speed-time problems , simple interest-compound interest, trigonometry and ratios. The coding section consisted of the following questions:

1. A basic string traversal question

2. A question similar to Rotate Array - LeetCode.

3. A question on finding previous smaller element ( Can be implemented using a stack).

4. Implementing Logistic regression from scratch.

For some reason , Java was not included in the list of available languages. Since I used Java , I was worried. So , I quickly changed my strategy and instead tried to solve all the questions of aptitude. I completed around 18 -19 questions correctly in around 45 minutes and then in the 15 minutes left , tried to solve the coding questions, With some basic knowledge and some common sense , I passed some test cases of all the questions(In 1 question , I passed 50 percent cases and in the others 20 30 percent ) and thus the test concluded.

Tips: 1.Try to have C++ or Python as your primary language and then study OOPS in Java for a well- rounded knowledge base. Even though I knew to solve the coding questions and would have solved all of them collectively in less than 10 minutes(but in Java), my rigidity with Java would have resulted in a costly fumble. 2.The aptitude section for AuxoAI was of a moderate to high difficulty level .I personally used my strong intuition of mathematics to solve the questions.While I had all the time in the world to solve the questions , it won't always be the same .I solved 18-19 questions .

Resources: This video is a goldmine for probability. PROBABILITY in 1 Shot | From Zero to Hero | JEE Main & Advanced

Overall 10 students were selected for the interviews and I was glad to be among them.

3. [Technical Round 1]: ( 10 Students appeared for this round)

The results for the OA were declared around 12 in the night and the interviews were scheduled from 11 in the morning.There were 2 interviewers in each panel.I introduced myself to the panel and then they asked me to select a project on which a deep dive could be possible . I chose the first project on my resume(It was a LSTM+ XGBOOST hybrid model ) , where I explained in detail the methodology of the project .They proceeded by asking the information about the columns used and why only those were selected, the source of the data , the number of rows present , and related questions. They then asked me to tell the metrics of the model (R2_SCORE and the MSE error) and inquired about the mathematical formulas of the metrics

and the intuition behind them.(Some questions such as "explain R2_score to a layman" were also asked. Then I was asked in detail (bohot depth me gaye) about XGBOOST and LSTM and the mathematical intuition behind them .I answered almost all the questions correctly and they were pleased with my fundamentals.They asked me about the gradient descent algorithm and how it works and its mathematical intricacies(fundamental understanding of coordinate geometry and curves is needed). Finally I was asked a bit about GEN-AI . To wrap up the interview , I was asked a simple DSA question. ( Sieve of Eratosthenes) . The expectation was to write a working code . I explained the brute force solution and then explained in detail the optimal approach . I coded the solution (easy tha) and they were pleased by it(it seemed) .Next I was asked about the TC and the SC of the solution ,and I correctly answered it. The interview concluded with me asking a question to the panel . The round lasted around 40 minutes.

Tips: 1. Have strong fundamentals of machine learning and mathematics.

2. Be calm.

4.Technical Round 2 : (5 students appeared for this round) The interview started with my introduction to the panel and another discussion on my projects ensued. They asked many questions on the projects , the technical difficulties and the non technical difficulties which I faced (This was a group project). I was asked about gradient descent and was able to answer almost all the follow up questions on it . Following this, I was asked to design a chatbot for some application (I think this was to check the understanding of the software development cycle ). While I initially stumbled , I was able to rectify and refine my approach iteratively . Finally I was asked a guesstimate on the number of pizzas eaten on a Saturday night in India. The round lasted around 30 minutes.

Tips: 1. In the guesstimate, I did all the calculations mentally , rather than on paper. This can help you . Also it is important to break the problem statement into smaller parts and then find the solution. 2.Be calm.

Round 5: HR ROUND (3 students appeared for this round): This was an informal round conducted by the MD of the company. It lasted around 10 minutes for me .It was just an informal chat wherein he asked me about my day , how do I feel about the situation and just some information on the company .

Tips:

1. A calm mind is the need of the hour .You might be put in unknown and extreme high pressure situations throughout the whole placement process and it is important to not lose your sense of reasoning .

2. Prepare answers for standard HR questions beforehand (jot down the main points) and then try to relate all these points to weave a story .

The interviews concluded by 7 pm on 12/09/25. After that, I departed for my home .But the results were not announced that night and also the following night .It was a really long wait and finally the results were announced on 15/09/25. I was selected finally.

Resources: 1.For Machine Learning and Deep Learning ,CampusX has the best playlist on YT.

1. Playlist name: 100 Days of Machine Learning

2. Playlist name:100 Days of Deep Learning 3.He is making some new playlists on advanced topics as well , do check it out .

2. 3BLUE1BROWN (YT channel ) has some playlists on mathematics. Do check it out . 3.For Puzzles: Since this is a machine learning role , puzzles would be asked mostly on probability(like coins and cards), also you can refer to GFG for top 100 puzzles. 4.DSA: Follow Striver's sheet and then specifically pick some questions from a topic which can help you revise the entire topic. Just do those questions before the OA.(just a suggestion).

General Tips and a small peek into my journey:

1. My placement journey would not have been possible without the constant support of my parents and friends. Have a strong group of people around you who genuinely wish for your success. I feel blessed and lucky to have so many good people in my life. Also , be genuinely happy about others' achievements.

2. Believe in God's plan.

3. My placement journey lasted 78 days.I cleared the online assessments of General Mills (summer intern ) , PhonePE , ZETA , IDFC , BrowserStack , BlackRock , Mahindra and then finally AuxoAI. I was rejected in the initial rounds in General Mills ( was asked a NP hard problem) , PhonePE( I was not confident enough and thus underperformed ), IDFC (was asked about cloud, Springboot ( topics which I did not study) ), Browserstack. I reached the last round in ZETA but was rejected. In BlackRock , I was not given a chance to give an interview even after clearing the OA (was waitlisted ). Throughout this process , I was not asked about any of the projects in even 1 of the interviews and then in AuxoAI , I was asked in detail about my projects(I honestly built the projects) . So , it was a bad streak of luck(for about 2 months) .The thing to note here is that it is fine to take a break of 1- 2 days after a rejection and then have a fresh start leaving everything behind .

4. Patience is something which is quite underrated in this journey. While people around you might be in a hurry to get placed, it is important to keep calm, think rationally, and then take any decision.

5. Luck and the importance of timing cannot be understated in this journey. While consistently getting the toughest questions in OAs (randomized questions in OA) broke me , I was really lucky that AuxoAI came for hiring. Luck evens out in the end (law of averages) but for luck to be on your side, you should be ready to work really hard even in adversity.

I sincerely hope that each one of you achieves more than what you dream of, finds great success, and be satisfied. May your batch perform even better than our batch.

All the very best !!

Feel free to contact me on WhatsApp : 8976801000 and LinkedIn: (19) Dhruv Deshpande | LinkedIn

1. Online Assesment Round:

The online assessment round was conducted on the HackerRank platform. It consisted of 36 questions to be solved in 120 minutes, covering topics from Computer Networking, Operating Systems, SQL, Logical Reasoning, Probability, and Puzzles, along with two DSA questions based on sliding windows and trees. The sliding window problem was easy, while the tree problem was of medium difficulty.

There were also multiple SQL query-based questions that tested the basics of joins, aggregate functions, and constraints. The non-technical questions focused on aptitude and logical reasoning, which included probability-based problems and short analytical puzzles.

We had to take the test from home due to heavy rainfall, which made it impossible to conduct the online assessment on campus that day. The overall difficulty level of the test was slightly higher. I was able to solve the sliding window question completely and the tree problem partially, along with most of the aptitude and core subject MCQs.

Note: This test was conducted for the OFSS Associate Application Developer role. Although I was not selected for the interviews for that position, OFSS returned a few days later to hire for the Consultant role. They shortlisted candidates based on the performance in the same test conducted

for the Developer role, and by God's grace, I was shortlisted. So, make sure to give your 100% in this test!

2. Technical Interview I:[ 27 students got selected for this round]

The interviews began soon after the pre-placement talk ended at around 12:00 p.m.

I was allotted to Panel 1, and I was the second candidate from my panel to be interviewed. As soon as I entered the room, the interviewer greeted me, offered me a seat, and asked me to introduce myself. After my introduction, he went through my resume and asked about the first project mentioned in it. He then questioned some of my technical choices, such as why I used JavaScript for the project, why I didn't use Next.js, and how I would convince him to use React instead of Next.js.

Since I had used a Sentence Transformer model in my project, he asked me whether I was familiar with NLP. I told him that NLP is one of my core subjects this semester. His focus then shifted to NLP-related questions -- he asked me about vectorization, tokenization, sentiment analysis, stopwords, and the difference between RAG and LLM. As I had my NLP mid-semester exam just two days earlier, I was confident and able to answer most of his questions well.

Then his focus shifted to DSA, and he gave me a question on valid anagrams to solve. I wrote the pseudocode for it on paper, and the interviewer seemed quietly satisfied with my approach. After that, he asked me to write code to sort a string, which I implemented using bubble sort.

Next, the discussion moved to DBMS and SQL. He asked me to write a query to find the second-highest salary, which I solved using subqueries. Then he asked for the average salary department-wise, which can be done using either GROUP BY or window functions--I chose to solve it using window functions. He further asked about the difference between SQL and NoSQL, how to optimize a database, and the difference between partitioning and sharding, as well as between vertical and horizontal partitioning.

He also questioned me about candidate keys, primary keys, and foreign keys. Since I had mentioned MongoDB in my technical section, he asked me how to fetch the second-highest salary using MongoDB.

After that, he moved to OOPs concepts and asked me to elaborate on the four pillars of OOPs with real-life examples. As my primary programming language is C++, he still asked whether multiple inheritance is supported in Java, along with some basic questions on memory management in Java.

He then shifted to React, asking about Hooks, followed by some basic questions on Postman, Thunder Client, Git, and GitHub.

At the end of the interview, he asked if I had any questions for him. I inquired about the type of work involved in the role and the training process. The entire round lasted for about 40-45 minutes.

Note: It is not necessary to give the correct answer to every question the interviewer asks. The key is to stay confident throughout. If you don't know the answer to a question, avoid directly saying "I don't know." Instead, try to relate the question to some relevant concepts and explain your thought process. If the interviewer is still not satisfied, you can politely say, "I'm not completely sure about this, but I'll definitely look into it."

3. Technical-Interview II [ Around 20 students got shortlisted for this]

For this round, I was the second candidate in my panel to be interviewed. This round was purely focused on databases and lasted for around 50-55 minutes. All the questions were based on SQL, MongoDB, and Database Management Systems (DBMS).

The interviewer first asked me to introduce myself, and then, similar to the first round, he asked me to explain my first project. He also asked me to design the schema of my project on paper. While designing, I explained my approach, discussed how I chose the primary keys, the cardinalities, and the relationships between tables.

After that, he asked me to write several SQL queries--around 7 to 8 in total--and I was able to solve all of them. There were also some output prediction questions. He asked me the difference between DROP, TRUNCATE, and DELETE commands, and in which scenarios DELETE is used. I explained that DELETE is used with the WHERE condition. Then he gave me the query DELETE FROM table; and asked whether it would work without a WHERE condition. I answered that it would work, but it would be slower than DROP since it deletes the rows one by one.

Next, he asked about ACID properties, deadlocks, and the types of SQL commands. I mentioned DDL, DML, DCL, and TCL. He then asked me to elaborate on TCL commands, and I explained COMMIT, ROLLBACK, and SAVEPOINT. He also asked a scenario-based question related to SAVEPOINT, which I was not completely sure about, so I politely told him that I was not very familiar with that concept.

Then he moved on to ask the difference between functions and procedures, gave me a query to write a trigger, and followed up with multiple questions on views, joins, aggregate functions, procedures, UNION, and UNION ALL. He also asked about cursors in databases--which I honestly didn't know--and several questions on indexing, including the difference between

clustered and non-clustered indexes, and whether indexing would be effective for a table with millions of rows, along with a few scenario-based questions.

I was able to answer most of the questions in this round, except for one or two. Overall, I was quite confident about my performance, and I was shortlisted for the HR round.

4. HR Round[ Around 12 students got shortlisted for this]

This round was more of a casual discussion and confirmation round, but I was quite nervous before it began. When I entered the room, the HR interviewer noticed my nervousness and kindly asked me to take a few deep breaths to relax.

He then asked me about my nationality, strengths and weaknesses, and my extracurricular activities. I mentioned that I enjoy playing and watching cricket. He asked me who my favorite cricket player was, and I said Virat Kohli. We spent the next 2-3 minutes discussing Virat Kohli's mindset and attitude, which made the conversation more engaging and comfortable.

This round lasted for about 7-8 minutes.

After the HR round, 12 candidates received job offers, and I was one of them.

1) Online Assessment Round: The online test was conducted on the HackerRank platform and consisted of 36 questions, including 2 coding problems, several SQL queries, and questions on Operating Systems and Networking. This test was common for both the App Development and Associate Consultant roles, and candidates were shortlisted for the Associate Consultant interview based on their performance. The coding questions varied for each candidate; for me, one of the problems was the Valid Parentheses question, which can be easily solved using a Stack.

2) Technical Round I : [27 students were selected for the technical interview]

The interview started after a PPT presentation from Oracle at around 12:00 PM.

It began with the question "Tell me something about yourself apart from your resume." Be prepared for this in advance -- try to include your strengths, hobbies, extracurricular activities, and any committee participation. Everything you mention should highlight how effective and valuable you can be for the company.After introducing myself, the interviewer asked me which programming language I was most proficient in. I said Java, as it's my favorite language and I usually solve coding problems in it.

She then asked me a few OOPs questions -- what is Abstraction, Polymorphism, why one should learn Java, and why Java is platform-independent. Since we had prepared well for topics like Collections Framework and Multithreading (as Oracle often asks these), I was confident. Next, she asked why I had chosen MongoDB for my projects. I had mentioned both MongoDB and MySQL in my resume, so I explained my choice based on schema flexibility and scalability, describing how MongoDB scales both horizontally and vertically. I also added that relational databases are equally important because they follow ACID properties, ensuring data integrity and security. She seemed very happy with this answer.

She then asked about the machine learning algorithms I had used in my projects. One of the questions was to explain Naïve Bayes, which I had used during the initial phase of my project. I didn't give a detailed example but explained how it works and why it's effective.

Tip: If you've implemented any functionality, make sure you understand the high-level flow, how you implemented it, and how it actually works in the backend.

Later, she asked a few questions on Authorization and Authentication, including how JWT (JSON Web Token) works.

After that, she moved on to two basic DSA questions:

Swap two numbers without using a third variable.

Reverse a string.

For on-campus interviews, string-related questions are very common, so make sure to prepare linear data structures thoroughly.

Finally, she asked some basic SQL questions -- definitions and the differences between DELETE, TRUNCATE, and DROP commands. Some questions about View how does data in view table get updated even it does not support DML

After that, my interview concluded.

2) Technical Round 2: [ around 20 students appeared for it]

Round 2 began with a quick greeting, and the interviewer immediately moved to a DSA question, asking for the solution in Java. The problem was: given an array of strings, convert all elements into camel case and then sort them based on the first character of each element. I wrote the complete solution, explained my approach, and he seemed satisfied with my explanation. After that, he asked two simple SQL questions -- one on LEFT JOIN and another on a basic aggregate function. I solved both queries and also mentioned that if a similar question appeared, I could handle it using the GROUP BY clause.

Afterward, he reviewed my resume and asked me to elaborate on any one of my projects that I could explain well. I confidently replied that I could explain any of the three projects mentioned in my resume, so he asked me to choose one. I described the project in detail, and he didn't interrupt or cross-question, indicating that my explanation was clear.

He then asked a few personal questions -- where I was from and about my role as the Point of Contact for the Alumni and Mentorship Program at SPIT. My advice is to answer such non-technical questions smartly. You can add a touch of personality or humor to make the conversation more engaging and reduce nervousness. Interviewers usually appreciate candidates who are not only technically strong but also have good communication and interpersonal skills.

For me, this approach worked really well -- the interviewer became more comfortable, and our interaction felt natural. We both enjoyed the conversation, and overall, the second round went very smoothly for me.

Round 3 : HR round : [ Around 12 students appeared for it]

The HR round was more of a formality. The HR asked a few basic questions such as my nationality, hobbies, and whether I was satisfied with the compensation offered. She also asked if I had any questions for her, to which I responded with two simple queries related to the company culture and growth opportunities.

After this round, there was a short waiting period of around 45 minutes while the panel discussed the results. Finally, the results were announced -- 11 students were selected for the role, including 6 from MCA and 5 from B.Tech.

1. Aptitude [total 4 people]

The aptitude round was one hour long and was divided into four sections - Reasoning, Aptitude, Verbal, and Emotional Intelligence - with 15 questions in each section. Topics covered included compound interest, speed and distance, ratios, and seating arrangements. Time was a constraint, but the questions themselves were manageable and solvable with good preparation. I was able to attempt approximately 10 questions per section.

Preparation Tips: Practicing from IndiaBix is more than sufficient for this round. Focus on time management and attempt easier questions first. Regular practice on compound interest, ratios, and seating arrangements is recommended.

Important Points to Remember: Do not spend too much time on any single question. Since each section has 15 questions and time is tight, move on quickly if you are stuck and come back if time permits. There was no negative marking.

All 4 candidates were shortlisted for the next round.

2. HR round [total 4 people]

This was a standard HR round that felt more like a casual conversation than a formal interview. It began with "Tell me about yourself." Other questions asked included how I feel about the work environment at Edelweiss, what I do apart from coding and what my hobbies are, explaining my projects and what problem they solve, and questions about my family background and what my family members do. There was also a discussion about how Edelweiss handles sensitive client data and why they cannot feed such data into LLMs. The HR had also asked me if I've researched about the company and if I have looked up any employees there. One candidate was unfortunately not selected after this round.

Preparation Tips: Be confident and conversational. Know your resume thoroughly, especially your projects

- be ready to explain what problem each project solves in simple terms. Research the company beforehand so you can speak about their work culture with some awareness.

Resume Pointers: Make sure your projects are clearly described with the problem statement and solution. List hobbies that reflect personality and aren't generic. Keep your personal background section ready in your mind even if it's not on the resume.

Important Points to Remember: Treat this round as a conversation, not an interrogation. Be natural, smile, and engage genuinely. Knowing basic facts about Edelweiss.

3. Technical round [total 3 people]

This round was conducted by the CTO and DVP. The questions covered OOP pillars with a request to give a real-world example from my own project where I applied them, a deep dive into my project and internship experience and how they work, the difference between NoSQL and SQL and a system design scenario where I was asked to build a PolicyBazaar clone and choose an appropriate tech stack.

For the PolicyBazaar clone, I suggested React for the frontend and .NET for the backend, reasoning that the existing team would likely be familiar with it. When asked about handling document uploads such as insurance documents, I proposed using a relational database like PostgreSQL where a documents table would have a foreign key referencing the primary key of the users table, and a column storing an array of URL strings pointing to documents stored in a private S3 bucket.

Preparation Tips: Revise OOP concepts (Encapsulation, Abstraction, Inheritance, Polymorphism) and have a concrete example from your own project ready for each. Be comfortable explaining your projects and internship work end-to-end. Practice basic system design - especially around databases, storage, and API design - as scenario-based questions are common.

Resume Pointers: Only mention projects and internships you can speak about confidently and in depth. Be ready to justify every technology choice mentioned on your resume.

Important Points to Remember: If you forget something mid-answer, do not panic or go silent. Just continue speaking and move forward. If you genuinely cannot recall something, say so honestly rather than fumbling. Interviewers appreciate composure and clarity of thought far more than a perfect answer delivered nervously.

4. HR round [total 2 people]

This final HR round was primarily informational rather than evaluative. The HR representative explained what Edelweiss does as a company and walked me through the benefits of joining, such as access to experienced mentors and growth opportunities within the firm. It was more of an onboarding conversation than a screening round.

Preparation Tips: Listen actively and ask thoughtful questions about the role, team structure, or learning opportunities. This is your chance to show genuine interest in the company.

Important Points to Remember: Even though this round feels relaxed, remain professional. Show enthusiasm about the opportunity and the company. Asking one or two genuine questions about the role or the team leaves a positive impression.

There were 2 groups each consisting of 4 people each. I was a part of the first group and 2 of us had received the offer letter.

There were 3 rounds for this process all within the span of 4-5 days. Schedule:

1. Pre Placement Talk (Microsoft Teams): 10-07-2025 from 11.30am - 12.30pm

2. Online Assessment(Hackerrank): 10-07-2025 from 4.30pm- 6.30pm .

3. Interview Rounds (SPIT Campus): 14-07-2025 Make sure you are prepared beforehand as you will be notified a day prior to the OA Test and the Interviews of shortlisted candidates.

1. Round 1: Online Assessment [ 197 students appeared and it was conducted in college]

Platform: Hackerrank Time: 85 mins Questions

● 15 Technical Questions: These questions were based on CS Fundamentals majorly focusing on DBMS, OOPS, SQL and Java.

● 15 Aptitude Questions: The questions were easy to moderate. They were based on probability, profit/loss, sets, finding missing elements in series, mirror images, and answering the question on the basis of a given graph and statistics.

● 1 Coding question: Given an array of integers representing the latencies of different servers, your task is to find all pairs of latencies with the minimum absolute difference. Each pair should be returned in ascending order (i.e., [a, b] where a < b), and the final list of pairs should be sorted in lexicographical order. Return the result as a 2D array of these latency pairs. For example, if the input is [4, 2, 1, 3], the sorted latencies are [1, 2, 3, 4]. The minimum absolute difference is 1, and the valid pairs with this difference are [1, 2], [2, 3], and [3, 4]. So, the output would be [[1, 2], [2, 3], [3, 4]].

Python approach i used: To find all pairs of latencies with the minimum absolute difference, first sort the array. Then, loop through the sorted array to calculate differences between consecutive elements. Track the smallest difference. If a new smaller difference is found, reset the result list with that pair. If the difference equals, add the pair to the result. Finally, convert the flat result list into a 2D array of pairs and return it. This ensures all closest latency pairs are captured and sorted correctly.

2. Round 2: Technical Interview[ 16 students were shortlisted for this round]

We were asked to report to college by 9:00 a.m., with the interviews beginning around 10:30 a.m. We had been informed a day prior to carry a fully charged laptop, an updated resume with a passport-size photograph affixed, and to be dressed in complete formals.

My interview began with a "Tell me about yourself" question, but the interviewer specifically asked me to walk through my journey like a story from childhood till now and talk about everything I had done or achieved. Then he asked me why I chose diploma. Since the interviewer wasn't familiar with the diploma system, I also explained the entire process and its structure.

The conversation then shifted to my projects. He asked why I chose to build them, what problems they solved, what challenges I faced, and how I overcame them. Most of my interview revolved around my major projects. I focused on explaining the logic, technologies used, and real-world relevance.

He then asked me about my favorite programming language and why?., and he gave me a to write a code on paper. The task was to print all missing numbers between a given list, like [1, 3, 4, 99]. After that he told me to walk through the code. I explained my approach: first sort the list, then use a loop to identify gaps and print missing numbers.

Next, the interviewer shifted to puzzles. He asked three logical/aptitude problems. The first was the classic Water Jug problem: how to measure 4 liters using 3L and 5L jugs. The second was the Torch and River puzzle involving four people with different crossing speeds (1, 2, 5, 10 minutes) and a single torch. I explained the optimal 17-minute solution. The third puzzle involved burning two uneven candles to measure 45 minutes which I solved using the trick of burning one from both ends. I answered all three correctly, which seemed to make a positive impression.

Toward the end, he asked me about my family background, including where I'm from and what my parents do. Finally, he gave me the chance to ask a question. I asked him what skills I should start learning if I got selected for this role.

Overall, the interview was a balanced mix of resume discussion, problem-solving, and personal insight and felt more like a two-way conversation than a strict Q&A.

3. Round 3: HR Interview[ Around 8 students were shortlisted for this round]

This round felt more like a personal interaction than a formal interview. The questions were mostly background-oriented they asked where I stay, what my parents do for a living, and about my general family environment. It seemed like they were trying to get to know me better on a personal level and assess whether I would be a good cultural fit for the organization.

They also asked me how my technical interview went and followed up with questions like why I didn't continue my engineering at the same college where I completed my diploma. The entire round was quite short, lasting around 10-15 minutes.

Even though it was a light discussion, I would still recommend preparing well for generic HR questions including your strengths, passions, future plans, family background, and work preferences. Also, make sure to attend the Pre-Placement Talk and take notes many HR questions indirectly relate to the company culture and role expectations discussed during the session.

Finally results were announced, 3 students got selected, and I was one of them.

If you ever get such opportunities, DO NOT MISS IT, being a winner of this hackathon gave me an edge in every interview I faced afterward.

For those who had to take the OA, it consisted of aptitude questions, MCQs on core CS fundamentals (like predicting code outputs), and one key coding problem. The coding questions varied--some received complex ones like greedy or 3D DP, while others got easier two-pointer problems. We had an OA round of exactly similar format during the hackathon selection process which shortlisted 11 people from the college for the hackathon at UBS offices. Clearing most of the test cases was critical, most shortlisted candidates passed nearly all, though a few made it with partial success too, via their good aptitude scores. So, performance mattered, but luck had its part as well.

2. Technical Round -1 [20 candidates were shortlisted]

We were asked to report to college by 9:00 a.m., with the interviews beginning around 10:30 a.m. My panel had 2 interviewers, one of them started with asking me about the problem statement i was given during the hackathon, and about the solution, I explained to him in detail about everything about the hackathon right from the start to end of the 24 hrs. Then since our solution consisted of an LLM, he asked me more about how would you ensure that the LLM gives correct answers? And asked why Gemini over other LLMs? He also inquired about OpenAI's Whisper model in depth since that was also being used in a lot of projects of mine. He then asked me how would you reduce the latency of Whisper for a large audio file to which I replied of an idea of dividing the audio file into various chunks and performing parallel processing (multithreading) on them to get the transcriptions in faster time. He was convinced about my solution.

Then the other panelist gave me a coding question on finding the longest palindromic substring -> https://leetcode.com/problems/longest-palindromic-substring/description/, this was a LC medium. I started with the brute force approach of recursively moving the 2 pointers and then memoizing it. She was satisfied with the approach and didn't ask for the most optimal one. After this I was asked some basic questions like why DSA in python and not other languages? To which my answer was clear that I had done everything from backend frameworks like Django, FastAPI to AI/ML, and had around 3+ YOE of using python. Lastly they also gave me a situation about how I would maintain data integrity in one of my projects.

After this the panelists asked if I had any questions. I asked them about how Agentic AI is being used and in what domains are UBS planning to do so. I also asked about reasons behind why their merger faced so many issues and how UBS plans to avoid those issues.

Note: For some candidates they took multiple technical interviews, while for some they took a technical & just an HR interview only

3. HR Round [10-11 candidates were shortlisted]

This was quite simple and straightforward unlike other HR interviews. She remembered my face during the hackathon as I was involved in the final pitch as well, so she didn't ask much about HR questions, rather a simple background check about my family and whether I am fine with relocation or not.

Tip: See, HR interviews may seem simple but you need to understand and play safe here, as this is also the round where you have a lot to lose. So don't take it lightly and be well prepared with your answers. Stick with a genuine smile throughout the interviews, so even if you make a

mistake, accepting that mistake with a smile would give a much better impression than pointlessly being fixated on that point.

6 students were offered the role and I was one of them.

As Companies like UBS can ask questions from either area--or both--depending on the interviewer's background. So, ensure that you're prepared with core CS concepts, practical development knowledge, and also practice solving logical puzzles, as these are frequently asked to assess your analytical thinking.

2.Know Your Resume--But Also Know the Why- Don't just memorize what's on your resume--be prepared to reason every line. Have solid, well-thought-out reasons for every project, internship, or achievement listed. Be ready to explain your decision-making process and choices (e.g., why you chose a particular tech stack, what your contribution was in a team project, etc.).

Tip: Tailor your prep based on the company's JD and recent trends. For example, during our time, everything somehow looped back to AI--so having at least one AI-anchored use case or understanding really helped. Keep an eye on what's hot in the industry and align your resume or project examples accordingly.

3.Ask Smart, Genuine Questions- Interviews are a two-way street. Asking insightful questions (e.g., about the interviewer's role, company innovation, or tech culture) shows that you're truly interested and not just trying to land a job.

4. Participate in Hackathons--Especially Company-Specific Ones General hackathons help you get comfortable with ideation, teamwork, and presenting under pressure. This will prepare you well for company-specific hackathons, which are more than just coding competitions--they're also a chance to understand the company culture, network with employees, and demonstrate your compatibility.

Tip: Don't be disheartened by rejections. There's always a factor of timing and luck involved, so keep showing up and learning from each experience.

5. Last but Not the Least -- Communication is the Salt- Like salt in food -- unnoticed but essential. You may know everything, but if you can't express it well, it won't land. So practice speaking about your work, projects, and decisions. Give mock interviews. Talk to friends, mentors, and seniors. Record yourself explaining concepts( i personally did this very much to know how i should express). The more you speak, the more confident and structured you'll become. Be open, interact with your team, make the most of mentor sessions, and enjoy the whole experience -- not just the coding part. It's a great mix of learning, networking, and fun. :)

2. Technical Interview [ 20 candidates were shortlisted ]

The technical interview process started around 10 AM, and each interview lasted approximately 45 minutes to 1 hour. My interview went on for about 50 minutes and was conducted by a panel of 2 interviewers. It began with a basic introduction, followed by a resume walkthrough. They went through my achievements and then moved on to my projects. I was asked to explain one of my main projects in detail. The questions that followed included:

● Is it an individual or group project?

● What was your role and contribution?

● How did you come up with the idea?

● Business-oriented questions like:

○ How would you scale the project?

○ Would a subscription model work for your application?

○ Why would a user choose your app?

○ How would you handle randomness in the generated results?

● Tech-specific questions like:

○ Why did you choose this tech stack?

After project-related questions, they gave me a few real-world scenarios. For example:

● "If you're building a loan allocation model, how would you prevent it from being biased based on gender, age, caste, etc.?" This led to a few follow-up questions based on the approach I explained.

● Another scenario: "If you're building an e-commerce platform, what modules would you include? What all aspects would you focus on? And how would you divide the work among a team of three?"

Next, I was asked some technical/conceptual questions:

● Minimum 5 key differences between C, C++, and Java

● Some DevOps-related questions

● Questions on frontend frameworks -- which ones I've worked with, and whether I've used Angular

They also asked a couple of classic puzzle questions to assess logical thinking:

● The 8-ball puzzle (find the heavier ball using minimum weighings)

● A father-child age puzzle (when will the father be thrice the child's age)

At the end, make sure to ask them a few questions as well. It's a good way to show interest and curiosity:

● I asked about their roles at UBS and how their journeys had evolved in the company.

● I also asked about UBS's innovation initiatives, specifically in the areas of blockchain and AI.

3. Technical Interview

I had another round of interview which was more of a techno-behavioral (tech + HR) round. It lasted about 40-45 minutes and this time there was just one interviewer. The round started with a basic introduction, followed by a detailed walkthrough of my resume. Interestingly, the interviewer asked me to narrate my journey as a story -- starting from school up to getting into SPIT. While I shared my story, he interrupted occasionally with questions about the decisions I had made along the way, just to understand my approach and reasoning behind them. He asked me weather I wasfine with relocation or not. Then we discussed one of my notable hackathon wins -- the Smart India Hackathon. He asked:

● What did you build?

● What was the overall journey like?

● What challenges did you faced?

● How many team members were involved?

● What was your specific contribution?

After that, the round became more analytical with a set of 4 puzzle questions:

1. Two candles , each take 1 hour to burn -- how would you use them to measure 45 minutes?- link

2. Bridge puzzle -- 4 people with different speeds, 1 torch, 2-person limit: how to cross with minimum total time?- link

3. Poisoned bottle puzzle -- 1000 bottles, 1 is poisoned, you have 10 test strips: how to find the poisoned one in minimum time? -link

4. 2 eggs, 100-floor building -- from which floor will the egg not break? - link

At the end of the interview, I asked him about his journey to UBS and his current role at the company and How does UBS support internal mobility -- switching teams, locations, or

roles?... it went like a normal discussion where the interviewer shared his complete journey with me.

3. HR Interview [ 10-11 candidates where shortlisted]

My HR round was conducted just five minutes after my second technical interview and was quite simple and fast unlike other HR interview rounds.It was a pleasant surprise when the HR greeted me with a smile, mentioning I was a "known face" , likely because of the interaction during the UBS hackathon. That instantly made the interaction feel more relaxed.

The questions were more of a background check than a deep HR evaluation. She asked:

● Where I stay

● How my technical rounds went and what kind of questions I was asked

● Details about my internships -- what I did, whether they were paid or unpaid

We also spoke briefly about my hackathon experience and how I contributed to the team.

While it may have felt informal, I understand the importance of playing this round carefully. HR rounds often assess not just communication skills, but also culture fit, clarity, and honesty. Keeping a genuine smile, staying confident, and being authentic helped maintain a positive impression throughout.

6 students were offered the role and I was one of them : ).

customSections.title: Advice & Tips for Juniors
customSections.content:
1. Maintain a Balance between DSA and Development Skills- It's important to have a balance between (DSA) and development skills. As Companies like UBS can ask questions from either area--or both--depending on the interviewer's background. So, ensure that you're prepared with core CS concepts, practical development knowledge, and also practice solving logical puzzles, as these are frequently asked to assess your analytical thinking.

2.Know Your Resume--But Also Know the Why- Don't just memorize what's on your resume--be prepared to reason every line. Have solid, well-thought-out reasons for every project, internship, or achievement listed. Be ready to explain your decision-making process and choices (e.g., why you chose a particular tech stack, what your contribution was in a team project, etc.).

Tip: Tailor your prep based on the company's JD and recent trends. For example, during our time, everything somehow looped back to AI--so having at least one AI-anchored use case or understanding really helped. Keep an eye on what's hot in the industry and align your resume or project examples accordingly.

3.Ask Smart, Genuine Questions- Interviews are a two-way street. Asking insightful questions (e.g., about the interviewer's role, company innovation, or tech culture) shows that you're truly interested and not just trying to land a job.

4. Participate in Hackathons--Especially Company-Specific Ones General hackathons help you get comfortable with ideation, teamwork, and presenting under pressure. This will prepare you well for company-specific hackathons, which are more than just coding competitions--they're also a chance to understand the company culture, network with employees, and demonstrate your compatibility.

Tip: Don't be disheartened by rejections. There's always a factor of timing and luck involved, so keep showing up and learning from each experience.

5. Last but Not the Least -- Communication is the Salt- Like salt in food -- unnoticed but essential. You may know everything, but if you can't express it well, it won't land. So practice speaking about your work, projects, and decisions. Give mock interviews. Talk to friends, mentors, and seniors. Record yourself explaining concepts( i personally did this very much to know how i should express). The more you speak, the more confident and structured you'll become. Force yourself to get comfortable with being uncomfortable. That's how you grow.

1. Online Assessment

2. Technical Round

3. HR Round

1. Online Assessment + UBS Campus Hackathon

In March 2025, I participated in the UBS Campus Hackathon selection process, which began with an online assessment consisting of 50 minutes of multiple-choice questions and a coding problem. The MCQs focused on Java and core computer science fundamentals such as data structures, OOP, operating systems, and databases. The DSA problem varied for each candidate mine was on the easier side, and I was able to solve it successfully, passing all test cases and completing the assessment early.

Following the results, 11 students from our college were shortlisted to participate in the hackathon. Teams were randomly allocated, and I was initially nervous since all my teammates were complete strangers. But it turned out to be a great way to connect, collaborate, and step out of my comfort zone. Our problem statement was about addressing the shortage of teachers in Zilla Parishad schools by creating a smart platform to connect them with volunteer educators, a solution that helped our team win 2nd runners-up at the hackathon.

One of the best parts of the hackathon was how supportive and involved the mentors and UBS professionals were. They were really friendly, easy to talk to, and genuinely wanted us to do well. We had regular check-ins with them, and they gave us helpful feedback on everything from our idea to how we presented it. If you're participating, make the most of those interactions, ask questions, share your progress, and take their suggestions seriously. It's not just about improving your project, but also about learning how things work in the real world and understanding what companies like UBS look for.

As a finalist, I also received a direct exemption from the UBS campus placement online assessment, which allowed me to proceed straight to the interview round.

2. Technical Interview [ 20 candidates were shortlisted ]

So, my UBS technical interview began on a pretty comfortable note. The interviewer asked me to introduce myself, and then we dove straight into my internship experience and projects. He seemed genuinely interested not just in what I had done, but also in the problems I was trying to solve, the features I had built, and my overall thought process. One of my projects was based on workflow automation, which led to an interesting discussion about the human-in-the-loop concept and where automation should be balanced with human oversight.

He also asked me about the UBS hackathon project, which I had mentioned on my resume. We discussed the problem statement and what I personally contributed to the project. Then he asked if I had used AI in any of my projects, and we had a short conversation about that as well.

After that, he moved on to ask about my 10th and 12th qualifications, which I hadn't included on my resume. It was a bit unexpected, but the flow was smooth and conversational, so I didn't feel nervous.

I had about 4 days to prepare for the interview, and based on seniors' experiences, I expected questions mostly around internships, projects, and CS fundamentals. So I focused my prep on those areas. But right in the middle of the interview, the interviewer surprised me by saying, "I'll be asking you 3 puzzles now." That definitely caught me off guard, because I hadn't focused much on puzzles during my prep -- apart from just reading the ones mentioned in previous interview experiences.

Puzzle 1: The Candle Puzzle (link)

He asked: "You have 2 candles and a matchbox. Each candle takes exactly 1 hour to burn. How can you measure 45 minutes?" My first thought was to break one candle in half, but he pointed out that wouldn't give an accurate 30 minutes. After asking for a hint, he told me, "The middle of the candle is the key." That's when I realized I could burn the first candle from both ends, making it burn out in exactly 30 minutes. At the same time, I'd light the second candle from one end. When the first one finishes, I'd then light the other end of the second candle, making it burn in 15 minutes, totaling 45 minutes. He appreciated the logic and said I had cracked the tough part well.

Puzzle 2: The Poisoned Bottle Problem (link)

This one was trickier. He said: "You have 1000 bottles, one is poisoned. You have 10 test strips, and results take 24 hours. How can you identify the poisoned one?" I wasn't sure of the exact approach but suggested dipping strips in multiples (2, 3, etc.). He said I was thinking about grouping but wouldn't be able to narrow it down precisely. He then gave a hint "Label the bottles" and asked me about bits. I realized he was referring to binary encoding, and I mentioned that I could assign a unique binary number to each bottle. But even with that, I couldn't fully figure out the logic. Before moving on, I asked if he could explain it. At first, he said no, but eventually, he shared the solution which was based on checking the bit pattern of the test strip results after 24 hours to pinpoint the poisoned bottle.

Puzzle 3: The Bridge Crossing Problem (link)

Before this one, he told me "You'll be able to crack this," which somehow made me feel more pressured. The problem: "Four people need to cross a bridge. They take 1, 2, 5, and 10 minutes. Only two can cross at a time, and they need a torch to cross. What's the minimum time to get all across?" I tried pairing the slowest with the fastest, with the fastest returning which gave me a total of 20 minutes. But he said the optimal answer was 17 minutes. I explained that my idea was to always have the fastest person return with the torch. He said I was thinking in the right direction, but I still couldn't land on the right sequence. He eventually explained it, and honestly, looking back, it seems so simple now. But in the moment, when you're under pressure, even the simplest things feel difficult if you're not calm.

At the end of the interview, I asked him two questions: one about what sets UBS apart technologically compared to other banks, and another about his own experience having spent 24 years in the investment banking sector, what made him join UBS and stay. He answered both very thoughtfully, sharing insights into UBS's strong tech-first mindset and what stood out to him compared to other firms he had worked at. It felt less like a formal Q&A and more like a genuine, engaging conversation and with that, the interview wrapped up.

Tips:

● Stay calm. Interviews can be nerve-wracking, but your ability to think clearly under pressure is just as important as your technical skills.

● Know your projects well. Be ready to explain why you made certain decisions, not just what you did. You should be able to defend your choices confidently.

● Think out loud. Don't go completely silent while solving problems. Share your thought process; it helps keep the conversation going and shows how you approach challenges.

● Be honest if you're stuck. It's okay to ask for a hint or say you're not sure, what matters is how you handle the situation.

Note: For some candidates they took multiple technical interviews, while for some they took a technical & just an HR interview only

3. HR Interview [ 10-11 candidates where shortlisted]

The HR interview was quite short and honestly felt more like a friendly conversation than a formal interview. The interviewer was from the Mumbai branch, and since I had already interacted with her during the UBS Hackathon, she remembered me, which immediately made things more relaxed and comfortable.

She started by asking whether I had participated in any other hackathons after the UBS one. I shared that I had, and she asked me to talk about the differences I noticed between those experiences and the UBS hackathon. After that, she briefly revisited my hackathon experience at UBS, asking how I found it overall. We then moved on to a basic background check. She asked about my family and whether I was planning to pursue higher studies like a master's degree (I said no). And that was it we wrapped up in under 10 minutes.

6 students were offered the role and I was one of them (5/6 were hackathon finalists).

Pre Placement Talk(PPT) + Online Assessment(OA): 10th July 2025 Interviews: 14th July 2025

Placement Process:

All candidates who had applied were to give a UBS culture test (not timed) and Aptitude test (2 rounds 6 minutes speed based pattern recognition + 6 minutes 18 questions paragraph based). This test was to be given from home by applying on UBS website.

Some failed to give this test and were not shortlisted for OA.
journey.prep:
1. Nervous? Don't worry, just go and give the interview, everything will be fine after the first round. That day I realized my communication skills were much better than I expected them to be (Well they are worse for some personal reasons). Your words should reflect wisdom.

2. I didn't win any hackathons but had attended some and had experience. I was asked about hackathons in each round so try to go for as many as you can and try to work in a team. Don't just make PPT but also develop something as a team.

3. I didn't have any internship, I had projects but having an internship would definitely help.

4. I always tried to make fun and useful projects.

5. I used Go as my main language for development (Try it if you have time it is way more fun than Javascript).

6. The core subjects, the system design for your projects and follow-up questions are must.

7. Attending coding contests or virtual contests on Leetcode/Codeforces will help to solve problems under pressure.

8. Of course know your resume inside out. DO NOT add anything that you don't know properly.

9. If you don't know something don't tell them beforehand unless asked.

10. If your answer is NO just say it loud and clear as if you don't regret it just like an army personnel or just without any hesitation but humbly. Don't say it softly like you are scared.

11. I talked to a senior and my friends and fine tuned my resume accordingly.

12. Many candidates were multiple time hackathon winners and had internships but were still rejected, so always get your fundamentals right no matter what you have achieved.

13. One final thing is whenever you contact any senior, don't just ask about how they did it, also ask about what mistakes they made and why they were rejected. I wasn't able to clear PhonePe OA and then went on to clear UBS and MSCI OA's and was selected for UBS.

journey.howSecured:
All candidates who had applied were to give a UBS culture test (not timed) and Aptitude test (2 rounds 6 minutes speed based pattern recognition + 6 minutes 18 questions paragraph based). This test was to be given from home by applying on UBS website.

Some failed to give this test and were not shortlisted for OA.

1. Online Assessment [ 173 candidates appeared ]

Platform: HackerRank (Oncampus) Time Limit: 90 minutes

Format: 15 Aptitude + 15 OOPS/Java/SQL/DSA + 1 Coding Question

Section 1: 15 Aptitude questions were pretty much doable based on sets, probability, statistics, and some could be just answered by looking at the given graph (It was initially not very visible, just pull the image then it'll be clearly visible).

Section 2: 15 OOPS/Java/SQL/DSA were very basic if you have fundamental knowledge. The OOPS questions were in Java but even if you are from C++/Python background then knowledge of OOPS would help you clear it. SQL was simple syntactical as well. Some questions were also MCQ based on DSA like inorder of a given tree.

Section 3: The coding question was a bit tricky to understand. I can't clearly remember it but it was to be done by using TreeSet / PriorityQueue in Java.

I tried the coding question first for about 20 minutes but was able to pass just 1 test case then my platform was stuck for about 10 minutes so I quickly informed the invigilator. After the problem was solved (I didn't get my time back) I proceeded to section 2 and did that quickly and then completed section 1. Then I went on to the coding question which then I tried using PriorityQueue till the end of the time it passed 9 test cases and the assessment was finally over.

6 of the candidates were part of UBS Hackathon who had appeared for an OA in March 2025 so they were directly shortlisted for interviews, so 14 candidates (including me) were shortlisted from July 2025 OA (A rather low number of candidates).

2. Technical Round [ 20 candidates appeared ]

The round started by the interviewer going through my resume in the meantime asking me to introduce myself. Then he asked me to tell me my favorite project among the projects in my resume. I was told to draw the architecture of that entire project on a paper and explain each and every component. 3/4 of my projects were in Go (Rare to find such people). Then I was asked some system design based questions.

1. Your setup is in Andheri (Mumbai) and a person accessing from USA is observing latency, what will you do?

2. How will you handle millions of users?

3. How will you handle large file responses?

Then I was asked to differentiate between SQL and NoSQL databases (Now keep in mind NoSQL doesn't just mean MongoDB there are many other than that like Cassandra, Redis etc. so answer accordingly). Then he asked me which one is better: SQL or NoSQL? I had also mentioned horizontal scaling so I was also asked about that.

Then I was given a SQL query to solve which included JOIN + GROUP BY + HAVING + COUNT. My approach was using LEFT JOIN but interviewers approach was using INNER JOIN. Both worked. I had mistakenly switched the table names (Do not panic, shrug it off like it never happened).

I was asked about my most favorite (Operating Systems) and least favorite (FOSIP) subject. I was asked how many threads does a core have? Do they run in parallel? How did I manage to clear my least favorite subject?

A very very simple programming question was also asked. Then he asked me about the internal working of HashMap, time complexity of each type of working then about sorting algorithms and their time complexity and how do the ones having logarithmic time complexity work.

I was asked about Hackathons and the role of each member. I mentioned I had gone to some but didn't win any so he said winning isn't important, the experience gained is much more important.

I was then given the bridge puzzle Link. My answer was higher so he told me to improve it. I wasn't able to do it (Do not panic, shrug it off like it never happened).

Then came some HR questions:

1. Strength and weakness?

2. How are you improving your weakness?

3. One mistake you never repeated?

4. What do you know about UBS?

5. Why do you want to work for UBS?

6. What is the latest news you have heard about UBS?

7. Family background?

Then he asked whether I had any questions for him. I asked:

1. First of all I asked his name since he didn't mention it.

2. How is your typical day at UBS?

3. What is your favorite part of the work at UBS?

It was such a long round that I don't even remember the time.

3. HR Round 1

This round was entirely based on behaviour. I answered it loud and clearly like an army personnel without flinching.

1. Tell me about your entire life journey from place of birth, 10th school and percentage, 12th college and percentage, CET score, how I landed in SPIT?

2. What was my first preference, SPIT or VJTI?

3. Favorite thing about SPIT?

4. Do you have any internship experience?

5. Have you been to hackathons?

6. What was the problem statement? (We had a long discussion on this)

Then he asked whether I had any questions for him. I asked:

1. What learning opportunities and certifications does UBS provide?

2. Are those certifications just relevant within UBS or even for outside companies?

3. How is the role switching process in UBS?

The round lasted about 10-15 minutes. I was so much in army mode that after the interview when the TPC asked me something I mistakenly said YES SIRRR!! loudly.

4. HR Round 2

This round was just a background check and behavioural of about 5 minutes.

1. Why Computer Science Engineering?

2. Hackathon experience?

3. Open for relocation?

4. Are parents open for relocation?

Finally after a long wait 6 students (including me) were offered the role.

● 1 tech interview was conducted for some people, whereas for some, there were 2 tech interviews.

● Eligibility criteria was above 70% in both 10th and 12th boards, CGPA : 7+.

1. Online Assessment [173 people appeared]

There were 2 tests focusing on aptitude (verbal and visual reasoning) and UBS cultural assessment, which everyone had to take (from home).

Then a hackerank test was conducted focusing on DSA and CS core which was skipped for hack participants.

2. Tech Interview [ 20 people] (25-30 minutes)

( 6 panels with 2 interviewers in some and 1 in some, Summer intern process was going on alongside as well )

It started with my introduction, then they asked me about one of my projects. I explained it in detail, including the tech stack used (what and why) and system design.

Then they asked me what changes I would make in the project.

Then some HR questions like :

1. If your friend is suggesting some other technology and you want to use something else, then what will you do?

2. If one of your team member is not giving his best, which is causing delays in deliverables, what will you do?

3. If a client has requested for some feature which does not align with the objectives of your project, what will you do?

4. What are the business opportunities of your hackathon project (which was made at UBS hack) ?

Then 2 puzzles:

1. A variation of this ( Hats puzzle ),The conditions were not specified properly or I did not understand them properly. ( I wasn't able to solve it, I thought this might cost me the opportunity)

2. Simple jug problem

Then about Inner,Left,Right and Outer join.

Then they asked me about any questions I had for them. ( Ask something relevant, either about their tech-stack, you can do some research beforehand.) I asked about their DevCloud project which was mentioned on GitLab.

[

Tips: Maintain eye contact with the interviewer, a smile would be helpful. Ask for hints if required. Be well versed with your resume (projects and internship if any). If you're explaining your project try doing it with a use case, it would show that it actually solves some problem.

Think before answering any questions as there will be follow up questions as well. Be ready for some HR questions as well; they can be asked in tech interviews as well. Answer HR questions carefully keeping the company's interests in mind.

]

3. HR Round [9-10 people appeared]

This round was just for 5 minutes, HR knew me from the hackathon so it helped. This round was chill, Questions:

1. Family background

2. Relocation

3. Other companies which conduct hackathons (Barclays specifically) and their procedure.

[ 6 students got the offer including me ]

1. Online Assessment Round ( 197 Students ) ( 11/07/2025 )

UBS had a criteria of 7+ gpa till 3rd semester( I was in Summer breaks of 4th Sem to 5th Sem when the company came for internships). So 226 Applicants Filled the google form but along with filling the google forms you also need to register on their website. Only 197 registered on their website and hence the rest were not eligible for OA round. Before OA round there were 2 assessments on their website

UBS culture matching test

Aptitude

You can prepare for this just by searching about those on google/youtube ,etc.

Next there was the OA round.

It was a 90min Online Test on HackerRank.

There were 15 java/dbms/data structure questions + 15 Aptitude questions + 1 DSA question

Aptitude Questions included :

Sets questions ( just revise the sets from 12th standard or DSGT)

Probability ( just revise class 12th probability)

Basic graph interpretation ( class 10th graph knowledge would work)

Passage based questions

For the passage based questions just remember to extract the relevant information only. Remember this is important. It will have a lot of irrelevant information and take a lot of time if you read it entirely.

DSA Question:

They asked pretty easy questions. Just based on Arrays, HashMap, basic techniques like sliding window,prefix-suffix,etc. So just preparing for basics would also work, no need to go through DP on trees,etc.

My question was:

You will be given an array of size n. You need to divide the array in 2 parts such that the sum of the number of distinct elements from the left part and right part is maximum. You need to return that maximum sum.

constraints : 1<n<10e5

Example : 3 1 4 1 5

So here , if i partition them like 3 1 and 4 1 5 then no. of distinct elements of 3 1 is 2 and for 4 1 5 is 3 so sum is 5 , where as if i partition them like 3 and 1 4 1 5 then the no. of distinct elements would be 1 and for the 1 4 1 5 it would be 3 so sum is 4. But by partitioning 3 1 and 4 1 5 we got the sum as 5. So that is the maximum that we need to return.

My Approach:

So obviously brute force won't work as constraints are 10e5, So what i want ?

I want the left distinct + right distinct as max. So , let's think that i will try at every index that by partitioning at that index , what can be the sum and i will find the maximum among that.

Ok , so it will take O(n) , now I need to find the no. of distinct elements from left and right in either O(1) or in O(n). So brute force is just finding the no. of distinct elements every time. What if we just precompute those. Yes, we will use the prefix and suffix approach and that's it. We are good to go.

You can check out the code at : https://pastebin.com/G7g3Pm2n

So I advise that you focus on java and aptitude , dsa questions were pretty much doable.

Just be chill, you can do it, don't get too stressed, that's the advice.

2. [Technical Interview ] [16 Students] 14/07/2025

It was an offline face to face interview.

So the first question they asked me was what's your CGPA. I answered it, I guess I was the only one of

whom they wrote the GPA on the Resume. ( Maybe because it was high(9.79)). Next they asked me about

the Barclays minor as I was part of that. Next they asked me to introduce myself.

Although I did say oops as my strongest subject they still asked only 3-4 theory questions and 1 written question.

Next they moved on to the Data Structures, they asked me a lot of questions on this. And asked very basic algorithm questions.

Then next they asked me 2 quizzes. One was on probability and other I avoided answering it.

Then next they asked me some DBMS questions. Then they asked me about github, leetcode,codechef profiles. Then they moved on to some HR questions. Although it was technical round but still they asked me

HR questions.(I don't know whether other's faced the same or not).Just make sure you attend the preplacement talk with them. That's enough for the knowledge regarding the company.

They also asked about my strengths, weaknesses, hobbies, extra-circular activities, where I live,what my parents do, etc all. Being a part of any committee and leading any position would work for extra circular activities.

For OOPS : java docs, Kunal Kushwaha, Durga Software Solutions and MOST IMP IS BY JUST RANDOMLY TRYING RANDOM CODES. I mean just write the random codes, what if i add static here , what if I add final here.

For Data Structures : As i said java they asked how internally java Collections implement these Data Structures, So make sure you see the actual implementation. Next, preparing well for even Semester exams was ok(not sufficient) for this. Just have a curiosity while preparing for semester exams you will learn some

Relevant things around the syllabus and that's sufficient.

For Algorithms : It was basic. Following any sheet might work. To be honest I didn't even refer to one. I just solved Random Questions. One of the key mentors is Sujal Das . Doing CP for this is extremely more than enough.

For DBMS : Pretty Basic Questions on this. But College Syllabus is not enough for this, You have to prepare

Well other than college syllabus.

3. [HR Round] [9 Students ] 14/07/2025

To be honest, for other people it was around 15-20 minutes grind. For me it was just 2 minutes of casual talk. They asked me where I live, what my parents do, from where I completed my 12th, why I didn't choose Walchand Sangli (I am from Solapur, I did my 12th from Walchand Solapur, They mis understood it as Sangli and hence asked). Also they asked what is Barclays Minor in my Resume. And that's it, I have literally listed entire HR round questions. They just asked me these questions and for others it was literal grind. So if you do well in the technical round, HR will be just a formality.

Finally 3 people got selected for Internships.

journey.prep:
Always keep a smile. It instantly lightens the mood and helps the interview flow more naturally. Even if you're nervous, a calm and pleasant expression makes a big difference.

Don't panic. Once you start panicking, it affects how you think and respond. Take a breath before answering it's okay to pause for a moment and gather your thoughts.

Never lie. If you don't know an answer, start with "I think…" and try to reason it out. But if the interviewer keeps digging deeper, be honest and admit you're not sure. They appreciate honesty more than guessing blindly.

For DSA, I'd recommend NeetCode 75 it's concise and covers all core patterns. But don't just focus on DSA. Prepare OOPs, SQL, and core CS topics like OS and Networking too.

For Aptitude, try solving from InterviewBit's aptitude section, it's straightforward and helps you build consistency.

Be thorough with your resume. Know every line of it and never include something you can't explain in detail.

Luck plays its part. Sometimes it's about the panel you get or the questions asked but solid preparation and the right mindset always tilt luck in your favor.

1) OA

2) Technical Interview 1

3) Technical Interview 2

4) HR Interview

1. Online Assessment Round:

The online assessment was conducted on the HackerRank platform, consisting of 36 questions to be solved in 120 minutes. The test covered a mix of topics including Computer Networks, Operating Systems, SQL, Logical Reasoning, Probability, and Puzzles, along with two coding problems based on Tree and Dynamic Programming (DP).

There were also multiple SQL query-based questions that tested basic to intermediate understanding of joins, aggregate functions, and constraints. The non-technical sections focused on logical reasoning and quantitative aptitude, including probability-based word problems and short analytical puzzles.

The good part was that we got to attempt the test online from home since it was raining heavily that day, which definitely reduced some stress. Overall, the OA was moderately difficult. The key was to maintain speed while balancing accuracy across both the technical and reasoning sections.

2. TECHNICAL ROUND 1 [ 27 students were selected for the technical interview]

The first question was the usual: "Tell me about yourself." I gave a brief overview of my education background, technical skills, and the projects I had worked on. From there, the interviewer moved straight into my project section.

I mentioned my CI/CD project, so most of her questions revolved around Kubernetes, kubectl, Jenkins, Minikube, replicas, and how Kubernetes detects high traffic. I was able to answer most of them confidently, though I struggled with a couple of deeper ones. She appreciated my overall understanding and moved on.

Next, she asked me to write a simple REST API using the @GetMapping annotation, and then to draw the architecture showing frontend-to-backend connectivity. After that, we shifted to Java -- she asked

about the differences between Java and C++, their advantages, data types in Java, and the types of for loops.

Then came a quick DSA question: reverse a string. It was straightforward, and I solved it easily. She followed it up with two basic SQL queries, one using WHERE and ORDER BY, and another involving an INNER JOIN.

After the technical part, she asked a few situational questions like "How would you disclose bad news if you were a manager?", "How do you handle stressful situations?", and "What did you learn from such experiences?"

We ended up having a really good discussion around these. At the end, she asked if I had any questions. I asked her two things "What advice would you give to freshers joining Oracle?" and "How is Oracle adapting to AI?" That sparked another nice conversation, and overall, the interview felt very friendly and conversational rather than intense.This round lasted for about 40-45minutes.

3. TECHNICAL ROUND 2 [ around 20 students appeared for it ]

The second round started almost immediately after the first barely a five-minute break. I greeted the interviewer, and we shook hands. He began by asking how my first interview went. Since it had ended on a friendly note, I felt quite confident and shared my experience with him.

He then asked me to introduce myself and followed it up with an interesting question, "What mistakes did you make in your previous interview?" I mentioned one of my small mistakes and explained how I had already learned from it and corrected it. He seemed to appreciate that honest answer.

Next, he started asking questions about my AI project mainly what it does, why it's needed, and how it works in practice. He even asked me to show the deployed version of the project. After that, we moved to SQL, where he asked about different types of joins and cursors, which I was able to answer confidently.

Toward the end, he asked if I had any questions. I asked him the same ones as before "What advice would you give to freshers?" and "Will the duties of an Associate Consultant be completely technical, or will they also involve functional responsibilities?" That led to another engaging conversation. I also mentioned that my previous interviewer had told me about Oracle's AI initiatives, so I asked him a bit more about that too.

Overall, it was a short and smooth round, around 15 minutes long. The discussion felt more like a conversation than an interrogation. I was lucky with my panel some other panels went on for over an hour and a half.

4. HR ROUND [ Around 12 students appeared for it]

The HR round was short, lasting about 5 minutes. The HR started with some basic questions about my nationality, and whether I was aware of the role Oracle was offering. She then asked if I would be comfortable with relocation.

Next, she asked if I was planning any further higher studies. I humorously replied that this is my "higher studies" since I'm already pursuing my master's degree. The conversation then moved to the internship I need to complete for my course. She asked what I would do if the company offered me a PPO. I lightened the mood with a joke, saying I definitely wouldn't reject Oracle.

That was essentially it, the whole round was relaxed and quite casual.

[12 students received offer, 6 of them from MCA ]
