Online Assessment - 15-09-2025 F2F Interviews - 17-09-2025

1. Online Assessment Round [~ 125 Candidates Appeared] Platform: HackerRank

Total Duration: 95 minutes

Sections: 4

Section Breakdown

1. DSA Question 1 - Basic problem on arrays (1 question)

2. MCQs - Computer Science & Related Topics

○ OS, Computer Networks, DBMS

○ Cloud services

○ Debugging

○ Data structures

○ Total: ~25 MCQs

3. MCQs - Aptitude

○ Quantitative and logical reasoning

○ Total: ~10-11 MCQs

4. DSA Question 2 - Slightly difficult problem on arrays (1 question)

My Approach

● Started with the first DSA question (array-based, straightforward).

● Then moved on to MCQs (CS fundamentals + cloud + debugging + DS + aptitude), which consumed

the majority of my time.

● Finally attempted the second DSA question, which was comparatively difficult. I managed to clear

partial test cases for it.

NOTE - DO NOT UNDERESTIMATE APTITUDE - IT IS JUST AS IMPORTANT AS YOUR

DSA AND PLAYS A CRUCIAL ROLE IN GETTING SHORTLISTED FOR THE NEXT

ROUND.

Links : APTITUDE (IMPORTANT)

1.https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLpyc33gOcbVA4qXMoQ5vmhefTruk5t9lt

2.https://www.indiabix.com/

3. If time permits - https://bodheeprep.com/free-cat-quant-practice-questions

2. Technical Round 1 [ 25 candidates appeared for this round]

The reporting time at college was 8:45 AM as OFSS was scheduled to conduct their Pre-Placement Talk

(PPT) for the shortlisted students. However, due to some delays, the PPT wrapped up only around 11:00-11:30 AM, after which the interviews began.

I was called for my first interview at 3:30 PM. By that time, most of my peers had already given two interviews, and some were unfortunately rejected.

I walked into the room, greeted the interviewer, and was pleasantly surprised to find that she was very chill and friendly. With around 15 years of experience at OFSS, she carried a calm yet professional demeanor that helped ease my nerves.

I began with a brief introduction, after which the conversation quickly shifted to my projects.

Project Discussion

● She asked me to explain the implementation details in depth of the first project I mentioned.

● Then, she posed a situational question: "If X problem occurs, how would you solve it technically, and what could be the potential reason behind it?"

○ Since I primarily work in Machine Learning, I clarified that I am not deeply into development but still answered based on my knowledge.

○ She seemed satisfied with my explanation.

● We then moved through all the other projects listed on my resume, and even discussed a few hackathon-winning projects that were not on the resume.

The interviewer also asked:

● "How do you distribute work in a group and handle conflicts?"

○ I shared my experience of working in teams and explained how we ensured smooth collaboration.

● "Which programming language do you prefer?"

○ I said C++, since it was the first language I learned.

○ She asked, "Why not Java?"

○ I explained that I was most comfortable with C++, though if given an option among Java, C++, and Python, I would still lean toward C++.

○ She pointed out that C++ is quite old and asked me to justify it. I confidently presented use cases and advantages where C++ still shines. She seemed convinced with my reasoning.

○ To show adaptability, I added that I would also love to learn Java since it's widely used and in trend, highlighting my willingness to learn new technologies.

Towards the end, she asked if I had any questions. I prepared and asked three questions, which led to a fruitful discussion lasting 10-15 minutes.

This Round Lasted for around 40-45 mins.

Learnings

● Be careful and confident while introducing and explaining yourself. Interviewers can easily sense if you're faking something. Authenticity matters.

● This round was heavily project-focused. It tested how well you can present your work, defend your choices, and explain your technology stack.

● Be 100% sure about what you have built. If it's on your resume, you should be able to explain it thoroughly.

After 10 mins I was called for Round 2

3. Technical Round 2 [~ 12-14 Candidates]

By the time my Round 2 came up, I was one of the last candidates to be interviewed. Many interviewers had already left, so I knew I had to give my best to make an impression.

I entered the room, greeted the interviewer, but initially, he didn't seem very interested. He skipped the introduction part altogether and jumped directly into project discussions.

Project & Technical Discussion

● He picked the third project on my resume and asked me to explain it.

○ I explained the project step by step in detail, covering the entire implementation.

● After the explanation, he shifted focus to Large Language Models (LLMs) and asked:

○ How do LLMs work (Encoder-Decoder Overview & How it generates response)?

○ Which models have I personally used?

○ Why is the quality of responses different across LLMs?

○ I answered all these questions confidently, and he seemed satisfied with my explanations.

Coding & SQL Tasks

● Next, he asked me to write a C++ code to count character frequencies.

○ I wrote the code systematically on paper (as they were evaluating written solutions).

● Then, he moved to SQL:

○ Task: Find the 2nd smallest number from a table containing duplicate values.

○ I solved it using CTEs and the DENSE_RANK() window function.

● After SQL, he asked me to explain the same project again, but this time on paper, step by step.

○ He also raised a few counter-questions, which I handled well.

● Finally, he asked:

○ "What is the difference between Machine Learning and Deep Learning?"

○ I explained the distinction clearly, which concluded the technical questioning.

Closing Discussion

The interviewer now seemed more engaged. We ended the interview on a positive note with a light discussion about:

● AI trends

● How the company is heavily investing in AI

● My views on the future of this domain

Learnings

● First impressions matter, but consistency seals it. Even if the interviewer seems disinterested, maintain energy and confidence.

● Projects are your strongest asset - be ready to explain them multiple times, even on paper, and defend your choices.

● Be thorough with basics in C++, SQL, and core concepts - they often act as filters.

● Stay updated with AI/ML advancements - it shows genuine interest in your field.

*Round Lasted for 40-45 mins.

Round 3

HR Discussion

● The HR directly informed us that we were selected.

● HR asked whether I had any questions.

● She also asked for our preferred job location.

● Before closing, she advised us to enjoy the remaining days of college life, as professional life would soon begin.

My Journey Before OFSS

Before getting selected at OFSS, I had already gone through a series of ups and downs in my placement

journey.

I appeared for InCred Finance and reached till the last round, but unfortunately got rejected there. Then

came an opportunity with BlackRock, where I was considered for a Data Operations role. Out of the

candidates, 10 were selected and 3 (including me) were waitlisted. That moment hit me hard being so

close yet not through was one of the most disheartening setbacks I faced.

I also participated in Nomura's Kakushin Hackathon, where I reached the presentation stage, but again

faced rejection.

These multiple setbacks took a toll on me. I remember being the most disheartened during the BlackRock

waitlist phase watching others move ahead while I was stuck in uncertainty. But through it all, my family

stood strong beside me. They constantly reminded me, "God has something bigger planned for you."

And truly, they were right. That bigger plan unfolded when I got selected at OFSS. Looking back, I feel

nothing but thankfulness and gratitude to my parents, to my friends for their endless support, and to my

college for providing me this opportunity.

Key Takeaways for Preparation

1. Maintain a Strong CGPA

○ A CGPA ≥ 7.5 is mandatory - aim higher to stay safe.

2. Know Your Resume Inside Out

○ Be ready to explain every detail of your projects and experiences.

○ Do not fake anything - honesty is valued more than exaggeration.

3. Focus on Aptitude

○ Aptitude is a crucial shortlisting factor - give it equal importance as DSA.

4. Practice DSA Daily

○ Strengthen your problem-solving skills.

○ Also, build an understanding of how DSA concepts are applied in real-world scenarios.

5. Master CS Fundamentals (priority order)

○ OOPS == DBMS → OS == CCN

○ These topics form the backbone of most technical interviews.

6. Showcase All-Round Skills

○ Highlight leadership qualities and extra-curricular activities.

○ Companies value candidates who are not just technically strong but also versatile.

7. Believe in Yourself

○ Confidence, consistency, and self-belief are key to overcoming rejections and moving forward.

journey.prep:
So here's a short gist of my college years. Honestly, I didn't have a great start--my PTR was 7.35(currently it's 8.25, keep it above 8), and it's not like I was busy with DSA or projects. In fact, the first two years I was pretty lost and didn't do much prep at all. Later, I finally buckled down and started DSA.I tried covering as much as I could before placements, but still couldn't clear the OAs. I sat for around 15 to 20 companies and got rejected in all of them. By the end, I was the only one in my group still unplaced.

I'm telling you this because the process can get really tough. Maybe everyone around you will get placed before you, maybe your PTR won't meet the cutoffs, and yeah--there'll be a lot of tough days. But don't give up. Enjoy the whole ride--the rejections and the successes--because that's what makes it easier to handle.

And the most important thing: have fun! It's college--you won't get this time again. And also everyone has a different approach to studying , if u have a different one dont think its wrong .

Before the technical round 1 we had a ppt where I asked 2 questions . It didn't play a very important role for me but it might help you , so ask if you have even a small doubt in your head don't hesitate to ask but if you don't it's okay, no pressure .

1. Tech Round 1 [ No of candidates who appeared for this round : 25] [30-40 mins]

The PPT was supposed to start at 8:45 but actually began around 10, and the interviews started at about 11:30. I know the waiting can be really nerve-wracking, but try to stay calm if possible.

During my interview, I went in and greeted the interviewer with a handshake. She started by asking me for my introduction, and then the very first question was: Why Oracle? (I was asked this in all rounds). I answered by mentioning something I remembered from the PPT--that Oracle has a presence in almost 125 countries--so she could see that I had paid attention.

Next, she gave me a very simple coding question: adding two numbers. She wanted to understand how I wrote the code. As a follow-up, she asked about function declaration vs. function expression. After that, she asked me to write an SQL query to select all names starting with my name using the like operator.Then, we moved on to HR-style questions. She asked me about my strengths and weaknesses, and then asked: If you had all the resources you needed, what product would you build using your skills?

I also got some puzzles. For example: If I had 1 cm³ cubes, how many would I need to fill a 9 cm³ cube?

She asked me CSS questions too. One was whether I had used a CSS framework (I said I had worked with Tailwind CSS). Then she asked about the main box styles in CSS. At first, I misunderstood and said flex, grid, etc., but what she was looking for was padding, borders, margins, etc. She also asked: What is absolute positioning? (and wanted me to show it by drawing) and What is the default positioning?

Another puzzle was the classic jug problem: You have a 5L jug and a 3L jug. How will you measure exactly 4L without any measuring device?

She also touched on OOP and C++ concepts, like polymorphism (and asked me to write it down), what I would call an overloaded constructor in the parent class, the difference between agentic AI and generative AI, and what inline functions in C++ are.At the end, she asked if I had any questions, and I asked her two.

Now, here's the important part: I did not know the answers to all the questions, and I wasn't able to solve both the puzzles. But I made sure to walk her through my thought process and explain the solutions I was considering. I also asked for hints when I needed them.It's not about always having the correct answer--it's about how you approach the problem and how you carry yourself throughout the process. Don't be scared. You'll feel very nervous outside, but once you're inside, just sit and talk as if you're chatting with a friend. And remember: it's okay if you don't know something. Nobody knows everything. What matters most is keeping an open mind and thinking freely.

2. Technical Round 2 [Duration : 30 mins ]

For Tech Round 2, I was called in within 20 minutes. The interviewer was very chill and said he wouldn't start with technical questions. Instead, he began by asking me where I live and Why Oracle. While I was answering, he noticed I mentioned AI and became very interested. Since I had completed an internship in generative AI, he asked me to explain it and draw the flow. This was a project I knew well, so I explained everything in detail. While I was drawing, he mentioned that he used to live where I do, and we had a short discussion about that.

After that, he asked a simple DSA question: detect duplicates and print their count. Then he asked me to write an SQL query to find the third-highest rank in a given dataset, and later to implement the same logic in C++.

He asked me Why Oracle once again, and I repeated the point I had mentioned earlier from the PPT. At the end, he asked if I had any questions, so I asked a few, and we discussed them.

3. HR round[10mins and 9 ppl]

This was NOT an elimination round,just a formality round .I was asked about my nationality, willingness to relocate, plans for a master's degree, who I live with, and my hobbies. She also mentioned that the final results would be based on Round 1 and Round 2. Finally, she asked if I had any questions.

1. Open Assessment (Sept 15, 2025)

2. Technical Interview - 1 (Oct 8, 2025)

3. Technical Interview - 2 (Oct 8, 2025)

4. HR Interview (Oct 8, 2025)

Note: The OA was common for both the Associate Consultant and Application Developer roles. Although I was not shortlisted for the Application Dev role after the assessment, I was later shortlisted for the Associate Consultant role based on the same OA performance.

1. Open Assessment [Eligibility criteria: 7 CGPA, with no current backlogs]

The OA was conducted on HackerRank, consisted of questions from the following:

● Data Structures & Algorithms (2 questions, everyone had different questions):

1. Based on Arrays - Easy difficulty

2. Based on Trees - Moderate difficulty

● Computer Science Fundamentals:

1. Computer Networks

2. Operating Systems

3. SQL (Joins, Aggregate functions, constraints)

● Aptitude & Reasoning:

1. Logical reasoning and probability based quantitative aptitude

2. Analytical puzzles

2. Technical Interview - 1 [27 students were shortlisted for this round]

The interview began with a brief self-introduction. I kept my response concise, summarizing what I have learned over the course of my studies, and highlighting my interest in Machine Learning. I also mentioned that Python is my primary programming language, while I'm comfortable with Java and SQL as well. I concluded with a short note on my long-term goals and hobbies.

The interviewer then moved on to discuss my projects. She began with my major project. I explained the idea behind it and what my specific contributions were. Next, she asked me about another project, which was an open-access platform for managing and exploring research papers. I described its main features and briefly outlined my role in developing its core functionalities.

After that, she reviewed the technical skills listed on my resume and asked several follow-up questions. When asked about my preferred programming language, I mentioned Python. She then asked why not Java, to which I explained that Python's simplicity, extensive libraries, and faster prototyping capabilities make it ideal for research or machine learning related tasks, which align more closely with my interests. When asked why many companies still prefer Java, I replied that Java offers better performance in large-scale enterprise systems, strong type safety, and a good support for multithreading and scalability.

She later asked some questions related to database design, including schemas and access controls along with some SQL functions. She then asked about the use of JavaScript - I explained that it is primarily used for adding interactivity to web pages and is essential for front-end development, especially when working with frameworks like React

She noticed I had mentioned Android SDK in my resume and asked whether I had built any Android apps. I mentioned that I had developed one as a mini-project during my second year in Java (though not listed in my resume) and asked me several related questions.

We also discussed the scalability differences between SQL and NoSQL databases, after which she moved on to Git and version control systems. I explained concepts like repositories, commits, branching, merging, and pull requests, and described how multiple developers collaborate using Git. I also shared a basic diagram to illustrate the workflow and mentioned common Git commands used for these operations.

The interviewer then moved to Data Structures, asking how linked lists work and their real-life applications. I answered honestly when I could not recall specific applications. I was then asked to write a function to calculate the first n Fibonacci numbers, which I implemented.

Next, she asked a few Linux command questions, which were fairly straightforward. She then asked about Tableau since I had listed it under my skills. When asked why Tableau and not Power BI, I responded that Tableau provides a more intuitive interface, faster data blending, and better integration with Python for analytics, making it a preferred choice for exploratory data analysis.

Finally, she asked a few questions about my certifications, which I had completed. When I was asked why I didn't have any formal internship experience, I explained that I didn't find opportunities that aligned with my interests at the time. Instead, I focused on personal and academic projects, which helped me apply my learning effectively.

3. Technical Interview - 2 [~20 students were shortlisted for this round]

This interview skipped the introductory "Tell me about yourself" and started directly with my projects. He began with my major project, asking me to explain it in detail again, and then moved on to some other project. He probed further into how I managed certain functionalities, how I implemented specific features, and posed hypothetical scenarios such as "If you were to implement X, how would you do it?". He also inquired whether the project was hosted, to which I replied, it was not, and asked a few other technical details. Overall, the focus was on being thorough and precise about my projects.

The discussion then shifted to SQL, where I was asked to write a query involving aggregate functions and GROUP BY. He also asked several Python-related questions, including the use of inbuilt functions, and explored my understanding of the language in detail.

He further revisited my technical skills listed on the resume, asking clarifying and in-depth questions. While he maintained a serious and formal demeanor, I remained calm and answered to the best of my ability.

_______________________________________________________________________________________

Note: Both of these interviews lasted for around 45-50 minutes and were manageable as long as you remain calm, honest, and well-versed with every little detail mentioned in your resume, as the interviewer may ask in-depth questions based on your listed skills, projects, and certifications. I have attempted to include all the questions I was asked, although I may have missed a few, this experience reflects the overall structure and focus of the interviews.

_______________________________________________________________________________________

4. HR Interview [12 students were shortlisted for this round]

The HR interview was short, lasting around 5 minutes. It started with some basic questions, first confirming my nationality, followed by queries about the role being offered and the compensation details. She then asked if I would be comfortable relocating to any of the mentioned work locations, to which I replied yes.

Next, she inquired if I was planning to pursue higher studies, to which I replied no. When asked why, I mentioned that I didn't have any such plans in the near future, but might consider it a few years down the line if I ever decide to. The conversation then moved to whether I had any current offers or PPOs from other companies; I said no, and when asked if I had appeared for other interviews, I told her this was my first interview ever.

Overall, the round was relaxed and conversational, and all candidates who reached this stage were offered the position.

_______________________________________________________________________________________

Personal Insights:

I was rejected in most of my earlier open assessments, and even when I cleared some, I was eliminated during group discussion rounds. I had been studying on and off for placements since they began in the month of July and by the end of September, I was honestly burnt out, mainly because I wasn't seeing any results despite putting in consistent effort and not getting shortlisted for interviews. Still, I kept reminding myself to stay patient and keep improving, and finally received this offer in the second week of October,

after nearly three months. I also started my placement preparation quite late compared to many peers (which in hindsight was a bad idea), but this made me realize that placement success isn't just about hard work, there's also a fair bit of timing and luck involved. What matters is staying consistent, realistic, and open to learning. Even if things don't work out right away, every attempt adds experience and clarity, and eventually, your effort finds its result.

Lastly, I had a CGPA of 7.66, which made me eligible for almost all companies, except maybe one (Zeta which had a requirement of 8+). Based on my experience, it's recommended to maintain at least a 7.5 CGPA, as that tends to be the minimum eligibility criterion for most companies during campus placements.

_______________________________________________________________________________________

Areas of Improvement:

Looking back at the entire placement process, there are a few areas I believe I could have improved on:

1. Early and consistent preparation: I started my placement preparation quite late, which added unnecessary pressure toward the end

2. Confidence and composure: Showing structured thinking and confidence in your answers makes a big difference in how the interviewer perceives you, even if you don't get every answer right. It's important to remember that interviewers generally want you to succeed and are looking for how you approach problems, not just whether you know the exact answer.

Overall, this experience helped me identify where I stood technically and learned a lot about what to focus on moving forward.

journey.prep:
● Communication skills and confidence are key and be you, be honest.

● Always take a pause and understand if the interviewer is keeping pace with you.

● Try hard, think out loud, ask for hints if you're stuck.

● If you need a minute to think or frame an answer, ask the interviewer for the same.

● Stay confident, a partially correct answer with 100% confidence is better than a fully correct answer with 50% confidence.

● Always give examples while explaining stuff wherever possible, preferably something relatable.

● Keep questions ready for the interviewer, they always ask if you have any questions for them, never say no here.

● Be attentive during the Pre-Placement Talk (PPT) as you'll get enough content to ask relevant questions.

● Your introduction should be short and to the point, and mention things you are good at as the interviewer may lead the discussion based on them.

● Be well versed with your resume from top to bottom.

● Don't just focus on DSA completely, make projects (do them yourself and try to participate in hackathons as winning is not important, the learning is) and have internship experience too.

● Always have a smile on your face and be interactive with your interviewer, even while solving something share your thought process.

● Interviewers are not just assessing your technical skills, they are also assessing your mindset and your approach.

● Don't follow previous interview experiences blindly, as those are from people who got selected but those who didn't may have had completely different experiences, so be confident in your strong points.

My few previous experiences :

I was also selected for the JPMC CFG hackathon (a hiring hackathon), and since my hackathon experience went great, I was quite hopeful of converting it into an offer. Unfortunately, it didn't work out. I even skipped some companies because I was confident about CFG, but sometimes things don't go as planned.

Throughout the placement season, I cleared almost all the OAs for which I applied, but I was not able to convert them into a final selection. This placement phase really tested my patience to the extreme. Even after doing well in interviews, selections didn't happen. I gave interviews for JPMC Fintech, PhonePe, MSCI, IDFC, Nomura (GM role), BlackRock, EDS, and finally got selected at Oracle.

Every interview taught me something new. I don't consider these as failures, but rather as a learning process that helped me finally get selected.

● MSCI interview: I was asked to implement a max heap from scratch (which I managed to do), system design of WhatsApp/messaging system (with focus on group messaging), syntax of sharding in MongoDB (which I didn't know), and to write a Node.js server connection code. The lesson here: always expect the unexpected.

● IDFC interview: I was grilled deeply on Java, Spring Boot, and core implementations of data structures like Map and Set. I was also asked the detailed system design of a URL shortener (my mistake was not preparing system design properly even after being asked about it in MSCI). On top of this, I had to code on their compiler. I explained my code perfectly, but the compiler wasn't running it. The interviewer thought it was my mistake, and that shattered my confidence, leading me to make further errors. Later, I found out their compiler had an issue, and my code was correct all along. The learning: be confident in what you know, and don't let external factors shake your confidence.

● EDS interviews: Both rounds went pretty well. But in the last round, it came down to me and one other candidate. The other candidate was selected due to CGPA and their primary language being Python. Sometimes, despite a good performance, external factors can decide the outcome.

Through all these interviews, I lost my patience many times and even thought of giving up. Giving 100% each time and still not getting through was extremely stressful. But looking back, every rejection just made me stronger. I now believe that some things fall apart to make way for better ones. This was just the start of my career journey, and it has made me tougher for the future.

Placements are honestly based on luck to some extent, but if you don't give your 100%, even failures won't teach you anything. So always keep a smile, keep working hard, and stay strong.

1 OA (Online) 1 Tech Interview (Offline)

1 Tech + HR (Offline)

1 HR(Offline)

1] OA [ No of candidates who appeared for this round : around 120 , shortlisting criteria : 7 CGPA and 70% in 10th and 12th]

So, our OA was actually supposed to be offline in college, but thanks to the rain it got shifted online at the last moment. The test was for 95 minutes.

It started off with 32 MCQs covering stuff like LLMs, Cloud, basic aptitude, api knowledge and some core tech subjects. There were also a few graph-related ones like articulation points and DFS traversal.

After that, there were 2 coding questions (everyone had different sets). Mine were:

1. We were given a list of requests, each having a user ID and a timestamp. The task was to decide whether each request should be allowed or not. A request could only be allowed if the user had made fewer than k requests in the last 1-minute window. Example: n = 3, user = [1, 1, 1], timestamp = [6, 10, 65], k = 2 Output → [1, 1, 0]

2. Two interns had to complete n tasks. Out of these, the first intern had to do exactly k tasks and the second intern would do the rest. Each intern had rewards for every task, and we had to maximize the total reward. Example: n = 5, reward_1 = [5, 4, 3, 2, 1], reward_2 = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], k = 3 Output → 21

Tip from me: Since you could navigate between questions, it's better to attempt the coding ones first (they weren't too hard) and then move on to MCQs. Completing both coding questions was super important to get shortlisted for interviews.

Only 25 students were shortlisted for interviews after OA.

They had the PPT (pre-placement talk) only for the shortlisted candidates. It lasted for about 45 minutes and started at 10:15 AM. The company gave a brief introduction about what they do. My advice would be to pay close attention during the PPT, because it really helps when you want to ask relevant questions later.

After that, the interview rounds started at 11 AM.

It turned out to be a pretty tiring day for me because there was no fixed order for interviews. First, they collected our resumes, and then the interviewers just picked any resume randomly. Whoever's resume they picked was called in. I was eagerly waiting for my turn, but no luck. By that time, many students were already done with their 2nd round, and a few had even completed their 3rd and final interviews--while I hadn't even started my 1st round yet.

Still, I stayed calm, because I had faced a similar situation during my BlackRock interview. Back then, I was also one of the last ones to be interviewed, and even though I did well, I wasn't shortlisted for the next round. This time, I just kept my patience. Finally, I was the very last candidate called in for the 1st round, and my interview began around 3:45 PM.

2] 1st Technical Interview [25 students appeared for this round] There were 4 panels for Round 1. For me it was a cakewalk -- mine lasted only about 10-15 minutes (I think being the last one actually helped). I heard other people's interviews went on for 30 minutes to an hour.

They started by asking me for a short intro and then jumped straight into four basic DSA questions: find the second-maximum element in an array, remove duplicates, check if a string is a palindrome, and write any recursive function (I wrote factorial and explained how recursion works). These were easy, but the interviewer was clearly testing how fast and clearly you think -- they asked me to write pseudocode for each one. I finished the pseudocode in about 5-6 minutes.

After that they asked what my primary coding language was and whether I'd done development in Java. I was honest and said I hadn't. Then we moved on to REST APIs -- I had to write a basic fetch request, explain query parameters and how they work, and discuss alternatives to query params. Finally they asked a basic SQL join syntax and that wrapped up my first interview.

I freaked out a little after because it was so short and I was last -- many people were already on their 2nd or even 3rd rounds while I hadn't finished Round 1. But within 5 minutes they called me for Round 2, so I relaxed a bit.

Tip: Some students were grilled pretty hard on Java -- things like file handling, inline functions, REST APIs, and Postman. A Postman question was "How would you test two APIs where the output of one is the input of the other?" -- so make sure you can explain chaining API calls clearly. Also, those who had knowledge of Spring / Spring Boot were questioned in much more detail, so be thorough if you mention it on your resume.Some candidates were asked about MongoDb and were asked to write basic fetch and how to save on db queries and connections queries.

3] 2nd Tech+ HR [15-16 candidates appeared for this round ]

This was the techno-HR round. Five minutes after I finished Round 1, I was called for Round 2 -- this one was taken by one of the directors of OFSS (the same person who did the PPT), so paying attention during the talk actually helped. This round was totally resume-driven -- no DSA, SQL, or puzzles.

The interviewer went through my resume and then we started with a short intro. He was super friendly and asked about my JEE journey, why I chose SPIT instead of an IIT/NIT, and why I went into engineering -- those are open-ended, so be honest. He asked about my primary coding language and what made me pick it, then asked me to explain a recent project and drilled a few follow-ups. He also asked about my positions of responsibility -- what my role was and how I balanced it with academics.

Since I'd been the marketing head, he gave me a Shark-Tank style task: imagine he was Jack Ma with 200 million to invest -- pitch one of your crowdfunding projects and convince him to invest. At first I started explaining the project, then realized I needed to market it -- so I switched to a pitch mode and that worked out well; the interviewer seemed happy.

He then asked some Java basics: what the import statement does, the difference between interfaces and abstraction (I gave examples), packages in Java, and to explain the static and final keywords. At the end he asked if I had any questions. From the PPT I remembered they mentioned AI models, so I asked whether Oracle (or the company) was building in-house AI models and how those models are affecting the company -- I also asked his view on whether AI is a boon or a curse for people in tech. We wrapped up, shook hands, and I left. It lasted for around 35- 40 mins.

In my opinion this round was mainly to assess mindset, attitude toward tech, and confidence. My tip: be yourself, be confident, and know your resume inside out.

Only 9 students were shortlisted further.

4] HR [ 9 candidates appeared for this round ]

As soon as my 2nd round ended, I was called in for the 3rd and final round.

This one was more of a formality -- the HR even mentioned it wasn't really an "interview," just a basic conversation. She asked me how my day had been so far, then a few simple things like my nationality and whether I was open to relocation. After that, she gave me a small situation-based question: "Imagine you're a team lead and a conflict breaks out between two high-temper teammates -- how would you handle it?" I answered confidently about keeping calm, listening to both sides, and resolving it fairly. She seemed satisfied with my response and told me to wait for the results once everyone else was done.

After some time, when all the interviews wrapped up, they finally announced the results. Out of everyone, 9 students were offered the job -- and I was one of them.

Useful Resources I Followed :

● DSA: Regular practice on LeetCode and giving contests on Codeforces and LeetCode. This really helps with clearing the OA. I also referred to Strivers A2Z DSA Course/Sheet for structured prep.

● Aptitude: It's just as important as DSA, so don't ignore it. I prepared closer to the placement season using Indiabix and CodeHelp Mock Test.

● SQL (Super Important): Practice in-depth because it's asked both in OA and interviews. I used Leetcode SQL problems. Make sure you cover:

○ Last Minute Revision (articles, cheat sheets, Interview Questions)

○ DBMS + SQL In depth

○ Advanced SQL topics like window functions, triggers, procedures

● OOPS (VVIMP): Don't leave this for the last minute. Learn in detail

● OS (Can keep for last-minute but practice properly): inDetail Important topics → Paging, Threading, Semaphores. Notes are handy here too.

● CCN (Computer Networks, can also keep for last-minute): CCN Revise important concepts, practice a bit in detail.

● System Design: A few companies do ask for it. Practice some examples to be safe -- YouTube System Design channels are helpful.

● Most important resource for me was GFG (GEEKSFORGEEKS ) -- for last-minute preparation it helped me a lot.

● If your primary language is Java, then practice advanced topics in detail such as synchronization, multithreading, exception handling, file handling, memory leaks, and implementation of various data structures in the Collection Framework.

customSections.title: Advice & Tips for Juniors
customSections.content:
● Communication skills and confidence are key and be you, be honest.

● Always take a pause and understand if the interviewer is keeping pace with you.

● Try hard, think out loud, ask for hints if you're stuck.

● If you need a minute to think or frame an answer, ask the interviewer for the same.

● Stay confident, a partially correct answer with 100% confidence is better than a fully correct answer with 50% confidence.

● Always give examples while explaining stuff wherever possible, preferably something relatable.

● Keep questions ready for the interviewer, they always ask if you have any questions for them, never say no here.

● Be attentive during the Pre-Placement Talk (PPT) as you'll get enough content to ask relevant questions.

● Your introduction should be short and to the point, and mention things you are good at as the interviewer may lead the discussion based on them.

● Be well versed with your resume from top to bottom.

● Don't just focus on DSA completely, make projects (do them yourself and try to participate in hackathons as winning is not important, the learning is) and have internship experience too.

● Always have a smile on your face and be interactive with your interviewer, even while solving something share your thought process.

● Interviewers are not just assessing your technical skills, they are also assessing your mindset and your approach.

● Don't follow previous interview experiences blindly, as those are from people who got selected but those who didn't may have had completely different experiences, so be confident in your strong points.

My few previous experiences :

I was also selected for the JPMC CFG hackathon (a hiring hackathon), and since my hackathon experience went great, I was quite hopeful of converting it into an offer. Unfortunately, it didn't work out. I even skipped some companies because I was confident about CFG, but sometimes things don't go as planned.

Throughout the placement season, I cleared almost all the OAs for which I applied, but I was not able to convert them into a final selection. This placement phase really tested my patience to the extreme. Even after doing well in interviews, selections didn't happen. I gave interviews for JPMC Fintech, PhonePe, MSCI, IDFC, Nomura (GM role), BlackRock, EDS, and finally got selected at Oracle.

Every interview taught me something new. I don't consider these as failures, but rather as a learning process that helped me finally get selected.

1) Online Assessment Round:

The online assessment was conducted on the HackerRank platform, consisting of 36 questions to be solved in 120 minutes. The test covered a mix of topics including Computer Networks, Operating Systems, SQL, Logical Reasoning, Probability, and Puzzles, along with two coding problems based on Tree and Dynamic Programming (DP).

There were also multiple SQL query-based questions that tested basic to intermediate understanding of joins, aggregate functions, and constraints. The non-technical sections focused on logical reasoning and quantitative aptitude, including probability-based word problems and short analytical puzzles.

The good part was that we got to attempt the test online from home since it was raining heavily that day, which definitely reduced some stress. Overall, the OA was moderately difficult. The key was to maintain speed while balancing accuracy across both the technical and reasoning sections.

IMPORTANT NOTE: We had given OA for the Associate Application Developer, and we weren't told that the selection for Associate Consultant would be taken according to this OA result. So if you are giving the test for Associate Application Developer then give it 100%.

2) Technical Round I : [27 students were selected for the technical interview]

The interview started after a PPT presentation from Oracle at around 12:00 PM.

We had 6 panelists and I was in the 1st 6 group. So I was taken to the room where my panelist was sitting. As soon as I entered the room, The interviewer stood and walked towards me to

greet me with a FIRM handshake (i have emphasized firm because it is important as it shows how confident you are). After all the greetings, he asked me about how my day was, and frankly speaking that day we had our MSE and we had just given our test and came for the interview. So I told the interview about it, and he talked about it for almost 5-10 mins about my day.

After this casual conversation, he asked me which programming language I was comfortable with. I told him I was comfortable with c++. So he firstly asked me the difference between for and while loop, is there any difference. I answered the way he wanted and then he asked me to print numbers between 5 and 10 using a while loop. I wrote the code directly and explained it to him. Then he gave me two strings, one with all capital letters and another string with the same letter but a mixture of small and capital letters, and asked me to return true if the string matched or return false if it didn't. There was no restriction in using the in-built function of the language. So I simply used the direct string comparison. Then he modified the question that he wanted two equal strings even though they have different ascii values to return true while comparing. Here I used the in-built function of string to capitalize the whole letter in both the string and then compared it. While coding he wanted me to include a try-catch function for any error handling, but I hadn't revised that topic so I honestly told him that I hadn't revised the error handling section but I explained how error handling would work if included. He was satisfied with my answer.

My interviewer then shifted to the DBMS topic and gave me 2 questions to solve.

1. Two table i.e. The Train and Destination table was given to me and he had asked me to find the cost of all the trains that stop and start from Mumbai. So this question was easy, we just had to join two tables and use the where clause to find the answer.

2. Same two tables and was asked the train with the highest travel time.

Later he asked me about all the projects I had done. He asked me whether the projects done were individual projects or not. All the projects I had mentioned were all group projects. As it was all a group project, he asked me what exactly my role was in each project and what was the purpose of our group choosing those topics for our project. And with these questions my interviewer concluded with the interview and asked me whether I had any question for him. I had asked him about his role in OFSS and asked him what role we would play in the company as a fresher.

So I was interviewed for almost 40 min and the interview ended on a good note.

NOTE: Don't throw things randomly on the resume and even while answering the question asked by the interviewer as it would lead to many follow up questions related to it and if you couldn't answer those questions it would affect your result. So be HONEST and give the interview with confidence, it's ok if you are unable to answer the question, you can tell the interviewer that you are unable to recall the concept, but would be able to tell it once revised. HONESTY and CONFIDENCE is the key for any successful interview.

2) Technical Round 2: [ around 20 students appeared for it]

After my round 1 interview, nearly 15 min later i was asked to be ready for round 2 interview. I was taken to the room for round 2 and the interviewer greeted me and immediately started with the interview.

The Interviewer asked me to explain one of my AIML projects in detail. He wanted me to explain the whole project in such a way that i am explaining it to a non tech background person. So I started with a brief description about my project and then dived deeper into the explanation about the models that I had used. I systematically explained to him how the system architecture looks like and works. He was satisfied with the explanation, then he moved on to my Web project. He asked me about the purpose of choosing a book reading website and what new features were added in comparison to the inspired website. So I explained to him about the project and the purpose of the project along with what new features we had added.

Then he started to ask me about the techstack that i had worked on and why those techstack were used. He later grinded me upon the programming language that I had written on the resume. He first asked me to write a code to open a file and read the file in python language. Before i started with writing the code i asked him a follow up question of what type of file does he want me to read, he gave me the benefit of doubt to use any file type. So I used a CSV file as the input file to be read, and I wrote the code in python. I used pandas to read the file and show the content of the file. After this he started with OOPS questions, he asked me to explain encapsulation, overloading and overriding.

My interviewer then shifted to DBMS and asked me a question where I had to use JOIN and GROUP BY to solve the question. So basically most of the round people are being asked questions related to JOIN and Clauses. So focus on these topics and practice it.

After this i was asked a guesstimate question where i want to find the fastest route and mode of transport from my house to my college. He gave me the benefit of doubt to choose any method or electronic device to find out the optimal route and transportation. I answered the question using google maps, so hi follow up question how would you choose the transportation. My answer for guesstimate could have been wrong or not, but I explained what I know and concluded with the interview.

NOTE: As you can see in this round it was mostly about my resume, so it would be best for you to know what you are writing on your resume, whether you actually know it or not, before interview LEARN EVERYTHING IN YOUR RESUME so that whatever you are asked from your resume you able to answer it properly.

This round also took around 45-50 min to conclude.

Round 3 : HR round : [ Around 12 students appeared for it]

The HR round was more of a formality. The HR asked a few basic questions such as my nationality, hobbies, and whether I was satisfied with the compensation offered. She also asked if I had any questions for her, to which I responded with two simple queries related to the company culture and growth opportunities.

After this round, there was a short waiting period of around 45 minutes while the panel discussed the results. Finally, the results were announced -- 12 students were selected for the role, including 6 from MCA and 6 from B.Tech.

7. HR Round Resume Screening Your resume is as very crucial a part of the entire selection process as any other. Building your resume is a time consuming process, so allot enough time for it. Try to tailor your resume to the role you are applying for. All resumes are screened by an ATS (Applicant Tracking System), so you can check your score on websites like "ResumeWorded". My resume had a score of 72. Key points regarding resumes - They should be 1 page resumes as that's what is expected from freshers. Make single column resumes in Latex format. Try to include all relevant coursework / competition / projects / internships in your resume. Having 1-2 good finance projects on your resume helps. Participate in case study competitions. Do some finance certifications and add them onto your resume. You can make minor changes to your resume that you are taking for your interviews. Results were announced 1 day prior OA Test around 9. Online Assesment (67 Students were shortlisted) The online test was conducted on campus. With a total of 45 marks, it consisted of 4 sections - Finance & Accounting (10): This section contains mostly accounting and corporate finance questions. I think it had 1 question about puttable bonds. Market Awareness (10): This section contained quite a few economy questions and market sentiment questions, I had something related to " what is the exemption on taxes for investing in government pension schemes", so focus on market situations and terms, be aware of

current affairs just to be safe Quantitative Aptitude (15): This section focused on permutations, probability, and algebra questions. So this one is out and out mathematics. Verbal Ability and Reading Comprehension (10): This is an English section, pretty simple if you try to stick with the basics. The time given was 45 mins, so there is a time crunch as the quant section is tough, the VARC section is easy but time consuming. So try to segregate the sections into time slots so you can attempt as much as possible. The results for this round were announced a day before the final day i.e. 1st July. So don't lose heart in the process and be prepared. Group Discussion (37 students were shortlisted) Group discussion Topic - "Central Banks' Diverging Paths Amid Geopolitical Stress - The Bank of England maintains rates at 4.25% due to global uncertainty, while Norway and Switzerland have opted for rate cuts. Explore how central banks should balance inflation control with growth risks, particularly in the context of conflicts or trade wars." The moderators also introduced subtopics during the discussion. As far as I remember, these included "Views on Forex reserves", "What are the impacts of having different views and policy of central banks" Ensure you contribute at least 3-4 meaningful qualitative points. Try to work as a team, acknowledge others points and add on to it. Make sure you speak for 45 sec - 60 sec per point so the moderator takes note of you. The discussion time was 20 mins and last 10 min were for summary We had 3 panels for GD Interview Round 1 (22 students were shortlisted) The round consisted of accounting questions, Corporate Finance, puzzles, mental maths, market awareness. The following are the questions that were asked to me. The change in depreciation and taxes and what are its effect on the financial statements. Latest IPO and M&A What is capital restructuring and why is it done. I had made a DCF valuation project, so I was asked questions about it. I was asked to calculate 57 × 63. Be sure to explain your approach. Other people were also asked the values of roots i.e 2,3,10 etc. I had done the forage investment banking simulation course, so a few questions on them. The round lasted for 30-40 mins. I was last in panel but was called early which took me by shock. If you are not able to answer anything don't panic makes sure you tell the thought process and approach for it. If you make a mistake or there is some misunderstanding in what you were supposed to answer DO NOT PANIC, --your interview isn't over. One or two mistakes are acceptable so keep your head down and focus on answering the rest of the questions properly. Once the GD is done you might receive the order of interview, but always be ready there can be changes in last minute and you can be called anytime

Interview Round 2 (12-15 students were shortlisted) This round was taken by the manager for CIB, the duration of this round was only 7-8 minutes. The round consisted of 30-35 rapid fire questions. We discussed the Flutter framework and Firebase. He asked if I had experience with NoSQL databases, to which I responded that Firebase Realtime Database is a NoSQL database. When asked about AWS and Kafka, I admitted I had read about them but didn't have in-depth knowledge.

Lastly, he presented a scenario: if a transaction occurred in Mumbai at 11:20, followed by another in Pune 20 minutes later, how would I detect fraud? I acknowledged that Iwasn't sure of the exact technology to use, but my approach would involve calculating the time difference and distance between the two locations to determine ifthe transaction was possible.

For this round, it'simportant to answer honestly. You're not expected to know everything, but relate what you do know to the topic.

3. HR Interview Round [15 students appeared, 13 were selected ]

This round was mainly HR-focused, but the interviewer also asked some basic technical questions. Itlasted about 20-25 minutes.

He began by asking which programming languages I've worked with. I mentioned that my primary language is C++, but I also have knowledge of Java, Python, and Dart. Then he asked me to explain Object-Oriented Programming, what polymorphism is,where I've implemented it, and the difference between the two types of polymorphism.

After that, the HR questions started. He asked what challenges Ifaced during my internship. I explained that I encountered issues deploying the app on the Play Store due to Google policy conflicts, and Idescribed how I resolved those issues.

Next, he asked why I chose Barclays and followed up with a few more questions based on my response. He then presented a hypothetical situation: What would I do if a superior said something rude to me in a meeting? He also asked how I would handle itif a junior told me I had spoken rudely to them, and how I would manage two team members arguing during a meeting if I were the team leader. For these questions, ensure your answers align with the company's values.

He also asked me to describe a situation where I experienced conflict with teammates and to share an experience where I led a team. I described my experience as the Mudra domain head here.

For HR questions, it'simportant to understand the company's values and tailor your answers accordingly.

This combination of theoretical and practical questions tested both my conceptual understanding and problem-solving skills in real-time.

Additionally, the technical test featured a high-weightage DSA question where points were awarded based on the number of test cases passed. The problem was quite challenging, with 8 hidden test cases and 2 visible ones. The task required constructing the lexicographically smallest string of length m+n−1, given two input strings of length m and n. The second string contained only 'T' and 'F', and wherever there was a 'T', I had to copy the entire first string from the start. For positions marked by 'F', the substring starting from that character in the result needed to be unequal to the first string. The solution had to return -1 if it was impossible to construct such a string. This problem tested my understanding of string manipulation and logic-based problem-solving.

2. Technical Interview Round (27 students appeared, 15 selected)

I was first asked to introduce myself, after which the focus shifted to DBMS JOINS. I had to draw Venn diagrams representing the different types of joins and write queries for each. The interviewer provided two tables, "employee" and "department," and asked me to explain the different joins--inner, left, right, and full--and how they differ.

We also discussed my projects, and I was asked to write basic for and while loops. The interviewer then posed an interesting question about the while loop: whether incrementing the loop variable before or after the statements inside the loop would make a difference.

They also inquired about my interest in the IT sector and whether I genuinely wanted to pursue a career in this field. This was a brief conversation before the technical questions started.

Next, I was asked to explain one of the projects I had listed on my resume. I selected a project and went into detail about it. The interviewer asked why I chose specific technologies for the project (e.g., "Why did you use Next.js instead of React?"). They also wanted to understand the relevance of the project: whether it had any real-life application and if it was solving a real-world problem.

After that, we moved on to questions related to computer science fundamentals. I was given real-life scenarios and asked how I would solve certain problems. One question I remember was about withdrawing money from an ATM. The question was: If money is debited from your account but not dispensed by the ATM, what could be the issue and how would you resolve it?

Another technical question involved synchronizing two APIs: If the result of the first API is used as input for the second, how would you avoid any errors or overlaps during this process?. Then, the interviewer asked few questions on OOPS and DBMS.

To clear this round, it's important to be thoroughly prepared with your resume and solid in your understanding of computer science fundamentals.

The interview started with the typical question: "Introduce yourself." After that, I was asked a series of behavioral and personal questions, including:

• When did you take a position of responsibility? What challenges did you face, and how did you overcome them?

• How many members are there in your family? Do you often have conflicts with your siblings?

• Can you share an experience where you worked in a team, and there were differences in opinions? How did you resolve the conflict or handle clashes between your views and those of your team members?

The interviewer also wanted to assess my general awareness and asked for my opinion on the current situation in Gaza and the Israel conflict. This round lasted around 20-25 minutes.

I wasn't fully prepared for this type of questioning, but I stayed honest and answered each question based on the STAR (Situation, Task, Action, Result) approach. It's crucial to stay calm and composed. Even if you don't have an immediate answer, take a moment to think it through and respond confidently.

That said, it's always a good idea to practice these types of questions beforehand with friends or family through mock interviews. This helps you prepare and handle such rounds more smoothly.

This was an online test conducted at college consisting of 14 questions of totalmarks 100. Among these, one was a coding question with 10 test cases for 50 marks that carried maximum weightage, one was an SQL query question for 10 marks and the rest 12 focused on CS fundamentals with a significant emphasis on DBMS and OOPS. To prepare for this round, I thoroughly revised the concepts of OOPS, DBMS, CN, OS and DSA. I practiced problems on Codeforces and also participated in many contests.

2. Technical Interview (Out of 27 students who appeared, 15 were selected for next round)

The interview lasted for about 30-40 minutes. Itstarted with the interviewer asking me to introduce myself. After hearing my introduction, he focused on my interest inmachine learning and asked me to explain what machine learning is.Next, he asked how machine learning actually works and what "data" is.After that he gave me a scenario: "What if some wrong or extreme values are included in the dataset? How would you make sure the machine stillgives accurate results?".

After discussing machine learning, the interviewer moved on to DBMS. He gave me a table and asked me to normalize itstep by step, explaining how to make the table more efficient by reducing redundancy. He also asked me about DML and DDL commands.Then he asked me one numerical question on alltypes of join.

Next, we shifted to data structures and problem-solving. He asked me a few questions about linked lists, including how to write code to detect if there's a cycle in a linked listand how to swap two nodes. He also asked how to swap two numbers without using extra variables. There was a pattern-printing question as well, where Ihad to write code to print a specific design using loops.Toward the end, the interviewer asked about my experience with competitive programming and rating as mentioned on my resume. At the end he asked about Git and GitHub.

For this round, it isimportant to be thoroughly prepared with your resume and solid in your understanding of computer science fundamentals and DSA.

3. HR Interview (Out of 15 students who appeared, 13 were selected for next round)

The interview started with the typical question: "Introduce yourself." After that, I was asked a series of behavioral and personal questions, including:

● Tell me about your experience during your last internship, and what challenges did you face? I shared insights into my previous role, detailing the projects I worked on and the challenges I encountered.

● What were your learnings from this? Ireflected on the skills Igained and how I tackled the difficulties during my internship.

● Why do you want to join Barclays as an intern? Iexpressed my enthusiasm for the opportunity at Barclays, citing the company's reputation for innovation and itsalignment with my career goals.

● Can you share an experience where you worked in a team, and there were differences in opinions? How did you resolve the conflict or handle clashes between your views and those of your team members? Idescribed this from my experience of amini project.

After these questions, the interviewer shifted focus to more specific topics related to the role. He noted my interest in machine learning but mentioned that the internship might involve work in different domains. They asked if I would be willing to work in another area.He also asked whether I had completed any projects using core languages like C or C++.

● Prepare SQL queries and database management concepts, as SQL questions often focus on real-world applications.

On the day of the test,ensure you manage time efficiently between the MCQs and the coding questions. Double-check your SQL query for syntax and logic errors.

Resume Pointers:

● Highlight projects involving coding, data structures, and databases.

● Include any relevant certifications in programming or SQL that demonstrate your skills.

2. Technical Interview (35 candidates)

After the online assessment, 35 candidates were shortlisted for the technical interview, which was conducted offline the next day. This round involved in-depth questions about:

● Your technical knowledge of programming languages, data structures, and algorithms.

● Problem-solving skills,where you might be asked to solve problems on a whiteboard or explain your thought process.

● Questions about projects listed on your resume, with particular emphasis on your role,challenges faced, and how you overcame them.

The interview lasted for around 30-40 minutes per candidate, and 15 people were shortlisted for the next round.

Preparation Tips:

● Review your resume thoroughly, especially the projects and technologies you mentioned.

● Practice explaining complex technical concepts in simple terms. Mock interviews can help with this.

● Prepare for questions on problem-solving using DSA (Data Structures and Algorithms) by solving problems from LeetCode and InterviewBit.

On the day of the interview, stay calm, maintain clarity in your answers, and don't hesitate to ask for clarification ifneeded. Always explain your thought process when solving problems.

3. HR Interview (15 candidates)

The final round was an HR interview, conducted offline in the evening of the same day. In this round, the HR panel focused on:

● Behavioral questions to assess your personality, teamwork skills,and how you handle pressure.

● Questions about your career goals, strengths, weaknesses, and why you're interested in the company.

● Situational questions, where you may be asked how you would handle a particular scenario in the workplace.

This round was relatively short, around 15-20 minutes per candidate. After this round, 13 candidates were finally selected for the role.

Preparation Tips:

● Practice answering common HR questions like "Tell me about yourself", "Where do you see yourself in 5 years?", and "Why should we hire you?".

● Be honest about your strengths and weaknesses, and give examples that show how you've worked on improving your weaknesses.

● Ensure you are well-versed with the company's background, culture, and the role you're applying for.

On the day of the HR interview, be confident, maintain good body language, and ensure your answers reflect apositive attitude and willingness to learn.
