journey.howSecured:
The process was as follows:

Online Assessment Based on Python, C++, Easy/Medium DSA

Technical Round C++/Python in depth, Medium DSA, Probability Stats

HR Round Standard HR questions

This is going to be a long one.

1. [Round 1 - Online Assessment] [ No of candidates who appeared for this round: 60-70 ]

The OA consisted of 5 sections and was conducted on Imocha safe assessment browser:

● C++ MCQs

● Python MCQs (mainly NumPy and statistics-based)

● Aptitude MCQs (standard, mostly easy)

● Python coding

● C++ coding

The coding questions were DSA/implementation based. Some candidates received harder problems, but mine were very straightforward.

Python coding question: You are given transaction data with categories and amounts. The task was to compute the total amount spent per category and print it as a float. Essentially, maintain a dictionary with category -> total amount.

C++ coding question: Given an integer k and an array, compute the running average over the last k elements. Example:

arr = [100, 200, 300, 400], k = 3 i = 0: 100 / 1 = 100 i = 1: (100+200) / 2 = 150 i = 2: (100+200+300) / 3 = 200 i = 3: (200+300+400) / 3 = 300

I don't remember the mcq questions well, but knowing intermediate c++ and python helped me. Also python mcqs were mostly around statistics and numpy functions like cumulative sum, median, etc.

The OA was in a very unexpected format and since the languages to use were so limited, many people gave up halfway in the test. (Also quite a few for being flagged as cheating)

My OA round, unlike everyone, was very eventful. Initially, I did not have access to a Windows laptop, which was required for the test, so I had given up hopes of even trying for the OA, but fortunately, my friend Asim helped me at the last moment. The OA program crashed midway (saying that I'm sus) and I had to wait till I got a fresh new link. The HR and support team were really very nice that they helped me and also arranged the new test (I was able to prove my innocence). I gave the OA after everyone finished and they stayed with me for invigilation as well. I hurriedly finished the OA and in the hurry, I wasn't able to think logically and thus, I couldn't solve the c++ dsa question. Again I had no expectations that I would even make it into the interviews.

2. [Round 2 - Technical] [ No of candidates who appeared for this round: 9 ]

My panel was conducting 1-1.2 hrs of interviews, mostly focused around c++ (in depth), medium/hard dsa, and probability statistics. My interview was by far the longest i.e. 2 hrs. It started with my introduction, surprisingly they weren't as interested in my projects and internship and only inquired basic information on it while also asking whether they are in c++ or not.

They then asked me if I am confident in c++ or python, choosing c++ he asked me what's the difference between struct and a class. He also asked me what's the difference between c and c++, I answered having objects, to which he responded that we can make objects in c too (he's right about it technically speaking). Then they asked me what I know about oops in c++. I answered with 4 pillars of oops. Then he asked me which one I know the best, I answered polymorphism and explained runtime and compile time polymorphism, with code examples and also how compiler evaluates them (the compile stage and how runtime is evaluated with vptrs and vtable, I didn't go much deep in this to the function pointers but he was satisfied with my explanation). After that he asked me about the second best oops pillar that I know of, I answered with encapsulation and explained intuitively with real life examples and had to write code for the same.

Then he asked me about my favourite topic in c++, to which I answered templates and then I explained how the compiler evaluates templates (in the compile time itself). Then we discussed about how and when std::vector resizes, how can we check when the vector resizes. I answered that we can check resizing by seeing the operation time consumed. He said that it may be possible that the CPU is too fast and we can't even measure the difference. Then he answered it for me, saying that the address of the vector changes. Hearing this, it clicked to me so I explained it further that

resizing is done by creating a new vector of double the "capacity" and then the elements are copied into the new vector. He then also asked me about size vs capacity in this context and asked whether I can implement it. After which he asked me the difference between std::array and std::vector.

The conversation then moved on to memory management, starting with the difference between "malloc" and "new" keywords in c++ (new just calls the destructor of the class automatically). Then I was told to write some code about runtime polymorphism using the malloc keyword, it was basically creating class pointers and showing runtime polymorphism with it. (I was used to using new instead but the interviewer kindly gave me a hint that it needs typecasting when used with malloc). Then I also explained about upcasting and downcasting using Class pointers.

After which he asked me why even bother using heap memory? I answered that we can use it for storing large objects, to which he replied that if I have lots of memory it won't be a problem. Then I said that we can use it for dynamically allocating memory at runtime, when we don't know the size of the object at compile time. To which he confirmed that I am correct and added that heap memory is much faster (I think he meant it is faster for larger objects). I also explained about the need for destructors citing examples of sockets and files.

He asked me if I knew anything else in c++, so I answered with smart pointers, after which he asked me about why they are used. Then he asked me whether I know about mutexes and locks, after hearing a yes, he asked me what is a spin lock? I couldn't answer it. Next, he also had a question which I found tricky because I didn't understand the question well enough. He asked me whether some memory allocated in the constructor for a non member of the class, then when do we release it.. I was assuming he is talking about a stack memory variable, but he meant heap one. The answer was to deallocate it in the constructor itself.

Then he moved on to asking if I know about any other core subjects. Judging from the first part of the interview, I felt that saying any topic which I don't know absolutely 100% would be a disaster. So I answered with OS CPU scheduling and deadlocks. After explaining that, he asked me whether I knew about TCP/UDP (which was written in the JD requirements btw) and which core subject it belonged to. He asked me difference in TCP, UDP and an example where to use them.

Then they came to dsa questions which I honestly didn't do well, first they started with standard min stack question, given a stack, create a getMin with O(1) complexity. I initially forgot the two stack approach code so I gave them a single stack of pair<int, int> where pair.first is the element and pair.second is the minimum till now. He acknowledged the solution was correct but he specified that I cant change the data type of the stack. then I told him about the two stacks approach, to which he replied that it is taking too much space complexity, finally after 15 mins of me struggling he told me the answer that we can instead store pseudo elements in the stack (I saw this approach at neetcode.io/solutions/min-stack but I forgot it during the interview).

Then he gave me a detect cycle in linkedlist, which as well I forgot the iteration condition, and then figured out after some time, communicating entire thoughts continuously is a must. Then he asked me to also find the node starting the cycle while pointing out possible segmentation fault in my code in three places. The last dsa question I was asked was find the missing element. After listening to this I felt very relaxed because it's an easy question. I answered with xor of array method, to which he nodded. Then he asked me about another approach, he said let's say if it's sorted, what

now? I was a bit stumbled so I answered binary search without thinking. He clarified I was wrong. He then said me that it needs to be faster. I assumed he meant faster than O(n), and I went ahead scratching my head for another 5 minutes. I answered that all I can think of is Sum of natural numbers formula. He said it's in the right direction. But I kept on thinking that he wanted O(logn) or O(1) solution. He clarified this miscommunication and then I wrote the code for it using std::accumulate method, to which he asked what's the complexity of that method.

Later the second panelist started by asking if I had done probability and statistics during my course. He started with linear regression, asked me about it, and then gave me some data to perform it and evaluate it.. I said I dont recall the formula. He then asked me about uniform distribution, to which I answered slightly correctly. I explained my thinking with examples. I also explained about PMF and PDFs (in general what they are). After which he looked over my projects, one with ML catched his attention which was "DsaBuddy", he asked for explanation on what I did in it. It was a Random Forst model predicting next dsa problem to give to a person to learn, I told him about features used. He asked me about Random forst and decision trees, I explained them in detail. He asked me how can I get which feature is most important, which I forgot at the time. He also asked me to give an example decision tree based on my project and then he asked me why use random forest over decision tree. Then he also asked me about some Classifier in tensorflow which I couldnt answer. Later, he asked me about Lasso and Ridge and what's difference between them.

He then asked me about a logical puzzle, given a revolver gun which has 6 slots and two bullets placed consecutively. Which is higher probability that next shot will fire the bullet? There were two cases here that in the first fire, the bullet was not in the slot, and second case that bullet was present and it had a malfunction. I plotted down the cases and in each case calculated probability of shuffling and not shuffling. He later informed me of a mistake that after the first misfire, the revolver moves one section ahead automatically which I didnt account.

Then he asked me about gaussian distribution, to which I could explain what it is and the standard deviation and mean in it. he asked me about expectation of x general formula which I couldn't recall. Then he asked me about the gaussian distribution's PDF which I could remember only some parts, and writing just some parts of it he was satisfied with it.

3. [Round 3 - HR] [ No of candidates who appeared for this round: 9 ]

Fortunately, every candidate was given the chance to appear for the HR round as soon as their Technical round was done. This meant all 9 candidates appeared for both the interview rounds without any shortlisting.

The HR interview was short, also luckily I met the same HR who stayed with me in the OA. I started with my introduction, then I was asked about my parents' professions and whether I have siblings. I was also asked about 3 positives and 3 negatives about myself (classic strengths and weaknesses. I made a slight mistake that after recognizing this question I kept on saying "strength" and "weakness" instead of positive/negative as they said). Then they asked me why I'm pursuing this degree, whether I have plans for higher studies, how I would rate myself in c++ and python and finally if I have any questions for them. I answered all the questions citing story-type examples from my work experience and school and college life.

After this round, two students, including myself, were selected, while two others were asked to appear for a confirmation round. Since no one was selected in the confirmation round, the company decided to conduct another hiring process, similar to the earlier one, for students who had not attempted the Online Assessment. In this process, one student was selected.

[ In total 3 students were offered the job ]

Lessons learned:

Maintain your composure at all times. I can't remember how many opportunities I lost due to this. My ability to perform in stressful situations was almost non-existent because for practicing dsa I was always in a learning attitude. In an interview this was never the case since it can determine your future. I would recommend doing codeforces and leetcode contests as much as you can. For this particular interview, I never really had any hopes because I thought my dsa skills are not worthy of a quant position. So I was again in the same learning attitude.

Be 110% confident in yourself, chances are that then they will perceive you at 70%. (But please justify it too) I never made my introduction good to catch attention, I was only speaking about what I did. No one is interested in what you did. You need to communicate what you can do that can benefit them. I learned this from my friend Asim. So in this interview, I played entirely on my strengths, i.e. understanding the language at a very deep implementation level. I had web development projects and experience, but in my intro I told them that I also made a small mini project in rust by parsing my linux configuration file. I use Arch Linux and I use vim btw. (I actually said this in the interview too)

Don't let any incorrect answer derail your confidence. I initially had a very good interview in the first half and mid was very bad, but I didn't mind it much so I caught up in the last parts.

Be humble. Placements are a humbling experience. The earlier you accept it, the easier it gets for you.

Communicate your thoughts well, and remember it is a two way street. My entire DSA answers were very bad, but since my interviewer was very nice, he gave me feedback on whether I am going in the right direction or not. In most of the common cases, you will have to judge this by yourself by observing the interviewer very attentively. I think I never realised this since I was always focused on the right answer and speaking it as fast as I can.

Have a good resume such that it looks filled completely, leaving any empty whitespaces signals that you haven't done anything and memorize your resume on your fingertips so that any keyword or any related keyword is known to you and you can talk about it for a good 2 minutes at minimum. For example, I mentioned "BERT" model in my projects section, then the interviewer asked me about Transformer architecture along with BERT. Also single keyword also has variations to ask on, like on WebSockets I was asked about the http upgrade packet to ws:// protocol and another time I was asked about how sockets communicate (classic socket bind/accept diagram). If you are short on time, I recommend you to look out on at least 25 common interview questions on each tech keyword you mention on your resume.

Practice speaking a lot. I was a dead silent introvert (my literal speaking capacity is 2-3 hrs after which I have a sore throat). I followed Vinh Gang youtube and Matt Huang youtube to learn how to communicate better. It does not matter how good you are if the person in front of you doesn't understand what you say.

Fomo is only as long as you let your emotions control you. In my friend group I was one of the last people to get placed, and most of the higher paying companies already came and went. It is easy to say but hard when it's on you. I did feel panicked but I was confident due to having a solid internship experience.

Saying that Placement is luck based is an understatement. It is Swiss cheese luck, there are lots of factors, many of which you can't even think of, which are needed to have good luck in order to succeed. I hope my case is evident for this point. But you do need to do the needful so that when the opportunity strikes you are ready to go in.

Research the company very well before giving any interview. I have been asked if I know the company's business even in technical rounds. I used perplexity deep research for this and it helped me understand their businesses as well as the HR stuff. Highly recommended. Also have a look at the Companies Expert youtube for prepping on all those HR questions. HR questions sound stupid at first, but they are very psychological in nature. Understanding what questions mean to ask what is very very important.

The last lesson I would say is to keep persevering. I was not able to accept the rejections at first, but then I heard my Uncle's story:

He graduated from a Tier-3 college and remained unemployed for 1.5 years in poverty. Eventually, he approached placement agencies that provide training and subsequent job opportunities in exchange for 50% of the candidate's salary after securing employment and also an upfront non refundable fee in lacks. While most candidates did not receive opportunities through this route, he succeeded and even outperformed a candidate from NIT Trichy in the interview. Today, he is working at Intel in Silicon Valley.

He also struggled for admission into college, it was raining heavily in Mumbai the day he went for admissions, and almost the entire college was empty because of the immense rains, he got the admission because he reached there when only 3 students came that day.

There are many such stories that we don't know the struggle behind. I am lucky that my employment was not critical for my family's survival. If that's not you, then I hope God bless you.

Resources I used (ordered in importance I gave them, YMMV):

DSA:

● I initially did some CP on codeforces and Atcoder, solving around 30 Leetcode problems, so before placements I did 90% of Neetcode 150.

● Overall I would say my strategy was bad, I was ok at Graphs, Dp but I wasnt as good at problem solving so I couldn't clear elite company OAs. Not knowing standard leetcode problems also put me at risk of bad interviews.

● I would suggest doing CP for at least 6 months, regardless of your interest in it and memorizing NC 150, in the sense that you can recognize the type of problem from NC 150 list. This would give the best of both worlds but I was a bit late in doing so.

● I wanted to do the striver sheet earlier but since it had 179 problems I couldn't have spared time for it.

● So for learning, I watch Striver A-Z course YouTube playlists on each topic like dp, graph, stacks and queues, etc. And for practicing I used Neetcode. (highly recommended)

● I was particularly bad at managing stress during OA and interviews, many times I went blank only to come out and solve the entire solution. Solving CF or LC contests can help with this.

● I had started CF with CP 31 sheet: https://www.tle-eliminators.com/cp-sheet

● I also solved a searching and sorting, dp, sliding window from CSES problemset to learn some patterns/ways to do things: https://cses.fi/problemset/

Aptitude:

● Since I was a DSE, I lacked good math skills, so I used this youtube playlist to gain basic understanding: Aptitude Preparation for Campus Placement - YouTube

● Then I went on this playlist but only for very important topics like speed-dist, trains, mixtures, etc: Quantitative Aptitude Tutorials - YouTube

● Then after that I felt I lacked speed so I kept on watching random trick videos on "imran sir maths" yt channel. By far this helped me most. I would suggest his videos as a must watch for "Time & work" and "Coding Decoding" topics. I was able to solve those questions in 30-45 seconds after some practice.

● The standard indiabix is also good, I personally never did it for all topics because many questions were too repetitive, and it takes a bit longer.

SQL:

● Since I had good fundamentals understanding, this wasn't even an issue. I was able to solve many Hard SQL problems just by intuition, but sadly those didnt accept any partial answer like Dsa questions.

● If you have no idea on sql syntax, start with this video and go in depth on joins, etc. I can vouch for this since I learned mysql from here about 4 years ago in my diploma: SQL Tutorial - Full Database Course for Beginners

● After knowing this, if you have time, please do solve Leetcode Sql 50 sheet. And try to go from naive to optimal query by learning as many new functions as you can.

● Once done with this, go onto understanding case statements and window functions in sql. I will suggest only 5 most common window functions are more than enough. I learned these from chatgpt. Learning case statements is best ROI on your time vs frequency of being asked.

● Learn about unions, I personally never used them but it is a good to know for your tech interview.

● After this, you can learn about Date and String functions. Understand how to use them and also memorize all the formats like %y, %B, etc. Learn about 20 most commonly used functions in both categories.

● SQL OA questions 90% of the time revolved around manipulating the type, extraction in string and dates like using instr(), left(), trim(), date_format(), etc. Know well about this.

● Finally boss of all topics, recursive CTE. I never learned this topic, but I forgot the count of how many OAs I couldn't solve just because I didn't know this.

HR questions:

● I only ever gave one HR interview, so I am not the best person for advice on this. I read just this one article with 50 hr questions: https://www.interviewbit.com/hr-interview-questions/

● I also had memorized 5 incidents, like 5 positive ones and 5 negative ones. Negative ones need to show your learning and how you overcame it, not that u still have it.

● I used one of these incidents in my "strengths" answer, where I said I have high versatality, citing example of my work at navy. I won't tell that to you here :)

● Also have at least 60-70% understanding on what company does and what they are. I used perplexity pro a lot to research about companies in one go.

Tech mcq stuff:

● I never really had to prepare for it because I was a core dev profile. I would say know about these topics well:

● Git: it was asked in workindia oa in detail, about commands.

● Java/Oops: many OAs asked java code for oops and their output.

● Python: 2-3 OAs also asked about python, won't say super necessary, but knowing more has always been helpful for me.

● System design: I heard many places asking about nosql, horizontal scaling and all, I will say Gaurav Sen's youtube playlist on this is more than enough.

● General languages: I recommend roadmap.sh for understanding depth on tech topics, it is an overkill though, so for short and sweet u can see: https://learnxinyminutes.com/

● Also keep a deep understanding on every tech keyword you mention on your resume. I was asked about WebSockets, the flow of info, the starting http upgrade msg etc.

OOPS:

● I had a solid understanding on oops because of my diploma. I will say these topics are important:

● 4 Pillars of OOPS all with a real world example.

● Java inner classes, static inners and stuff. (vvimp)

● Constructors logic, when which one gets called on which object.

● Know about the final keyword on all classes, methods and variables.

● Know all ways to use super and this keyword.

● Know access modifiers.

● Know about Object class methods like hashCode(), toString(), etc.

● Know about deep and shallow copying (in all languages preferably, Python, Java and C++)

● instanceof operator

● Why and how string is immutable in java

● Composition vs Inheritance (vimp for interviews)

● I won't say this list is exhaustive, so please refer JavaTpoint for OOPs in Java. best resource for it, but takes time.

Schema Design:

● I won't say this is important but may get asked sometimes. This is just writing down relations and/or making ER diagrams.

● Important to know about:

● ER diagrams, EER constructs.

● Plot out entities and just keep on joining them with relations.

● Be alert when making relationships and entity structure, you may get told to write a query for the same.

Finally, if you wish to connect or ask any questions, feel free to reach out to me on my Linkedin.

Wish you the best of luck.

journey.prep:
Why I Got Selected & What Helped Me

One of the key things that helped me was consistent LeetCode practice over a long period. I didn't just aim to solve problems--I made sure I understood why certain solutions worked and why others failed. For particularly tough problems, I sometimes spent 2-3 hours just breaking them down, revisiting them until I gained full clarity.

After exams, I specifically revised graph algorithms, solving the entire graph section on CSES Problem Set and also picked some hard problems on trees and graphs to stretch my thinking. That gave me a strong base for several questions that came up during the tech interviews.

Another factor that I believe played a big role was my calm and composed attitude during the Tech Round 2 and the Hiring Manager Round. I didn't panic, even when I didn't know a solution completely--I asked clarifying questions, discussed trade-offs, and tried to reason through the problem.

Areas I Could Have Improved

Despite the positives, there were definitely areas where I could've done better:

● I didn't prepare enough for system design. While I had some basic understanding, I could have been more confident if I had practiced it more through mock interviews or small-scale design exercises.

● I should have invested more time in revisiting my own projects. Especially the ones I had mentioned on my resume--some schema-level or implementation-specific details were fuzzy, which could have been avoided with better preparation.

General Tips for Candidates

● THINK OUT LOUD during the interview.

● Solve a lot of DSA . For DSA, start with neetcode.io , then move on to Striver's A2Z sheet. I first completed about 15 problems from each topic on neetcode.io [Around 2.5 months] . After that, I focused on DP, Arrays, and Binary Search from Striver's sheet [Around 3 months]. For graphs, I followed the YouTube channel https://www.youtube.com/@codestorywithMIK , which has many solved questions across topics--definitely check it out. I also solved the CSES graph section and used ChatGPT to get questions combining multiple topics like DP on graphs and graph + bitmasking.

● And as I said, don't just run behind getting the correct solution--explore the wrong solutions also. Wrong answers teach 10x more than the correct ones. Spend good time around each question. Don't be in a race to finish off questions; it's about understanding deeply, not just ticking boxes.

● A correct code/approach in the interview does not guarantee your selection, nor does a wrong one deny you. It's all about how well you are able to explain and articulate your thoughts.

● Revise your resume and projects thoroughly: Be ready to discuss your contributions, system design choices, and technical decisions. Know the why behind each decision, not just the what.

● Stay calm and composed during interviews: Your attitude matters as much as your answers. If you get stuck, ask clarifying questions, explain your thought process, and don't panic.

● Avoid comparing yourself to others: On the interview day, many people will be talking about how their rounds went, what questions they got, or how confident they feel. Don't let it overwhelm you. Stay focused on your own preparation and performance.

● Be humble and helpful: Everyone around you is equally nervous and aiming for the same goal. Be kind, share a smile and help others if they need it. You're not competing against each other--you're just trying to show your best.

● Take notes during the Pre-Placement Talk: Interviewers often refer to company-specific terms, metrics, or philosophies. Jotting them down can give you an edge during interviews.

● Be mindful of your grooming and energy: Wear something you're confident in (formals preferred), get a good haircut , get enough sleep, and arrive on time. First impressions do matter.

● Don't take failure personally: Not every round or result defines your intelligence or hard work. Learn from it and move forward. You only need one opportunity to click.

● Believe. If you're someone who places faith in God, then trust that everything happens in its own time--God has a plan for you.

You can contact me on WhatsApp. +91 9152752492.

journey.howSecured:
1. Online Assessment [ 200+ Candidates , 7th July]

The Online Assessment was conducted on 7th July 2025 via the DOSelect platform. It was a 90-minute test originally scheduled to begin at 4:00 PM but was delayed due to technical issues, and my test eventually started around 4:40 PM. Despite the delay, I stayed calm and maintained a composed attitude. I proactively communicated with the DOSelect support team to resolve the issue. Interestingly, the same individual who assisted me during the technical glitch later appeared in my HRM interview, and I believe my calm response left a positive impression.

Before the OA began, a pre-placement talk was held from 2:30 PM to 3:30 PM. I made it a point to take notes during the session, especially on important points such as the company's vision, founding inspiration, growth metrics, and their underlying technologies and architecture like microservices and scalability. These notes proved useful in later interview rounds, particularly when I had to refer to PhonePe's infrastructure, scalability, and database systems.

All students who applied were allowed to take the OA, and there was no shortlisting prior to the test. Shortlisting after the assessment was based on problem-solving accuracy, the efficiency of code, the number of passed test cases, and behavioral logs captured by DOSelect's secure browser, which monitors for tab switches, fullscreen exits, and suspicious activity.

Test Structure & Questions

● 1. Friendship Clusters Problem: Given a list of integer pairs representing friendships, determine the minimum number of additional friendships required to make all people directly or indirectly friends with each other. If person A is friends with person B, then all their friends are also friends. Approach:

○ Modeled it as a graph.

○ Used DFS to find the number of connected components (disjoint sets).

○ Final answer = number of disjoint sets - 1.

○ Issue: Got a stack overflow on one large test case due to recursion depth but chose to move on since I had to manage time.

○ Could have used DSU

● 2. Array Assignment with Max Difference Constraint Problem: Given an array with some pre-assigned elements and a constraint k, find the number of valid ways to assign the remaining elements such that the difference between adjacent elements is at most k. Each element must be between 1 and 100. Approach:

○ Used recursive backtracking with memoization.

○ Solved 7 out of 12 test cases.

● 3. Pair with Bit Position Sum Constraint Problem: From an array, pick two numbers (a pair) whose sum is exactly s such that the total of positions of set bits in both numbers is less than or equal to k. Count the number of such pairs. For example, consider the number 12. Its binary representation is 1100, and the set bits are at positions 2 and 3 (starting from position 0 on the right). So, the sum of bit positions is 2 + 3 = 5. Approach:

○ Brute-forced through all pairs.

○ Calculated set bit positions using bit manipulation.

○ All test cases passed except one.

● 4. House Assignment with Friend Constraints Problem: Given friend pairs and their house preferences (4 houses with limits), assign each student a house such that:

○ Friends don't get the same house

○ House limits are respected Input Challenge: Input was provided as a complex nested list (e.g., [[h1, h2], [h2, h3]]) with no clear count of friend pairs.

● Approach:

○ Due to lack of time and complexity of parsing, printed "possible" as a fallback solution.

○ Managed to pass approximately 60% of the test cases.

During the test, I faced a Wi-Fi issue and had to switch networks. Since DOSelect tracks activities like fullscreen exits and network changes, I immediately called the representative to inform them and ensure they witnessed the switch. I also followed up with the POC to document the situation properly. Transparency during such incidents is crucial, as it helps protect against being falsely flagged for violations.

The test results were released around 9:30 PM, leaving me with very little time to revise or prepare. We were asked to report the next morning by 8:00 AM, so I had to make the most of the limited time. While traveling in the local train and metro, I made sure to quickly go through some previously asked problems and revise key topics like graphs.

Additionally, it's important to groom yourself well before the interview. Dress professionally--wear formal attire--as it helps create a good first impression and shows that you're taking the process seriously.

Round 2 - Technical Interview (First Tech Round) [30 students]

I reached campus at 7:30 AM. At 8:30 AM, interview batches were announced; I was in the second batch. The first batch started at 9:00 AM, so I had an hour to calm down and prepare. At 10:00 AM, my turn came. I knocked, entered, shook hands with the interviewer, who introduced himself as an App Developer at PhonePe. I gave a brief self-introduction, then the interview started.

Question 1: Minimum Number of Operations to Sort a Binary Tree by Level

He opened with a medium-level tree problem and asked me to explain the logic before jumping into code.

I explained that I would do a BFS traversal of the tree, level by level. For each level, I'd collect all the node values into a list. Then, I'd make a sorted copy of that list. Using a map of value → index from the original list, I would compare the original and sorted arrays index by index. If the values at index i didn't match, I'd swap them in the original array and increment a counter. I would also update the map after every swap. This technique is similar to solving the minimum swaps to sort an array problem.

He listened carefully and seemed satisfied. After a few clarifying questions, he asked me to write the code and then discuss the time complexity. I did both. Although he mentioned he was expecting a graph-based approach, he acknowledged that my solution was valid and handled the problem efficiently. We had a brief back-and-forth on potential optimizations and edge cases.

Question 2: Find the K-th Smallest Sum of a Matrix With Sorted Rows

This was a tough one. I started with a brute-force approach: generate all possible sums by combining one element from each row and storing the results in a max-heap of size k. He immediately asked why I was using a max-heap instead of a min-heap.

I explained my reasoning -- that the max-heap would help keep track of the k smallest sums by discarding the largest as new smaller ones come in. He looked a bit surprised but agreed with my logic once I did a dry run of the approach.

Then he asked me to optimize the solution. I took a pause to think but couldn't come up with an efficient algorithm on the spot. I admitted that I was stuck and asked for a hint. He kindly walked me through a more optimized method.

He then asked whether duplicates could occur in the sums. I answered yes. He asked why, and I gave a correct explanation. When he asked how to avoid duplicates, I suggested using a HashSet to track visited combinations. He nodded and seemed happy with that answer.

Post-Interview Conversation

After the technical questions, he asked if I had any questions for him. I asked about a couple of app features and their color palette choices--he smiled and admitted those weren't part of his responsibilities but still gave me general answers. Then I asked him about their tech stack, and he shared that they had recently started using React Native. Before I could ask why, he explained the reasoning behind the shift in detail, which I found really insightful.

Post-Interview Reflection

The interview ended around 11:00 AM. Although I was relieved it was over, I didn't feel too confident, especially about the second question. I overheard a few other candidates saying they had solved it, which made me a bit anxious.

The results were expected soon, but they didn't come until 3:00 PM. During this waiting period, some candidates were called for Technical Round 2, while others moved on to HR interviews.

To keep my nerves in check, I spent the time revising System Design concepts, casually discussing things with friends, and grabbing some refreshments. Those small breaks helped me ease the pressure and clear my head for whatever was coming next.

3. Round 3 - Technical Interview (Final Tech Round) [ Around 11 students]

Time: Around 3:00 PM onward Duration: Approx. 1 hour

By 3:00 PM, I had gotten quite relaxed after the long wait. I made sure to stay composed and walked into the interview room calmly. I knocked, asked for permission, and entered. The interviewer greeted me with a handshake and introduced himself. He mentioned that he works on KYC, user verification, and database systems at PhonePe.

I introduced myself in a similar way, giving a brief about my background, skills, and a short description of one of my projects. Without wasting any time, he jumped straight into the first question.

Question 1: Lava Brick Heat Loss in Matrix

Problem Description: Given a matrix where each element represents the heat removed from a lava brick when it passes through that cell. Starting at position (0, 0), you must reach (n-1, m-1) with minimum total heat loss.

● At any point, you must move exactly 3 steps in one direction (up, down, left, right).

● After completing those 3 steps, you must immediately change direction (no continuing in the same direction).

● You cannot reverse direction.

My Approach: I immediately recognized that the problem could be treated as a graph traversal problem.

● I considered each cell as a node, and the edges as moves with the weight equal to heat loss.

● I suggested Dijkstra's Algorithm and explained in detail about the characteristics of Dijkstra and why it was suitable for this weighted graph problem.

● I also highlighted the need for a modified state: i, j, direction, steps_remaining, total_weight.

He asked me to explain it visually, so I first drew a standard Dijkstra graph, showed how it processes nodes, and then extended it to demonstrate why additional state parameters (like direction and steps) were necessary in this case. I justified this as expanding the graph to a more detailed representation of possible paths.

Code Implementation: He then asked me to write the code. While implementing:

● I paused to ask him a few clarifying questions regarding direction changes and boundaries, and he was supportive in answering.

● I realized I had missed the relaxation condition, so I asked if I could write a generalized version elsewhere in the code. He agreed.

● Some directional code blocks were repetitive, so I asked if I could omit them with comments for clarity. He agreed again.

I then completed the code with detailed comments and added placeholders for repeated blocks and the generalized relaxation. After that, he asked me to explain the code again and discuss the time and space complexity, which I did thoroughly. He verified the logic and moved to the second question.

Question 2: Painting the Walls - Leetcode

Problem Setup: He presented the problem in an incomplete form (as I understood it), giving only a partial description and asking me to proceed with a solution based on it. I kept asking for clarification, but he insisted that this was all the information I would get.

My First Attempt: I assumed a possible setup and gave him a brute-force-style solution. For the sample test case, it passed. However, he then gave me another test case where my approach failed. I revised my logic and proposed another solution. He pointed out that it would also fail and asked me to come up with a counter-example that would break my logic.

I took a moment to think and asked if I could get a glass of water. He nodded. I joked, "Will this disproving of my own solution count?" He smiled and said, "Yes, yes," while laughing. Eventually, I did manage to find a test case where my solution would break.

At this point, he provided the full problem statement, mentioning that it involved dynamic programming. I initially struggled to grasp the direction of the solution, so I asked for the constraints. Once I had them, I was able to identify the DP approach.

My Final Solution: I explained a recursive + memoized solution, wrote the code, and discussed both time and space complexity. I also explained how the solution could be converted into a bottom-up (tabular) DP formulation.

Post-Interview Interaction

Once the technical questions were done, he asked if I had any questions for him. I asked about:

● The challenges faced in KYC and verification systems

● What is that random message which gets sent when someone links their UPI/Bank?

● His most impactful contribution to the PhonePe ecosystem

He answered each of them in detail, sharing both technical and team-level insights.

Before I left, he smiled, shook my hand again, and said:

"You're the most calm and relaxed person I've spoken to today."

With that, the interview ended on a positive and memorable note.

Round 4 - Hiring Manager Interview

Time: Just 10 minutes after Round 3 Interviewer: Same person who handled my technical issue during the Online Assessment (OA)

I wasn't sure if he remembered me from our earlier interaction during the OA when I had technical issues, but he greeted me with a smile and a handshake. Without much small talk, he asked me to introduce myself.

Self-Introduction and Resume

I gave the same structured introduction I'd prepared--covering my name, background, skills, and a quick summary of my project. He asked me if I was tired to which I replied yes but equally excited.

He scanned my resume for about a minute and then asked me to pick the most exciting and challenging project and walk him through it.

I began by explaining:

● What the project was about

● The goal and motivation behind it

● The tech stack used

● My specific role in the team

When I mentioned that my role involved designing model schemas, he immediately asked me to list down the tables and their schemas. I admitted I couldn't recall all of them in full detail but shared the key tables and schema structure from memory.

He then asked me to walk through the user flow in the project. Since the project involved GenAI, he had several follow-up questions on how I integrated it. I explained the RAG (Retrieval Augmented Generation) architecture and how I approached prompt tuning. I also admitted that my tuning approach wasn't based on any specific methodology--it was entirely experimental and observation-driven.

He asked what hallucinations in GenAI meant, and I explained that too.

API Design & Project Ownership

He then asked about a few specific APIs used in the project. I clarified that I didn't personally implement those but had a rough understanding. I even drew a high-level diagram of how I thought the flow might look.

To show stronger ownership, I brought up another project I worked on using MERN stack, where I had built the APIs myself. I explained:

● API structure

● How user authentication worked

● Use of JWT tokens and hash functions

He then asked, "Where is the hash code stored?" I answered "in the virtual environment," but he pointed out that this would be a security issue, which I acknowledged, adding that I hadn't deeply explored that side yet.

System Design: YouTube

Next, he asked about my most used app. I said YouTube, and he asked me to explain how its APIs might work. I confirmed whether he wanted a project-level view or a system design-level view, and he chose the latter.

I started explaining:

● DNS lookup

● API gateway

● Load balancing

● Service-based architecture

● Horizontal scaling

He then asked how I would handle video feeds. I explained that:

● Videos would be delivered in chunks

● Additional content would load only when the user finishes scrolling the current chunk

Then came the key question: "How would you decide which videos to send?"

I said that would be handled by a recommendation system. He challenged me further: "Assume you're just launching YouTube--how would you build a basic recommender without ML?"

I proposed a rule-based scoring system, explaining that:

● We'd gather user data like subscriptions, likes/dislikes, history, location, etc.

● Each video would have associated tags

● Based on parameter weights, we'd assign a score to each video

● The highest scoring videos would be sent as feed chunks

He seemed satisfied with the logic and the non-ML approach.

Behavioral and Personal Questions

He shifted toward more personal questions:

Q: "How has choosing CSE in SPIT changed your personality?" I responded:

● I've moved beyond solving only textbook problems to asking what, why, and how behind everything

● I now approach problems by fixing first, identifying root causes, then redesigning

● My curiosity has grown, and I challenge myself often

● I introspect and verify facts before raising questions

Q: "What would you do in case of a conflict with a manager or teammate?" I gave a real example where we had to choose between Django and MERN for a project. Although we had used Django in a previous winning hackathon, I convinced the team logically to go with MERN this time based on:

● Current requirements

● Ease of debugging

● Flexibility of tech

I emphasized that I prefer direct communication, avoid miscommunication, and back my arguments with facts and logic.

Q: "How have the past 6 months been for you?" I highlighted:

● The value of courses like Machine Learning, Distributed Computing, Blockchain, Business Analytics

● How they improved my clarity of concepts and curiosity

● Every course had a mini project, which taught me about deadlines, collaboration, debugging, quick learning, handling people and team-building

Questions I Asked the Interviewer

He then gave me the chance to ask questions. I asked:

1. " I referred to points from the pre-placement talk. PhonePe was launched in 2016, what was its founding inspiration?"

2. "Why hasn't PhonePe moved to AWS, Azure, or GCP? How do you handle so many transactions on your own infra?"

3. "How has PhonePe managed to capture such a huge customer base in rural India, despite strong competitors like GPay?"

He gave thoughtful answers and mentioned:

● Hiring the right people

● Emphasis on financial discipline

● Focus on long-term survivability and execution

As the conversation wrapped up, I smiled and said:

"So that saying about pressure turning coal into diamonds is true?"

He smiled back, and then I asked him if he had any feedback for me.

The results came at 7:45 PM. 7 people got selected.

Why I Got Selected & What Helped Me

One of the key things that helped me was consistent LeetCode practice over a long period. I didn't just aim to solve problems--I made sure I understood why certain solutions worked and why others failed. For particularly tough problems, I sometimes spent 2-3 hours just breaking them down, revisiting them until I gained full clarity.

After exams, I specifically revised graph algorithms, solving the entire graph section on CSES Problem Set and also picked some hard problems on trees and graphs to stretch my thinking. That gave me a strong base for several questions that came up during the tech interviews.

Another factor that I believe played a big role was my calm and composed attitude during the Tech Round 2 and the Hiring Manager Round. I didn't panic, even when I didn't know a solution completely--I asked clarifying questions, discussed trade-offs, and tried to reason through the problem.

Areas I Could Have Improved

Despite the positives, there were definitely areas where I could've done better:

● I didn't prepare enough for system design. While I had some basic understanding, I could have been more confident if I had practiced it more through mock interviews or small-scale design exercises.

● I should have invested more time in revisiting my own projects. Especially the ones I had mentioned on my resume--some schema-level or implementation-specific details were fuzzy, which could have been avoided with better preparation.

General Tips for Candidates

● THINK OUT LOUD during the interview.

● Solve a lot of DSA . For DSA, start with neetcode.io , then move on to Striver's A2Z sheet. I first completed about 15 problems from each topic on neetcode.io [Around 2.5 months] . After that, I focused on DP, Arrays, and Binary Search from Striver's sheet [Around 3 months]. For graphs, I followed the YouTube channel https://www.youtube.com/@codestorywithMIK , which has many solved questions across topics--definitely check it out. I also solved the CSES graph section and used ChatGPT to get questions combining multiple topics like DP on graphs and graph + bitmasking.

● And as I said, don't just run behind getting the correct solution--explore the wrong solutions also. Wrong answers teach 10x more than the correct ones. Spend good time around each question. Don't be in a race to finish off questions; it's about understanding deeply, not just ticking boxes.

1. Online Assessment [ All the students who had Applied appeared for it Nearly 200+]

We were Asked to report at 1 : 40 PM for PPT (Pre Placement Talk) followed by OA.OA was initially scheduled at 3 : 30 PM however it started nearly at 4 : 00 PM.

Total 4 Questions were there in this Round and duration was 90 Minutes (1 and Half Hour)

Question 1 :

Reference Question : Connected Components in an Undirected Graph

It was mostly Like this same question we have to figure out the Number of Connected Components and we were asked to finally print the final cost where cost was 1 for connecting 2 different components.

I instantly came up with approach of DSU and coded it in nearly 8 to 10 Minutes as DSU is my favourite Data Structure. I got all the Test cases Passed and got AC on it.

However, few people also solved it by using BFS / DFS. But One common mistake which I noticed was alot of people even after realizing that it was a DSU question were not able to code DSU. So, I would suggest stop using Templates at least one month before Placement. It was an easy one If you have command on DSU. I would strongly recommend to learn DSU as it is favourite Topic of every PBC.

Question 2 :

Reference Question : Array Description

It was Almost same as this question from CSES. A slight change was there that At max Difference can be till k instead of 1 where k was an Integer Provided in the Input. I had solved this problem alot of times before still was not confident to code it that fast so decided to go for 3rd one and then came to it and coded it. I was able to solve all the test cases apart from 5 test cases which I was not able to figure out initially but later on realized that I was not doing Modulo 1e9 + 7 and the moment I did that all the test cases got Passed.

Question 3 :

You were provided with an Array of length n and a variable s and a Variable k. Your task was to print the number of pairs where sum of two elements was equal to s and sum of bit positions of 1 of those numbers should be less than or equal to k.

Ex.: n = 5 arr = [1 2 7 3 5] This is the Array and say s = 10 and k = 5

So, Answer will be 1 in this case as 3,7 is the Only Pair satisfying the conditions. Here 3 + 7 = 10 and In binary 3 = 011 and 7 = 111. For 3 There is a 1 at 0th position and another one at 1st position so sum of bit positions = 1 and for 7 there is 1 at 0th,1st and 2nd Position so sum of bit positions = 3. So, total sum of bit Positions = 1 + 3 = 4 which is less than k in this case.

The trick in this question was the constraint as n was at max equal to 1000 so O (n*n) can be easily passed. So, without even a single thought I applied Brute Force I got all the Test Cases Pass. One thing I noticed was though I read the question completely but while Implementing I forgot to check the bit positions condition and just checked the condition of pairs sum equal to s but still I got and all the test cases got passed. But after realising that later on I again came back to it even after getting AC I improved the code as we were Informed that code will be seen and on the basis of that shortlisting will be done. This was an easy Problem mostly was there for speed solving.

Question 4 :

Reference Question : M-Coloring Problem

It was mostly like this same Problem with Proper story Plot but the Main trick in this Problem was to take the Input as they didn't mentioned that what number of edges were to be taken as an Input. I didn't met a Single Person who had solved it completely. I was nearly having more than half an hour. I tried Applying all the different techniques which I knew mainly I tried using getline as I code in C++ but that didn't worked. One thing which alot people did was they directly Printed possible as answer can either be Possible or Impossible. On printing Possible nearly 7 of 11 test cases were getting Passed. I knew this trick but didn't used it as it was Mentioned in PPT that code will be reviewed by Phone Pe Team. I also knew that last year with 2 complete and half Partial submissions candidates have received call.. So, I was almost sure that I will be getting the OA shortlisting.

30 Candidates were Shortlisted after OA Round. List came nearly around 10 : 00 PM and we were asked to report at 8 : 00 AM the next day.

2. Technical Round 1 [ All 30 shortlisted Candidates gave this Round ]

There were 3 Panels. I was in 2nd Panel. So, have to wait for 1 hour from 9 to 10. Then some of my friend from panel 1 after first Round told me that they were asked questions on Binary Search and Binary Lifting. I was quite confident afterwards as these are My most strong topics in CP. Then Finally I went for Round 1. Interviewer Didn't at all looked at my resume and not even asked for My Introduction. He tried to make me comfortable and then directly started with the Problem. He was very helpful in entire Round. Question 1 : I had never seen exact same question Previously.

Problem Statement : You are given a Binary Tree and for each level you have to find minimum number of swaps to sort nodes of that Particular level and at the end you have to return the total Number of swaps required for all the levels of tree.

I started with explaining that how we'll take all the nodes of each level using queue and store it in vector. So, question boils down to finding minimum number of swaps required for sorting the elements of a vector and likewise we can do for all the Levels. Now, thing was How can we solve it for a particular vector. I directly gave him the Merge Sort approach which seemed appropriate to me at that time. However he didn't looked satisfied with merge sort. So, I decided to go for another approach through I was not having any other approach but with nearly 3 minutes of strong thinking I cam up with Approach of DSU (As I mentioned earlier it is my most favourite data structure so I almost try it in every question)

I explained him that we can find Number of cycles using DSU and total number of swaps will be equal to size of a Particular component - 1 and likewise we can add it for all the components. But then He asked me how will I code DSU as Numbers can be 1000,200 or any big number then I told him about Coordinate Compression and with that it becomes a standard DSU Problem. He just looked too satisfied with approach. Then He asked me to code it. He asked me to write complete code along with syntax with Proper Assumptions on Paper. I was completely Comfortable in it and coded it Properly.

Question 2 :

Reference Question : Maximum Sum Combination

It was exactly this same Problem but the change here was that there can be n arrays not necessarily 2 Arrays. I had solved the above mentioned Problem. So, directly came up with Priority Queue but was not able to figure out for n arrays. I tried alot of Approaches but was not able to come up with a complete correct solution. At once even Interviewer stopped looking at me and was doing his own work. But I was still explaining him My approach without stopping which I have learned from Striver's Media.net Experience that you should never sit Blank in Interview even if you know that your Approach is complete wrong. As in real life Industry work not necessarily you will be having solution of every Problem but one thing which should be there in you to continuously try for finding the solution.

3. Hiring Manager Round [ Around 16 students]

After hearing everyone's experience I was not quite confident that whether I will be getting call or not. But all of sudden I received a call from my TPC and all of sudden I ran for taking my resume from My Bag and went for HM Round. He was Managing Head at PhonePe and was just too good and helpful.This round was highly focused on my Resume.

Even He didn't looked at hard copy of my resume and instead he was having my resume open on his Laptop. Even he didn't asked me the Standard Introduce Yourself Question and rather directly started with my Projects and asked about my One project on which I was confident enough. I explained him my Test My Case Project which is a Chrome Extension I made for Codeforces for validating Test Cases. He looked interested to know how it exactly worked I explained him it's complete working and then he asked why I made this to which I replied I made it for myself as I was facing that issue on Codeforces which I think made a Good Impression on him. Then he grinded me on my resume with questions like My leadership qualities, My role as Executive in IETE and a lot of such questions. Then he asked me

My most frequent used App to which I replied Youtube as I knew he will be asking me the System Design / Architecture of Youtube. I had read a lot of Past Year Experience of PhonePe due to which I knew this is sure shot question for PhonePe HM round. Later on he asked me to tell how Youtube Recommendation system works to which I took him to complete Core CS, ML and DSA which is My strong zone. (I wanted to show that I had good command on Core CS) Then He asked me a lot of Behavioral questions on which I was almost prepared. He also asked me my weakness to which I replied that I over optimize things as I come from CP background and then told him that I am continuously trying to Improve it. Then at the end, He asked me Tell me a Reason why we should not hire you to which I replied that I don't think so I have any such qualities and I do possess all the main qualities required for SDE 1 at PhonePe and even If I don't have I will learn them faster. He then asked me to ask any questions I had then I asked him few questions which I prepared during the PPT (Pre Placement Talk) which made him feel that I was highly focused during PPT. He looked Impressed and I almost knew that I am getting the call for final Round.

4. Technical Round 2 [ Around 11 students]

I received the Message that I have been shortlisted for 3rd and Final Round of the Day which is Technical Round 2. At the very beginning of this I was told that I have been strongly recommended by Manager Sir. The Interviewer was very helpful and talked with me for a while to make me comfortable. Then He started with DSA questions

Question 1 :

Reference Question : Drunken Maze

Don't worry It was not the same Problem but it was very easy as compared to the above Problem with just Direction condition. As I had solved this Problem just recently I directly told him the Approach to which he was satisfied and directly told me to do the code. I asked him what is the Expectations with Quality of code to which he replied he has to show My code to the Team. So, I maintained High Quality of Code which I had practiced a lot for Interviews. He looked satisfied with the code and then fast forward he asked me the follow ups to which I replied very faster. (Graphs have always been my strongest Part in my Complete Coding Journey thanks to Striver for that)

Question 2 :

Reference Question : Painting the Walls

Interviewer directly Showed me on Leetcode Itself and asked me for the Approach after looking directly at constraints I directly replied with DP without a Second thought to which he agreed. I gave him 4 different recursive functions on the spot all of which were correct. But he wanted me to tell the approach using only those dp states which he want. I was not able to figure out exactly the states he wanted but eventually with certain talk with him I gave him the approach he wanted. I asked him that should I go for code to which he said Time's Up. But then He said that don't worry You are good guy for PhonePe to which I replied "Ok, So let's meet in the Office" This was something I had never thought I will say to my Interviewer. He replied with yess for sure. With that I came out from Interview Room.

I was the first one to Complete all the 3 Rounds and So, I knew that I have to wait for nearly 2 hours and eventually all of us ended up waiting for nearly 3 to 3 and half hours and finally Shortlisting Came. 7 of Us were hired with (Internship + FTE offer). Later on I got to know that I was the first one ever from EXTC department to get into Phone Pe. To someone like who always wanted a PBC to work on it felt like dream come true and that everyday grinding just seemed worth it.

1. [Online Assessment] [ 219 candidates appeared]

The assessment was conducted around 1hr after the ppt presentation (~4.30pm - 5pm). It was conducted on the DoSelect platform. The test contained 4 questions to be solved in 1hr 30 mins.

The webcam was on for the entire duration. There were also constraints on usb devices, so external keyboard and mouse may malperform. Do ensure a proper laptop with a webcam, keyboard and trackpad. The college wifi was not working properly so some of us had to use our own mobile hotspot to give the test, so ensure you have adequate internet connection.

I personally faced lag during the contest where the text input was delayed 3-5s, I was writing entire 2-3 lines and the UI would update it seconds later. Also there was no VIM or EMACS mode for editing, so keep that in mind.

The running test suite and customs tests feature in this platform was abysmal.

A. You are given 'n' people, labeled from 1 to n. There are 'm' existing friendships represented by 2 arrays 'A' and 'B', each of size 'm'. The i-th friendship is between person A[i] and person B[i].

Two people belong to the same friend group if they are direct friends or have some indirect friendship.

Find the minimum number of friendships to be added such that every person belongs to the same friend group.

Input: The first line of each test case contains two integers n and m (1 <= n, m < 2*10^5) The second line of each test case contains m integers, a1, a2, … , an (1 <= ai <= n) The second line of each test case contains m integers, b1, b2, … , bn (1 <= bi <= n) Output: A single integer - the minimum number of friendships to be added.

Example input 4 2 1 3 2 4 Output 1

This can easily be solved by counting the number of connected components and returning the number of connected components - 1. I used DSU here and passed all test cases.

B. You have 'n' employees and have been given an array 'A' of size 'n', where A[i] indicates the number of ladoos the i-th employee receives. If A[i] = 0, it means the ladoos are not yet assigned. You are also given 2 integers 'm' and 'k'. Where 'm' is the maximum number of ladoos a single employee can get. And 'k' is the maximum allowed difference between adjacent employees.

Find the number of valid ways to assign ladoos to the unassigned positions such that. Each unassigned position gets a ladoo between 1 to m and the absolute difference between adjacent employees is at most k.

Input: The first line of each test case contains two integers n,m and k (1 <= n <= 10^4) (1 <= m <= 100) (1 <= k <= 30) The second line of each test case contains m integers, a1, a2, … , an (0 <= ai <= m) Output: A single integer - the total number of valid ways to assign the ladoos mod 1e9 + 7

Example: Input:

5 5 2 0 3 0 0 4

This was a simple 2D DP problem on counting, i just kept an array 'dp' of length 'm + 1', where dp[i] represents the number of ways to i ladoos currently. Calculated the dp by iterating over the n elements in array 'a'.

I passed most of the test cases except 2, where I didn't account for the first element being 0.

C. You have been given an array 'a' of length 'n' and an integer 'k'. For each element the value of a[i] is defined as the sum of (bit * position) where bit is the bit at the position starting from 1 from LSB in the binary representation of a[i]. E.g. for a[i] = 13; Binary representation of 13 = 1101 1 1 0 1 Position 4 3 2 1 Value = 4*1+3*1+2*0+1*1;

Find number of pairs(i ,j) such that value(a[i]) + value(a[j]) <= k

Input: The first line of each test case contains two integers n and k (1 <= n <= 10^5)(1 <= k <= 10^5) The second line of each test case contains m integers, a1, a2, … , an (0 <= ai <= 10^5) Output: A single integer - the total number pairs(i ,j) such that value(a[i]) + value(a[j]) <= k

Input: 4 20 5 6 7 8 Output: 1

The expected solution for this problem was to make the value array first, and then using sorting + 2 pointers to find the number of pairs in ( O(n.logn)). But I was running low on time so I wrote a brute force solution ( O(n^2)) in 5 minutes and it passed all test cases.

D. I don't remember this question, it was related to harry potter or something. The input format for this question was also not clear, so instead of wasting my time on it, I checked how the output was. We were supposed to print possible or impossible.

I just wrote cout << "possible" << endl; and it passed 6/8 test cases 💀

In total I attempted 2 Complete + 2 partial questions, and I advanced to the next round. 30 students were shortlisted. The list of the students eligible for next rounds was released around 11 pm. And the next rounds were on the right next day.

2. [Technical Round 1] [ 30 candidates were shortlisted ]

We were told to arrive at college at 8am, as the order of panels was not confirmed. But the interviews started at around 9am.

Problem 1: given an array of n integers return the maximum subarray sum of a subarray where the first element and last element is the same. Can be done by simple map in linear time.

https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/dsa/maximum-sum-subarray-such-that-start-and-end-values-are-s ame/

Problem 2: given a tree with all unique elements and queries of the form [currnode, value], you are supposed to output the maximum of (value xor node) over all nodes from root to currnode. This was solvable by a binary trie. Where you have to perform dfs and dynamically add and delete the visited nodes from the trie. And answer queries for currnode.

https://codeforces.com/blog/entry/66434

I did the first problem entirely and the second one with some hints. From every slot of panels 3 students were asked to give HM round first. From the 10 people in my panel, 3 students including me were asked to give HM round first. I wrote code for both the problems. And was expected to know the implementation of trie.

As time was running out, I did not ask any questions to the interviewer, but you should prepare some questions to ask them.

3. [Hiring Manager Round] [9(from directly tech round 1) + 5(after both tech rounds)]

This was a resume round, typical HR questions were asked. Conflicts with coworkers? How did you resolve it? Your weaknesses? How would you learn fintech?. I was lucky enough to get asked about my 6 month internship and projects I did in it. My normal projects section only had a single project (NOT RECOMMENDED) about employee management systems, I was not asked a question regarding this. Do not depend on luck, have both good internships and projects. He then asked me to give me my favourite feature any app has made in recent years. I told him about the apple natural handwriting to math feature and explained its design. This is very

common system design question and it is generally a good idea to be prepared in advance for this.

4. [Technical Round 2] [11 were shortlisted for the final round]

Some people who completed the HM round first were also rejected, so do not panic if you were not in the 9 people who were chosen to give HM round first. The format of this round was the same as the Technical Round 1. But the difficulty of the questions was high. Problem 1: given an array of strings return true if concatenation of any two strings makes a palindrome. This can be solved using trie. And I was again said to write the whole implementation of the trie.

https://leetcode.com/problems/palindrome-pairs/description/

Problem 2: this problem was 2700 on codeforces, in my entire codeforces run i have solved at max a 2500 question. I would not even explain this just go to the link below. This was just to test how the student thinks and I don't think they expected any of us to solve this question.

https://codeforces.com/contest/1270/problem/G

I solved the first problem without any hint. But I could not solve the second problem with any hints. My interview was the longest by far. Around 1hr 45 mins.

Out of 11 students 7 were selected, I was one of them.

journey.prep:
1. Strong DSA skills are essential - PhonePe places heavy emphasis on problem-solving, with this year's difficulty being higher than usual. Topics like Tries, Binary Lifting were commonly asked.

2. CP is a bonus, not a requirement - Being comfortable with CP is a big plus as it improves your problem solving skills. I didn't do any competitive programming, but regularly attempting Leetcode contests and upsolving problems (sometimes trying to understand the 4th question) helped me grasp advanced topics and perform in a time bounded environment.

3. Internship experience adds value - My interview started with questions about my internship. It's important to clearly explain what you worked on and the impact you had.

4. Know your resume inside out - Be fully prepared to talk about everything on your resume, including freelance work, projects, and technical contributions.
