1. [Online Assessment] [219 candidates had applied]

4 Questions were to be solved in 1 hour 30 mins

a. You are given n people, labeled from 1 to n. There are m existing friendships represented by two arrays A and B, each of size m, where the i-th friendship is between person A[i] and person B[i].

Two people are considered friends if there is a direct or indirect connection between them (i.e., if they belong to the same connected group of friends).

Your task is to determine the minimum number of new friendships that must be formed so that every person is connected directly or indirectly--in other words, so that everyone belongs to a single connected group.

Input: N = 4, M = 2, A = [1, 3], B = [2, 4] Output: 1

This is essentially a connected components problem, where each group of friends forms a component, and the minimum number of new friendships required is simply:

Answer = Number of connected components − 1

This is because each new friendship can merge two components, and to connect k components into one, you need exactly k−1 connections.

b. You have N employees and are given an array P of size N, where P[i] indicates the number of ladoos the i-th employee receives. If P[i] = 0, it means the ladoos for that employee are yet to be assigned. You are also given two integers M and K:

● M is the maximum number of ladoos any employee can get.

● K is the maximum allowed difference in ladoos between adjacent employees.

Your task is to determine the number of valid ways to assign ladoos to the unassigned positions such that:

● Each unassigned position gets a value between 1 and M.

● The absolute difference between the ladoos of adjacent employees is at most K.

Input: N = 5, M = 5, K = 2 , P = [0, 3, 0, 0, 4] Output: 80

Initially, I approached this problem using backtracking. For each position with value 0, I tried assigning all values from 1 to M and recursively explored the possibilities while maintaining the K difference constraint between adjacent employees. I maintained a counter to track the number of valid configurations.

This approach worked for a few test cases and passed 4 of them. However, it was too slow for larger inputs due to recomputing overlapping subproblems, and I quickly realized that this was a Dynamic Programming problem.

Although I identified that memoization was required, I struggled to define the exact DP state due to time constraints.

Dp State: Let dp[i][prev] represent the number of ways to fill the array from index i onward given that the previous value was prev. Try all possible values from 1 to M at unassigned positions and memoize results to avoid recomputation.

c. You are given an integer n, an integer k, and an array arr of size n consisting of integers. For each element arr[i], convert it to its binary representation and define its value as:

Sum of (bit × position) where position is 1-based from right in the binary representation.

You need to find the number of pairs (i, j) such that:

value(arr[i]) + value(arr[j]) == k

Input: n = 4, k = 20, arr = [5, 6, 7, 8] Output: 1

● I looped from the least significant bit to the most significant bit, checking if each bit was set using (num >> bitPos) & 1.

● While doing this, I maintained a position counter (1-based from MSB) and added bit * position to the score.

After calculating the custom value, I stored it in an array and this transformed the question to check if the array has a pair for which the value is equal to k, I solved this using hashmap storing the frequencies and incrementing the count of the final answer.

This approach passed all regular test cases. However, one test case had a missing array input despite providing n. To handle this edge case, I wrapped the input parsing in a try-catch block, and in such a case, I returned 0.

Thanks to the optimized bitwise handling and proper input validation, I was able to solve all test cases correctly.

d. You are given:

● Four houses from Harry Potter: Gryffindor, Hufflepuff, Ravenclaw, and Slytherin

● Two integers: n: number of students m: maximum number of students allowed in each house

● A list of friendships: pairs of integers (a, b) where student a and student b are friends and must be placed in different houses

● A strings, where the i-th string contains the allowed houses for the i-th student (e.g., "[["pref1, pref2"], [pref2]]" you had to parse the string and split them accordingly and store their preferences)

Your task is to determine if it is possible to assign every student to exactly one of their preferred houses such that:

1. No pair of friends is placed in the same house

2. No house has more than m students

3. Each student is assigned to one of their preferred houses

Print "possible" if such an assignment exists, otherwise "impossible".

This was the final and most complex question, especially due to the tricky input format:

● I had to read n and m

● Then an unknown number of friend pairs

● Followed by a single line of strings indicating preferences for each student

Because I was short on time and the input parsing itself was time-consuming, I chose not to attempt this question.

2. [Technical Round 1] [30 candidates were shortlisted]

In this round, we were divided into three panels of 10 students each, with each session lasting approximately an hour. I was a part of the third panel. Some candidates were asked to introduce themselves, while others were immediately given DSA problems. The interview followed a similar pattern to the previous years, although the difficulty level had noticeably increased this time, with topics like Trie and Binary Lifting also making an appearance.

I was first asked to introduce myself, after which I was presented with a DSA problem:

Problem: Given an array of integers (which may include both positive and negative numbers), find the maximum sum of a subarray that starts and ends with the same value. If no such subarray exists, return the Integer.MIN_VALUE.

I initially explained the brute force approach -- iterating through every possible subarray and checking if the first and last elements matched. Then, I discussed an optimized solution using a hashmap to store indices of elements and computing prefix sums to calculate the subarray sum in constant time. However, the interviewer pointed out that in cases where all elements are the same, this method could degrade to brute force in terms of time complexity.

To solve the problem efficiently, I used a prefix sum array to compute the sum between any two indices in constant time and maintained a hash map to track the first occurrence of each number. While iterating through the array, if a number had been seen before, I calculated the sum of the subarray between its first occurrence and the current index. If this sum was greater than the current maximum, I updated the answer. In cases where the computed sum was negative, I reset the first occurrence of that number to the current index to allow for potentially better subarrays in the future. For numbers appearing for the first time, I simply stored their index in the map.

This logic struck a good balance between efficiency and edge case handling. The interviewer seemed satisfied with the clarity and completeness of my explanation and asked me to write down the code for it.

The second question I was asked involved a binary tree and multiple queries, where each query was a pair (node, value)--and the same node could appear multiple times with different values. For each query, the task was to find the maximum XOR between the given value and any of the node values along the path from the root to the specified node. I initially proposed a brute force approach where, for each query, I would traverse the path from the root to the node and compute the XOR on the go. However, the interviewer asked me to optimize it. Recalling a previous problem I had solved involving maximum XOR using a Trie, I adapted that idea here. At first, I was constructing a new Trie for each query, but after a few hints from the interviewer, I realized that I needed to build the Trie dynamically as I traversed the tree, inserting values on the path and using a counter mechanism to keep track of the presence of values. While backtracking, I would decrement the counter or remove the value to reflect that the node was no longer in the current path. This allowed me to efficiently query for the maximum XOR at any point without rebuilding the Trie for every query.

After explaining the optimized approach using a Trie with dynamic insertion and backtracking, I was asked to code out the solution. I implemented the logic by building the Trie on-the-fly during a DFS traversal of the binary tree, maintaining a counter to manage insertions and removals as nodes entered and exited the current path. The interviewer seemed satisfied with both my thought process and implementation. The interview wrapped up with me asking him a couple of questions.

3. [Hiring Managerial Round] [14 candidates were shortlisted for round 2 (a mix of both HM and Tech Round 2]

After each panel finished, the students who showed strong technical skills were directly sent for the Hiring Manager (HM) round. I think this was done to check their communication and soft skills. In this round, many students were rejected even though they were very good at coding, so it was clear that this round tested more than just technical knowledge. My HM interview was taken by the Engineering Head at PhonePe. He started by asking how I was feeling and then asked me to introduce myself. He looked at my resume and began asking questions based on it. Since I had mentioned my internship, he started with that. I also told him about the freelance work I had done. He then asked in detail about the things I had built during my internship. After that, he moved on to my projects. All of my projects were from hackathons, so I was confident while explaining them. Then he asked me to choose one of my favorite apps and design its system. I explained my choices clearly and walked him through my thought process. At some points, he said my design might not handle large traffic, so I broke those parts down further and improved the design. In the end, he was happy with my final solution. The second half of the interview was mostly HR questions. I tried to answer honestly and gave real examples, even mentioning times when I was wrong and how my friends helped me understand things better. Showing a balanced and honest mindset helped. I ended the interview by asking him a few questions.

4. [Technical Round 2] [ 11 students were shortlisted for the final round]

This round was quite similar to the first technical round, where we were asked two DSA questions. The first question was: given a list of strings, return true if concatenating any two of them forms a palindrome. I started with the brute force approach, but the interviewer asked me to optimize it. I then explained a Trie-based approach where, before inserting a string into the Trie, I would reverse it and check if it already exists. I also maintained a pointer i to check if the remaining part of the string formed a palindrome. After some back and forth and dry runs, the interviewer was satisfied with my logic, asked about the time complexity, and then told me to write the code.

The second question was an array problem that was mostly greedy/observational. Despite several hints from the interviewer, I wasn't able to come up with the correct solution during the interview. He later shared the solution and asked me to prove why the approach worked mathematically. I tried to reason it out but couldn't come up with a complete proof. However, I did manage to explain a valid DP-based approach and correctly identified the DP state. Since time was up, we had to wrap the round, and I asked him a few questions before ending. I also requested him to walk me through the proof of the solution I couldn't solve. I checked the second question was rated 2700 on Codeforces (Problem Link), which explained its difficulty level.

Out of the 11 candidates, 7 were selected in the end and I was one of them.

1. Online Assessment [219 candidates had applied] Platform: DoSelect || Questions: 4 || Time: 1hr 30mins

I would advise you to skim through all the questions first and start with the one which seems familiar/ easy. I started with Q3, which I solved in 7-8 minutes. Then I moved to Q1, got stuck on an edge case due to limited debugging options, but managed to solve it in 20 minutes. I spent the rest of the time on Q2, implemented a recursive solution, and passed a few test cases.

1) You were given n people and 2 array A and B of size m, where each pair (A[i], B[i]) means that A[i] is a friend of B[i]. Also, friendships are transitive, so if x is a friend of y and y is friend of z, x is also friend of z. You were told to find the minimum no of new friendship such that everyone is friend is each other. Approach: The question can be easily solved by counting the no of components . I used DSU to find the no of connected components and return it -1, A DFS or BFS approach would have worked too.

2) You were given an array A which represented the laddoos given to n employees. Each person must receive atleast 1 and atmost m laddoos. You had to assign laddoos to employed who had received 0 laddoos such that the absolute difference between two employees is not more than k. And finally, you had to print the no of valid ways distributions. Approach: I thought of writing a recursive solution first and then optimizing it using memoization, but was only able to solve 5 test case. Thought of debugging it but the platform didn't allow to see print statements (tho after the test I got to know that you can see print statements via custom inputs). Gave approx. 45 mins to this problem but was not able to solve it completely

3) You had to find the count of unordered pair such that their sum is s and the total of set bits in both the number is <=k

Approach: As the constraint was small enough for O(N2) to work but I solved it in O(N) as it was quite similar to the famous 2 sum problem. So used a map to store numbers and if the complement (s-a[i]) is present in the map checked for the set bit condition.

4) The question didn't specify the no of edges so didn't even look at this question as I had no practice on how to take input of this kind. However, as the question only needed to print possible or not possible and each test case having only one result so just printing possible was enough to get 6/8 testcase right. And further as one of the wrong testcase was the sample one so hard coded it and got 7/8 right. Well, they did mention that code quality was being considered but taking into consideration that no one was able to solve this optimally and almost everyone printed possible, this question may as well have not been considered for the selection.

I solved 2 problems completely and 2 partially which was enough for being selected for the next round.

2. [Technical Round 1] [ 30 students appeared] All the 30 students were divided into 3 panels of 10 each. I was part of the 1st panel.

The interviewer introduced himself and ask for mine as well. I kept my into short as I wanted more time for the 2 problems.

Question 1: Find the peak element in a 2d matrix. Where peak element is defined as the element which is greater than its 4 adjacent neighbors.

Before starting the question, I made to fully understand the problem by clarified the constraints, is it 4-directional or 8-directional adjacency. I started with the brute force solution which was to iterate and see if the condition is met.

Then I showed him how monotonicity is maintained in a 1d array for finding the peak element and how we can use binary search to implement it. Thought of flattening the 2d array and applying binary search on it. However soon found out that it does not work. With the help of some hints from the interviewer, found the optimal solution which involved binary search with the search space as the range of rows/cols. He then asked me to code the solution of paper.

Question 2: You were given a tree and q queries. Each query had a start node, an end node and a destination. The task was to find the node which is at a minimum distance from destination while also being on the path from start to end node.

Ex: Consider the n-ary tree And the query [2,5,7].

The path from 2 to 5 would be 2->1->3->5 and out of all the node the node 3 is at minimum distance from 7 so the answer is 3.

It started by saying that we can precompute the distance between all pair of nodes (MSSP algorithm) by using Floyd-Warshall algorithm and then for each query find the path using dfs/bfs while also maintaining a parent array to track the path. And using the parent array to trace the path we see which node has the minimum distance from destination.

However, as the distance matrix takes O(N3) time to compute, it wasn't optimal so the interviewer asked me look the answer in terms of LCA (Lowest common ancestor). I tried to find some observations from the testcase and found that the answer can be one of the LCA (start, end), LCA (start, destination) and LCA (end, destination). Once these 3 nodes are found we can calculate the minimum distance from the destination. However, it was not optimal and time was up so left it there.

The interviewer then asked for any questions for him . I had researched about it and asked him .

I was not able to solve both the question however don't let it demotivate you. The interviewer is more interested on how you approach the question so be open to him and read out your thoughts out loud and ask him for any hints if needed.

To save some time, from each panel 3 were fast-tracked to give the HR round before 2nd tech round.

3. [Technical Round 2] [ 14 students appeared] My 2nd tech round happened after my HR round. And similar to 1st tech round we were asked to solve 2 questions. I was not asked for my intro this time.

Problem 1: Given a matrix of size m*n, each element had a heat value which I gained if I landed on it, I had to return the minimum heat with which I could reach bottom right corner from top left corner under the following constraints:

1. I could move left, right, bottom or top.

2. I could not retrace my path at any point.

3. I couldn't move the same direction more than 3 times.

I initially approached the problem using BFS, but since we're trying to minimize a cumulative cost (heat), I pointed out that Dijkstra's algorithm would be more suitable here.

I took 5 states in my heap as heat, x, y, prevDirection, countOfPrevDirection and implemented the standard Dijkstra with the constraint on the paper while considering the code quality as well. I was asked a follow up that what if I had to move k steps before changing direction. I handled that as well

Problem 2: The exact problem from leetcode I started with a greedy solution which as expected didn't work on a few cases. Then I thought about dp to which the interviewer said I was on the right track. I was able to find the state which is quite similar to 0/1 Knapsack but the interviewer was not satisfied. I then dry runed the test cases given by him and my solution worked. He was satisfied by my answer till the end of interview I then asked him what would the optimal solution be. He opened the leetcode question itself and showed the editorial. The editorial had the same solution as mine. He then shook hands with me and said "Well Done".

4. [Hiring Manager Round] [ 11 students appeared]

PhonePe's HR round isn't a typical HR round; it revolves more around the resume so be have good projects on it and (internship if any).

The interviewer was the engineer manager at PhonePe. He started by asking me to walkthrough my projects. Since two of them were hackathon-winning projects, I had a clear strategy on how to present them: I first explained the problem or need , then walked him through how I approached and solved it, which helped build curiosity around the tech stack I had used. He asked me about jwt and RSA algorithm. I was not sure about the e xact implementation of it but gave a rough idea to him. In one of the projects, I had worked on the entire software development lifecycle , and I made sure to highlight that experience specifically.

I also made sure to explain him about a dev Ops experiment that I had done which wasn't mentioned on my resume. He was quite impressed by this.

He then asked me about my favorite app and its most used feature and I answered with reddit. He went forward to ask me to implement the post feature from the DB selection to the schema and optimizations (Pagination, caching, etc.).

He then followed with typical HR question. I gave honest and diplomatic answers to him using real life examples.

I was one of the first to have concluded with all the rounds so had to wait 4 hours for the results to be announced

7 students received the offer.

1. Online Assessment [219 candidates appeared for this round]

4 coding questions were to be solved in 90 minutes.

Problem 1 You are given n people, labeled from 1 to n (<=1e5). There are m existing friendships represented by two arrays A and B, each of size m, where the i-th friendship is between person A[i] and person B[i]. Two people are considered friends if there is a direct or indirect connection between them (i.e., if they belong to the same connected group of friends). Your task is to determine the minimum number of new friendships that must be formed so that every person is connected directly or indirectly--in other words, so that everyone belongs to a single connected group. Approach: I figured it is a connected components problem, I had 3 options - dsu, dfs and bfs. I went with dfs as it was quicker to implement, the answer was the number of connected components - 1. I passed all test cases.

Problem 2 You are given n (<=1e4) employees, some already have been assigned ladoos and some aren't, you need to assign ladoos to the second type of employees such that the difference between ladoos assigned to adjacent employees doesn't exceed k (<=30 i believe) and the maximum number of ladoos any employee has is m (<=200). You need to return the number of valid ways to assign ladoos. Approach: I initially thought this was a greedy/math problem but the ambiguous case of adjacent employees with 0 ladoos led me to think it is a dp problem, also n*m being close to 1e6 assured me that it was. I applied backtracking and memoized it. My state was memo[i][prev] which is the amount of ways I can assign ladoos to employees from [i,n-1] with the value of the last employee's assignment being prev. The tricky part was to decide the lower and upper limit of how many ladoos to assign to the ith employee. I took it from max(1,prev-k) to min(m,prev+k). I could solve 11/13 test cases with this approach with a few hidden cases not budging even after optimizations.

Problem 3 You are given an integer n (<=1e3), an integer k, and an array arr of size n consisting of integers. For each element arr[i], you can find its value using the following operation: convert it to its binary representation and define its value as: Sum of (bit × position) where position is 1-based from right in the binary representation. You need to find the number of pairs (i, j) such that: value(arr[i]) + value(arr[j]) == k.

Approach: Due to the low constraints I didn't think much and applied 2 nested loops. I checked each pair using a lambda function for the condition mentioned by iterating bitwise over the numbers and incremented the response. I passed all test cases.

Problem 4 You are given:

- Four houses from Harry Potter: Gryffindor, Hufflepuff, Ravenclaw, and Slytherin

- Two integers: n: number of students m: maximum number of students allowed in each house

- A list of friendships: pairs of integers (a, b) where student a and student b are friends and must be placed in different houses

- A list of strings, where the i-th string contains the allowed houses for the i-th student (e.g., "[["pref1, pref2"], [pref2]]" you had to parse the string and split them accordingly and store their preferences)

Your task is to determine if it is possible to assign every student to exactly one of their preferred houses such that:

1. No pair of friends is placed in the same house

2. No house has more than m students

3. Each student is assigned to one of their preferred houses

Print "possible" if such an assignment exists, otherwise "impossible" Approach: The question did not specify the number of friendships and the size of the list of strings, we were supposed to take the input as a stream. Since I didn't practice this type of input parsing, I couldn't solve this question. But since the input was small it could've been solved using backtracking i suppose.

Round 1 Summary: I could solve almost 3/4 questions and it was good enough to get me to the next round. My advice would be to not waste time on a question if it doesn't click, solve others and come back later. I solved 1->3->2 and due to increased confidence after solving 3, I could think of 2 without any pressure.

2. Technical Round - 1 [30 candidates appeared for this round] This round consisted of 2 coding questions which we were supposed to explain and code on pen paper. The interviewer asked for a brief introduction and then introduced himself before moving to the coding problems

Problem 1 Given an array of n (<=1e5) integers lying in the range [-1e9,1e9], return the maximum sum of a subarray that starts and ends with the same number. I could immediately think of hashing the minimum prefix sum of each unique number in that array to that number, when I encounter another instance of that number I could subtract the current prefix sum with the minimum prefix sum hashed to that number to get the max total sum of the subarray. Then I updated the map using the current prefix and continued. Finally I coded the solution for my approach. The interviewer was satisfied with my answer and asked the time complexity which was O(n).

Problem 2 Given a parents array of size n (<=1e6) which represents a binary tree and q (<=1e6) queries where queries[i]={node,value}, For each query, the task was to find the maximum XOR between the given value and any of the node values along the path from the root to the specified node, I initially gave a brute force dfs solution which ran in n*q, the interviewer asked me to optimize it and since values differed from query to query memoization wouldn't work. I thought for some time and then the interviewer hinted at using a trie data structure for storing nodes, I mentioned it had been a long time since I used it for solving problems and still attempted it, with a few more hints I could reach the solution. I needed to dynamically

create the trie and for each leaf node(in the trie) I could solve the queries that comprised of the tree node it represents. Since the query value is at max 1e6, its bitwise representation comprises 17-18 bits, making that the height of my trie. The interviewer then asked for the time complexity, which was O(17*17*n).

At the end he asked me whether I had any doubts and I asked about the async nature of PhonePe's systems and how a payment inconsistency is resolved which he explained stating that they constantly poll the NPCI servers for a response after a payment request has been initiated.

3. Technical Round - 2 [14 candidates appeared for this round]

This round had the same format as technical-1.

Problem 1 Given a matrix of size m*n (m*n<=1e6), each element had a heat value which I gained if I landed on it, I had to return the minimum heat with which I could reach {m-1,n-1} from {0,0} under the following constraints:

1. I could move left, right, bottom or top.

2. I could not retrace my path at any point.

3. I couldn't move the same direction more than 3 times. I mentioned that this seemed like a dijkstra problem to which the interviewer agreed, I considered the state of my heap as: {heat,x,y,prev,count} where {x,y} are the coordinates of the point that I landed on, heat is the accumulated heat, prev is the last move and count is a counter for move repetition. I maintained a matrix h[][] for storing minimum heat of each position and coded the solution. I mentioned that I could reduce my coordinates from 2 to 1 and compress the matrix h, but I went with this for simplicity. The interviewer agreed with my solution and asked a follow up question. He stated that if there was a minimum limit for moving in one direction before changing direction(say k) how would I adapt my solution. I stated that I could move k distance to the right and bottom of {0,0} and push those as the starting points to neglect minimum criteria to which he agreed.

Problem 2 Given 2 arrays cost and time each of size n where cost[i] and time[i] represent the cost of the ith painting and time required to paint it respectively by a paid painter. There was also a magic painter who could paint for free and painted 1 painting per unit time. But the magic painter could only work when the paid painter was busy. I had to return the minimum cost to paint all n paintings. I mentioned that there was a tradeoff between 1)choosing the cheapest painting c for the paid painter and for time t[c] the magic painter could paint t[c] expensive ones, and 2)choosing the most time consuming painting for the paid painter so that magic painter could paint more. I stated that in such a problem I had to consider all paths and hence it is a dp problem to which he agreed. I asked for a minute to think and came up with a state dp[i][rem] which is the minimum cost to paint [i,n-1] paintings where rem is the remaining paintings from [0,i-1]. There are essentially two options, use the paid painter and move to dp[i+1][max(0,rem-t[i])] or don't and move to dp[i+1][rem+1], at the base case check if rem is 0. He agreed and I coded out the solution.

In both of these rounds I made sure to communicate my thought process with the interviewer which is essential for them to understand how you approach a problem.

4. HM - Round [11 candidates appeared for this round] My HM interview was taken by the Engineering Manager at PhonePe. He started off by asking for my introduction and then started questioning me based on my resume. He asked about my internship experience

and what I learnt from it. I answered with an emphasis on the exposure I received to a real world codebase and system, and the design/devops concepts I could implement during it. He asked about the most difficult project, what made it difficult and how would I reapproach it if i could start over. He went on to ask similar behavioural questions regarding my projects and experiences. He then asked me about how I would design instagram stories to which I responded with a rank based algorithm where I'd assign points to each story according to the interaction with that user and give them a rank, I mentioned I'll use a map data structure to hash a pair of {rank,userId} to the array of urls of the photo/video content in the story and then cache stories using redis, or use a cdn. He then asked me about my most recent project and how much help did I take from llms in it to which I honestly replied stating that I used it for the ui of screens which I had a hard time figuring out, and also for debugging code. At the end he asked me if I had questions, I mentioned that in the PPT it was stated that there's a flat hierarchy structure at PhonePe, and I asked what it meant. He explained the hierarchy structure in depth. I also asked about the sports culture at PhonePe which he happily explained. The round went well overall and he wished me luck at the end. The key is to brush up your system design knowledge, both in general and PhonePe in specific, and be honest and expressive with your answers.

1. OA ( Coding Round) [All those who applied (200+)]

Patform : DoSelect || 90 minutes || 4 Questions

Each Question has 100 points (Total 400 points)

1. 1. There are some n friends and needed to find components, as soon as I read the question I understood it was a DSU (Disjoint Set Union) or Union-Find question so I wrote the DisJoint Class and was able to solve this question within 10-15 minutes. It was simple just had to count the total components. I was able to pass all test cases (12/12 testcases).

2. You are given an array of length n representing the number of laddoos distributed to n people standing in a line. Each person must receive at least 1 and at most m laddoos. Some people have already been assigned laddoos (represented as numbers between 1 and m), while others are yet to be assigned and are marked with a 0 in the array. Your task is to assign laddoos to the unassigned positions (i.e., the 0s in the array) such that the final array satisfies the condition: for every pair of adjacent people, the absolute difference between the number of laddoos they receive is less than or equal to k. You need to determine the total number of valid ways to make these assignments such that all constraints are satisfied.

For Example : n=3, m=5, k=3. Array = [5 3 0] Expected Output : 5

Solution : So for the last person as we can assign (1 to m i.e. 5 laddoos) as the adjacent element is 3 the condition of <=k holds so here I have 5 different ways ( [5 3 1], [5 3 2],.., [5 3 5]) My Approach : I was able to solve it partially I used recursion , it could also be further memorized for all testcases to pass.

3. Given an Array of n elements have to find 2 elements whose sum is equal to m and the bit addition is <=k. Suppose sum should be 10 and I have elements 6 (110 in binary) and 4 (100 in binary) So for 6( the bit sum will be 2 + 1 = 3) and for 4 (2) The total sum 3+2 =5 and if it is not more than k it will be considered.

My Approach : I had sorted the array (Time Complexity : nlogn) so that I can use 2 pointer concept to find sum = m, and if the sum condition holds then I check the bit condition . For checking bit condition ran loop to all bit position from 0->31 Suppose we have 0 1 0 1 0 1 ( left is msb while right is lsb) position : 5 4 3 2 1 0 sum : 4 + 2 + 0 = 6 (so this way easily can just add the positions of 1) I was able to solve this question fully (8/8 testcases)

4. Sorting Hat : You are given n students and m, the maximum number of students allowed per house. There are four houses: Slytherin, Gryffindor, Hufflepuff, and Ravenclaw. Each student has a list of preferred houses they can be assigned to. Additionally, some pairs of students are friends and must be placed in different houses. Assign each student to one of their preferred houses such that no house exceeds capacity m and no friends share the same house. Determine if such an assignment is possible. Solution : It can be solved using backtracking as can assign in a particular friend group n try different ways and in end if all get assigned can print "Possible" else "Not Possible" I was able to solve it partially.

Tip : When the number of friend relations is not specified in the input, using Scanner in Java is not ideal, as it relies on knowing how many inputs to read. In such cases, BufferedReader is preferred since it allows reading input line by line until the end. This makes it important to understand how to handle different input formats across programming languages.

In total I was able to solve 2 questions fully while other 2 partially. I had solved question 1 and then jumped to question 3 n then proceeded to solve it completely. I think had around 50 minutes to try ques 2 and 4 and was able to do that both partially. Total 30 candidates were selected for next round.

Tip : Don't waste time on 1 question first try the questions which are able to solve and even if able to solve partially some question its ok, Partial Marking does helps so try to increase the number of total testcases passed across all problems.

2. Technical Interview 1 [ 30 students appeared this round ]

This was offline interview, there were total 10 panels so the round happened in 3 batches a there were total 30 students. My Technical Round 1 happened in first batch. It was a 1 hour round where 2 Coding questions are asked. My Interviewer didn't asked me for a Intro and told me he will be giving 2 questions and he expects to have 1 coding question with proper optimized code on paper with complexities and the

2nd problem if not able to code out completely atleast properly discussed optimized solution and having written something on paper to even stand a chance to reach to the next round.

1. Given a NxM matrix have to find the peak element Example : [ 1 2 3 2 1 5 3 1 2 ]. Solution : Here Peak Element is 5 as 5 is greater than all its adjacent numbers in all 4 directions ( if a number is on boundary assume out of boundary all elements have a negative infinity ) We had to return any peak element from the matrix

My Approach : I first explained the obvious brute force solution which would be check for each number if peak n when find peak return. It would take time complexity of O(n^2) . As we wanted any peak element for each row we can perform binary search space , in normal binary search we need the array to be sorted but here binary space search would work as just need any element. I explained with example if we have 1 4 3 5 4 3 2 6 1 here middle element would be 4 we see on left of 4 we have 5 which is >4 so now right boundary mid -1 So search space : 1 4 3 5 middle = 4 which is greater than both left and right so its peak elemnt for a particular row. So my approach included for every row find the peak element n then just need to check for the above and below row if its peak element and can return. Time Complexity : O(nlogm) Space Complexity : O(1) Interviewer was looking for a n(logm) solution and he told my approach was correct and I proceeded to code out the whole solution on paper.

2. The second question was based on n-ary tree Example : 1 level 0 / \ 2 3 level 1 / / | \ 4 5 6 7 level 2

Q queries will be given : [startnode, endnode, node] Example if q [ 2,5,7] If path of 2-> 5 includes nodes 2,1,3,5. From node 7 - node 3 is the nearest which is also present in path. It was a LCA ( lowest Common Ancestor) Question and a Competitive programming concept Binary Lifting can be used for most optimal solution.

My Approach : As the question was been explained I understood it had something to do with LCA and I told LCA and the Interviewer smiled as I was able to guess the type of question very quickly. For startnode and endnode first find LCA so for node 2 and 5 it would be 1 and then I told I can run a dfs for the node and find nearest node from the path, he told me I can optimize more and don't need a dfs so was able to come up with the solution where using parent node

information and the depth the traversal was not needed. I coded out the solution on paper , also implemented the LCA function. Interviewer was satisfied , we had also discussed time and space complexity for every approach. He asked me do I have any Competitive Programming Experience I Told yes as I had given contests on codeforces and codechef along with Leetcode. Interviewer was satisfied as I did further optimizations in the LCA Approach. It was a binary lifting question where can find using logn and its most optimized approach, interviewer was ok if not able to code binary lifting in my case as I was able to achieve a similar optimized approach and had wrote code for it.

He asked do I have any questions for him-

I asked him about NPCI and the system design for UPI payments in general, we had a discussion on NPCI and his work experience and his role in company.

3. Technical Interview 2 [ Around 14 students appeared]

My Technical Round 2 took place after the HR round. For some students, the HR round happened before Technical Round 2. This might have been done to speed up the process or to save time. Technical Round 2 was similar to Round 1 - we were asked to solve two coding questions on paper. I gave a quick introduction before starting the questions.

1. Given an array [ "abc", "or", "xyxcba", "cba", "xz"] Check if a palindromic string exists after concatenation of 2 strings. For above example : we have abc + cba = abccba OR abc + xyxcba = abxcyxcba There might exist many palindromic string can return any 1.

My Approach : First discussed the brute force where for every pair check if palindrome and then the optimized version included usage of Trie , in trie can store the reverse string suppose in trie abc is already stored in reverse as cba and for string cba later can see c exists and a word exists so can return , now for a case like xyxcba also forms palindrome with abc right so now see that xyx is itself a palindrome so from the rest it forms palindrome so it will form a palindrome. It had TC : O(n*k*k) n= length of array , k=length of a string I asked is there any further optimized approach and interviewer said no and I proceeded to code out the Trie solution.

2. It was the exact question from Codeforces with Rating 2700 which is around International Grandmaster (IGM) level - https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/1270/G My Approach : Explained the brute force and the Interviewer gave hint to focus on the constarints 𝑖−𝑛 ≤ 𝑎𝑖 ≤ 𝑖−1 and separate the dependent variables

I was able to derive that i-ai lies between (1 to n ) and it was 1-indexed array so even I lied from (1 to n) Drew edges from i to i-ai and saw it formed a cycle, I understood that the sum will be 0 where there will be cycle. He asked to explain why the cycle leads to 0. This was a question No student in any panel was able to come to optimized solution on its own. I think this particular question was asked to see thinking process and if can reach to solution with help of hints maybe. I dry ran the approach of cycle, didn't completely wrote the code as time was up but the basic idea I wrote on paper.

Interviewer asked if I had any questions -

We had a discussion on overall experience also in PPT they had mentioned they used T-store internally in PhonePe I asked about it and had a discussion over same. Also how UPI payments can be made using SMS service too.

3. Hiring Manager Round [ Around 11 students appeared]

During the interview, I began by greeting the interviewer with a "Good Afternoon." He asked me to start with my internship experiences, where I explained both roles, my responsibilities, and key learnings. We then moved on to the projects on my resume - two web projects and one mobile application. I had the app on my phone and offered to demonstrate it, which he agreed to. The app included an ML model, leading to a discussion on how the model was integrated and called from the backend. He appreciated the design of the app. He then asked if I had worked on any team projects. I shared a project that contributed to my team winning an international hackathon featuring participants from over 10 countries.

Since I had mentioned teaching experience on my resume, he asked how I got that opportunity and what I taught. I explained that I had taught 11th and 12th-grade students, helping them with computer science and clearing doubts in other subjects for college entrance exams. I also spoke about my volunteering experience with an NGO, where I taught 7th and 8th graders. The NGO had on learning about my prior teaching background asked me to help students prepare for Olympiad topics. Following that, we discussed one of my major projects in detail, including the system architecture. I explained the flow using paper diagrams and covered topics like authentication, how OAuth works, OTP-based verification, and how API calls are made.

Toward the end, the interviewer asked about my most-used application, and I said YouTube. He then asked me to design a system for YouTube Shorts. I drew a high-level system design on paper and explained various components, including how the system dynamically adapts video quality based on network bandwidth. We also discussed why I am pursuing a minor in management from SP Jain, and wrapped up with a few HR-type questions - one of which was how I handled conflict. I shared an example from the JPMC Code for Good Hackathon, explaining how our team resolved a disagreement.

This round primarily tested knowledge of my resume and understanding of system design.

When Interviewer asked do I have any questions - I asked 1-2 questions and discussed topics related to it. We also had discussion over if in future payments can be done using facial recognition and the challenges and how it can be misused.

A total of 7 students received the offer, and I was one of them.

The process consisted of 3 rounds 1 Test and 2 technical rounds. The Entire process including interviews was online.

1. Technical and Aptitude Test

The round had a mix of technical and aptitude questions, with a total duration of about 90 minutes. It was a proctored test and divided into three sections: Aptitude, DSA, and SQL. All the questions were MCQ-based, so no actual coding was required.

For the aptitude part, the questions were pretty standard--quant, reasoning, and problem-solving type. Practicing from Indiabix is more than enough. I'd suggest taking timed mock tests, because I personally lost a few easy marks just due to time running out :(

The DSA section had MCQs on topics like BSTs, AVL Trees, Merge Sort, time complexities, and guess-the-output questions. Nothing too unexpected, but you need your basics really clear. GeeksforGeeks (GFG) is the best prep source here.

Finally, the SQL section was entirely Oracle SQL based. Lots of questions on joins, subqueries, aggregate functions, etc. If you're comfortable with writing and analyzing queries, you'll be fine

Overall, it was a balanced test--no coding, just solid concepts and quick thinking.

2. Technical Interview I [ 40 - 50 mins]

here were two interviewers, and the interview began with a quick introduction where I had to talk about myself and my general hobbies. After that, they asked me about the programming languages I was comfortable with, and I said Python. From there, the discussion moved to OOPs concepts in Python. They asked me to share my screen and write a simple Car class with a few objects. Then they followed it up with questions on types of constructors and some magic methods I had used. They specifically asked about the use of __new__ and __call__ methods.

Next, I got a string parsing question where I had to convert data into a list of dictionaries. The problem was straightforward, and I felt communication skills played a big role in explaining my thought process clearly.

They also gave me a SQL question where I had to calculate the average ratings for a movie using two tables with joins. After that, there was a question on data warehousing concepts, which I wasn't familiar with and I straight away said I dont know it.

The interview wrapped up with a few questions about BlackRock as a company and why I was interested in working there.

3. Technical Interview II [16 Students ][30-40 mins]

This round had one senior interviewer who handled all the questions. He began with a quick introduction and even asked me to recall who had taken my Round 1, which I honestly couldn't remember .

Next, he went through all the projects from my resume and asked about the tech stack used. Since the role was for Data Engineering and most of my projects were in ML/Data Science, he wanted to know why I still felt I was a good fit.

After that, he asked me how to store a polynomial and gave around 5-6 SQL queries verbally. I requested to share my screen and solve them on notepad, and he was fine with that.

He then moved on to questions about RAG (Retrieval Augmented Generation) and asked if I was comfortable with it. Towards the end, the questions shifted to my daily use of AI, and he wrapped up by asking a thought-provoking one: "Why hire people when AI can already generate code?"

journey.prep:
1. Placement preparation should start 3-4 months prior to the placement season. You can do it during your 5th semester. Preparing 1 month before placements will create huge pressure and stress. You will get no time to learn before OA or Interview Day. Ultimately, it depends on you how you manage your time.

2. If preparing for non-tech, do not fully rely on non-tech roles, as only 10% of roles are non-tech and 90% of jobs on our campus are tech roles (a mix of SDE and data roles). Always have a backup and prepare for the tech side by side. Read my story below to avoid this mistake.

3. Practice DSA and Aptitude and be well-versed before the placement season begins. It cannot be done one night prior or one week prior. And DSA & Aptitude done one night prior cannot help you clear OAs easily.

4. Once the OA-related part is cleared, focus on practicing for interviews. Try to give mocks to friends or try to improve communication skills in front of a mirror.

5. Prepare an approximate 2-3 minute introduction talking about your academics, internship/work experience details (showing its significance and what impactful work you have done), academic achievements (if any), and your interest in the role offered. This is the starting punch in which the interviewer understands you as a whole, analyzes the candidate, and prepares the next consecutive questions.

6. Always have a smile on your face and try to connect with the interviewer instead of just answering questions like a robot. Do not panic or be nervous, try to handle the situation.

7. Always ask effective questions to the interviewer at the end. Frame questions that can impress the interviewer and leave a lasting impression. Asking questions also shows that you are curious about the company. Do not ask vague or very basic questions.

8. Be very well-versed with the projects you prepare or put in your resume. You can expect deep questions about them. Diversify your projects, which will help you apply for various roles.

9. Usually, people say "do not compare yourself with others," and that's true--comparing yourself with others will always put you under stress and pressure. But what I would suggest is just keep a short analysis of your competitions, so that you know you need to perform better to clear tests & interviews.

10. Balance your preparation. Do not focus on only one skill. For eg. Do not do ONLY DSA & no Dev and Similarly do not do ONLY Dev & no DSA. Balance both things, plus additional CS Fundamentals and AIML concepts.

11. Do not get depressed by rejections. Rejection is a part of placements, and every rejection gives a learning. You should not give up and should keep trying again and again. Switch ON your beast mode and never settle until it is achieved. Trust on God's plan. Even God takes our exam before giving results.

12. Always remember, placement is the joint result of hard work and luck. Luck is not in our control, but hard work is in our control. And Hard work increases the probability of Luck favouring you. You need to put in all your efforts to stand out from the crowd . AND if you are lazy and unambitious, then trust me you are already behind in the race.

Back Story - My story is that I was purely preparing for JPMC non-tech roles during my third year, and I was not focusing much on tech roles. I was confident enough and took a risk that I would prepare for JPMC ONLY and get selected there. But things became uncertain, my resume didn't even get shortlisted for JPMC. I had thoroughly prepared for the OA, GD, interviews, and many more, but I was not even able to cross the initial step, i.e., resume shortlisting. That was a depressing night for me.

After that, I was unable to clear tech role OAs (because I was less prepared) and kept getting rejected. So, I decided to give my best at that moment and started very hard preparation for tech roles. Meanwhile, by that time, I already had an inclination towards data-related roles because I was also interested in machine learning and data science. So next, I purely focused on clearing OAs. I prepared all the stuff that is required for OAs and practiced aptitude. Companies were coming, I was getting rejected, companies were running out, but parallelly I was preparing harder. After much efforts, the time came when I was finally able to clear my first OA, which was BlackRock, and I was confident enough for the interview (not overconfident) that I could be able to impress Interviewer. Interview is nothing but selling yourself. I prepared all the stuff related to the data role (as I was shortlisted for Aladdin Data) and prepared each and everything about my resume, my projects and technical concepts. I gave the interview confidently. Later, the results came out, and I was able to enjoy the fruit of my hard work.

General Advice -

Decide what you want to pursue Tech or Non tech. Tech people need not worry much because there will be a greater number of opportunities. But for Non tech people, kindly note that opportunities for Non tech are fewer and limited. So if preparing for Non Tech, then also prepare for Tech side by side as a backup. Luck plays a very vital role and you never know what is the next move of your luck. The only thing you can do is be an ideal person who has knowledge of all skills and be ready for every kind of job. At the end, you are the captain of your own destiny . Placement Observations -

Below are the observations that I found during placements, and these can help you note down things in advance. THIS IS JUST an observation, do not rely completely on it.

1. The average hiring ratio is 5:1. Example - if 30 students shortlisted for interviews, then on avg 5-6 students will be selected. The number can be higher or lower as well, but averagely its 5:1.

2. Copying can be very risky. If found, you might not be able to sit for next 2-3 companies (which may be good companies).

3. Students with ONLY DSA skills were unable to answer web development questions in interviews, and students with ONLY development skills were unable to answer DSA questions in interviews. You need to prepare both.

4. There's no fix date or time of any company. Anybody can come anytime. Or even may not come.

5. Communication skills matter most in interviews and GDs. Even if you are intelligent but unable to convey your answers, you might not move forward.

6. You might see your friends or peers getting placed, but you should not take that as depression. Depression will slow down your productivity and willingness. Instead, you should learn from your mistakes, learn from your peers, put in more efforts, do not give up and achieve your goal.

7. Things to consider about Bad Luck -

- You might not get selected in your dream company.

- Your resume might not get shortlisted even being perfect.

- Your server may crash during test and you are out.

- You might get hard/strict panel for interview.

- Your interview might get scheduled in the last slot. By the time your slot comes, the company may have already made decisions.

- Undeserving students might get shortlisted.

8. About Good Luck - it will come surprisingly.

Resources: These are general resources for both roles. You can also refer individual company interview experience sheet and previous year sheets for more detailed prep.

Tech and Data Roles -

1. DSA/Coding - Striver's A to Z sheet. If not able to complete full sheet then atleast try to cover concepts from each topic from the sheet. Problem solving on Leetcode, HackerRank etc platform. For SQL you can do basics on https://sqlbolt.com/ and advance on SQL 50 on Leetcode. For OOPS and CS Fundamentals like DBMS, OS, CCN you can refer any resources of your own.

2. Projects - hackathon project or any impactful project which can impress interviewer. For data roles, you can do analytics or machine learning project.

3. Aptitude - Indiabix, GFG. Refer each topic of indiabix individually from YT or any other resource. Practice aptitude as much as possible because practice only can help you solve questions in OA quickly, with fast calculation, saving time, completing all questions and build confidence for even selecting tukka option.

4. Puzzles - refer GFG puzzles.

5. For data roles, make sure to do machine learning concepts and implement models for better understanding. Non tech Roles -

1. Aptitude - same as like mentioned above. Also do current affairs, market awareness of last 1 year.

2. Finance, Case Study, Guesstimate - Best resource sheet prepared by my senior. Refer this. https://drive.google.com/file/d/1Nwf3VM4tBb92TxsgUxDtghXyLeSLHU_v/view?usp=s

3. Additional resources -

- This is all-in-one course for Finance. No other course required - https://www.coursera.org/specializations/finance-and-financial-markets

- Note that only JPMC requires Finance knowledge. Rest other Non Tech roles require knowledge of Consulting, Marketing, Supply Chain, Markets & Economics etc. So you can practice Case Studies of various non tech fields.

The process consisted of 3 rounds 1 Test and 2 technical rounds. The Entire process including interviews was online.

OA on 22/8/2025 Interviews 2 rounds on 28/8/2025 .

Eligibility criteria was 7.5+ CGPA. I would recommend to maintain CGPA of 8 which is eligible for almost all companies except for few.

Preplacement Talk was conducted on 20/08/25. And this was a Pool Campus Recruitment Drive.

1. OA Round [100+ Candidates ] Test was conducted on eLitmus platform and it was camera proctored. Duration was 1.5 hrs consisting 3 sections. Since BlackRock visited our campus for the first time, we didn't had any previous interview experience so I searched on Web and Interview experience in YT to prepare and understand the pattern. The actual test pattern was similar to what I researched.

1. Aptitude section.

- It consisted of Quantitative Aptitude, Data interpretation and Logical Reasoning.

- The key point here is that calculators were not allowed, so you need to be fast with your mental maths and logic.

- Practising various questions and giving mock aptitude test on any online platform will help you to develop quick maths skill.

- Also prepare all types of aptitude topics because which type of question can come you never know.

2. Technical/Programming.

- This was not a coding section, but an MCQ based on coding/programming questions. It consisted of 2 types: Flowchart and Pseudocodes.

- Guess the output of code snippet and guess the output of flowchart were asked. Flowchart were not easy for sure. They were complicated and require practice to tackle such kind of question s. Some questions were fill in the blanks in flow chart.

- Pseudocodes were on Data Structure operations mostly related to Trees.

3. SQL Section -

- It consisted of SQL Code snippets. It was actually Oracle SQL which has slightly different syntax but overall logics were same.

- I suggest cover every topic of SQL right from basics, joints, subqueries etc. In MCQ, options are very closely differentiated from each other, so firm remembrance of syntax and logic is important for time- based questions.

Overall, Test was moderate level and balanced. Time management is very important, you need to be very fast in identifying the logic, calculating the maths for quant questions, imagining the outputs and understanding the code snippets. Practicing such questions beforehand boosts confidence and improves critical thinking ability.

2. Technical Interview Round 1 (Online) [25 to 30 were shortlisted (including waitlisted students)]

My first interview round began with a polite greeting and a brief introduction about myself. I prepared my introduction which aligned with the role offered, matching my skill set with the role and showed that I am interested in this role. Then a follow-up question was asked based on my work experience, what skills I gained, and what were my learnings there. Then the conversation moved on to the projects in my resume. Imp pointer - Always put the project which you are very confident about in the first place. I was asked for an overview of all projects mentioned in my resume and a detailed explanation of the first project. In-depth questions were asked regarding the project. It was an ML project, so questions related to Python, which library was used, which model was used, why that model, what were the results, what were the challenges, how the dataset was formed, etc., everything in depth was asked. Also, they asked twisted questions like if dataset columns are changed or a new column is added, then how the model will react. Then what was the outcome of the project, what problem does it solve, etc. Make sure to know the in-and-out of your project (also about the coding part) so that you can answer confidently. I was asked to explain a function of my project code.

Next, the interviewer jumped to the coding part and asked me to open an online compiler and gave a question to code in Python. I was familiar with CPP, so I asked him and coded the solution in CPP. He then changed the input array and asked me to print the solution. Then he asked about time and space complexity, then how I can optimize it, and so on. The question was easy - print the frequency of each element.

At last, the interviewer asked me about what BlackRock does and why I wanted to join BlackRock. Then he asked me how I stay updated about Finance and AI. Luckily, I used to read the news, so I was able to answer. He asked for any latest news regarding AI, and I answered him with three news. Then the interview ended, and I was given an opportunity to ask them any questions. So I asked them two appropriate questions. Overall, the interview went very well. My preparation helped me to answer confidently in the interview.

3. Technical Interview Round 2 (Online) [15-16 students approx] My second round was a little bit stricter than the previous round. The interviewer directly asked me for my introduction and straightaway asked me a DSA question. He asked me which language I code in and to name the data structures of that language. Then he asked me some micro questions which then layer by layer ended up asking the "Kth largest element" question and its optimization. Then he asked scenario -based questions which were based on HashMaps. Then he asked OOPS concepts. Then again, I was grilled o n the first project mentioned in the resume. Similarly, in round 2 also, the interviewer manipulated my project inputs and project dataset and asked how my project would perform on manipulated data. This conveys that you should know each and every function , code, input-output scenario, and limitation of your project. Overall, the interview went medium (according to me). But answering confidently and being transparent would have impressed the interviewer even though he was strict.

Also, always keep a smiling face and do not show your anxiety or fear. A happy and good conversation between you and the interviewer always results well .

4. Temporary Round [10 students] On the interview day, i.e., 28 Aug, all results were already announced to the TPO. However, an AI copy-case incident happened during our interview rounds. The company caught some candidates using AI, which was very clearly evident to them. So, they decided to cancel the recruitment from SPIT. We all were tensed and anxious because, due to some candidates, everybody would have to suffer. So, the next day, Sikka Sir called 10 students for the next round, and Sikka Sir took an HR kind-of interview of us. Later, they discussed the copy-case incident and how they convinced the company not to cancel recruitment from SPIT, as BlackRock was visiting SPIT for the first time. After a stressful situation, Sikka Sir finally announced the names of the selected candidates, and we were very happy. The ones who copied using AI were straightaway rejected from the process.

[ Total 10 selected students -> 6 for SDE + 2 Aladdin Data + 2 Global Marketing]

customSections.title: Advice & Tips for Juniors
customSections.content:
1. Placement preparation should start 3-4 months prior to the placement season. You can do it during your 5th semester. Preparing 1 month before placements will create huge pressure and stress. You will get no time to learn before OA or Interview Day. Ultimately, it depends on you how you manage your time.

2. If preparing for non-tech, do not fully rely on non-tech roles, as only 10% of roles are non-tech and 90% of jobs on our campus are tech roles (a mix of SDE and data roles). Always have a backup and prepare for the tech side by side. Read my story below to avoid this mistake.

3. Practice DSA and Aptitude and be well-versed before the placement season begins. It cannot be done one night prior or one week prior. And DSA & Aptitude done one night prior cannot help you clear OAs easily.

4. Once the OA-related part is cleared, focus on practicing for interviews. Try to give mocks to friends or try to improve communication skills in front of a mirror.

5. Prepare an approximate 2-3 minute introduction talking about your academics, internship/work experience details (showing its significance and what impactful work you have done), academic achievements (if any), and your interest in the role offered. This is the starting punch in which the interviewer understands you as a whole, analyzes the candidate, and prepares the next consecutive questions.

6. Always have a smile on your face and try to connect with the interviewer instead of just answering questions like a robot. Do not panic or be nervous, try to handle the situation.

7. Always ask effective questions to the interviewer at the end. Frame questions that can impress the interviewer and leave a lasting impression. Asking questions also shows that you are curious about the company. Do not ask vague or very basic questions.

8. Be very well-versed with the projects you prepare or put in your resume. You can expect deep questions about them. Diversify your projects, which will help you apply for various roles.

9. Usually, people say "do not compare yourself with others," and that's true--comparing yourself with others will always put you under stress and pressure. But what I would suggest is just keep a short analysis of your competitions, so that you know you need to perform better to clear tests & interviews.

10. Balance your preparation. Do not focus on only one skill. For eg. Do not do ONLY DSA & no Dev and Similarly do not do ONLY Dev & no DSA. Balance both things, plus additional CS Fundamenta

journey.prep:
I wanted to share some of my thoughts after going through the interview process with companies like Baker Hughes, Dolat Capital, Quantiphy, and BlackRock. My main interest has always been in mathematical coding, and mathematical problems solving (which was thoroughly asked in dolat capital) rather than traditional DSA, so it was a surprise when my journey led me to a global marketing role.

What really struck me across all the interviews was that confidence is a huge part of the game. The interviewers valued direct and clear answers, and how you present your thought process seems just as important as the final solution. They almost always threw in a couple of really tricky questions that felt designed to see how you handle pressure. Honestly, getting through one of those tough problems gives you a major boost and makes the rest of the interview feel much more manageable.

A major wake-up call for me was in the Dolat Capital interview when they started asking deep questions about C++, which was definitely not my strong part. It taught me what I now call the "30% rule": even for your weakest subjects, try to have at least a basic, 30% level of understanding. It's far better than being caught completely off guard. Similarly, the BlackRock interview was an eye-opener. They did a deep dive into my project's architecture, asking about the data preprocessing pipeline and my storage choices. It made me realize that interviewers want to see that you can think about the entire system, not just the code you wrote.

In these 4 interviews, the common question was on my project. They told me to go through my projects and ask deeply on that one.

First, only list projects you are 100% confident you can defend, because they will ask tough, detailed questions. Second, be careful about listing an outlier tech stack. If one project uses a technology that doesn't fit the rest of your story, interviewers will zoom in on it.. Your projects should highlight your strengths, not create traps.

So, while my path took an unexpected turn, the technical interview process itself was an incredible learning experience. The biggest lesson was the importance of a balanced strategy: know your strengths, strategically cover your weaknesses, and always be ready to explain your thinking with confidence.

There were 3 rounds in this process. (For GM role)

1. Online assessment

2. Technical interview

3. HR round

1. Online Assessment[ 100 students appeared for this round]

This round was conducted on E-litmus platform and was proctored.

It consisted on mainly 3 sections and all were of objective type(mcqs):

1. Logical reasoning,verbal reasoning,aptitude

2. Coding / algorithms

3. DBMS and SQL

This was of 90 minutes, but each section and subsection had its own time limit set.

There were 4 subsections in 1st section, like verbal reasoning, logical reasoning, quantitative aptitude, and assertion reasoning type.All these subsections were easy to solve but lengthy, especially the quantitative aptitude one.Each sub section had its own time limit and navigation in subsection was not allowed, so had to carefully answer or leave the question. The questions were of cat-type basic aptitude and english questions, like speed and time, height and distance, work and efficiency, upstream and downstream, profit and loss, missing number or wrong number in the sequence.

The 2nd section had flowchart type questions based on an algorithm or a scenario like lottery system, shopping mart. It had 4-5 questions based on each scenario, so had 4-5 such scenarios and each flowchart had a missing box to fill for that algorithm. There were some loops based mathematical coding questions as well, like to test the divisibility by 17 , what should be the main line :- first n-1 digits - 5* last digit should be divisible by 17. Then there were lengthy loop questions to calculate some mathematical sequences, like agp, gp, sum of squares.

The 3rd section was of dbms and sql and had queries and database concepts like normalization, acid properties. Major questions were output type questions to the queries, like sysdate from dual, to_char function, and many more based on dual .

In the OA, try not to spend more time on just 1 question, as it was very much time bound, especially the flowchart questions and quantitative aptitude.

2. Technical Interview[Nearly 35 were selected for this round (7 waitlist) ]

I was selected for the Global Marketing role which had 7 shortlists (3 waitlists).This round started with my introduction and the interviewer asked me to go through my projects. I mentioned about my film recommendation project, on which the 2 panelists asked me to explain its architecture, how will I expand the project to industrial level, which tech stack I used, and why so. Later, they asked me to explain about data collection and preprocessing at industrial level.

That was it, I felt that I stumbled upon some questions based on the architecture. 3 students cleared this round and went to the hr round.

3. HR[ 16 total shortlists- 3 for GM role] (Technical interview-II ,HR for GM role)

It started with my introduction, followed by my projects. HR later asked me some questions like:

1. What do I think about the use of AI and its extent in next 5 years?

2. Does AI make you lazy?

3. Where do you see yourself in next 5 years?

4. What are your weakness and what plan do you have to improve those aspects?

5. Few questions about BlackRock as a company and what does it do?

Total of 10 students were selected overall. 2 for Global marketing role.

Online Assesment - 22-08-2025 Technical Round 1 - 28-08-2025 Technical Round 2 - 28-08-2025 HR - 29-08-2025

1. Online Assessment Round [] Level: Medium - Hard

Platform: eLitmus

Duration: Somewhat 1 Hr 30 min or 1Hr 45 min

● Timed sections on various topics like:

○ Aptitude

○ Reasoning

○ Verbal

○ Flowcharts

○ SQL

● All sections will be timed and there will be a window after each section

where you can take a break after every section.

● For every question you can answer, go previous or skip for the time.

● When all questions of the section are done then the system will throw the

skipped question so don't panic and waste your time on questions that you

are not able to do at that moment.

● Just do all the questions as fast as possible.

● The DSA will be easy to medium.

○ Most questions in DSA was from tree data-structure, specially BST

formation, preorder, postorder, and formation of the same.

○ I would recommend doing and practicing AVL Trees as well

As some of my friends were asked questions based on that

● The toughest question was from the critical thinking :

○ There was a problem statement and there was ﬂowchart for that

particular problem, for example platform assignment for a train.

○ You have to analyse the pseudo code and understand the ﬂow

chart.

○ There were 3-5 question on one ﬂowchart.

○ There were around 2-3 ﬂow-chart.

○ Every ﬂow-chart was very big, bulky and contained around 5-8

decisions.

○ There were some empty blocks in the ﬂow-chart which we had to

ﬁll by understanding the ﬂow chart and by options given in the

mcq.

● Last section was SQL, all about DBMS, do have a closer look to DBMS,

specially very in-depth topics which no one teaches.

2. Technical Round 1 [ 35 candidates appeared for this round]

So my technical round was scheduled at 9.30 am and it was an online interview on Webex Platform Interview began with my introduction , keep it short and crisp , REMEMBER your entire interview will go around your introduction so make sure to say things you know , dont fake it As well as dont even think or try to cheat on online interviews as many of them were caught by TPO and strict actions were taken Then the very first question was asked to me about What was my most recent project I have worked on ? Explaining the entire project , I started explaining The architecture of the project and the purpose of the project. There will be a lot of cross questioning on your projects so have thorough understanding on them After some more chit chatting on projects and resume , panelist jumped on DSA I was asked a famous question of Linked List (How to detect a Cycle in a Linked List) As soon as i started with the optimal approach of Slow and Fast Pointers , the interviewer said me not to use this method and think of an optimal approach other that this KEY Point - Never jump directly on optimal approaches , walk through brute better and optimal in a structured manner Then after some time the next questions was on my primary language , I answered C++ Follow up question immediately - WHY C++ and not JAVA , what are the primary differences between them and some more questions around it were asked Then the interviewer started asking about OOPS concepts About Four Pillars and differences between them , I answered it very confidently using examples to demonstrate better understanding ,

Q) Applications with examples on all four pillars with understanding on each one of them and what are the differences between between some concepts of OOPS in java and c++ like in c++ we can inherit from multiple parents and in java we cant , then whats the solution for java he asked and follow up on what i was saying REMEMBER - he will ask follow ups on what you say and grill till a point he knows that you know the concepts well , so dont fake it answer it honestly. Q) Difference between interfaces and abstraction , static , can we instantiate objects or not Q)I am creating my own language in which we can instantiate static , What will be the core difficulties and challenges and how would you resolve them. KEY - Deep Understanding of OOPS was very essential as half of my interview revolved around it In between some Managerial HR type questions were also asked , just communicate well here nothing much for these questions,

Dont let any awkward silence to be created at any time , You can take some time from the interviewer to think and then answer , So just be confident and you are good to go

At the end of the interview he asked me about how good knowledge do you have about finance and like some common questions on do you manage your portfolio , what type of investments do you do and We discussed on that for about 5-10 minutes , Here you can show how eager you are to learn and break into finance The discussion went so well that the interview started becoming a talking session . Then he asked me about current affairs and what latest news I had read on BlackRock

I had read some news so I could answer these questions very well . Then I was asked, "Do I have any questions for them ? Never say no , always prepare some good questions to be asked at the end of the interview which gives them the feeling of eagerness to learn

TIP- However good your technical skills might be , but if you can't communicate and convey and make them understand about your thought process then its no use So yes work on your soft skills as well

3. Technical Round 2

Dont know how many got call for 2nd interview Round 2 was a bit more formal and short than the previous round , as usual started with my introduction and then on projects and resume as i mentioned in round 1

Then on a specific project he started grilling me Q)Screen was shared and i was asked to open Notepad and write down schema of my project , how i passed that data on backend and questions related to storing them on databases Q)I was asked to write a few SQL queries regarding the schema i made Have a good knowledge of JOINS , GROUP BY , WINDOW FN , DATE FN and you are good to go

After this schema design and querying again we moved to OOPS Started with fundamental questions and gradually complexity was increasing , so even if you dont know the exact answer , try to gather some points and convey the thought process in between Q)I was asked on how i used concepts of OOPS in each project and how i utilized the four pillars Here explain the architecture and gist of project and then go on with the answer to how OOPS played a major role in each projects in some or the other way

I wasnt asked many development questions , but my friends were asked questions on React and Backend , so read the JD for the role you are applying for and have ideas in some way or the other.

PRANK ROUND (THERE WAS NO HR ) During the BlackRock process, after finishing my two technical rounds, our TPC told us about the prank round that had been taken earlier by our TPO head, Mr. Vinod Sikka. On the same day, I also had an EDS interview scheduled at their office, so I was really stressed trying to manage both. While waiting for the BlackRock result, the tension kept building, but finally, my name was announced for the SDE role. That moment was such a big relief and honestly one of the happiest feelings--I realized how important it is to stay calm under pressure and I felt super excited to join BlackRock.

Read some more interview experiences on GFG as well of students from VIT
