There was an Online Assessment followed by 2 Technical Interview Rounds.

Since it was Pool Campus Placement various other colleges also participated in it.

1. [Online Assessment Test] (After PPT)

The online assessment round was fully MCQ-based with a total duration of two hours. The test was divided into three main sections: Aptitude, Technical, and Flowchart-based Coding. Each section had 3-4 subsections with individual timers ranging between 10 to 20 minutes, which made time management a very crucial factor. Students with cgpa>7.5 were allowed, and only a smaller percentage were shortlisted based on sectional performance and overall accuracy.

The Aptitude section consisted of questions from quantitative aptitude, logical reasoning, and verbal ability. Topics like speed, time and distance, profit and loss, probability, puzzles, and data interpretation were commonly asked. The verbal subsection included paragraph-based comprehension questions that were strictly timed, requiring quick reading and precise answering. My approach here was to eliminate wrong options quickly and focus on accuracy instead of random guessing.

The Technical section tested core programming concepts, primarily object-oriented programming (OOPs) in Java, C++, and Python. Questions asked us to identify differences between abstraction and encapsulation, select the correct definition of method overloading versus overriding, or point out the role of garbage collection in Python versus destructors in C++. SQL-based MCQs included queries for finding the second highest salary, identifying invalid JOINs, and error-checking. There were also input-output questions where code snippets were given and we had to predict the exact output or the type of error (runtime or compile-time). I prepared for this by revising OOPs fundamentals and practicing SQL queries in advance, which helped me trace the logic accurately during the test.

The flowchart-based coding section was slightly different from standard coding rounds, as it involved tracing algorithms presented in flowchart form. Questions asked us to trace a given flowchart and select the correct output from the options. I managed this by simulating the flow on rough paper step by step, which reduced mistakes and saved time.

To prepare for this round, I practiced aptitude questions regularly on IndiaBix and GeeksforGeeks Aptitude. For technical sections, I revised OOPs concepts in depth and solved SQL MCQs from GeeksforGeeks SQL MCQs. I also focused on understanding common compile-time and runtime errors in different languages, as error-based MCQs were common. For flowcharts, I brushed up on the basics of loops, conditionals, and algorithm tracing.

On the day of the test, I made sure to keep rough paper ready for quick calculations and flowchart tracing. Since the subsections were auto-submitted after the timer,

I was careful not to spend too much time on any one question. Overall, the key points you need to learn is to manage time effectively, stay calm during timed reading comprehensions, and have strong fundamentals in OOPs and SQL.

2. [Technical Interview Round 1] [ 27 appeared (excluding 8 waiting not allowed)] .

The first interview round began with a polite greeting and a brief self-introduction, where I highlighted my academic background, project work, and any relevant experiences. The interviewer then asked me to explain my projects in detail, focusing on the technologies used, the challenges faced, and the outcomes. I was also asked about my work experience, hobbies, and the skills I had gained from practical exposure. From there, the discussion moved to technical fundamentals, where I was asked about the four pillars of Object-Oriented Programming and to name the programming languages I was most comfortable with.

The interviewer also touched on role-fit and motivation questions, such as why I wanted to join BlackRock. I answered honestly, focusing on my interest in working with a global firm known for innovation and technology in finance.

When asked about my knowledge of finance, I admitted that I did not have sufficient background but emphasized my willingness and eagerness to learn, which the interviewer seemed to appreciate. Toward the end, I was given the opportunity to ask a question, and I inquired about his routine and experience at BlackRock, which led to a more casual and insightful exchange.

Throughout the interview, I made sure to remain confident and articulate in my responses, even though I knew it was challenging to stay composed in such situations. The interviewer maintained a friendly and supportive approach, which made the conversation more comfortable. My key takeaway from this round was that confidence, clarity in explaining one's projects, and openness to learning new domains like finance are crucial.

Links:

https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/java/object-oriented-programming-oops-concept-in-java/

https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/aptitude/puzzles/

3. [Technical Interview Round 2] (16 students appeared)

The second interview round was more project-focused and technical in nature. The interviewer began by asking me to choose one project that I would like to deep dive into. Once I selected the project, she asked detailed questions about its architecture, schema design, and the reasoning behind my technical choices. A key discussion point was on database design, where she asked me to compare SQL vs. NoSQL and explain which one I preferred in different scenarios. I elaborated on aspects like structured vs. unstructured data, scalability, and consistency, while also discussing how collections, documents, and sub-collections work in NoSQL databases.

The interviewer then shifted the conversation toward financial awareness, asking how I keep myself updated with current financial situations. I responded by mentioning sources like financial news portals, online articles, and business publications, while also admitting I was still in the process of building deeper financial knowledge. Moving further, I was asked data analysis-oriented questions such as how I handled datasets in my projects, what tools I used, and importantly, whether I had deployed my work or kept it at an experimental stage. I clarified the scope of deployment in my projects and described my exposure to end-to-end development.

Overall, this round tested my ability to defend my project choices, my database knowledge, my awareness of financial trends, and my practical experience in implementation. The interviewer maintained an analytical approach, probing deeper into technical and real-world application aspects, which made it important to stay structured in my responses and connect technical knowledge with practical use cases.

https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/dbms/introduction-to-nosql/

https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/reactjs/react/

Prank Round

During the BlackRock process, after finishing my two technical rounds, our TPC told us about the prank round that had been taken earlier by our TPO head, Mr. Vinod Sikka. On the same day, I also had an EDS interview scheduled at their office, so I was really stressed trying to manage both. While waiting for the BlackRock result, the tension kept building, but finally, my name was announced for the SDE role. That moment was such a big relief and honestly one of the happiest feelings--I realized how important it is to stay calm under pressure and I felt super excited to join BlackRock.

BlackRock shortlisted candidates for four different roles based on the online assessment and the preferences we had selected. The roles were: Aladdin Data (5 shortlisted + 1 waitlisted), Global Marketing (3 shortlisted + 3 waitlisted), Software Engineer (15 shortlisted + 3 waitlisted), and Software Engineer AWT (3 shortlisted + 1 waitlisted), making a total of 34 candidates including waitlists. I was shortlisted for the Software Engineer role, and I will be explaining my experience for this role further.

2. Technical Round 1 [18 candidates shortlisted]

My first technical round was conducted on the Webex platform and was scheduled at 12:00 PM. Since it had to be attended from the TPO office (on campus), I reached beforehand to ensure everything was set. Interestingly, my panel was moving faster than expected, and I was called in at around 11:30 AM, slightly ahead of time. When I joined, there were already two panelists present in the session.

The interview began with the usual greetings and the request to switch on my camera. Soon after, the panel directly moved into DSA-based questions.

The first problem given to me was:

Sort n elements (assume 100) in O(n) time complexity.

At first, I was taken aback because the sorting techniques I was confident with, such as Merge Sort and Quick Sort, typically work in O(n log n) time. I mentioned this to the panel, but they clarified that they were looking specifically for an O(n) solution. After taking a few minutes to think, I demonstrated the sorting of three elements in O(n) time using simple swapping. The interviewers seemed satisfied with my attempt, and they later explained that this problem could be efficiently solved using Cyclic Sort. I pointed out that this might increase the space complexity, but they assured me that it was acceptable. This exchange highlighted an important takeaway:

If you don't know the exact answer, keep communicating and explaining your thought process. Interviewers value your problem-solving approach as much as, or even more than, the final solution.

The next question was a classic 3-Sum Problem. I began with the brute-force approach, then optimized it by explaining the two-pointer technique. While presenting, I carefully analyzed and conveyed the time complexity of each approach. The panel seemed pleased with my structured explanation and progression from brute force to optimal.

After this, I was asked about my preferred programming language. I responded that I primarily use Java for problem-solving and Python for development. One of the interviewers, who was an expert in Java, proceeded to ask me several Java-related questions. These covered concepts from OOPs, threads, and exception handling. Since I had prepared well in these areas, I was able to answer confidently, and the panel appeared satisfied with my responses.

Finally, the round concluded with a puzzle question -- the famous 4 Litres Bucket Problem (reference link). I asked for some time to think and gradually explained my thought process while attempting different possibilities. Although I got stuck briefly, I managed to work through the problem and eventually reached the solution. The interviewers appreciated my persistence and logical reasoning throughout.

Towards the end, I was given the opportunity to ask questions. I asked a couple of role- and company- related questions, which I believe is always a good practice as it demonstrates genuine interest in the company and the position.

3. Technical Round 2 [8 candidates shortlisted]

My second technical round lasted for about 40-50 minutes. It began with a polite exchange of greetings and a brief introduction from both sides, which helped create a comfortable environment. Unlike the first round, this interview was entirely based on my resume (resume_link) and my past experiences.

The interviewer first asked about the SCOPE program at JPMC that I had mentioned in my resume. I explained what the program was about, my role in it, and the key learnings I gained from the experience. She then shifted the focus to my internship, asking in-depth questions to understand my contributions and learnings better. During this discussion, she also asked whether I was comfortable working with Git and GitHub, which I confidently confirmed.

Next, she moved on to the projects listed in my resume. I described two of my projects in detail, focusing on their features, the technologies used, and the real-world problems they aimed to solve. Since one of my projects was from Smart India Hackathon (SIH), where I had emerged as a winner, it particularly caught her attention. She found it inspiring and appreciated how the project had a practical impact on real-world challenges. Her feedback was very encouraging, as she praised my problem-solving mindset and the relevance of my work.

Towards the end, she asked if I had any questions for her. I took the opportunity to ask two:

1. How BlackRock has contributed to her personal and professional growth.

2. How BlackRock is adapting to GenAI and AI/ML modules in its work environment.

She responded warmly, providing detailed and insightful answers to both questions, which gave me a deeper understanding of BlackRock's culture and vision. The interview concluded on a positive note with final greetings.

A small but important takeaway from this round is to always carry a smile and maintain a confident, positive demeanor throughout the interaction -- it goes a long way in leaving a lasting impression.

4. HR Round (Prank Round) [9 candidates shortlisted]

The next stage was supposed to be the HR round, but due to some unfortunate circumstances, BlackRock decided to terminate the process midway. However, our TPO was in constant discussion with them, trying to request and resolve the situation. As a result, instead of a formal HR interview, we had a small, unofficial one-on-one interaction with Sikka Sir, who offered valuable guidance and reassurance.

Later, the final results were announced by Sir himself in the conference room, where he also shared some inspiring words with us. In the end, 6 students were shortlisted for the Software Engineer role, and 3 were placed on the waitlist.

o The Pseudocode subsection contained three MCQs based on different algorithms and data structures. customSections.title: Advice & Tips for Juniors
customSections.content:
• Don't lose confidence even if you face multiple rejections. I interviewed in 8 companies before BlackRock, and though I often felt demotivated, I eventually realized that things fall into place at the right time.

• Even if you feel others less deserving are getting placed, remember that your journey is unique. I had won multiple hackathons but wasn't placed initially -- yet I ended up in a top MNC like BlackRock, which I never even dreamed of.

• Stay confident and keep a smile throughout your interview. It creates a positive impression and shows your enthusiasm.

• Always interact with the interviewers. Don't stay quiet -- even if you don't know the exact answer, explain your thought process. Many times, they are more interested in how you approach the problem rather than just the final solution.

• Practice explaining your projects clearly in bullet points (features, technologies, and real -world impact). This not only shows clarity but also highlights your problem -solving ability.

• Know your resume inside out. HR and technical rounds can both heavily focus on what you've mentioned, so be prepared to discuss every detail confidently.

• Prepare both technical and behavioral aspects. While DSA and technical knowledge are crucial, soft skills, communication, and genuine interest in the company matter equally.

• Ask questions at the end. Always have 2-3 role- or company-related questions ready. This shows curiosity and genuine interest in the company.

• Be consistent in preparation. Whether it's aptitude, SQL, or programming, practicing regularly (LeetCode, mock tests, etc.) makes a big difference.

• Network smartly. Connect with seniors, peers, or professionals on LinkedIn to get insights into the process. Sometimes even small tips can give you an edge.

• And most importantly, trust the process. If one door closes, another one will open with an even better opportunity.

If you have any further doubts, feel free to connect with me on LinkedIn :)

The pointer requirement for applying was 7.5cgpa and above luckily I had just reached to 7.64 in sem 6 but I would recommend keep a steady pointer above 8 if possible to not miss any company or at least above 7.5(even before sem 5 as that's considered when placement initially starts) and don't make the same mistake as me, the role options were software engineer, global marketing, aladdin data and open for all(which I went with) after resume shortlisting 100 participants from our college were selected for the OA

1. [Round 1 OA] [ 100 participants from our college ]

There were 3 section calculators not allowed(always carry them with you though never know when they might be allowed) All MCQs allotted time was 2 hours but I didn't see any overarching timers.

Technical 20 minutes (10 questions) - Coding questions mostly based on trees like find the position, prefix, postfix , what will be the output pretty easy you could do good with only in class knowledge.

SQL 20 minutes (10 questions) - Most were find the correct syntax, command as well as some theory based questions you should be ok if you practice a bit on geeksforgeeks

Aptitude I don't remember the exact time it was split in 4 sections like(6+8+11+9) mins or something like that 2 sections were like in you're average aptitude maths and logic I think, the other 2 I remember better cause they were unique

flowchart section - 2 flowcharts with blanks and 4 questions each to fill them they might look challenging especially given the time crunch but the first one had branches (switch case) so essentially you just had to compare the options for the blank cell with that spot on the other branches the second one had shorter variable names so it was much harder.

Reading section - I don't know what else to call it but essentially there was a table with construction material names and serial numbers, all questions were on matching them.

You can practice aptitude on geeks for geeks but I didn't find any questions like these 2 sections during my practice.

2. [Round 2 Interview 1] [ 35 candidates shortlisted]

The interview was held on webex in the TPO office itself. I was in the first morning slot so I consider myself lucky. I got a call from them and they told me they'll call again at time of joining and be ready. I entered the allotted room and set up my laptop and opened webex and checked my cam and mic, I also practised my intro out loud which I would recommend to you too if you have the time cause in the previous interviews I'd end up speaking in a low voice without noticing. I got the call and the interview started there were 2 interviewers my introduction went smoothly and they asked me about my projects, I had three projects all of which were all group projects, I went through them briefly after which they asked more in depth about each like my contribution in them, why python? Why next.js and not node.js? Is next.js worth upgrading to if you know react? Who made react? I had actually forgotten that one I said "I know a famous company made it but I forgot" even with this mistake the interview went pretty well like a normal conversation maybe because the interviewers chill and I was less tense. There was one question about if my website suddenly had a lot of traffic how would I handle it. Finally they asked me if I had any questions for them and I asked about their experience in the company.

3. [Round 3 Interview 2] [ 16 candidates]

Just as I stepped out of the room I got a call to join my second round of interview I rushed back and set up my laptop and joined the meet this time there was only one interviewer he also asked about my projects but mostly focused on one, what do you mean by scalable? How is your project scalable? How is it Accessible? Why do you call it easy to use? All these are the points I wrote about the project in my resume so only write the truth. I was able to explain all of his questions then he asked me to share my screen and open notepad and write a basic SQL code for inputting data from a source as I was typing there was a connection issue I switched to my hotspot and reconnected and explained what happened (Its possible unexpected things happen during an interview its important to keep calm and not panic) then he told me to stop typing and just explain there were follow up questions like what to do if there is no primarykey? journey.howSecured:
This was a pool campus recruitment process so probably it took place simultaneously in other colleges too. Pre-placement talk was conducted along with VIT Pune students on Webex. Total 3 rounds took place after Pre-placement talk.

● OA (Technical and aptitude test)

● Tech Interview 1

● Tech Interview 2

1. Online Technical+Aptitude test [Approx. 100 students appeared for this round]

The CGPA criteria to apply was 7.5 and above. Having a proper resume format (Jake's preferably) and one good project with unique features(Can be Major project) along with a couple of basic personal projects is sufficient to make your resume get shortlisted in campus placements. Make sure to write the project description in the form of pointers(the various features). Also, don't completely rely on gpt instead list down in your own words and refine it using gpt. Try to keep the project that sells more at the top.

The test was conducted on the eLitmus platform and was proctored. As Blackrock visited for the first time, we had no interview experience to refer to. So, I searched the web for test formats/questions and prepared accordingly and the test format/topics were not different. Test duration was 1.5 hours , having 3 sections: Aptitude: Had 3 subsections - Quants ; Data Checking/Data Accuracy(was easy) ; Logical reasoning(pattern recognition,sequences,etc).Solving maximum without wasting time is key!

Programming : Had 2 subsections - Flowcharts.Given 2 flowcharts of some basic problem and contains 5-6 blanks which we were to identify and MCQs based on those. 1 was some string matching algo and the other was easy enough ; Pseudocodes. They gave 3 pseudocode based MCQs. Two were based on binary trees/BSTs(basic insertion,deletion,traversal,depth) and one on AVL trees(rotateLeft,rotateRight operations). I prepared on these topics beforehand and thus was able to solve this section confidently.

SQL: There were 20 MCQs on Oracle SQL and were mostly theoretical.Time given was more than enough. I was aware of most of the functions in mySQL and solved SQL50 on leetcode. Though Oracle SQL is a bit different syntactically, I tried to trust my gut and marked accordingly in some questions.

One thing I had learned about OA's in 2 months of placement season is that YOU NEED TO HAVE TRUST IN YOURSELF AND IN YOUR PREPARATION. This doesn't mean you have always prepared all the topics completely and have an overconfident attitude.Instead, you are well aware of what all you have prepared and what not and need to own that truth. Enjoy the test when the time comes. Breathe and take it slow , keep your mind focused in the present! THE MOST IMP THING: PLEASE PREPARE APTITUDE (Quants,LR,everything) properly from Indiabix. I fumbled a lot in aptitude tests till I was confident and became good.

2. Technical Interview 1[ 27 students appeared for this round ]

A total of 27 students (across all 3 roles) got selected for the interviews. 8 additional candidates were on the waitlist but they didn't get a chance for an interview at the end. For the SE role, 18 appeared for interviews.The interview process was conducted online on Webex. The interview started with a warm greeting followed by my introduction. After that he told me to walk through and explain my Major project(which was the highlight). I explained what it is, what problem we are solving (the need) and the main features of the project. Further, he asked me to explain the tech stack used which led to a detailed conversation about how the architecture of the project was, about the database used, about Next.js . He basically was testing the low-level implementation details and whether I have actually worked on the project. He also asked about any conflict which might have occurred while working on the group project.I was prepared for such questions. After that he asked me to explain what OOP is. I explained about how some languages are functional programming languages and others object oriented languages.gave an example - python being more on the functional side(i was wrong) and explained it further how python supports both upon intervention.Then he asked to explain encapsulation , Inheritance, polymorphism. Always remember to give examples! To end off , he asked me a very common puzzle. I was very aware of such common puzzles but I had never read the solutions :( Though I very well knew they were interested in the approach. So I was able to smartly handle this and come up with a solution. Then he gave a last minute effort to optimize it and was able to do so.Lastly, I asked him one question regarding the technologies used at Blackrock. Before leaving, he himself said that the HR will inform me about the next round shortly!

3. Technical Interview 2[ 16 students appeared for this round ]

The 2nd tech interview was a techno-HR for some of my friends.For me, it was completely a tech round. This round started with greetings and a short conversation on how was my experience of the 1st round to which I told him honestly how I tackled the last puzzle in the previous round. Then he asked me to explain one of my favourite projects. I explained my major project.Then I was asked about my contribution ;I spoke about the features I worked on. Then he asked me to explain the kanban board functionality which I built, supabase db used. Further he asked me to explain what is authentication and authorization which led to a to and fro conversation on how exactly it works behind the scenes. He was not interested in the token generation-cookies and session storage part but on whether the database is queried on each auth request and similarly for authorization. Further I was asked about enum in Java.I explained that it is a special class in java , where it is used (Gave an example of how I defined roles using an Enum in db schema. It is good if you bring up a concept which you have used in your project). Then as I spoke about

RBAC in my project he asked me to open notepad and design the Roles table and how authorization will take place. For this I designed 2 more tables to explain him properly about the end-to-end flow. Remember to be confident in what you explain and always keep talking! He then posed an open ended question: If you have data which is coming from multiple sources, what rules will you define to normalize/preprocess it and store correct data? I started with the use of python for data preprocessing and the different techniques used as I got a sense that he was not expecting 1NF,2NF,3NF. Then he clarified that I just need to give a rule to be imposed(low-level). For which I answered :A very general and straightforward rule would be to check matching data for each attribute.If it matches, there is high probability that the data is correct. Further for unmatched fields, I will check existing database and look for a match. I honestly did not know what he was expecting, but he was satisfied with my answer. The last part of interview was: A binary tree implementation and function to search for a value in tree. He told me to open notepad and code. It is a good practice to talk about each and every line of code on what you are doing. Further he gave 2 followups- finding the no. of occurrences of that element and the deepest level of that element. He wanted me to implement all 3 in the same function .I tried but afterwards, I used global variables and stored the value for each and explained. He told me it can be done without this but what I did was correct. At the end I asked for a feedback (he said good things!) ; asked him about some interesting project which he has worked on and a pleasant 2 min conversation went on.

4. HR Round(Prank round) [13 students]

We were told due to some unfortunate reasons, Blackrock is terminating the process but TPO is requesting them. 10 students were called the next day for an HR round. This was just a small unofficial 1 on 1 conversation with Sikka Sir after which the results were announced by Sir himself in the conference room along with some words of inspiration.He announced that 10 students were selected and 3 were on waitlist. (7 SE, 2 Aladdin data, 1 GM)

10 students were offered the job and I was one of them!

journey.prep:
1. Craft a solid self-introduction -- it's your first impression, so make it count.

2. Take notes during the pre-placement talk -- they can help you frame personalized questions during the interviews.

3. Practice a backend framework like Django or Express -- learn to set up a server, design schemas, and build basic APIs beforehand. I had done a Django course on Udemy - Django Masterclass : Build 9 Real World Django Projects

4. I personally did Neetcode 150, then practiced LeetCode daily and previous contest questions. Focus on mastering fundamentals and recognizing patterns, not chasing streaks or ratings. You can also do Striver's A2Z DSA sheet.

5. Use Indiabix and GFG to revise fundamentals of DBMS, OS, OOPs and CCN. DBMS is the main priority, as the interviews revolved around being able to apply the concepts you learned in DBMS. Just some basic knowledge of OS, OOPS and CCN was required for the rapid fire round.

6. LeetCode's Top 50 SQL Questions are more than enough to get a strong grip on SQL basics and variations.

7. Don't panic in interviews -- it's okay to ask for help; interviewers are usually very supportive. Think aloud throughout each interview -- it helps the interviewer follow your approach and gives them a chance to guide you if needed.

Feel free to contact me on LinkedIN - https://www.linkedin.com/in/manankher/

1. Rapid Fire Round [ 72 candidates appeared for this round ]

This was the first round, and we were all asked to arrive by 8:25 am, and were asked to assemble in 103 by 8:50 am. We thought that we would first receive instructions on how the rapid fire round would be like. But at 9 am sharp, we all receive an email, containing a google form link, and one of the WorkIndia coordinators comes into the room, and tells us to start the test immediately, and that the form will stop taking submissions after 9:15 am. So make sure you have your wifi and laptop battery charging setup. Luckily I was already connected to the wifi and had my laptop charged, so I was able to start the test immediately.

It was an MCQ test which contained basic technical questions on Java, Python and C++, like answering the time complexity, space complexity and output of code snippets. Some questions on basic OS and CCN like deadlocks and DNS, some github commands like listing all branches, stash and pop. Some questions on prefix and postfix increment operators, and some basic data structure questions like which data structure is LIFO, FIFO. The objective is to answer as many questions as you can within 15 min. It contained around 40 to 50 questions. I was able to answer all of them, some with a little uncertainty, and submit.

2. Debugging Round [ 46 candidates appeared for this round ]

For this round, we had to join the meet link on our laptop. The interviewer then asked whether I prefer Django or NodeJs. I chose Django. Then he sent a link to a small existing django codebase containing an Attendance Tracker project, with a README file containing instructions on what was to be performed. Initially, while starting the server, there were 2 bugs that were required to be fixed.

One bug was in the models.py, a syntax error in the choices parameter passed to a models.CharField.

Expected syntax: status = models.CharField(max_length=20, choices=[('active', 'Status active'), ('inactive', 'Status inactive')]) Given syntax: status = models.CharField(max_length=20, choices=['active', 'inactive'])

The second bug was in the views.py, another syntax error in which the key of a python dictionary was being accessed incorrectly.

Expected syntax: [s["name"] for s in students] Given syntax: [s.name for s in students]

After fixing the errors, I started the server. The server was running now. After this, I was asked to implement an API endpoint to mark a student's attendance. For this, I was initially adding an attendance field in the existing Student table. But the interviewer asked me for a better way. So I made a separate table, Attendance, which can contain the student_id as foreign key and a date field, to store when the attendance was marked. Then, there was another constraint that a student cannot mark attendance again on the same date. For this, I used the unique_together model option within a Meta class to make the composite field (student_id, date) unique. The interviewer was happy with this. Then I started implementing the API endpoint, and wrote the url and the handler function. But time was running short, so the interviewer just asked to write a comment inside the handler function on how I would implement the endpoint.

Throughout the round (around 45 min), I kept telling the interviewer my thoughts and the steps I am taking. Also, googling and using stack overflow was allowed, but no LLMs. The interviewer will judge you based on your knowledge of the programming language, the backend framework, and most importantly your ability to ask the right questions and google them, and find out the answers. I had googled the syntax for using choices parameter, the syntax for implementing the unique together and also the date field.

3. DSA Round [ 15 candidates appeared for this round ]

The DSA Round was also conducted in online interview form, and we had to write code on google docs. The questions were of leetcode easy and medium difficulty. The interviewer first asked me to introduce myself. Make sure you have a proper introduction ready, which briefly covers your education, your internship experience and high impact projects. Also, create an introduction which aligns with the company's principles.

First question: You are given a positive integer N. Find X such that the sum from 1 to X-1 equals the sum from X+1 to N. For this, I first suggested the brute force algorithm of iterating through all elements from 1 to N, then for each element, running 2 for loops to calculate the 1-X-1 and X+1-N sum, giving a O(n^2) TC. I then optimized it by suggesting a prefix sum approach. First, we calc the total sum using the sum of n natural numbers formula, and then iterate from 1 to N, calc prefix sum, and subtract from total sum. So whenever left and right sum become equal, we return that element X. I wrote this code, then the interviewer then told me to optimize it further. So I suggested a binary search approach, and conditions would be if leftSum>rightSum, e=mid-1 and if leftSum<rightSum, s=mid+1, else return mid. Also, I was asked to optimize space complexity as well, so I used the same formula to calculate leftSum (1 to X-1 sum), instead of prefix array. I wrote this code, then the interviewer asked to optimize it even further. I took some time, but thought that if I want to optimize from O(logn), there must be a direct formula. Thats when it clicked me, that I can write an equation, and solve it for X.

leftSum = rightSum (x-1)x/2 = totalSum - leftSum - x (x-1)x/2 = n(n+1)/2 - (x-1)x/2 - x (x-1)x = n(n+1)/2 - x x^2 - x = n(n+1)/2 - x x^2 = n(n+1)/2 X = sqrt(n(n+1)/2)

The interviewer then asked, what does this signify. I said that X will be the sqrt of sum of the n natural numbers. He was happy with this, and explained me that for a solution to exist, the sum of the n natural numbers must be a perfect square.

Second Question: https://leetcode.com/problems/majority-element/description/ I first suggested a brute force approach by creating a hashmap (dictionary in python) and storing the frequency of all elements. Then iterating through the hashmap, and returning the element whose frequency is greater than n/2.

The optimal approach with constant space complexity is Moore's Voting Algorithm. Majority Element - Leetcode 169 - Python

During the DSA round, I was asked why I preferred using Python. I explained that I initially used C++ and had solved around 150 questions on LeetCode in it. But later, I switched to Python because its simpler syntax allowed me to focus more on understanding the logic behind each problem, rather than the boilerplate code. This helped me improve my problem-solving skills more effectively.

Tip: If you switch languages for DSA, be clear about your reason, it's not about which language is "better", but what helps you learn and think better.

Third Question: https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/dsa/find-a-repeating-and-a-missing-number/ For this, I was only able to suggest the approach with the frequency array / hashmap. The interviewer wanted me to optimize the space complexity. I started thinking in terms of slow and fast pointer, but on dry running, that approach didn't work. Then the interviewer gave me a hint that I can modify the array in-place. I started thinking along those lines, maybe swapping the numbers. But time was up, and I

wasn't able to optimize it. The interviewer then asked me if I had any questions. I asked them about the various microservices they have built, and what different architectures they have used, along with the methodology they take while deciding the appropriate architecture for these services.

Finally, after receiving the answer, I thanked every person on the call, by their first name.

At this point, I felt I might not get selected for the next round, since I couldn't come up with the most optimal solution for the third question. Still, I kept my hopes up and didn't give up. I began preparing for the next round anyway, asking ChatGPT to help me build schemas for applications like a job recruitment platform.

After quite some time, I finally received the link for the next round! The waiting period can be really nerve-wracking, but it's important to stay calm and think positively. Don't be disheartened if your interview doesn't go as expected, it's never truly over until the list of shortlisted candidates for the next round is out.

Bonus Question (asked to one of my friends): https://leetcode.com/problems/minimum-size-subarray-sum/description/ A further variation of this was asked, by allowing negative integers to exist in the array.

4. Schema Design Round [ 7 candidates appeared for this round ]

In this round, I was given a problem statement of an Ecommerce Platform on google docs, along with its various requirements. Also, 2 bonus requirements were given of implementing coupons for orders, and a referral system. Initially, I focused on the main requirements, and identified the main entities from them. I wrote down the table names. Then I started building the relations between these tables, with the help of foreign keys, along with the necessary attributes for each of them. While building the schema, I made sure to obey the normal forms like 1NF and mentioned these terms while making the schema. Make sure that you keep properly explaining the interviewer your thought process behind each and every step, and also make sure to ask doubts on things that might not be clear in the problem statement. I had asked some questions, like should I also focus on the merchant's side, or only on the customer's side, and difference between inventory and warehouse, as it was not very clear from the problem statement. Explain the cardinality of each relationship you are creating (one-one, one-many, many-many).

After creating a rough schema, the interviewer then identified certain areas that could be improved, normalized further. I listened thoroughly and made these changes, and explained how this approach would be more effective in preventing data redundancy. I was then asked to write 2 SQL queries on the schema I had built. This included finding the delivery times of the recent orders, along with their delivery locations. I used JOIN, ORDER BY, LIMIT, DATEDIFF function for subtracting the placed_at from the delivered_at. Then I was asked to find the average delivery time, for which I used the aggregate function.

As I had time remaining, I also went ahead and implemented the bonus requirements. The referral table would be a unary, many-many relationship, and contains referred_by and referred_to (both foreign keys to User table)

Finally, the interviewer asked if I had any questions. I asked him what his first six months at WorkIndia were like. He mentioned that he had joined recently, and that while the initial weeks can be hectic, things become smoother as you get familiar with the processes.

I shared my own experience from an internship at a startup, where the first couple of weeks were also hectic for me, since I was learning a new tech stack while working on live features. But once I got used to the codebase, I was able to contribute meaningfully and build exciting features. That sense of solving real-world problems was deeply satisfying. The interviewer appreciated this and mentioned that I would be a good fit for a startup like WorkIndia.

I would advise learning CTEs while solving SQL 50, because they are a powerful way of dividing your SQL query into manageable and easy-to-understand sequential steps.

5. Culture Round [ 4 candidates appeared for this round ]

The culture round felt more like a meaningful conversation than an interview. The interviewer was very friendly, and there's truly no need to be nervous. We spoke about my journey, passions, values, and experiences. It was a heart-to-heart.

The questions covered:

● What got you into this field? Why engineering and not any other role?

● Tell me about your journey so far, your internship, and what you learned from your peers.

● Lowest point in your life and academics.

● Your family, your interests, your short- and long-term goals.

● What do you consider as "good work"?

I answered honestly, sharing how I got into tech through PC gaming and modding, inspired by my grandfather's tech-savviness. I spoke about learning QBasic in school, then Java, and how my love for coding naturally led me to engineering, where I could solve real-world problems and innovate.

I reflected on my regret of not joining any committee in first year, which limited my exposure, but after second year, I made it a point to step out of my comfort zone: applying for internships, connecting with people on LinkedIn, and seeking out opportunities.

I also shared my internship experience, the meaningful features I built, and how much I learned from my mentors and colleagues. I opened up about my family's support, and my goal to help them by becoming financially independent and making them proud.

When asked about what "good work" means to me, I shared how participating in hackathons changed my perspective. Earlier, good work meant building something cool solo using a new tech. But through hackathons, I realized that true good work is about team collaboration, communication, and building something together that no one could have done alone. It's about leveraging each person's strengths, validating each step as a team, and delivering something meaningful as one unit.

Finally, I asked the interviewer:

● How did WorkIndia start, and what impact were you hoping to create?

● How do you deal with scam jobs on the platform?

● From the core values in the WorkIndia PPT, which one do you consider most important?

It was a genuine and fulfilling conversation where I could truly be myself.

Tip: Don't prepare scripted answers. Reflect on your journey, speak from the heart, and be honest. This round isn't about checking boxes, it's about understanding who you are and what drives you. Also, have a good idea about the companies that you have interned at. The interviewer might ask certain questions like when was the company founded, or how old was your mentor in the company, not to grill you, but to verify authenticity and see how well you know your own experiences. Be honest, and don't try to bluff. It's totally okay to say "I'm not sure" rather than guess.

2 students were offered the role. It was a long day, and the results weren't announced immediately. They got announced after we went back home.

2. Take notes during the pre-placement talk -- they can help you frame personalized questions during the interviews.

6. LeetCode's Top 50 SQL Questions are more than enough to get a strong grip on SQL basics and variations.

7. Don't panic in interviews -- it's okay to ask for help; interviewers are usually very supportive. Think aloud throughout each interview -- it helps the interviewer follow your approach and gives them a chance to guide you if needed.

After that i was asked 2-3 SQL queries on my own schema. I took a lot of time and patience to solve this as 4-5 joins were required in each query so the important thing here is to keep talking about what you are thinking and why are you making a particular join. I was not able to design only one thing where i was asked to model categories like consider an Iphone with choices like size(small,medium,large), colour(red,green,blue) and RAM(4,8,16) so there are like 3^3 combinations possible so i want to store all this in MySQL lets say, i tried but could not reach a solution, so i offered a trick where i take the primary key from products and store these categories and their values as arrays in MongoDB. They told the solution is correct but can be done entirely in MySQL also to which i honestly replied i am not aware of that so in case you get stuck try to atleast give some solution rather than staying blank and silent. Hackathon main kaisa thoda jugaad lagate hai to quickly achieve something waise kuch kar sakte ho, now this was accepted in WI which was good for me but i have no clue as to how other companies will perceive this so BE CAUTIOUS.

This was due to the question where i shifted to MongoDB. Answer - Mixture of DB is used.

3) Ask unique questions : As WorkIndia will face a challenge of verifying the authenticity of Job Postings, to counter this does WI use a rule-based model or some AI algorithm or a decentralized approach with smart contracts on a blockchain. Answer - Rule based algorithms.

I answered honestly by saying the process can be considered as wholistic judgement for an SDE role where DSA,DBMS and Dev everything is evaluated. Initially there was a Resume Shortlisting and a list was shared of candidates applicable to attend the interview process. The entire process was scheduled on 9th July itself from morning to evening and all interviews were conducted in an online mode.

1. Rapid Fire Round [ 72 students were present for this round ]

As the name suggests, we had to attempt 40-50 questions in a 15 minute window so both accuracy and speed were essential. The questions were like : time/space complexity of code snippets, calculating the expected output of a given code and fundamental questions like if a = 10 then what will a++ + ++a equal to - answer is 22. The snippets were a mix of Python,CPP and Java codes so cannot isolate one language to focus on. There were also CS fundamental questions like OS,CCN and Git commands.

2. Debugging Round [ 46 students appeared for this round ]

We were sent a GMeet link where the interviewer asked for a choice between JS or Python. As I did DSA in Python and was aware of both Flask and FastAPI, I chose Python. I was a bit scared as the codebase shared was in Django so i told the interviewer honestly that I was aware of Flask and FastAPI so he asked if I wanted to switch to Express and JS or would I like to try Django as Google/StackOverflow/Documentation (everything except AI) was allowed so I stuck with Django and was able to debug the errors. Specific questions were

asked related to the errors so it is important to understand the error and explain your intuition as to why the error may have occurred and then solve it. General questions related to Git or the MVC folder structure in a codebase were also asked.

3. DSA Round [ 15 students appeared for this round ]

This was the ﬁrst time I was told to introduce myself, I was not prepared for this so always be prepared for this question else it sets an impression that you are not even prepared for the basic most obvious questions. I was lucky enough that this did not affect me. Overall the panelists asked candidates to only write pseudocode on Google Doc but i was expected to code and run it on GDB probably bcuz i code in Python so they wanted to see the output. There were 2 interviewers in the GMeet and I was asked this question :

In a gaming tournament unique ids are to be assigned from 1 to N to N participants, there might be some invalid ids already assigned in between and we need to assign them values acc to the next smallest valid number from 1 to N. So if the given array is 1,0,2 then 0 is invalid then answer should be 1,3,2. Another example test case :

Input : 2,0,4,-6,9,6 Output : 2,1,4,3,5,6

So my initial approach was to iterate over the array and put numbers already valid in a Set in Python which translates to a unordered_set in CPP. Now start a loop from i = 1 to N and check if it exists in the set , if not then replace the ﬁrst invalid number in the array with the current i. This is O(N) time and space. I was asked to reduce the space after this. I asked if the order matters while assigning values, so the interviewer cleared that the only expectation is 1 to N, nothing else matters. So my next approach was to sort the array and check if 1 to N exists in it with Binary Search( lower_bound ), if not replace the ﬁrst invalid position with the current missing number. This is NlogN time and constant space. I was asked to bring time back to O(N). I took a lot of time here and asked for hints where the interviewer told me try to establish some relation between indexes and validity of a number which eventually led me to a Cycle Sort solution where there is a special case that if the input is strictly between a given range like 1 to N then sorting can be done in O(N). Pls read about this on GPT/Google, the solution goes as : We will try to place the already valid numbers on their correct indexes which will leave only invalid numbers on indexes where there should have been something else, now in another iteration from left to right we change the invalid numbers to valid because based on indexing we know the next valid number. I was able to code my initial 2 solutions but messed up something in the last one but the interviewer said that was ok.

A key part here is to take the smart guess when not sure. Some of them are objective based theory while some will be solving according to a data structure or so.

2. Round 2: Technical Interview Round [18 Candidates appeared for this round]

This round will last for about 45 minutes to 1 hour. The best tip would be to remain calm and smile in this situation. The interviewer is judging you on the depth of your knowledge and the way you explain which highlights your communication.

As any interview would start, the first question asked was - Introduce yourself. The key part here is to spend a bit more time and highlight the aspects that you want the interviewer to ask you. This is

going to form the base of your interview. I talked about my internship experience and current projects in web development and also the brownie points that I had won multiple hackathons and worked at NGO. Consequently, the first half shifted on my projects and work experience where I was asked to explain about it in depth and then further was asked situational based questions - Were these collaborative projects? If yes and a conflict arose then how would you manage it? (Another question) If some of your team mates were not on the same page then what would you do? (Another one) How would you approach people when you had to build a project on a tech stack th at you don't know? The way I answered these questions was that I took examples of the projects and explained each one of them highlighting that I have been in these situat ions and have leadership qualities.

Then the next part of the interview was on the aspects they had mentioned in their job description - Data Analytics and Cloud Computing. (Questions like - What is cloud computing?) They don't expect me to have in depth knowledge on them but I gave an overview on them and they were happy about it.

The third phase of this interview spanned on the DBMS. I was asked about SQL and what I knew about it. Then I was asked to design a schem a for a School. I used the "Thinking Out Loud" method

- which is essentially whatever I wrote I spoke about why I wrote it and then added the constraints (NOT NULL, UNIQUE, PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY). I did this so that the interviewer know the process in which I am thinking. After this I was asked to explain the Schema. The interview then asked me SQL Queries on the same. The queries were related to the Schema I made, and one of the questions on which the interviewer emphasized was the difference between the HAVING and the WHERE clause.

Since I had an interesting resume, they again came back to my work experience and then ended the interview by asking - Why choose General Mills? Researching about the company helps here. Overall the round was based on resume and you should know it thoroughly anticipating the questions that can arise.

9 Candidates went to the next round.

3. Round 3 - HR Based Round [9 Candidates Appeared for this Round]

This was a purely HR based round with common questions. Mine was the shortest one lasting about 20 minutes. There were two people in the panel. They were looking at how you are going to tackle these questions. It started by walking them through your resume. This similar was as in the Technical Round but here my focus was on the fact that I worked at NGO which resonates with the company policy of giving back to society. Some of the questions were:

• Where do you see yourself in 5 years ?

• If not engineering then what will you be doing? And why?

• One impression - good and bad that your friends will have about you? Why would they have that?

• What do you know about General Mills?

• Why choose General Mills?

The answers that you give can lead to follow up questions on that. The key is to keep calm and have a smile on your face and then give the reply to best of your ability. Highlighting points relevant to the company is always beneficial as they see that your goals align with theirs.

In the end 4 people got the internship offer.

This round lasted for 45 mins to 1 hour . The interviewer began by asking which subject excites me the most and I chose App development. I was given a case study to design an app. The task began with me asking relevant questions to understand the requirements thoroughly. I had to consider factors like the app's functionality, user experience, and the overall system architecture. Once Ihad enough information, I proposed a design that detailed both the frontend and backend components, explaining how they would interact. A key focus was on scaling the app from 3,000 to 30,000 users, and I discussed strategies like efficient data storage, user management, and backend optimization to handle the increased load. The interviewer tested my ability to break down the problem, gather requirements, and present a robust, scalable solution.

Following this, I was asked about storing large amounts of data using Firebase, which had been a core part of my previous app development experience. The interviewer wanted to understand if I knew how to handle scalability issues in Firebase, especially with large databases. I explained Firebase's strengths in handling real-time data but also discussed its limitations when itcomes to scaling beyond certain thresholds. This led to a deeper conversation about database management, where I was quizzed on concepts like BCNF and normalization. I answered these questions, elaborating on whether normalization is needed for small databases. While I wasn't very familiar with microservices, the interviewer was helpful in explaining key concepts, and Ipicked up the basics quickly, which allowed me to respond to further questions.

Toward the end of the interview, the case study was revealed to be based on an app the interviewer had already developed, providing a real-world context to the task. I asked how they had solved the scalability problem in their app and was curious about their experience at General Mills. The interview tested my ability to think critically,learn on the go and apply theoretical knowledge to practical challenges. It wasn't just about technical expertise but also about showing my problem-solving skills and willingness to engage with new concepts and feedback. Overall, it was an insightful experience that showcased my strengths and highlighted areas where I could continue to grow.

In my HR interview, the panel consisted of two interviewers who started by asking me to introduce myself and share a bit about my family background. After that, they posed an interesting question--if I hadn't chosen to pursue engineering, what other career path would I have taken. They then moved on to ask where I see myself in the next five years and how my friends would describe me, giving me a chance to reflect on both my professional goals and my personal traits.

Finally, I was asked why I wanted to join General Mills, which allowed me to express my interest in the company. At the end of the interview, I had the opportunity to ask them questions.

The key is to stay calm and maintain a friendly smile throughout the process. Answer the questions confidently and ensure that your responses reflect genuine interest while aligning with the company's values and goals.

They were curious about my interests beyond my degree, and I was asked what I enjoy doing that isn't related to academics. Another question focused on my reading habits, asking about the most recent book I had read and to discuss it. Additionally, I was asked how my friends perceive me, both in terms of strengths and weaknesses.Overall, it was a smooth and comfortable round where the main focus was on being authentic and honest in my responses.

journey.howSecured:
Before the OA, only students belonging to CE or CSE branch and having CGPA 7.5 and above were shortlisted for the OA, so a significant number of students were in-eligible to apply.

SO PLEASE MAKE SURE TO MAINTAIN GOOD CGPA. (AT LEAST 8)

Pay attention in PPT and interact with the company employees so that they remember you.

1. Online Assessment

Around 66 students appeared for the test, since IDfy had come for two roles ( SE and ML ) ,there were two different tests, one for SE and other for ML ( students had to choose a role before giving the OA).

The test for SE was conducted on Hackerrank for 90 minutes, and everything was proctored. The test consisted of 3 sections having 1 DSA, 2 SQL , 2 REST API questions respectively.

Every candidate did not get the same DSA question, I had got an easy one. The question was to check whether a password was strong or weak, for the password to be weak there were certain conditions that had to be satisfied like "contains only lowercase or uppercase letters" or "contains only numericals" or "contains a substring which is present in banned_words list". The constraints were also not very big so brute force worked here, just remember to put the words present in banned_words list in a set for fast lookup otherwise certain test cases won't pass due to TLE. Since this question was easy, I finished solving this question in 10 minutes.

Next was the SQL section, this section was tough and this is the game changing section because very few people know SQL very well so solving this section completely will definitely give you an edge over others. Both SQL questions had multiple tables, so I don't remember the exact questions, the first question could be solved by join and using group by and aggregate function. The second question was a notch above the first one, this question involved multiple joins and we had to use subquerier to further process the table before joining with other tables ( eg : adding a new column of data ) . The inner queries further contained aggregate and group by clauses, so this can become overwhelming to understand the exact flow, the trick here was to use WITH clause to separate out the inner query logic to make the query more readable and understandable. This section took most time because of the complexity involved. Since I had quickly solved the DSA question, I could devote more time to this section.

PLEASE TAKE SQL SERIOUSLY, IT SEEMS EASY UNTIL IT ISN'T, SO PRACTISING SQL IS VERY IMPORTANT.

Leetcode SQL 50, CodeChef, Hackerrank, are some of the good resources to start with. A day prior to the OA I practised from this site to brush up my SQL knowledge.

Next was the REST API section, each question instructed us to create a get method using any language like C, C++, Java, JavaScript (Node JS) , Python etc and hit a URL to get data and apply the given filter and return the filtered data. But the catch was, we had to do it from scratch, no framework, no code autocomplete, no external help, so knowing the exact syntax was the key here. I knew how to make a REST API in Java using Spring Boot Framework but I had no idea how to create the Get method from scratch in Java and since most of time had gone in SQL section, I did not have time to think about the syntax in JavaScript, so I could not solve both REST API question.

Since I had solved the DSA and SQL section completely I got shortlisted for the interview but some of the other shortlisted candidates had solved some sections partially. But to remain on the safe side, try to solve all questions, even partial is enough SOMETIMES, not every time.

I feel clearing the OA is the toughest task because of the competition and time pressure. I was fortunate enough to have only 66 students for the OA, other times I had to compete with 100+ students, so focus on getting proficient in DSA, SQL , Computer Fundamentals and Aptitude. I had given the OA of 5-6 companies before IDfy and cleared the OA of only 3-4 of them because I couldn't solve a DSA question fully or due to aptitude, so please focus on them early on.

2. Technical Round

Only 8 out of 66 candidates were shortlisted for the interview round. The shortlist came at 7:30 pm a day before the interview and we also had Baker Hughes PPT and test a day before the interview, so I did not have much time to prepare for the interview. Since I had read previous year interview experience, I focused on the projects listed on my resume, like tech stack, features, architecture diagrams etc.

We had to arrive by 9 am. There were three panels. I was first in my panel, my interview started around 10:30 am. So my interview started with the interviewer downloading the results of OA. He saw my results and said that I had the highest score so he was impressed by it. Then he introduced himself and his role at IDfy ( he also asked some points from the PPT, so remember to pay attention in the PPT ), then he read my resume, each and every point, then he told me to introduce myself. I mentioned my education background, a short description about my projects, and my interests ( prepare a good 1-2 min introduction beforehand, use chatgpt or other AI tools to refine it ). I had mentioned Formula 1 as one of my favourite sports to watch, fortunately my interviewer was also a formula 1 fan so we had a good brief conversation about the sport. Then the interviewer said that he would focus on three sections of my resume, technical skills, projects and internships. He started with a question, in which programming language was I most comfortable in and how would I rate myself in that language. I mentioned Java. He then started with Oops in Java, he asked me about polymorphism, diamond problem, how interfaces solve the diamond problem, static keyword, how static variables and static methods are different from each other. I answered all these questions correctly and gave examples where ever needed to explain the concept. Then he asked me to write the code for Destructor in Java. I was unsure whether Destructor existed in Java, so I mentioned this at the start but since I was unsure, I thought for a while and said that, to implement a Destructor we have to make the object null so that Garbage Collector will destroy the object. The interviewer said that my initial answer was correct that Destructor did not in Java, so he told me to have more confidence in my answer ( honestly I did panic a little after this so I drank water to calm myself ), after this he gave me a DSA question to solve, the question was there are a list of transactions given , the format was same as the ones given in a passbook , so there was a transaction description, credit amount, debit amount and current balance. Initial balance was given and we had to flag any transactions which are erroneous, the transaction was erroneous when current balance was not correct. For example, if the initial balance was 100 , credit was 10 , so the current balance should be 110 , if it was otherwise then we will flag this transaction as wrong. This was an easy question, simple math was required, only thing required were string functions like split, parseInt to get data from string. First, I verbally explained my approach then proceeded to write the code on paper ( remember to write clean and readable code ). Once this was done the interviewer proceeded with SQL queries, he gave me two schemas, Employee and Department. He asked three queries, I don't remember exact questions but I had used joins,

group by and aggregate functions to solve them ( remember to think clearly, ask for time to think and break down the problem, then join the solutions)

Next, the interviewer asked which was my favourite project, he read the project description. I had mentioned JWT, so he started by asking what is JWT and describe its structure, how did I implement it in my project, then he asked about REST APIs, difference between get, put , and post, whether we can create a new entry in db using get request (we can by sending the data as path variable or query parameter, but its not a good practise).

Then he said he was done with the interview and asked whether I had any questions. I asked two questions and the interview ended, my interview lasted for around 50-60 minutes.

After finishing my interview, I was instructed by our TPO to wait for the results till 1 pm. We initially thought that we would have to wait for another round at least, but then the company official said that no more rounds will be taken and final results will be announced on the basis of the first interview round. Two of the candidates had a second interview round but I did not.

Around 3:30pm, the results were announced, a total of 5 candidates were selected and fortunately I was one of them.

Additional Tips and Resources:

● Placements are tough, remember to stay calm, and patient. I was so disappointed with myself when I could not even crack the first round of many companies that I started to self-doubt myself. Keep your head down, and keep grinding.

● Luck definitely plays a part in placements, so focus on what you can control which is skills. Remember consistency is key, whether it's DSA or academics. I had a good CGPA, but since I was not consistent enough in DSA so I could not crack other high paying companies.

● Have good projects, and remember to justify specific things about the project, like tech stack, architecture etc.

● If you are familiar with Java, then master it, if not, at least know the basics like OOP concepts.

● I did not give a single HR Round, so I don't have any experience in that, but prepare for HR Round because it can happen that you clear all technical rounds but fail to clear the HR Round.

● Practice giving answers in front of a mirror or give mock interviews to your friends, this improves your communication skills.

● Follow Striver's sheet for DSA, give contests on leetcode, codechef, codeforces, this helps because you get a habit of solving questions with time pressure.

● Aptitude is very important, a lot of companies ask in OA, use this. Practise timed tests to really mimic the test environment. I started aptitude late, don't make this mistake.

● Puzzles are a common way to test critical thinking in interviews so practise from GeeksForGeeks.

● System design is a common question in interviews even for freshers so practise from GeeksForGeeks. Use chatgpt to understand the specific terminologies, and practise questions like how to scale a specific system ( for example your projects ).

● Guesstimates can also be asked, so prepare them if required ( this should be done only when you have ample amount of time ).

● During interviews, maintain eye contact while answering, be calm and ask for help if required, interviewers don't mind giving hints, they want to know your thought process.

● Remember to fill all the required application forms while applying, companies are strict and don't accept any excuses for any delay or missing application details. I missed filling one registration form while applying for IDFC First Bank, so I could not even give its' OA. Don't make this mistake.

● A lot of companies also hire through hackathons like Nomura, JPMC, Morgan Stanley, Adobe etc so keep an eye on them and practise development side by side.

journey.prep:
To prepare for the process, I practiced aptitude questions on IndiaBix and referred to the "1000 Sanfoundry MCQs" focused on OOPs and Java. I ensured that my fundamentals in JavaScript and SQL were clear, as questions from these areas are commonly asked.

One key piece of advice is to have complete clarity about your projects--know every detail thoroughly. Only mention technologies or features on your resume that you have actually worked on, as interviewers often ask in-depth questions about them.

The most important factor throughout the interview process is confidence. Your body language reflects both your personality and your capability, so it's crucial to maintain composure, answer every question with confidence, and wear a smile. Even if you realize that your answer is incorrect, acknowledge it politely and assure the interviewer that you will work on it.

Although I was anxious at the start--since this was my first interview experience--I treated it as a win-win situation: either I would gain valuable interview experience, or I would get placed.

The real challenge came in the coding section. We had 3 questions to solve in just 30 minutes. One was the classic House Robber problem, which I tried to approach using binary search. My logic and functions worked fine when I tested them with static input, but I struggled a lot with handling input and array initialization in the given environment. Even the enhanced for-each loop wasn't working as expected. I ended up trying 3 different variations, but none passed due to these input issues. Because of that, I couldn't solve any coding problem, which was very disappointing since the logic part was actually clear to me.

On the aptitude prep side, I realized that platforms like IndiaBix are no longer enough. Even after solving everything on IndiaBix, I got rejected in many companies , because their aptitude level was higher. For serious prep, I would strongly recommend going through R.S. Aggarwal's aptitude book, because companies are raising the bar year by year.

2. Group Discussion [ 60 students ]

After the OA results were out, I found myself shortlisted for the Business Analyst (BA) role. Honestly, I wasn't very interested in BA and had only planned to attend to avoid any demerits.

The next morning, I got to know that candidates could apply for a role change, but it required HR approval and would be considered purely on the basis of the resume. The catch was: before applying for any other role (like Framework Engineer or MLE), all BA-shortlisted candidates first had to clear the Group Discussion (GD) round. If you failed the BA GD, you were out of all roles.

There were about 60 students shortlisted for BA, divided into 6 groups of 10 each. For the GD, we were given 1.5 minutes to jot down points and structure our thoughts. My group's topic was: "9-to-5 Job vs Startup."

The discussion went really well for me. I didn't start or conclude, yet I still made it to the next round. This made me realize an important point: it's not always mandatory to be the first or last speaker to get noticed. What really matters is how meaningful and relevant your contributions are during the discussion.

3. BA Round 1

The interview started with the classic "Introduce yourself," where I briefly covered my projects, achievements, and interests. The interviewer immediately pointed out, with a smile, that my resume didn't have a single mention of the word "business" -- and we both laughed at that.

He then picked up on my Profit View project (Virtual Trading System) since he himself was very interested in the stock market. He asked me to explain it in detail, which I did confidently. The follow-up questions were challenging:

● "Suppose you have 8 billion customers next day -- how would you handle scaling, and what would be your revenue model?"

● "What is the highest stock in the Indian stock market?"

● "Why did you integrate AI into this project?"

● "Which is better: AI or human intelligence?"

I answered these from a market perspective, staying practical and confident. He also tested me on current market knowledge: "The market is bad right now, which sectors would you invest in?" Another situational question was: "If you're in a 3-member team (1 stock market expert, 2 developers), and the industry stakeholder wants a new feature X that clashes with your ideas -- whom will you listen to?"

Then, he switched to my Legal AI project. He grilled me on technical details -- models like BERT, PEFT, Microsoft Phi-2, and why I chose them. He also asked: "How many cases are filed daily in the Mumbai High Court?" (a guesstimate question linked to my project domain).

Towards the end, he challenged me on role alignment: "Why join Quantiphi as a BA when your resume shows you're a developer?" I explained my reasoning, and he also asked me about Quantiphi's competitors. Finally, he pressed me multiple times on my preference -- BA or FE. I stayed consistent and confidently said Framework Engineer every time, despite the follow-up trick questions.

The interview lasted around 40-50 minutes, and it was intense but engaging. Before wrapping up, I asked him if he was personally interested in stock markets. He smiled and said yes -- he actively invests too. That made for a nice ending to the discussion.

4. FE Round 1

After being promoted to the Framework Engineer role (based on my resume), my interview started with the usual introduction. The interviewer then moved into some basic technical questions, like the difference between C++ and Java.

From there, the focus shifted to my projects.

● On Profit View, he asked me about the working of the system, why I chose specific technologies, and the role of message queues and Redis caching.

● Next, we moved to Mark Me. I explained for 2-3 minutes straight, covering why I chose the project, the problems we faced, and how we solved them.

● Chronologically, he then asked about Legal AI. Specifically, he wanted me to explain what RAG is. I gave a detailed 2-3 minute explanation of my pipeline -- including saving data in Astra DB and the flow of the retrieval process. He seemed quite impressed with this project. ●

Since my primary language is Java, I expected some heavy DSA questions, but surprisingly, he only asked very basic ones. For example:

● "Given the area of a circle, find its radius."

● A couple of easy SQL questions -- one on filtering (like names ending with "YADAV") and one on simple joins.

The entire interview lasted 40-45 minutes.

Key Takeaways:

1. The interviewer was more interested in my projects because they had practical use cases and impact.

2. For one of my friends, the interviewer asked a much tougher question: "Write code to fetch live coordinates of the user without using any reference docs " So the difficulty can vary a lot.

4. FE Round 2

My second interview was quite short and casual, lasting only about 15-20 minutes. It began with a simple "Introduce yourself," and I kept my introduction brief and to the point.

The interviewer mainly focused on my projects:

● He first asked about Profit View (Stock Market Project).

● Then he moved to Mark Me. Since I mentioned that I am a follower of ISKCON, he lightly questioned me on how I manage to work on stock market projects, considering it's not typically encouraged. This part felt more like a conversation than a formal interview.

After that, he asked about the databases I knew and a couple of very basic questions on the difference between SQL and NoSQL. He also asked about the backend technologies I'm familiar with, but only at an informational level -- there was no deep cross-questioning.

Towards the end, he asked the standard "Why Quantiphi? Who are Quantiphi's competitors?" and reminded me that the Pre-Placement Talk (PPT) is very important, as it helps us understand the company better before interviews.

Overall, it was a light and comfortable interview -- more of a discussion than a grilling session -- and the interviewer seemed satisfied with my answers.

5. HR Round

Unlike a typical HR round, this one focused on management and stakeholder questions. The panel began by asking me to introduce myself -- but specifically told me not to mention any projects. They then asked several situational questions like:

● "If your team members are not working, how would you tackle them?"

● "How would you convince stakeholders to buy your product?"

At one point they said: "You are linking each question to your project -- what possible flaws can you detect in the project? If you knew them, what actions did you take to overcome them, and how would you still manage to retain consumers even after those problems?" I explained everything properly: how we identified flaws, the corrective steps we implemented, and the communication/mitigation strategies we used to keep users engaged despite issues.

Since I was leading a team of four on my ongoing project, I used those experiences to answer the management scenarios -- showing concrete examples of problem detection

After nearly 3 hours of waiting, results were announced around 9:30-10 PM: 8 students were selected (3 FE, 2 MLE, 3 BA).
