journey.prep:
Stay Positive and Believe in Yourself : The placement process can be long and stressful. Losing hope or feeling demotivated is absolutely normal, but always believe in yourself and keep putting in consistent effort. Better things are on the way. Talking to your friends and family during tough times really helps keep your mind calm and motivated.

Prepare Based on Company Patterns : Go through previous interview experiences for the company you're targeting. Some companies grill your resume thoroughly, some focus on Java or DSA, while others might focus on computer fundamentals. Knowing the pattern helps you prioritize topics effectively.

Know Your Resume Inside Out : Be prepared for questions like "Why did you build this project?" or "How would you improve it further?". Small bluffs are fine, but avoid putting anything on your resume that you can't confidently explain.

Cover Both DSA and Fundamentals : Don't limit yourself to DSA alone. Computer fundamentals like OS, DBMS, OOPS, and Networks are equally important. For DSA, go through Striver's Sheet and give contests on CodeForces and LeetCode. For computer fundamentals, practice from Sanfoundry or GFG. These will help you in Online Assessments as well as interviews.

Stay Calm During Interviews: Interviews can be nerve-wracking. I once felt nervous in an interview and ended up answering wrongly, which got me frustrated and affected my confidence

for the remaining questions. To avoid this, practice mock interviews with friends or seniors. They help you get comfortable under pressure.

Trust the Process and Don't Compare :Trust God's plan and your own journey. Failures are an unavoidable part of growth. Don't compare yourself with others--it only adds unnecessary stress. Virat Kohli waited 18 years to win his first IPL trophy, while Rohit Sharma lifted his first one just a year after the league began . Everyone has their own timeline; enjoy your journey without rushing through it.

JUST TRUST THE PROCESS. ALL THE BEST !!!

1. Online Assessment [ 191 applied on unstop and 133 shortlisted for test ]

The test was held on campus via Unstop with rigorous proctoring. It contained three sections - Aptitude, Technical MCQs, and Coding. Each section had a sectional timer.

● Aptitude (40 questions in 35 mins) - The questions in this section were easy, but the main challenge was time management. Don't spend too much time on a single question; try to solve as many as possible within the time limit.

● Technical MCQs (33 questions in 25 mins) - This section included Web Development (HTML, JavaScript-based) questions, as well as questions on OS, DBMS, and OOPS. The questions were mostly standard, but some were tricky and required careful attention.

● Coding (3 questions in 30 mins) - There were three coding questions:

1. Minimum Robbing Speed - A thief wants to rob all the houses in a village. Given an array representing the number of houses in each neighborhood and the

maximum amount of time (in hours) available, find the minimum speed (houses per hour) required to rob the entire village.

2. House Robber Problem - This was the classic House Robber problem from LeetCode, solvable using a standard Dynamic Programming approach.

3. Maximum Loot on Islands - Given an undirected graph of n islands, each with a loot value, and edges representing travel paths with travel times, a pirate can start from any island and visit each island at most once. The total loot is the sum of the visited islands' values, while the total time is the sum of the travel times along the chosen path.The task was to find the maximum loot which can be solved by direct Dijkstra's Algorithm.

I was able to solve the first two questions but couldn't attempt the third one due to time constraints.

2. Technical Interview - Round 1

The interviews were conducted the next day and FE was my first preference . I was shortlisted for FE role . Although there was an option for students to switch roles as well.Some students had their interviews in online mode, while others had them offline. Mine was in offline mode.

The interview started with my introduction.Then the interviewer asked me about my Major Project focusing mainly on its real-world application .Next he asked me about my Internship project at TCS and asked me to explain it in detail which I have implemented using Google Cloud Platform.Then he asked me simple programming question of Checking whether a number is pallindrome or not. I have started with brute force approach and then explained the optimal one .He also asked me questions about the other projects mentioned in my resume, focusing mainly on how I implemented specific features and the reasoning behind them .Finally I asked the interviewer a question and the interview was concluded.

I was able to answer almost every question in this round and felt confident that I would advance to the next round. This interview lasted for around 45 mins.

3. Technical Interview - Round 2

After about 30 minutes, I was informed that I had been selected for the second round and was called in for the interview.

This interview started with a self-introduction. Then, the interviewer asked me about my internship project. He further asked about the difference between SQL and NoSQL in DBMS, followed by a discussion on normalization. After that, he asked me to design a database schema for a company with users as students, employees, teachers, and staff. His main objective was to assess my understanding of storing data in a normalized form. Next, he asked me to write a SQL query on the schema I had designed, having GROUP BY and ORDER BY operations. After this, he asked about the difference between JWT and Cookies. He then moved on to Sockets and Polling concepts. Further, he asked some basic Python questions such as the difference between lists and tuples and how multiple inheritance works in Python. Finally, he asked me about my Major Project.

In this round, the interviewer cross-questioned frequently to test my depth of knowledge . I was able to answer almost every question except for the one on Sockets, where the interviewer gave me a hint, after which I was able to respond correctly.

Tip: Try to answer theoretical questions with real-life use cases or examples to demonstrate a deeper understanding of the topic

4. HR Round

After about an hour, I was informed that I had been selected for the HR round.

The HR round began with my self-introduction, followed by questions about my family background and where I live. Then, the interviewer asked me to pitch one of my projects of my choice in one minute as if I were pitching it to an investor. He also asked about the challenges I faced while working on that project.Next, he moved on to behavioral questions such as:

If I assign you a project about which you have no prior knowledge, how would you approach it?

If you are assigned three tasks with tight deadlines, how would you prioritize and work on them?

He also asked a guesstimate question to estimate the number of daily users on YouTube. Lastly, he asked me why I want to join Quantiphi and where I see myself in the next five years.

Around 9 PM, all interviews were concluded, and the team went inside the conference room to discuss the results. Everyone waiting outside was very tense, and I was silently praying to God. Finally, around 9:45 PM, the results were announced--8 candidates were selected, including me (for the FE role). Among the selectees, 2 were for MLE, 3 for FE, and 3 for BA roles.

The process had 4 rounds.

1) OA

2) Technical Interview 1

3) Technical Interview 2

4) HR Interview

Quantiphi offered 3 roles, FE (Framework Engineer), MLE (Machine Learning Engineer) and BA (Business Analyst). We were supposed to order our preference in the Superset Application.

(To read the ML Interview Experience skip over to page 3)

1. OA [ 133 Appeared ]

We had 3 sections

1) Aptitude, Logical & Verbal Reasoning: 40 Questions - 30 Minutes

2) CS Fundamentals: 33 Questions - 25 Minutes

3) Coding Problems 3 Questions - 30 Minutes The amount of time was limited, so speed was the key to getting through in this round.

The first section was mostly as expected, but there were quite a few difficult problems on permutations and a few other topics. There were also a lot of problems on Area and Volume calculations (What is the profit if you sell the material extracted from a pyramid (and a cone) for 10 Rs/cm^3 and you bought the pyramid for 200). But I had to skip most of these because the time was limited and we didn't have calcis allowed. My advice would be to attempt this section in multiple iterations, solving the easiest questions in the first one, then the next and so on. Can't stress this enough, but time is a huge constraint here so manage it well. The second section was CS fundamentals (and little dev too). We had general theory based questions from OOPs, DBMS and OS. This was pretty standard. There were unexpected questions though that were the you know it or you don't type. The final Section had 3 coding problems. An easy one, an easy-medium and a difficult one.

● A thief wants to rob all the houses in a village. There is an array of the number of houses in each neighbourhood and the maximum amount of time(hours) he can take. At what minimum speed in houses per hour does he need to rob to clean the entire village ? You just need to take the sum of the houses and divide this number by the total time to get the rate of robbing. Round it off to the higher number and return the integer answer.

● A question very similar to the House Robber Problem from Leetcode. It was a basic include-exclude DP problem with one if condition. I didn't even need to apply DP as the first Recursive code that I ran passed all testcases. Link

● You are given an undirected graph of n islands, each with a loot value, and edges representing travel paths between islands with their travel times. A pirate may start from any island, traveling along available paths, and can visit each island at most once. The total loot is the sum of the visited islands' values, while the total time is the sum of the travel times along the chosen path. Find the maximum loot the pirate can collect. I was able to solve the first 2 problems but ran out of time attempting the 3rd one.

2. FE Interview 1 [ 17(FE) + 17(MLE) + 58(BA - GD followed by interviews)] [ 4:30 PM]

I had mistakenly selected FE as my first preference so I informed my FE Interviewer that I wanted MLE. We had been notified of this inward mobility for Roles in the Presentation. I was asked to complete this interview after which my request would go on to be processed.

We started with this round with me introducing myself and the interviewer going through my resume. We discussed all my projects (2 ML, 2 Dev) one after another and he asked plenty of questions as I was explaining. Be thoroughly prepared with your projects and don't fake anything. You should be prepared to answer questions like "Why did you use this service and not the other (Postgres vs Mongo, AWS vs Azure, etc) ?", "Are there any live applications that provide this service, how does your project compare to theirs ?", "What changes would you make if you wanted to serve 10k users with your project (Scalability is a very popular question) and other questions that question the inner mechanics of your project like "What purpose does this feature resolve ?", "Couldn't you have simplified things this way, your approach is very inefficient." and so on. Not every interviewer goes in this deep but there are ones that do.. (Baker 😭)

After the resume we started with his questions. He didn't ask any really difficult questions on DSA or SQL that needed time, this was more of an itinerary of easy to medium theory and coding problems. Here are a few of those:

● Do you know about normalization ? What is the difference between 1NF and 3NF normalization ?

● What is polymorphism ? How do we implement it ?

● Can you tell me about Indexing ? What are the drawbacks of Indexing ?

● Write an SQL query to remove duplicate entries from a database. (I used row_number() and partitioned by PK, after which I removed all entries with a row_num higher than 1)

● Can you do this problem without using windowing functions ?

There were quite a few questions around this difficulty level and I was able to answer most of them. After this round I was asked to appear for Interview 2 where I was informed that I will now be taken to their ML Engineer to appear for MLE Interview 1.

3. MLE Interview 1 & 2 [ 6:30 PM & 7:30 PM]

I would like to start this section with an overview of what I think of ML Interviews. These are just the views of a guy that has given 2 ML interviews so read them with a grain of salt. There is no defined structure to gauge a candidate's ability for an ML position at the graduate level. So Interviewers are going to ask you a very wide variety of questions and your selection depends on how much you can impress them across the duration of the exchange. Here is my personal order of importance for the subjects of your interview:

1) Your Projects: Can't stress this enough, but your projects are your best shot at showcasing your skills to the interviewer and showing how deep of an understanding you have in the concepts you've used in these projects. The interviewer can't just ask you to explain the architecture of a GNN Model to test you because that isn't something you can expect the average candidate to know. You need to dominate this discussion and tell the interviewer of every sellable skill you've utilized. Tell him about the nature of the dataset you used, about the challenges you faced in feature engineering, about the tools you used to clean/filter the data and augment samples. Tell him about why you chose your Model over the alternatives (for me it was why I chose BiLSTM over LSTM and GRU) and about the architecture of your model and what understandings you derived while working on the model and so on.

2) Fundamentals: The interviewer will then start asking questions to test your fundamentals such as

● What is regression ? How do you differentiate between it and classification ?

● What do you mean by clustering ?

● What will you do if your dataset has a lot of missing values ?

● Why do some models with good training accuracy have bad test accuracy ?

● What is bias vs variance tradeoff ?

● What are false positives and negatives ?

● What are precision and recall and when do they become useful ?

● What metrics did you use to judge your model and explain the significance of each metric ? (I answered the confusion matrix, classification report containing accuracy, precision, recall, f1- score, and the Learning curve comparing training and validation sets) There will be plenty of questions like this and they can be prepared for in advance.

3) Your Knowledge of ML Models: In the midst of the questions focusing on fundamentals, the interviewer also kept asking me questions on popular models. These included

● What is Linear Regression ? Is it related to Logistic regression ?

● Please explain how a Decision Tree works ? Can you draw an example for us ?

● Why do we need Unsupervised Learning ? Can you talk about any popular models Unsupervised Learning holds ?

● What is an ensemble model ?

● What will you do when faced with an Image based dataset. Having a basic understanding of these models is sufficient, you don't need to be an expert in everything.

I think this discussion includes most of the questions asked to me during the interviews. I'll list the few remaining questions here:

● The interviewer asked me if I had deployed any models ?

● He asked me if I had worked with NLP ? (I started talking about the need to process words and the Bag-of-Words Model. I had very surface level knowledge on this matter..)

● He then started to ask more detailed questions related to NLP but I was unable to answer them, from his body language it seemed like he expected a little more. In popular ML culture we see everyone talking about Deep Learning but NLP spans a whole lot of projects too and is not as much talked about. Can read a few things up.

● He presented to me a situation where I had a dataset of sentences that were classified as good and bad and we needed a model that could predict sentences in this manner.

This concludes almost all of what I was asked in MLE Interviews 1 and 2. I haven't separated the interviews into two sections because the flow of the interviews was very similar and it didn't make sense to separate them. The only difference was that the second interview didn't involve as many fundamental questions as the first one and was a little more intense. There was a bit of grilling involved in both the interviews and the first one went on for over an hour. The second one was a bit short at 30 minutes. This was followed by the HR interview. The selection from FE/MLE/BA Interview 1 to Interview 2 was very brutal. The rate of progression from Interview 1 to Interview 2 at Quantiphi was far lower than the average company.

4. HR Interview [ 13 shortlisted, 3 MLE and 10 FE+BA] [ 8:30 PM]

This was a typical "HR Interview". There weren't any tough questions, just enquiring things about you. Questions included. It lasted a relaxed 15-20 minutes. After the HR interview we had to wait for almost an hour as all the Interviewers and Execs discussed amongst themselves. Finally the shortlist was released around 10 PM and 8 candidates were selected. The selectees were 2 from MLE, 3 from FE and 3 from BA.

journey.prep:
1. My first interview was for an SDE role at WorkIndia. I cleared all rounds and interviews, making no mistakes from my side, answering all questions, and solving all the given DSA questions in an optimized way, yet I was still not selected for the HR round. The thing I learned is that placement remains a game of luck given that you have all the skills.

2. Tailor your resume according to the job description of the company, and make sure to include all the skills and projects relevant to the role you're applying for. Check for grammatical errors, as they can instantly create a bad impression. Also, check your ATS score online (websites like Enhancv and Resume Worded can help). Most importantly, never fake information in your resume, if you're caught, it leaves a lasting negative impression. Be true and genuine.

3. Always attend the PPT, as information such as the company's values or history shared during it is often asked in the HR round.

4. If you have consistently worked hard for your placements from the start, then even with some hard luck, you will eventually end up with a good placement. Just don't give up, keep trying and believe in the work you've put in so far.

5. I have always loved participating in hackathons, and I would highly recommend you take part in such coding competitions to continuously learn and grow your skills. You can read my post about my hackathon experiences here - link.

6. Focus on basic concepts, practice DSA regularly, as it requires consistency. Revise DBMS theory and SQL questions (especially the Top 50 SQL questions from LeetCode), review OS and CN, and try to learn Java, as it is required by many companies.

7. Whenever you learn new skills, make sure to first understand the basics and build a strong foundation. For example, if you're interested in machine learning, start with linear algebra and statistics, and try to understand each algorithm mathematically, you'll enjoy it even more.

8. Try to make open-source contributions and participate in events like Hacktoberfest, GSoC, etc. For that, your skills are your weapon, build strong foundations in whatever you are learning, and then collaborate with other developers online to expand your connections.

The interviewer was polite and seemed genuinely interested in my projects and my Data Science degree from IIT Madras. This part lasted about 15-20 minutes.

Next came the coding round. I was given a database schema and asked three SQL questions based on it. The first two questions were easy, similar to this question: Average Selling Price, while the third was of medium difficulty similar to this question: Monthly Transactions 1. The topics included aggregate functions, joins, and subqueries. I'd recommend practicing the "Top 50 SQL Questions" from LeetCode for such rounds.

After that, the Data Science/Python coding round began. The interviewer provided a CSV file and asked me to use any notebook platform (Google Colab, Kaggle, or Jupyter Notebook). The questions were based on Pandas and NumPy, and I was asked to:

customSections.title: Advice & Tips for Juniors
customSections.content:
1. My first interview was for an SDE role at WorkIndia. I cleared all rounds and interviews, making no mistakes from my side, answering all questions, and solving all the given DSA questions in an optimized way, yet I was still not selected for the HR round. The thing I learned is that placement remains a game of luck given that you have all the skills.

2. Tailor your resume according to the job description of the company, and make sure to include all the skills and projects relevant to the role you're applying for. Check for grammatical errors, as they can instantly create a bad impression. Also, check your ATS score online (websites like Enhancv and Resume Worded can help). Most importantly, never fake information in your resume, if you're caught, it leaves a lasting negative impression. Be true and genuine.

3. Always attend the PPT, as information such as the company's values or history shared during it is often asked in the HR round.

4. If you have consistently worked hard for your placements from the start, then even with some hard luck, you will eventually end up with a good placement. Just don't give up, keep trying and believe in the work you've put in so far.

5. I have always loved participating in hackathons, and I would highly recommend you take part in such coding competitions to continuously learn and grow your skills. You can read my post about my hackathon experiences here - link.

6. Focus on basic concepts, practice DSA regularly, as it requires consistency. Revise DBMS theory and SQL questions (especially the Top 50 SQL questions from LeetCode), review OS and CN, and try to learn Java, as it is required by many companies.

7. Whenever you learn new skills, make sure to first understand the basics and build a strong foundation. For example, if you're interested in machine learning, start with linear algebra and statistics, and try to understand each algorithm mathematically, you'll enjoy it even more.

8. Try to make open-source contributions and participate in events like Hacktoberfest, GSoC, etc. For that, your skills are your weapon, build strong foundations in whatever you are learning, and then collaborate with other developers online to expand your connections.

(I have included CGPA)

1. Resume/CGPA Shortlisting: (In this case it was CGPA shortlisting , but still I have provided guidance for Resume shortlisting )

Always tailor your resume to align with the specific job description of the role you're applying for. These adjustments don't need to be major -- simply swapping a project, updating certifications, or modifying the skills section can make a significant diff erence.

Ensure that your resume maintains visual and structural consistency. Avoid mixing date formats, bullet styles, or using bold/italic formatting inconsistently across sections. A clean, well-organized resume gives a strong first impression.

Once your resume is finalized, evaluate its compatibility with Applicant Tracking Systems (ATS). Tools like Resume Worded can help -- aim for a score of 65 or above.

Initially, the CGPA eligibility criteria for th is role was set at 8.5, but it was later relaxed to 7.5. The shortlist of candidates selected for the Online Assessment and Pre -Placement Talk (PPT) was released on 3rd August 2025 at 7:00 PM.

2. Pre-Placement Talk:

The Pre-Placement Talk was conducted online on 4th August 2025 at 5:00 PM.

The information shared during Pre-Placement Talks is extremely valuable, so it's important to be attentive -- not just to the content of the presentation, but also to the names and roles of the presenters. I made it a point to take multiple screenshots and jot down the specific examples used while the speaker explained some of the company's financial services. These details often come in handy during interviews.

While it's a good idea to ask thoughtful questions at the end of the session, it's even smarter to hold back a few insightful ones. Save them for your interview -- this gives you an opportunity to show continued curiosity and engagement with the company during later stages.

3. Online Assessment: (Approx. 160 students appeared, invigilated by the company) The online assessment comprised 70 questions to be completed in 90 minutes. It was conducted via Google Forms at the college premises. The marking scheme awarded +1 for each correct answer and imposed a -0.25 penalty for incorrect ones. The assessment covered four major sections: Java, Python, SQL, and Aptitude.

Java (18 Questions): This section focused heavily on fundamental OOP concepts in Java. Topics included the Collection Framework (TreeMap, HashMap, LinkedHashMap, ConcurrentHashMap, ArrayList), access modifiers, threads and multithreading, keywords like synchronized and volatile, compile-time and runtime polymorphism, interfaces, abstract classes, exception handling, enums, and functional methods like map, filter, and reduce. Most questions were of the "guess the output" type. Although my primary DSA language is C++, I had thoroughly studied and revised Java concepts beforehand. A great resource for MCQ practice: Java Practice - Sanfoundry

Python (17 Questions): Similar to Java, the Python section included "guess the output" questions involving OOP concepts, inheritance and MRO (Method Resolution Order), shallow vs deep copies, list comprehensions, slicing, dictionaries, sets, stacks, and queues. Many questions required careful dry runs and a strong grasp of Python's internal behavior and edge cases. A good practice resource: Python Practice - Sanfoundry SQL (5 Questions): This section tested practical SQL query-writing skills. The difficulty level was moderate, with questions based on GROUP BY, JOIN, ORDER BY, UPDATE, DELETE, and various date functions. Some tricky questions involved updating joined or aggregated tables. Attempt only if

confident. Highly recommended: Top 50 SQL Questions - LeetCode

Aptitude (30 Questions): This was arguably the most challenging section. It covered clock problems, speed and distance, trigonometry, upstream-downstream problems, probability, combinatorics, statistics, geometry, family relationships, and financial mathematics (including stocks and investments). Some questions were quite verbose and difficult to interpret, and I couldn't solve a few. Two great resources for aptitude practice are:

 YouTube Aptitude Series by CareerRide

 IndiaBix Aptitude Practice

I performed well in the Java, Python, and SQL sections but found the Aptitude section challenging. In total, I attempted around 50-55 out of 70 questions. Fortunately, I was among the 44 students shortlisted out of 160.

Final Tips: Keep your technical concepts in Java and Python fresh, practice aptitude regularly to build speed, and remain calm under pressure. Time constraints will challenge everyone equally -- focus on accuracy, avoid panic, and read questions carefully.

4. Technical Round 1: [44 student appeared] 2 interviewers in my panel

As I mentioned earlier, I was unsure of whether I 'd be selected for interviews or not. So, I was keeping my cool and doing last minute revisions for Java. Around 12:15 pm we received the shortlists and I was delighted to see my name at the 17 th position. I quickly had a small snack before the interviews start so that I am not empty stomach (make sure to eat at least a little and not be completely empty stomach due to stress/tension). I was very lucky with my interview slot and timings, I was scheduled for 2nd interview in my panel. My interview lasted about 30-40 minutes. And there were 2 interviewers in my panel. Even if your interview gets scheduled late, don't worry and do your best.

I will keep my experience as detailed as possible.

I entered the cabin and greeted both the panelists, they asked me about my name and branch (Didn't ask me to introduce myself). They asked me why did I choose Data Science branch. I was honest and said that during that time I was naïve and wanted to pursue a career in data science without much understanding of it, I basically explained how I understood and explored other options and found my interest in software development. They asked me what backend technol ogies I had explored, I had done Node.js + Express framework and Django in python. He disappointedly asked whether I had not tried Java for backend. I answered this question very carefully and told him that I had studied Java for my

2nd Sem and then I had developed games like Snake and minesweeper using Java, and like justified that I know Java. Whereas for backend development my fundamentals are clear enough that switching the language won 't be an issue for me. He was happy with my response. Then he shifted the interview towards Java OOPs, He showed me one of the question from Java section in OA.

He started asking whether do I see something wrong in Class Person or a way we can make it better. I suggested making string private and having getter and sette r method to ensure that the name string is not directly accessible from outside of class and only via getter and setter method. He asked me which concept was OOPs is this, I answered Encapsulation and explained what it meant in this scenario .

He then asked me about the output of the code, I answered "2 100". Later they asked me how can I make the output to be 1 100. So, I suggested overriding equals and hashcode methods provided my HashMap class in Person class to behave such that if the name is equal, It will treat it as same object otherwise as different object. He also asked to improve the declaration of HashMap object. At first, I couldn't understand what exactly was needed to be done, I suggested having Person class object be immutable as there is a risk of key getting corrupted due to change in data within a Person object. Then they asked a follow up on what is a immutable class, I explained how to make a class immutable and also mentioned about enums. For the earlier question, Later they give me hints and I understood and explained that having a ref of parent and object of child class is a better practice in Java, as you can change the object to any other child of the parent without having to change the ref.

Map<Person, Integer> mp = new HashMap<>();

was the answer they were looking for. I needed hints but I caught on to it at the very end. They asked me to write a very simple program to remove all the white spaces from a string and return the string. I requested whether I could use C++, and I wrote it on piece of paper, I started by writing #include<stdio.h> but they said it's fine and write the logic, so I made a function with proper name like removeWhiteSpaces and passed in the string and simply iterated over it and checked whether if the character is non space then append it to ans string and return ans. The interviewer commented that he liked how I made a function instead of writing in Main.

Then they asked me about a simple S QL query involving a join and order by and limit to get the first row. I also said that it's possible to use max(date) to get the row with latest date.

The interview questions ended on a brighter note.

Questions I asked to interviewers:

1. I asked them to introduce themselves and their role.

2. How is AI being integrated within I SS and what's its impact has been for ISS. (I tried to enter the convo when they jokingly said that people in the company sometimes don't understand their own code as they use AI and that is why they do code reviews. Here I tried to showcase how I personally use AI as more of a tutor for learning and deep diving into concepts)

3. I don't remember exactly how but they were talking about data scrapping , and I took the opportunity and I replied that I have experience with data scrapping as well and how I made a s cript to scrape linkedIn profile data from their user urls using selenium and beautiful soup.

By the end of this, they asked me where do I stay and whether commute will be a problem.

And just after 10 minutes of leaving the cabin at 2 pm, I was notified that I have been shortlisted for next round. Why I Think I Got Selected:

 Timing & Luck: I got an early interview slot, which helped.

 Confidence & Communication: I stayed composed and articulated my thoughts clearly.

 Honesty: I was transparent about what I knew and didn't.

 Engagement: I asked meaningful questions and engaged in a two-way conversation. Even if you don't know something don't stay completely silent and keep processing your thoughts out and don't panic. Your personality and confidence also matters, try to work on soft skills and effective communication. Give as much mock interviews as you can to better prepare yourself.

In total 15 students were shortlisted for HR round including me.

Tips:

 Do not lie on your Resume but you can smartly change phrases so that your resume looks good.  Do not throw the sheets/papers in which you did your OA questions. They can be asked in an interview.  Make sure if you are adding any links then they are clickable in your resume  Prepare well around your resume projects & its tech stack. You can ask your friend to keep on cross questioning you on them  Prepare a couple of scenarios (even if fake) about disagreement in the team, or any times that you have shown leadership/ team spirit. These questions are very common too.  If you don't know the answer or you are not able to recall it, try to put it across politely instead of saying something wrong  Think out loud when solving a DSA problem/ SQL query but when saying a theory answer try to sort of structure it in your mind first. Make use of technical terms & examples where possible

5. HR Round: [15 students Appeared] 2 panelists

My HR round started at around 3:50 pm, I had prepared in advance for all the common HR questions which could be asked. Even if you get caught off guard do not panic and be calm and collected, answer it genuinely. My HR round lasted for about 30 minutes.

I entered the room and greeted the interviewers, their first question was do you know us. I had paid attention to PPT so I knew their names and I h ad mentioned that their cameras were not working properly so I didn 't realize it instantly but by listening to their voice. They first asked me about my education from 10 th, 12th and College CGPA and Cet score. I answered the question by making a narrative about how I wasn't very studious and how I got serious about studies and answered each question. They asked me about my family background, make sure to answer only what is needed and not more than that. I showcased how being a single child, my parents have been supportive and available for me. She also asked whether I knew the office location and visited the NESCO IT park, I replied with correct answer and was honest that I hadn't been there.

She asked me about why did I pursue CSE DS, I again answered gen uinely and told her the truth. She asked me about my 1st coding project, I mentioned I had gotten into game development using Unity and later using Java built snake and minesweeper games. She also asked me about masters and would I want to pursue it. I answered no (I genuinely hadn't planned for masters) mentioned that how skills, experience and practical knowledge in industry is required to stay relevant and masters is more theoretical and academia focussed. So, I would rather up skill myself while working in a job. She pressed on even more about the fact that aren't my parents insisting for me to do masters since I am a single child. Again, I thought carefully and answered that it was different during my father's time where a degree was required to grow in pharmaceutical companies. Whereas in tech I don't need as much

education, having experience and skills are the most important thing. (Try to justify the trade off between masters and job)

How do I stay relevant about the tech news. I said Youtube, Reddit, Twitter and justified my perspective. She started asking me about my perspective about AI, I made sure to answer everything positively. I said AI is a tool and won't completely replace a human, at least not until there is a very fundamental change in how AI works. I made sure to cover the positive aspects of AI, she said would it have any impact on jobs? And I said that due to this for example 10 people doing some work would be reduced to 5 -6, but there could be other jobs for managing agentic AI systems. She asked me how would I make sure I don 't get replaced with AI. I again answered that not staying in the comfort zon e for a long time is the key and always having continuous growth and learning is essential.

She also asked me about my hobbies, I answe red reading, table tennis, badminton, swimming. I made sure to elaborate on how reading was not my strong point and how I developed that skill effectively. Sir had only asked me a single question about what is my preference regarding application developer and AIML. I made sure to answer diplomatically, I said my primary focus is on developing software either for clients or for some internal company usage, and within software development I want to keep my options broader and so that I am able to figure out my interests, etc. And how I could maybe help others get a new perspective in software development processes using my ML and Gen AI knowledge, so no knowledge ever goes waste. She lastly asked where do I stay and whether commute would be a problem for me. I live in thane so I said it won't be a big issue for me as I have been travelling for SPIT for the past 3 years. And if I do find it difficult, I would simply shift closer towards the company and ensure it doesn't hamper my work.

I made sure to ask decent questions:

1. How is data staleness managed as old data cannot be served to clients

2. Since ISS is multi -national company serving over 15+ countries , how do they manage and maintain regulatory compliance for each country.

3. How does team and project allotment work for interns and freshers in ISS

HR Interview Tips:

1. Maintain Eye Contact Ensure steady, natural eye contact with the interviewer. It shows confidence and helps build a connection, but avoid staring as it may come across as forced.

2. Be Mindful of What You Share Avoid oversharing personal experiences that don 't directly address the question. Focus on relevant, concise answers that highlight your suitability for the role.

3. Use the STAR Method Structure your answers to behavioral questions using the STAR me thod (Situation, Task, Action, Result). It provides clarity and demonstrates a problem -solving mindset.

4. Show Respect in All Responses Be polite and professional. Even casual or off -topic comments should be delivered respectfully to avoid unintentionally off ending the interviewer.

5. Frame Strengths and Weaknesses as Narratives Share your strengths and weaknesses with context. Use short stories or examples (real or carefully crafted) that showcase growth and self -awareness.

6. Avoid Monologues Don't treat your ans wers like speeches. Keep the conversation balanced, concise, and interactive. Know when to stop and where to elaborate.

7. Display Confidence and Personality Strong communication and soft skills often outweigh technical skills in HR rounds. Let your personality come through --be confident, composed, and clear.

8. Always be Positive Always answer all questions in a positi ve manner and I 'll suggest don't ask for feedback in an HR interview, you can in a technical round if you feel that you 've done great.

9. Always Deny plans for Higher Studies

Never show interest or accidently hint your passion for academia and research . Prepare solid reasons to justify why you're choosing industry over academia, or it may become your reason for rejection.

Lastly, 12 students were selected out of 15, including myself. 2 for Data quality, 2 for software testing, 8 for Software Engineering.

The questions were on easy to medium level but all the options looked similar at first sight - but had slight differences, making it a bit time-consuming and needing a double check.

She then asked for a brief explanation of one of my projects, followed by a few questions on its implementation.

Since I had stated Java as my primary programming language, she asked me a few questions about JDK, JRE, and JVM, and then about how and why Java is considered platform -independent. Make sure you are clear on these basic Java architecture concepts.

The discussion then moved to SQL queries. The first was to find the maximum salary in each department, followed by the query to find the top two salaries in each department. I had to write the queries on paper. She then added gender and city columns to the same table and asked for the names of female employees with the maximum salary in their respective departments.

Next, the discussion moved to OOP concepts in Java. I was asked to briefly explain the four pillars of OOP. Then, the interviewer presented a few classes -- Shape, Rectangle, Square, and Circle -- and asked me to apply inheritance to them. Initially, I designed Shape as an interface and implemented hierarchical inheritance, where Rectangle, Square, and Circle each implemented the Shape interface. She then encouraged me to think of a more convenient approach. That's when I realized she was expecting multilevel inheritance, such as Shape → Rectangle → Square, since every Square is a Rectangle . Following that, she introduced a Rhombus class and asked me to integrate it into the inheritance tree. Initially unsure, I asked about its properties and understood that, just like every Square is a Rectangle, every Square is also a Rhombus. I then attempted to inherit Square from both Rectangle and Rhombus, which led to a discussion on the diamond problem in Java, its solutions, and the use of the super keyword.

Then came the DSA questions, the first question was to remove all occurrences of a given key from a linked list. I explained my approach in detail before writing the source code. I fumbled slightly while handling the pointers but kept thinking aloud and explaining my reasoning. I la ter wrote the correct code and dry -ran it on both the given list and an additional test case to check for edge cases. The second DSA question was straightforward -- return true if there are three consecutive odd numbers, else return false.

Finally, I was asked a commonly known puzzle: Mislabelled Jars

The interview concluded with me asking the panelist about her own experience at ISS -STOXX -- current role in the company, and experience in the tech industry.

4. HR Round: [ 15 students appeared ]

There were two interviewers in this round -- the same ones who had conducted the pre-placement talk. I would advise remembering their names, as interviewers sometimes ask if you know them. I was again the last candidate for the HR round, which lasted about 30-35 minutes and ended around 10 PM.

The conversation began with an introduction about myself and my family background, followed by questions about my 10th-grade percentage, diploma percentage, and current CGPA. My diploma caught their attention, and they asked why I chose to pursue a diploma instead of completing 12th grade and attempting JEE/CET. I'd advise all DSE students to prepare well for this question, as it is frequently asked in interviews.

Next, they asked about my interest in technology. I shared that I had been passionate about full stack development since my diploma days. This led to a question about my favourite project, for which I described one of my ML projects. They probed deeper into it -- asking how I came up with the problem statement, the overall design, the reason behind my choice of technology, possible alternative technologies, and potential edge cases. They also asked about the challenges I faced during development.

Since my resume listed two ML projects and only one fully dedicated full stack project -- and I had chosen an ML project as my favourite -- they expressed concern about my fit at ISS-STOXX, as the company doesn't work extensively with AI/ML. I clarified that although the projects were ML-based, their core still relied on full stack development fundamentals -- including a robust backend, scalable database, and interactive frontend. When given a hypothetical choice between working on a completely full stack project or a purely ML project at ISS, I confidently said I would choose the full stack one, as it has always been my forte and I am excited to explore the technologies ISS uses.

The interviewer knew that the last company which came before ISS-STOXX was Nomura, and asked why I couldn't clear its process. This led to questions about how many interviews I had given before, and why I thought I couldn't clear them. My suggestion to others would be to answer such questions honestly, showing self-awareness about areas of improvement and demonstrating that you have worked on them.

The interview concluded with me asking if the company organizes internal hackathons or other competitive events for employees. They replied that, at present, they do not, but expressed strong interest and agreed that it was indeed a great idea that I gave them. I added that hosting such events could enhance interaction among employees, encourage exploration of new technologies, and ultimately benefit the company.

The final results came at around 11 PM.

Finally, 12 students got the offer !!

journey.prep:
● Get used to rejections. Don't give up. During the entire placement season, I was very sick (even hospitalized before it began), had severe side effects that caused excruciating joint pains, and still had to travel 1 hour daily for online assessments and interviews. I faced rejections in interviews from PhonePe, Barclays, Nomura, and in the HR round of MSCI. Even during the ISS process I was not well. But I kept pushing myself -- just a little more every time.

● Stay connected to your friends. They help more than you can imagine -- conduct mock interviews, build projects together, prepare in groups. It really helps in keeping the momentum and staying motivated.

● Know all your projects well. I've often heard people say, "It was a group project, and I didn't work on that part." Personally, I'd strongly recommend not saying that. You usually have 3-4 projects on your resume, and you're expected to know all of them thoroughly.

● Some common resume/project questions:

○ Why this project?

○ Why this tech stack? (know as much as you can about that technology)

○ Alternatives to the technologies used?

○ Your exact role?

○ What did you learn?

○ What are the drawbacks?

○ What can be improved?

○ Can it scale? How is the architecture?

● While answering, never talk negatively about alternatives. Instead, explain why your chosen approach suits your project best.

● Avoid saying I don't know unless you have zero idea about the question.

● Don't restrict your thoughts completely, convey them to the interviewer and clarify doubts. During some interviews out of nervousness I didn't say a few things which potentially could have been answers which I regretted; avoid it.

● Don't be fooled by simplicity. After reading such experiences, you might feel that questions are easy/basic. That's a myth. Many people get easy panels or familiar questions. But rejections happen due to several other reasons -- timing, panel, tricky questions, or just not being the right fit. It's not always about luck or coincidence either -- some part of it is, but you should try to be as prepared as possible. Sometimes, when the panel has too many shortlisted candidates, they go tough. And if you answer those tough questions, you automatically stand out. The questions aren't impossible -- they're just a little tricky and layered.

● Never lose your calm. Always smile. Communication plays a huge role. Your presence, gestures, tone -- all matter. Highlight key words during your answers to guide the interviewer and keep the flow in your control.

● Read the Job Description. Align your strengths and weaknesses with the company's values and goals.

● Avoid last-minute prep. Don't rely on learning or reading something right before the interview.

● Have basic knowledge of System design not all companies ask them but phonepe, MSCI, Zeta, etc does.

● Prepare for a few HR questions beforehand.

Resources:

● Java and OOPs (refer at least the oops part): https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PL9gnSGHSqcnr_DxHsP7AW9ftq0AtAyYqJ

● Dbms: Complete DBMS in 1 Video (With Notes) || For Placement Interviews

● OS (Multithreading should be enough): Complete Operating Systems in 1 Shot (With Notes) || For Placement Interviews

● Indiabix for aptitude

● Sql top 50

● Striver Sheet for dsa is more than enough (unless you are appearing for phonepe).

Feel free to connect on LinkedIn.

All the very best!!! 😀

journey.howSecured:
A total of 3 rounds were conducted - 1 Online Assessment Round, 1 Tech Interview Round & Finally 1 HR Round. All were conducted on the same day 5th Aug. The CGPA Criteria for SDE was 8.5, later reduced to

8. It was further reduced to 7.5. May not be the case for next year if they don't want more applicants, so it is preferable to maintain a pointer of 8.5 and above. We were supposed to enter 2 preferences and mostly all of them were selected for their 1st preference. Some were asked personally whether they would like to sit for their interviews for the 2nd preference. So choose your preferences wisely.

1. Resume based shortlisting

My resume The first round was a resume-based shortlisting. While the exact criteria were not disclosed, CGPA likely played a role. Here are some key points based on my experience:

● Mention only those skills in your resume that you are genuinely confident and comfortable with. Including too many skills can lead to complex and unexpected questions during the interview if not fully prepared.

● Try to have at least one solid project. If the project is unique it's awesome but irrespective of if it is or not, focus on scalability and optimizations techniques.

● Ensure that all links in your resume are valid and clickable. Interviewers do check them. Also, make sure your projects have a proper README to give a quick overview of the project.

● Making your resume quantifiable using metrics or measurable impact is a good practice, though it is not strictly necessary.

● Try to align your resume with the job description or your selected preference. In our case, we were asked to choose two preferences (i chose SDE and Data Quality). Fortunately I was selected for the SDE role otherwise my resume didn't have any data science projects.. But that might not always be the case so make your resume smartly.

● Even if a company lists many technologies in the JD, you don't need to include all of them in your resume--focus on those that match your strengths and the role you're aiming for.

2. Preplacement talk

Although the process was initially planned to be offline, it was later conducted online at 5 PM on 4th August.

Pay close attention to the PPT. Note down the names and roles of the presenters--it helps during interactions. It's also a good idea to do some basic research on the company beforehand, like the founding year, CEO, and tagline, as such questions can be asked and showing awareness leaves a good impression.

You may ask thoughtful questions at the end of the PPT session to show engagement, though it's not mandatory. Alternatively, you can save your questions for the post-interview phase if that feels more comfortable.

3. Online Assessment [Around 160 candidates]

This round was held around 9:30 AM. It consisted of 70 questions in 90 minutes, conducted via Google Forms at the college premises under the supervision of company professionals. The marking scheme was +1 for correct answers and -0.25 for incorrect ones. Only desktop calculators were allowed.

The test was divided into four sections: Java, Python, SQL, and Aptitude.

The Java section had easy to medium-level questions, mainly covering OOPs, collections, multithreading exception handling, enums, etc. Most questions involved code snippets where we had to predict the output. Although my primary language was C++, I had to prepare the Java Collections Framework separately. Previous years, topics like streams, generics, concurrenthashmap were also included, so it's advisable to prepare Java thoroughly. I remember I had solved 15/18 questions in this section. One or two were flukes.

The Python section included questions on OOPs, MRO (Method Resolution Order), list comprehensions, Counter, stacks, sets, slicing, and similar topics. Understanding the internal workings of Python is important--such as knowing when a copy is created, how mutability affects original data structures, and what happens when using mutable default arguments in functions. These concepts are frequently tested and can be tricky if not well understood.

The SQL section was straightforward. An input and a problem statement were given, and we had to choose the correct option--no actual coding was required. Questions were based on basic concepts like JOINs, WHERE and BETWEEN clauses, and GROUP BY. Preparing fundamental SQL queries is sufficient for this part.

I spent around 30-40 minutes on the Aptitude section after quickly completing the others. It was the toughest part of the assessment, with long and time-consuming questions, mostly based on IndiaBix. I avoided guessing and managed to attempt a fair number confidently. Topics included core areas like profit and loss, interest, speed and distance, permutations, and data interpretation, along with less common ones like banker's discount and stocks.

4. Technical Round 1 [45 students]

I wasn't very confident about my OA performance, but I still began revising key concepts like Java Collections and reviewed my resume. The shortlist was announced at 12:15 PM, and I was delighted to see my name on the list. There were two interviewers in my panel, and they started asking questions simultaneously. The first question was a self-introduction, where I briefly mentioned my name, branch, projects, internship, committee role, and achievements--keeping it concise.

Next, I was asked to explain the four pillars of OOPs. I gave clear explanations with relevant examples. They followed up with questions on common interview topics like the difference between encapsulation and abstraction, and abstract classes vs. interfaces. I was specifically asked about constructors, instantiation, and whether these classes can have methods with their own implementation.Up to this point, I answered confidently. However, I got confused when asked if abstract classes and interfaces can have variables. I recalled that abstract classes can, but wasn't sure about interfaces due to less hands on practice with OOPs. I answered that it's possible but not commonly practiced--something I feel I shouldn't have said, as it didn't make much sense. These small gaps in lesser-practiced topics can create confusion, but the interview moved on smoothly after that.

They then asked if I was comfortable with Java Collections, and the same question was repeated for Python. Saying no directly could have been a red flag, so I answered honestly yet strategically. I mentioned that C++ is my primary language and that I'm very comfortable with DSA in C++ and OOPs in Java. I also said that while I may not have in-depth hands-on experience, I have a good understanding of Java Collections and know the basic concepts well. This seemed to satisfy them.

The interviewers continued with OOPs-related questions and asked about the different types of inheritance. When I mentioned multiple inheritance, they asked whether it's allowed in Java. I explained that it's not supported in the same way as in C++, but it can be achieved through interfaces. That led to a follow-up: why it is designed that way, what the diamond problem is, and how Java solves it.

Next, they asked whether an object can be used as a key in a HashMap. I recognized this question from the online assessment and replied that yes, it's possible. They then asked me to code it. Instead of creating a new example, I intentionally used the same one from the OA. I had been advised to try and control the flow of the interview, and since I had already explored this problem further (including using GPT), I was confident about the follow-up questions.

I used the following structure:

This naturally led to the expected question: what is the size of the map?(because the value is same) I answered correctly--it's 2. The next question was how to make the size 1, even after inserting two objects.My first response was that using String keys with the same value would result in one entry due to string interning, but they asked me to solve it using the Person class itself. I took a moment and recalled that the .equals() method is used to compare keys. I explained that we need to override .equals() to ensure objects with the same attributes are treated as equal. The interviewer seemed happy with this answer. Though the answer should also have included the hashcode() function which I realised after the interview.

After that, the discussion moved to SQL. The questions were mostly basic, such as types of joins and the difference between left and right join. I explained that they are technically the same, and the only thing that changes is the order of the tables. I backed it up with an example, and the interviewer nodded in agreement.I was then asked how to filter results after using GROUP BY, to which I responded with the use of the HAVING clause. They also asked about the order of execution of SQL statements and whether it's possible to update a table using joins.I paused to think and said that while I haven't performed such operations directly, I believe it's possible if the update depends on the output of a join. I added that joins return a new table, so it might be a bit tricky. The interviewer pointed out that updates could depend on another table involved in the join, and that's when I realized the gap in my understanding.

I was also asked the difference between the PUT and POST methods. I gave the correct explanation, but since I hadn't actually used PUT in my projects, I became a bit unsure when asked if I was confident. I stuck to my answer but on questioning I accepted that I hadn't implemented it in any of the projects listed on my resume. In hindsight, if you're confident in your explanation, it's better to respond with certainty.

After this, I was asked to write a program to find the frequency of words in a sentence. I asked for permission to write it in C++, which they allowed. I used maps for storing frequencies and implemented the logic using stringstream. However, after writing the code, I realized I wasn't very clear about how stringstream works, though I still gave a rough explanation of its functionality. One part of the code included the operation map[word]++. The interviewer asked how I was incrementing the value if the word was not already present in the map. I explained that in C++, the default value for an int is 0 when a key is accessed for the first time, so the increment works. Then he asked about the default value for a string, and although I wasn't sure, I responded that I hadn't checked it specifically but assumed it would be null.

He then asked how to store the frequency using words like "one" or "two" instead of numbers. This caught me off guard. I said that it couldn't be done unless we predefined the mapping of numbers to words using another map. He still encouraged me to try, but I got confused. A few seconds later, he told me to leave it and moved on. I think the operation he asked for wasn't actually possible without an additional mapping.

He then asked about exception handling and this part went very smoothly. He gave a scenario with two catch blocks, one handling Exception and the next one IOException, along with a finally block. He asked how the code would behave if there was an exception during file reading. I replied that the code would not compile because the more specific exception, IOException, should come before the more general Exception. He then switched their order and asked again, and I answered correctly. After that, he asked what would happen if

there was a return statement in the try block. I said that the finally block would still execute. He further asked whether the return statement would still return a value, to which I responded yes.

The interview ended with me asking them a question. After coming out, I noticed that my interview had gone on for quite a long time--more than 45 minutes--while others were mostly done within 30 minutes, and some even in just 15-20 minutes. This made me nervous because it could mean many things. I also kept thinking about the few silly mistakes I made during the interview, like being unsure about a few answers as mentioned earlier and I had answered slightly wrong on the sql execution statements. Thankfully, friends came to the rescue again and helped calm me down. I then shifted my focus toward preparing for the HR round by going through common HR questions and the job description.

Tips:

As you might have noticed, my confidence was tested multiple times during the interview, and there were situations where the questions had logical answers, but I wasn't able to respond properly. Be prepared for this kind of pressure. According to a friend, one of my biggest weaknesses is being too honest in interviews--I tend to openly admit when I haven't done something, and I did that multiple times. It's better to avoid this.

Always try to relate your answer to something you know, even if you're not fully sure. Simply saying "I don't know" or "I haven't done this" isn't the best approach. Instead, respond strategically to keep the conversation in your control. Also, to understand your weak points and improve your delivery, I highly recommend doing mock interviews with friends--it really helps.

While explaining concepts, using examples is always the best approach as it makes your understanding clearer and more practical. While coding, speak out your thought process and approach unless you're specifically asked not to. This helps the interviewer understand how you think.

Also, keep a smile during the interview. Sometimes interviewers intentionally don't react to test your confidence. The way you enter the room, sit, and use gestures--all these non-verbal cues matter to some extent. While speaking, emphasize keywords intentionally. This can guide the interviewer to ask questions in areas you're comfortable with--for example, mentioning the diamond problem can lead the conversation in that direction.

5. HR Round [15 students]

The HR round took place around 6 PM and lasted approximately 30 minutes. The interviewers included the HR representative and the Managing Director of ISS.The first question was whether I recognized them, as they had presented the pre-placement presentation earlier. I answered correctly and acknowledged the importance of paying attention to such details.

Tip: Be prepared with another version of a non-technical introduction. In my case, I was asked only about my academic scores -- SSC, HSC, CET percentile, and CGPA -- and I gave a brief, to-the-point summary.

Next, I was asked why I chose computer science. I backed this up with a personal anecdote from my childhood and explained how my interest developed over time. I emphasized the genuine joy I feel when building real-life, working projects. I repeated this mindset throughout the interview to reflect my authenticity and passion for the field.

I was then asked about my family background. When they learned that my sisters had stable careers, they questioned why I wasn't pursuing a master's degree. I responded by again expressing my love for building applications and explained how I wanted to take the next step -- to move beyond smaller-scale projects and work on larger systems that could help me grow and contribute more meaningfully. This response seemed to resonate with them.

They also asked how I planned to commute to work.

Then came a question to explain my favorite project, to which I described my internship project. However, this part brought back an old memory -- in a previous HR round at MSCI, I was asked technical questions and didn't respond well, which may have contributed to my rejection. Similarly, here too, I was asked a technical question about the scalability of my internship project. My response wasn't very good. However, the Managing Director reassured me that he was more interested in my thought process, which helped a bit, but it still bugged me afterwards and reminded me of the earlier rejection.

They followed up by asking how I got the internship, what I liked most about it, and what differences I observed between working with college teammates versus an industry team.

Another important question came up -- they asked how I'd feel if I had to work with a completely new tech stack or domain, and whether that would make all my prior learning go to waste. I confidently said no, explaining that no matter the stack, core concepts like APIs, databases, and clean code remain relevant. Every tech stack has its own strengths, and if the use case or project demands change, I'm ready to adapt.

The interview ended with me asking them some basic questions.

Everyone was asked to go home and results would be announced late evening. Finally a list of 12 shortlisted individuals came out which had 8 SDEs.

If you can't think of any good questions, take screenshots during the PPT if it is online and then you ask chatgpt to give some good and unique questions.

1. Online Assessment [ Around 150]

The OA consisted of four sections and it was taken on Google Form and there were a total of 70 Mcq questions to be done in 90 minutes. 1 mark was awarded for every correct question and 0.25 marks were deducted for every wrong answer.

Java (18 questions) The questions were mostly based on guess the output on topics which included multithreading, OOPS, enum, access modifiers, collection frameworks, interfaces, streams. Though my primary language was C++ and I knew the basics of Java, I thoroughly prepared for OOPs and a few advanced topics of Java . I tried to guess the output questions based on java from multiple sources on the internet.

Python(17 questions) The questions were based on topics like lists comprehension, stacks, OOPs, shallow and deep copies and on basic concepts. I prepared for python in a day and tried to solve as many questions as I could from the internet.

SQL(5 questions) There were queries based on Group by, Where, Joins, Order by and Delete. The options were very close to each other so read it carefully.

Aptitude (30 questions) The questions were based on topics like stocks, profit-loss, train problems, probability, permutation-combination, boat-stream problems, speed-distance.

Tips So for Aptitude I was left with only 32-35 mins as I spent much time in java and python and also started 10 mins late so I tried to solve only those questions that were easy in the first go and skipped the ones which I thought might be time consuming. So I would advise you to first just solve those questions which are easy and not waste your time solving the difficult ones as there might be questions ahead which can be solved in seconds and due to time constraints you might miss them.

For Java, prepare in depth and have a good understanding of java and do practice as many guess the output questions as possible.

2. [Techincal Round] [ 45 students (8 students in Testing)]

My interview began with the interviewer asking if my primary programming languages were Java and Python. I clarified that my strengths lie in Java and C++, and that I am not very well-versed in Python. This led to the follow-up question, "Then how did you clear the Python test in the morning?"

I answered honestly, explaining that I had researched the company's past interview patterns on Google and found that Python was frequently used in their tests. So, I prepared for it in advance--just enough to clear the assessment--while still having only a basic understanding of the language. I also mentioned that certain programming concepts, such as object-oriented programming (OOP), are similar across Java, C++, and Python.

He then asked me to elaborate on these similarities. I spoke about OOP concepts like encapsulation, polymorphism, overloading, and overriding. The conversation shifted to access modifiers, where I initially forgot to mention "default" but quickly remembered and explained all four in detail.

Next, he asked questions about my projects. Since two of my projects were built using Flutter with Firebase, he wanted to know why I chose Flutter as my tech stack and why Firebase was my database of choice. He also asked why I didn't use React Native, given its similarities to Flutter. I realized the importance of being ready to justify tech stack decisions, so I explained my reasoning clearly.

He then moved to my third project, which was based on the MERN stack. Here, he asked why I used MongoDB, what specific problem my project was solving, and why I chose React. He also asked me to explain JWT authentication. So I explained its three parts in detail and he asked me scenarios like handling invalid tokens.

From there, the questions expanded to cookies--what they are, how they work, and how I implemented them in my project. Since my project also used WebSocket, he asked a few technical questions on that as well. I noticed a pattern: most of his questions were based on what I had mentioned in my answers, which made me realize the importance of only bringing up topics I could discuss confidently.

The technical section also included a DSA question based on strings. The problem was to count the number of words that are the same in a given substring. Initially, I was a little confused because of the word "substring," so I asked for an example to clarify. Once I understood, I confirmed my approach with him, then provided a HashMap-based solution, which he approved. I wrote the solution in C++ on paper, and he later asked me to traverse the map in a different way, which I did successfully.

He then tested my database knowledge by asking which databases I was familiar with. I mentioned SQL, MongoDB, and Firebase. This led to an SQL query question involving two tables with a common attribute id. He wanted me to update the category column in table1 with values xyz only for rows where the id was present in both tables. My first query was a bit complex, so he asked me to simplify it, which I managed to do.

He also asked HTTP status codes and basic API concepts--first the full form of API, then how it works.

At one point, he paused the technical discussion and invited me to ask questions. I asked about the merger between ISS and STOXX and how it affected the company. He explained and then he mentioned that now they are shifting from Angular to React. I followed up by asking why that shift was made. I also asked a question related to the testing role, which he answered in detail.

After the short break, he asked about my favorite subject in 12th grade. I said Chemistry, so he asked basic questions like the symbol for water, what happens when hydrogen is added to water, and symbols for nitrogen and nitrogen oxide.

The topic then moved to testing. I explained the two types--manual and automation--and further broke them down into functional and non-functional testing. When asked if I had ever done testing, I shared an example: during my curriculum, I cloned a banking website from GitHub and ran various test cases, including edge cases. He then asked about the Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC), which I couldn't answer so he gave me a brief explanation.

Since testing was my second preference, he asked if I was genuinely interested in it. I reassured him that I was, stating that I am equally interested in testing and development, though I am not looking to work in machine learning or data roles at this point.

Before wrapping up, he also asked where I live and about my family background.

Tips One key takeaway was that the interviewer often picked questions based on what I said, so it's important to speak about things you can confidently explain in depth and you should be knowing your resume really well. Mention only those things in the resume which you know in detail and if you are adding any project from github you should know it in and out. If you have chosen Testing as your second preference make sure you prepare a proper justification for that and also make sure you have some basic understanding of Testing.

3. [HR Round] [15 students]

My interview started with me greeting them and they began to ask me where I live and then how much I scored in CET, JEE, SSC and my current CGPA. Then they asked me what is testing and what are different types of testing. I explained whatever I knew in detail. They were still not convinced since Testing was my second preference and questioned me that you have no project related to testing so is it that you are sure you want to do the role of Testing Engineer. I said Yes and gave them an explanation of whatever I could think of at that point of time. Then they asked how I decided to choose the Testing role but I told them that I don't know anyone who has knowledge about Testing so I googled about testing role and then I decided to take it. But this was not the correct way of saying because it seems that an uninformed decision was taken so make sure you show them that you take decisions wisely and be prepared for giving such kind of explanation. Then they asked me to go out and talk to my senior or professors about the testing role and what it is exactly and what a Testing Engineer exactly does. At this point I thought they would reject but I went out and Thanks to TPO that helped a lot to connect to me seniors of ISS Stoxx and they

explained me clearly and then I went to interviewer again after they were done taking others interviews and I explained them in detail whatever I understood and they also asked me who did I talk to and then I thanked them and left the room.

[12 students were offered the role including me ]
