journey.howSecured:
A total of 3 rounds were conducted - 1 Online Assessment Round, 1 Tech Interview Round &

Finally, 1 HR Round. All were conducted on the same day,5/08/25. The CGPA Criteria for SDE

was 8.5, later reduced to 8. It was further reduced to 7.5. It may not be the case for next year

if they don't want more applicants, so it is preferable to maintain a pointer of 8.5 and above

1. Resume/CGPA Shortlisting: [ Approx 150-160 students]

Tailor your resume according to the JD of the company and your strong skills. Once your resume is finalised, evaluate its compatibility with ATS. Tools like Resume Worded can help and aim for a score of 65 or above. The shortlist of candidates selected for the Online Assessment and Pre-Placement Talk (PPT) was released on 3rd August 2025 at 7:00 PM.

2. Pre-Placement Talk:

The Pre-Placement Talk was conducted online on 4th August 2025 at 5:00 PM. The information shared during Pre-Placement Talks is extremely valuable, so it's important to be attentive -- not just to the content of the presentation, but also to the names and roles of the presenters. I made it a point to take SS and jot down the specific examples used while the speaker explained some of the company's financial services. You can make use of all these points in the HR round and also while asking questions at the end of your interviews.

3. Online Assessment: (Approx. 160 students appeared, invigilated by the company)

The online assessment comprised 70 questions to be completed in 90 minutes. It was conducted via Google Forms at the college premises. +1 was given for each correct answer and -0.25 for incorrect ones. You were allowed to use the system calculator.

The assessment covered four major sections: Java, Python, SQL, and Aptitude. The Java and Python part was mostly output-based MCQs, with a prime focus on OOPS concepts, errors, exceptions, stack, queue and all types of sets in Java. The SQL part was relatively easy with just queries as an answer. The aptitude had a total of 30 questions, and it had all types of questions you could find on Indiabix. So I would suggest solving questions whose concepts are known to you.

4. Technical Round 1: [44 students appeared] 1 interviewer in my panel

I was the 2nd last person in my panel, and the panellist was the same who invigilated my classroom during

the test. In the panel distribution list, the name of the panellist was given, so I had looked her up on LinkedIn (it helps to ask questions at the end of the interview). My panellist was very careful and also cheerful while taking the interviews, as I gave my interview at 6:30 in the evening when many students had already given their HR round and had gone home. So do not panic and get stressed the whole time ur sitting outside TPO. The interview started by asking my name and how my test was. I explained that I solved most of the Java and Python part, but the aptitude was a little lengthy. No introduction was asked to me. Then she asked me what I had prepared for the interview, and I said that I had prepared DBMS, OS, SQL, OOPS, JAVA. Be careful what you say in this part, as they will ask in depth about these topics. She asked me briefly about my first project and then started asking SQL queries. The first question was about giving the maximum salary in each dept, and then followed by a query for the top 2 salaries in each dept. I had to write the query on paper. Then she added a gender and city column to the same table and told me to give names of female employees who have the max salary in that dept.

Then she asked me two puzzles:

1: https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/aptitude/puzzle-mislabeled-jars/

2: There is a lotus in a pond that grows double its size each day. On the nth day, it covers the entire pond. On which day will it cover 1/8 th the pond?

I knew the 1st puzzle as I had prepared the top 100 puzzles from GFG. But the 2nd one was new, but I tried to solve it on paper while explaining my approach. Then, when I could not explain, I asked for hint and then was able to solve it.

Then I was asked OOPs in JAVA. Where I was given the shapes, rectangle, square and rhombus, and to use oops concepts to depict their classes. So Shape was interface, rectangle and rhombus were abstract classes and square extended both rhombus and rectangle. Which led to the discussion on interfaces, abstract classes and the diamond problem in Java. The keyword super was also asked.

Then at last I was asked the DSA question of replacing a certain value from a linked list via in-place no using another linked list. I was told to write the code on paper.

Remember to be honest and think out your solutions loudly. If you do not know the answer, ask for hints; the interviewer is there to guide you.

5. HR Round: [15 students appeared] 2 panellists

Started with my family background, why CSE-AIML as a branch, where do you live, would travelling be easy? I was asked only about my academic scores -- SSC, HSC, CET percentile, and CGPA.

Then came a question to explain my favourite project, to which I described my major project. Then they went deep by asking me in detail about this project. How I came up with the problem statement, the whole design of how it works, my role in it, as I did the Ml part, they asked me about the data used, models used and the whole pipeline. Problems I faced while working on the project. They also asked the same questions about my other project. As my resume was inclined more towards ML and genai, they were concerned about my role in ISS, as they don't use much AI and ML in their projects. But I convinced them that to use mML models we need proper backed knowledge too, which I had in Flask and my basics were clear in the languages of Java and Python, so coding would not be a problem. They also asked how I keep myself updated with the latest technologies to which I answered I read news on the inshorts app. The interview ended when I asked the interviewers a question about my day as an intern at ISS

This round was a little more inclined towards my projects and my understanding of it. Very few Hr questions were asked.

*Be Thorough with the Basics of the Courses you have mentioned in your resume.

Eligibility criteria -7.5 CGPA and above

Round 1: Online Aptitude Test

Approximately 150-160 students participated in this on-campus round. The test was divided into four sections with a marking scheme of +1 for a correct answer and a penalty of -0.25 for an incorrect one.

● Java (18 Questions): This section focused on fundamental concepts, including output-based questions, threads, Object-Oriented Programming (OOPs), and the Stream API.

● Python (17 Questions): Similar to the Java section, it covered basic Python principles like slicing and OOPs concepts.

● SQL (5 Questions): This part involved basic SQL queries where I had to select the correct query for given table structures from multiple-choice options.

● Quantitative Aptitude (30 Questions): This section featured a wide range of topics, including questions on stocks, simple and compound interest, speed of a boat, probability, and permutation and combination.

Round 2: Technical Interview

Forty-five candidates were shortlisted for the technical round. My interview, which lasted about 15-20 minutes , began with the interviewer asking me to introduce myself. Following my introduction, I was asked to explain one of my projects in detail.

Key discussion points included:

● Java Collections Framework: I was asked, "What do you know about the Collection framework?". I confidently answered that the framework consists of interfaces like List, Map, Set, and Queue, and classes such as ArrayList and LinkedList. When asked about the hierarchy of the framework, I replied that I didn't remember it completely.

● Code Explanation: The interviewer presented a code snippet from the aptitude test related to encapsulation and asked me to explain its functionality and output. I explained how the code worked and what the result would be.

● Object-Oriented Concepts: As a follow-up, I was asked how I would initialize a variable without using a setter method. I answered that I would use a constructor. I was then asked how to make the class immutable. I explained that I would make all variables private and final, remove the setter methods, initialize variables only through the constructor, and make the class final so it could not be extended. The interviewer questioned if I was sure about making the class final, and I confidently confirmed that it is necessary for immutability.

● Data Structures: I was then asked to explain the output of a code snippet from the aptitude test that used a Map and a List. I had to describe what the output would be if I used a HashMap, HashSet, TreeSet, and LinkedHashSet for a specific input.

It was noted that the interviewer for my panel conducted interviews quite swiftly, with some lasting only 10 minutes.

journey.prep:
1. The most important advice for any interview I could give you is to always smile. Be graceful about your mistakes.

2. Do not claim to know something you do not know. That is a massive red flag.

3. The interviewers are human. Appeal to their human nature. They're tired and bored after long days of continuous interviews too.

Resources (For the lazy folk):

1. SQL: DataQuest for LMR, SQLZoo for a one sitting full syllabus study. Practice Leetcode SQL if the syntax tends to slip from your mind and if application of certain functions tends to slip from your mind.

2. DSA: The usual resources are great. Follow those diligently. If you have the time and you love coding, give the CSES Problemset a shot. I'm at the Mathematics section and it's really fun!

3. OS: Any YT course will do if you're studying it for the first time. If you're reading this the night before the interview, just read up on Processes and Threads, Process Scheduling, Synchronization, Memory Management, Filesystems and I/O. If you have more time, this Overview by InterviewBit is pretty swell!

4. CCN: Same as OS. LMR. Very, very LMR (Ye toh karke hi jao pls).

Mistakes that I made that I feel you can learn from:

1. I thought Aptitude was silly. It still is, but trust me, it's better to be able to do it faster than to have to walk yourself through every problem every time. That is tiring and gets old fast, and you often end up running out of time. Practice Aptitude. It never hurts.

2. Keep your primary language your primary language. That means that if you do DSA in C++, please know the ins-and-outs of the language. Do not go about mastering all languages. If you're just starting out, it may be simpler for you to do your DSA practice in Java, just to cover your bases with technical MCQs (Russell didn't care about language, they cared much more about the depth of your technical understanding, but not all companies are like this)

3. Write. Code. Feels dumb? Trust me, it isn't. That notebook is the OG IDE.

PS: Read all the interview experiences in the folder. Everyone has covered what they remember of the process, so everyone may have missed something or the other.

Placements need skill and practice. But they're also, to an extent, very much a game of LUCK. Do not be demotivated by rejections. Be confident in yourself.

OFF-CAMPUS IS VERY MUCH A THING, AND YOU MUST WORK FOR THAT TOO. All career migrations post-college will be off-campus! So prep for off-campus!

I'm always available on LinkedIn! You can also reach out to me on +91 8779410757 (Whatsapp)

Best wishes for your placements!

journey.howSecured:
The process had a resume shortlisting round, after which we had 3 rounds at their office in Goregaon.

Round 1: Written Test (MCQs, and some Coding Questions)

Round 2: Technical Interview I

Round 3: Interview With the Director (Techno HR, with a focus on Tech)

1. Resume Shortlisting [Not really sure about the number for App Dev specifically, but across about 5-6 intern roles they had 9k applicants]

The application and shortlisting were entirely run by Russell Investments on Workday. SPIT's placement office circulated a short form so they could see who had applied, but the company did the actual screening, communication and interviews. HR communicated with students directly.

I remember receiving a call from HR around 5 o'clock somewhere around the end of February. Keep in mind to be polite and courteous during all such calls. That means, you must:

- Wait for the person speaking to complete what they've said.

- Slowly and carefully articulate any questions (and I mean, ANY) you may have. Be diplomatic in their framing.

For your reference, things that may have influenced their shortlisting:

a. My LinkedIn b. My GitHub

Not linking my Leet/CF because it wasn't there in the resume I shared with Russell.

2. Written Test (40 mins) [ 87 candidates were shortlisted for this round ] [NON ELIMINATORY]

We were invited to Russell's office at Oberoi for this round. It was a pen paper test, with 10 Technical MCQs on CS Fundamentals (DBMS, CCN, OS, OOPS, Data Structures), 10 Aptitude MCQs, and 3 DSA problems out of which we were expected to solve 2. The first problem expected the implementation of the Bubble Sort Algorithm. The second was to Find the duplicate in an array in O(n) and by using O(1) extra space, and the third was to check if a given string is valid, given certain heuristics (Valid Parentheses problem) [Use a stack]. These were not very complex problems. (I'm not sure how much it really mattered, but a lot of us (including me) attempted all three coding problems. Make of that what you will)

For this round, I encourage you to keep a calm and collected mind, and to practice writing code by hand. Do not, and I repeat, do not use ChatGPT while writing code in your primary language as much as you can avoid it.

3. Technical Interview 1 [ All candidates who wrote the test ]

We were slowly called for an interview with a panel of 2 extremely experienced professionals. My interview was actually pretty late, but it extended so long I remember some of my friends scolding me for taking so long.

My interviewers were of varied domains. One was a highly experienced app developer, and the other was a DevOps engineer. This is important context to understand the rest of the interview

I walked in (asked their permission before entering), smiled, and extended my hand to them to shake. Start with the person closest to you, it's more natural. This gesture automatically familiarises you to them (especially since in tech, handshakes aren't all that common, so it helps break the ice).

We moved onto the interview.

They asked me to introduce myself. By then, we'd already had a short laugh over the water glass. This made the interview start with all of us smiling. I had a 3-min elevator pitch (fancy term for your answer to 'tell me about yourself') (I've memorized this and timed myself to stick to 3 minutes)

Then, we had the technical knowledge part of the interview first.

DSA:

1. Have you studied DSA? Yes, I have. What data structures comfortable with? I am comfortable with Arrays, Linked Lists, Stacks, and Queues. While I do know and have studied Graphs and Trees, I cannot claim mastery.

2. How would you reverse this array in-place?

3. They had my sheet. They asked me to walk them through my implementations for all 3 codes.

4. Suppose you're building a news aggregation app. A user searches for "climate policy India". Your backend search engine finds matching articles. But instead of just showing the title + link, you want to show a snippet of the article text that contains all three search terms, so the user immediately sees the context. To do that, you need to find the smallest window in the article text that contains all the query words. This is a classic sliding window + hash map/frequency counter problem. [Note: this is not the exact question, I have forgotten the exact one. But I remember the implementation, so I have done my best to create a similar problem statement so you can relate to the scenario]

DBMS:

1. A JOIN Query (joining 3 tables)

2. Do you know what a view is?

3. What's an index?

4. Find the Top-N Highest Salary

CCN:

1. TCP vs UDP

2. What happens when you click a URL?

3. What's a REST API?

Now, here's a place where my resume got me into a spot of trouble.

I have mentioned I know 'RESTful APIs' in my skills. I do know REST APIs. Thing is, I didn't know what the '-ful' part meant. (Arre REST, RESTful, same hi laga tha) So my interviewer asks me, this is a REST API. You've mentioned a RESTful API. What's that?

I didn't know at all. So, I smiled and said, I know how REST APIs work and I've built them, but I'm not fully sure what the '-ful' part means. I assume it has something to do with the principle of REST → statelessness, resource-based URIs, use of HTTP verbs, etc. [PS: I made this up. I didn't know at the time either. By sheer luck, this is the right answer. So, the moral of the story, say something]

Resume:

1. I had an Embedded systems experience on my resume. Interviewers are usually more than happy to hear about your experience. Talk about it with as much passion as you can muster. You must be able to explain what the company does, how you contributed, so on and so forth. If you were at a startup, highlight how you wore multiple hats, learned quickly, and adapted to a fast-moving environment. If it was a larger company, talk about working within established systems, collaborating across teams, and how your work contributed to the bigger picture. Personally, I talked to them about the product of the startup, how my work was on the product itself, and how I fixed a critical bug in the firmware code.

2. One of my interviewers was an experienced App Developer. He was extremely interested in the BLE (Bluetooth Low Energy) work I'd done at my internship. Here's what he asked me: -> How does BLE connection establishment normally work? -> Why did you need a custom three-way handshake instead of relying on BLE's built-in connection mechanisms? -> How did you measure the "74% reduction" in sync issues?

None of this may apply to you. But the questions were pretty in-depth (BLE is just one line on my resume) so be prepared for this kind of deep-dive

3. The other interviewer, a DevOps engineer, was very interested in my project Percy, an AI-driven system optimizing CI/CD pipelines, automating testing, enhancing the developer experience. She asked me for the system design, which I drew on a sheet with simple boxes and arrows. She had many questions about my design choices (Why are you maintaining the data in a JSON, why are you using Celery here, how would you integrate this into an existing CI system) She asked me what an AST was, and how it helped in documentation generation. She also interspersed some technical knowledge questions, like what's the difference

between on-prem and cloud servers, what you'd have to take care of in an on-prem server which cloud providers cover for you (I probably didn't answer this as well as I could have)

Once they were done with their questions, they asked me if I had any questions for them. Honestly, I did (like have actual questions. Not just 'ask for the sake of asking, ask something')

1. What does the work of an App Developer look like at Russell?

2. Do you attend client meetings?

3. How are teams structured?

4. What are your office timings like?

5. How does your CI/CD pipeline work, could you please give me a very very quick overview?

4. [Round 3 Name] [ 14 candidates appeared for this round ]

My round 2 was with a senior director who sits in London. He'd come to India for some other work. He was in charge of their data (very important in any financial firm) and had a very intimidating presence. I will admit, I was very terrified. It had been a long wait (this interview happened at 4:30, when my previous interview had ended at 1ish) so the tension had had time to build up as well.

He was very polite. I shook his hand with a smile. He asked me to work him through my resume (the same 3 min elevator pitch)

He was very, very interested in my experience. He wanted to know all about the product, the use, and the clinical trials associated with the product. He asked me about how a day working at a startup as a firmware intern was, how I debugged the cause of the lag in transmission, how the fix was approved, and how we tested it. He wanted to know about my knowledge of Alpha/Beta testing, SDLC.

Then, he asked me to write a simple SQL query to find all entries for October 2024, sorted by day, given that each entry was in DATE format in SQL. Now, this is an easy question, but I blanked. I cannot explain why. I could not remember LIKE in SQL, probably because I was so intimidated. In this situation, drink water. If you know something, but you're unable to answer, drink water. It provides a separate stimulus to your mind and helps clear stress.

Then, I said - the exact term is slipping my mind, but this is how the query would be structured. And as I wrote that down, I remembered LIKE and wrote that down as well.

He seemed happy with the answer. He moved onto some technical questions:

1. On-prem versus cloud (here, I ended up cross-questioning him a bit too. Keep it conversational! He seemed to want to talk)

2. How data is stored in a financial firm

Then, he shifted to cultural fit questions.

1. Tell me a situation where you were frustrated with a team mate. How did you work past the frustration?

2. What, according to you, is the most challenging part of working with a team?

The rest has slipped my mind, but it was somewhat around this.

Once he was done, he asked if I have any questions for him. I asked questions based on the talks we'd had in the morning with the Director of Application Development-

customSections.title: Advice & Tips for Juniors
customSections.content:
1. The most important advice for any interview I could give you is to always smile. Be graceful about your mistakes.

2. Do not claim to know something you do not know. That is a massive red flag.

3. The interviewers are human. Appeal to their human nature. They're tired and bored after long days of continuous interviews too.

Resources (For the lazy folk):

1. SQL: DataQuest for LMR, SQLZoo for a one sitting full syllabus study. Practice Leetcode SQL if the syntax tends to slip from your mind and if application of certain functions tends to slip from your mind.

2. DSA: The usual resources are great. Follow those diligently. If you have the time and you love coding, give the CSES Problemset a shot. I'm at the Mathematics section and it's really fun!

3. OS: Any YT course will do if you're studying it for the first time. If you're reading this the night before the interview, just read up on Processes and Threads, Process Scheduling, Synchronization, Memory Management, Filesystems and I/O. If you have more time, this Overview by InterviewBit is pretty swell!

4. CCN: Same as OS. LMR. Very, very LMR (Ye toh karke hi jao pls).

Mistakes that I made that I feel you can learn from:

1. I thought Aptitude was silly. It still is, but trust me, it's better to be able to do it faster than to have to walk yourself through every problem every time. That is tiring and gets old fast, and you often end up running out of time. Practice Aptitude. It never hurts.

2. Keep your primary language your primary language. That means that if you do DSA in C++, please know the ins-and-outs of the language. Do not go about mastering all languages. If you're just starting out, it may be simpler for you to do your DSA practice in Java, just to cover your bases with technical MCQs (Russell didn't care about language, they cared much more about the depth of your technical understanding, but not all companies are like this)

3. Write. Code. Feels dumb? Trust me, it isn't. That notebook is the OG IDE.

PS: Read all the interview experiences in the folder. Everyone has covered what they remember of the process, so everyone may have missed something or the other.

Placements need skill and practice. But they're also, to an extent, very much a game of LUCK. Do not be demotivated by rejections. Be confident in yourself.

OFF-CAMPUS IS VERY MUCH A THING, AND YOU MUST WORK FOR THAT TOO. All career migrations post-college will be off-campus! So prep for off-campus!

I'm always available on Lin

● 15 Feb 2025: Application form released.

● 22 Feb 2025: Registration deadline.

● 4-5 Mar 2025: Shortlist calls sent out.

● 12 & 13 Mar 2025: Interview dates offered (I attended on 12th March).

● 18 Mar 2025: Results declared. Resume: at the time of applying:- Russell_Resume.pdf

How applications & shortlisting worked:

● The application and shortlisting were entirely run by Russell Investments on Workday. SPIT's placement office circulated a short form so they could see who had applied, but the company did the actual screening, communication and interviews. HR communicated with students directly.

● The opening received applications from many colleges (VJTI, IIT Bombay, Thakur, Somaiya, VESIT, DJ Sanghavi, etc.) -- so this was effectively a campus-pool + off-campus hybrid. It wasn't restricted to a single campus TPO.

● Russell had over 9,000 applications across approximately 5-6 internship roles. They selected a very small number of candidates out of that pool (23 across all roles and 6 for app dev).

● Make sure to have a refined resume, a good cgpa (I'd recommend having 8+, but try to keep at least 7.5+ otherwise you'll miss out on a few), some achievements to get shortlisted (there were people with very good resumes but were kept on waitlisted).

● Along with a good resume also try to keep linkedin and github maintained. (My github & linkedin).

Interview Day schedule:

1. Arrival & welcome (9:30 AM): We were asked to come to their Goregaon office by 9:30 AM. The day began with HR welcoming everyone and explaining the schedule.

2. Orientation sessions: The HR Head gave a brief intro followed by sessions from senior leadership -- the Managing Director and various Directors. Each speaker explained what Russell does, company culture, client focus, and what the tech teams build. These talks were delivered in a training room (like a PPT walkthrough) and were surprisingly detailed.

3. Written Assessment (~11:00 AM): After the intro sessions we took a pen-and-paper assessment (details below).

4. Panel interviews (L1 - about 5-6 panels): Post-assessment we moved into technical rounds -- there were multiple panels running in parallel across the day. My technical panel was mid-morning/early-afternoon and lasted roughly 50-60 minutes. Several other panels ran alongside it.

5. Refreshments and waiting: Between rounds we were given refreshments and asked to wait in a common area. There were several short breaks.

6. Final rounds (L2 - 2/3 panels): After the technical panels, a small batch of candidates (about 10 for app dev) were shortlisted for final Director-level/ hiring-manager conversations. Those rounds lasted about 25-30 minutes each. After finishing, we were sent home around 6:00 pm and informed that the results would be shared via HR in a few days.

7. Result: On 18 March 2025 Russell announced the results; six technology interns were selected for the Application Developer role (four of us were from SPIT).

1. Written assessment [around 30-35 candidates on day 1 had given for app dev role]

● Format: Pen-and-paper, 40 minutes total, weightage 5 marks. Note: the test was explicitly not eliminatory -- it contributed to evaluation but was not a strict knockout.

● Sections & content:

○ 10 aptitude questions -- pattern recognition, sequences, next-word / next-number style problems (IndiaBix-style).

○ 10 CS fundamentals MCQs -- typical core topics (DBMS, SQL, OS, networking basics, OOP/OO design).

○ 3 very easy coding problems -- solve any 2 (but I personally solved all three):

1. Valid parentheses (stack application).

2. Missing number in an array of size n−1 containing numbers 1..n (classic sum/XOR trick).

3. Binary-search style problem.

● My experience: The test was easier than I expected -- I finished all sections comfortably and had time to attempt the third coding question as well. The coding questions tested basic logic, nothing too difficult.

● Preparation tips for this round: Regular aptitude practice (IndiaBix, common OA Questions) and brushing up on core CS topics (DBMS, OS basics, OOP) is sufficient. For the coding questions, having a command of stacks, arrays, binary search and basic bit tricks helps, you can extrapolate to covering linear structures and basic sorting algorithms.

2. Technical interview 1 [All candidates who had given round 1]

Duration & setting: About 50-60 minutes, weightage 10 marks, in a room with a senior technical panel. There were 5-6 panels running -- mine was led by a very experienced interviewer (16 years of experience). The panelists were senior, technically-minded people who actually head teams.

Flow of the round (how it started):

● We began with a firm handshake and a short personal introduction. I handed over my resume and gave a structured 1-2 minute elevator pitch touching on my background, projects, and what I enjoy building. The interviewer asked me to go tell something that was not on my resume, followed by a deep dive into overall technical discussion.

Project deep-dive:

● I had listed a mobile app project that used Firebase as the backend. The panel headed into why I chose Firebase, how I implemented authentication, how I structured the database, how I handled sync/real-time aspects, and where I would change things for scale. They liked concrete answers (why a NoSQL approach was chosen for an app prototype, when SQL would be preferable in industry scenarios, etc.).

● Be ready to explain the what, how, and why for each project -- not just what you implemented but design tradeoffs and alternate approaches.

System design & architecture discussion:

● They asked higher-level architecture questions: how to design an auth flow, how to approach scalability, where to put the session store, and how to handle concurrent users. They deliberately pushed to see whether I understood tradeoffs.

● They asked "cloud feels slow -- how would you improve performance?" -- this opened a discussion on caching, caching DB queries, denormalization vs normalization tradeoffs, and batching or asynchronous processing for heavy tasks.

● They explored my approach to problem statements and use cases, focusing on how I solve problems, the technical considerations I account for, and how I tackle challenges while building a project from scratch.

● My hackathon experience, particularly winning at SIH, impressed them due to the scale of the hackathon and demonstrated my ability to design and plan projects effectively, both technically and strategically.

Data structures & algorithms:

● Two easy to med DSA problems were asked (Linked Lists and Stacks were explicitly covered). For each, the panel expected: clarifying questions, a brute-force approach, and then progressive optimization to a satisfying solution with complexity analysis. I emphasise thinking out loud -- walking through examples and edge cases, and then writing pseudo-code. They also expected short runtime/space tradeoff discussions.

● Important behavioural tip from this round: do not pretend to know an optimized solution even if you do -- state the brute-force first, then show how you would improve it. They frequently picked words I said and asked follow-ups, sometimes on tangential points I mentioned casually.

● A brief discussion about the assessment questions was held; the questions were relatively easy, and the interviewer was very relaxed. There was a lighthearted moment when I mentioned solving all three questions, after which they asked me to explain the approach for just one of them.

● In some panels, if a candidate solved only two questions, the third question (from the assessment) would be asked in the interview. The assessment questions were generally easier than the interview questions, so solving and explaining one clearly in the interview left a positive impression. So if you know all 3, you could just solve 2 and take a chance that you might get asked the 3rd one in the interview.

SQL & fundamentals:

● A simple SQL query was asked (a simple JOIN query with some conditions). Beyond writing the query, they asked how to optimize it (indexes), and what a stored procedure and trigger is.

Cloud & deployment:

● We discussed on-premise vs cloud: I explained that cloud simplifies scaling and managed services but can have latency trade-offs; for performance-critical pieces, edge or hybrid approaches might be appropriate. They asked about packaging and deploying an app, so mention containers, CI/CD pipelines and dockers but I was not much aware of it so just stated my limited knowledge of those terms and didn't elaborate much.

● ! DO NOT SAY ANY THINGS THAT YOU ARE NOT AWARE OF !

○ It is always good to say that you don't know rather than saying something wrong or the interviewer sensing that you are not much aware of the topic.

Behavioral & communication expectations in the round (key):

● Think out loud, ask for constraints, write the brute force approach and then optimize, and write pseudo-code once the approach is agreed upon. Test your solution with 1 example.

● If stuck, say "I need a minute to think" (they prefer structured thinking). Interviewers will often ask to justify your step; do not be defensive if they probe -- it's expected.

My personal takeaways from Round 1:

● Be crisp about your projects. When you mention an implementation detail casually, the panel will latch on to it and probe deeper -- so be deliberate with your words.

● Explain tradeoffs instead of one-line answers. For example, saying "I used Firebase" should be followed by why (speed of development, managed auth, real-time DB) and when you'd not use it (complex relational joins, transaction-heavy systems).

● It was a varied experience from panel to panel, some panels had hard DSA Q solving, some evolved around resume, some went in depth with SQL, some were in detail about sorting algos, so you can't exactly predict what can be asked but it is good to cover basics and know your resume well.

3. Hiring Manager Round [On day 1, about 8-10 students had been shortlisted ]

● On paper, this round was worth around 10 marks, but the final decision largely rested with the directors and hiring managers. Although marks were assigned, I don't think the selection was purely based on scores.

● After the technical panels, Russell conducted further shortlisting: they called a small set of candidates (about 10) for the director/hiring-manager-level conversation. Some candidates were taken aside and told they would not be moving forward. There were moments of waiting and refreshment breaks while panels and shortlists completed.

● My final round was with the Director at app dev (about 23 years of experience) -- this round was intentionally more conversational and lasted around 25-30 minutes. The Director started with a friendly tone (asked about my day, understood nerves, and deliberately relaxed the conversation). He dived on my ability to:

○ Break down end-to-end use cases and how I would approach them from design to deployment.

○ Explain the SDLC and the phases where I'd focus depending on a product's maturity.

○ Discuss DevOps basics -- pipelines, infrastructure, monitoring, and release strategies.

○ Handle behavioral scenarios: working under deadlines, facing ambiguity, collaborating with non-tech stakeholders.

● This round evaluated structured thinking, cultural fit, communication and ownership more than raw coding skill.

Result & offer:

● Results were declared on 18 March 2025. For the Technology Intern (Application Developer) role, 6 interns were selected; 4 of those were from SPIT.

● The entire hiring process felt based on merit: there were students from many colleges in the applicant pool, and Russell reviewed candidates from across campuses.

My internship (brief reflection on the actual internship work):

● Now that I have completed the internship and am writing this, I can say it was very valuable. I worked on two substantive problem statements that had real ownership and impact. Weekly cross-team sessions introduced us to internal flows -- not just tech teams but business and product -- which helped me understand financial domain flows. Mentors were supportive and assigned meaningful responsibilities; interns even presented to Heads across offices and the MD at times. The exposure to the financial-services ecosystem, real production constraints, and presentation experience was invaluable.

What I did well (strengths that helped):

● Clear, confident resume projects articulated with "what/how/why" rather than surface-level bullets.

● Practiced think-out-loud approach during DSA -- started with brute force and improved the solution.

● Paid attention to system-design tradeoffs (Firebase vs SQL, on-prem vs cloud) and explained reasoning.

● Maintained composure in the final director round (honest about nervousness, but confident on substance).

● Prepared practical examples and could tie academic knowledge to project reality.

What I could have done better (honest learnings):

● I could have prepared a more concise elevator pitch specifically tailored to the role.

● I could have rehearsed a few more behavioral stories with specific metrics (S-T-A-R with numbers).

● I could have been even more deliberate when using throwaway words (they sometimes pick up on casual mentions).

● Improve clarity on when to choose SQL over NoSQL in enterprise scenarios -- have ready examples of data models to explain the choice (this is one thing I learnt really well during my internship).

What all to focus on (not just for Russell but for overall on campus tech placements):

i. Core CS fundamentals (must-do):

● Refresh DBMS basics: normalization, indexing, JOINs, transactions.

● Review Operating Systems basics.

● Networking fundamentals.

● OOPs: basic patterns and why you'd use them. (for other on campus companies, focus on doing OOPs in Java, Russell evaluated me on my overall knowledge, not a particular language)

ii. Coding & DSA (practical):

● Do arrays, linked lists, stacks/queues, trees, hashing, binary search.

● Practice medium problems on NeetCode or Striver; quality > quantity.

● When solving: ask clarifying Qs, present brute-force, optimize, write pseudo-code, test with examples, always dry run.

iii. System design / architecture:

● Practice small designs: auth flow, notifications system, basic microservice breakdown.

● Read about caching strategies (LRU caches, Redis, Hive), CDNs, load balancers, queues, and patterns for scaling. Head First Design Patterns helps for design patterns; for system design, learn common building blocks and tradeoffs.

iv. Cloud & DevOps basics:

● Know the basics of Cloud, how to deploy and its performance metrics.

● Be familiar with the basic terminologies of DevOps.

v. SQL practice:

● Do focused practice: LC SQL 50 and W3Schools/TutorialsPoint for syntax and edge cases. Learn and read the basics of indexing.

vi. Aptitude & fit:

● Warm up with IndiaBix style aptitude practice; be fast and accurate for the OAs.

vii. Project preparation:

● Know your resume projects inside-out. For each project, be ready to answer: architecture diagram, deployment steps, bottlenecks encountered, alternate designs, and "if I had more time, I would…".

viii. Soft skills & behavioral:

● Prepare 6-8 STAR stories: leadership, failure & learning, conflict, impact, ownership. Use metrics where possible.

● Prepare a few smart questions tailored to the interviewer's role (not generic company questions).

ix. General longer-term preparation (CGPA, internships, hackathons):

● CGPA: Maintain at least 7.5+; higher CGPA helps in shortlisting. Beyond ~8 it doesn't add much (except for firms like ISS & JPMC which prefer 8.5+).

● Internships: Even a small/unpaid internship adds credibility -- shows real-world exposure, teamwork, and practical application beyond coursework.

● Hackathons: Actively participate in hackathons; they build problem-solving under deadlines, give concrete projects to showcase, and often impress interviewers more than certificates.

x. Always tailor your resume according to the role and JD provided but never lie on it.

Interview day strategy:

Before the interview:

● Sleep well (8+ hours), eat a light breakfast, arrive 15 minutes early.

● Review bullet points of your projects, resume, and a short list of behavioral stories.

● Carry multiple printed copies of your resume (ensure it's set to A4 size in Overleaf for proper length and accurate print layout).

During the interview:

● Start strong with a calm introduction -- firm handshake, clear voice, concise 1-2 minute summary.

● Think out loud. Interviewers care about the process. Say constraints aloud; ask clarifying Qs..

● Brute force → optimize. If you can't find the optimal immediately, start with a simple solution and refine.

● Write pseudo-code and test it with sample input (edge cases included).

● If stuck, request a minute to organize thoughts -- better than blundering through.

● Ask intelligent, role-specific questions at the end. Tailor them to the interviewer's background.

After the interview:

● Be polite and composed. Hope for the best and prepare for the worst.

Questions to ask the interviewer (tailor them):

● Have some questions prepared beforehand but there's no need to just stick to those, listen to when the interviewer introduces themselves and ask questions that would be relevant to them and their team, not just company related questions that you had looked up earlier.

● For a technical interviewer: "What are the core problems the team is solving this quarter?" / "What does success look like for an intern in just 8-12 weeks?"

● For a manager/director: "How does the team measure impact?" / "Which areas should new joiners focus on to be productive quickly?"

● Avoid generic questions like "Tell me about the company"; tie your question to the person (e.g., "You mentioned X in your talk -- could you elaborate on how the team handles Y?").

Final tips & mindset:

Confidence + Humility: Be confident about what you know; be humble and honest about gaps. It's far better to say "I don't know that detail, but here's how I'd find/approach it" than to bluff.

Clarity of thought: Structured answers beat long-winded ones. Use short steps and call out assumptions.

Consistency over cramming: Daily steady practice (2-3 hours) is more effective than a single marathon.

Focus on learning concepts, reasoning, and fundamentals: Don't just chase numbers and get behind solving X number of Qs, achieving Y rank or winning Z hackathons, always keep learning as your core, pay importance to understanding from basics, success will follow.

Build projects that teach you tradeoffs: Real projects (even simple ones) let you answer "why" questions convincingly.

Health & mental prep: Sleep, minimal caffeine, and small relaxation techniques (deep breaths) before a round help dramatically.

Common pitfalls (avoid these):

● Jumping straight into code without confirming problem constraints.

● Not testing solutions with examples and edge cases.

● Overpromising or fabricating experience from your resume.

● Being too generic in behavioral answers -- always add specific outcomes and numbers.

● Not asking any questions at the end or asking questions that show lack of preparation.

Useful Resources:

● Aptitude: IndiaBix practice problems.

● DSA: NeetCode / Striver.

● SQL: W3Schools, practice LC SQL 50 problems.

● Design patterns & architecture: Head First Design Patterns (intro).

● CS Fundamentals: Make use of GPT to generate a list of topics, and Claude to make elaborate notes, use GFG, InterviewBit for core subjects as well.

● General interview prep: Do refer to interview exps, look up ambition box as well.

● Practice & exposure: Participate in hackathons -- the learning is often more valuable than winning (projects + deadlines teach you a lot).

Remember, placements can be a tough journey. It's important to realistically assess your chances, see which companies visit your college, and understand what opportunities align with your capabilities.

The main thing in on campus placements are LUCK, LUCK and LUCK!

So, if you get an opportunity for a good summer internship, it's wise to take your best shot at it and secure a strong backup. Then, you can focus on preparing for off-campus opportunities if you feel you can achieve even more. On-campus, apart from 1-2 exceptions, most companies fall within a similar range of CTC, and nothing is guaranteed. Even after solving thousands of questions, unexpected issues like technical errors can occur on d-day.

In short: aim for a good summer internship, keep a solid backup plan, and prepare for off-campus placements at a steady pace.

ALL THE BEST! You can contact me any time for any help and guidance: (+91 8169617362) / https://www.linkedin.com/in/sanjeev-ratnani/

journey.prep:
For preparing for placements and internships, be prepared with:

DSA: It is asked by most companies in Online Assessments and Interviews. Without DSA, you won't be able to clear OA and appear for interviews. Apart from doing DSA sheets also give contests to practice solving questions randomly with a time limit. If possible, do CP. It is not necessary but being good at CP gives an edge in OA.

Aptitude: Some companies ask aptitude questions in OA. I did not explicitly practise as I was confident about it but do practise if you are not sure.

CS Fundamentals: These are very important for interviews and OA.

OOPS in Java (and your preferred language as well), SQL, DBMS are most important. OS, CCN and system design are also important.

Resume: You should know your resume well. Have 2 good projects in your resume. It's good to have internships but not necessary.

Communication is very important in interviews and be prepared for HR Type questions as well. Companies might have other requirements like Machine Coding Rounds, Puzzles, Group Discussion, guesstimates, etc.

CGPA is important. Try to keep your CGPA above 8 (ideally 8.5). Many companies had their shortlisting criteria for OA as 8 and for some it was 7.5 and so on. The higher your CGPA, the more companies you get to appear. Initially, only CGPA till 5th semester was being considered for placements. From 2nd week of august, CGPA till 6th semester was considered. Also make sure you don't have any active backlogs

journey.howSecured:
Russell Investments conducted their first internship drive in India for our batch which included many roles. TPO informed us about 3 roles: Technology Intern, Business Process Automation Intern, Investment Research Intern. The rest of the interview process was done completely at their office or through online interviews. The HRs informed us directly about rounds through mail or calls.

1. Written Test (40 minutes)[30 on day 1 and approx. ~25 on day 2]

● 10 Aptitude MCQ

● 10 CS Fundamental MCQ

● 3 coding questions (Attempt any 2) - Valid Parenthesis, Binary Search Pseudo code, Find Second Max Element in array.

This test was very easy. Also, this was not an elimination round.

2. Technical Interview 1 [30 on day 1 and approx. ~25 on day 2]

This interview was conducted by a Frontend Developer and Devops Engineer.

The interview focused mainly on my resume. The discussion was regarding my internship and my projects. Apart from this I was asked 1 leetcode easy question - find common elements in 2 strings. A few database related questions were asked as well.

3. Technical Round 2 [ No of candidates who appeared for this round ]

This round was conducted by the Director of Application Development.

The interviewer focused on my resume. He asked me questions about my projects from a business perspective. Like why would organizations choose my applications above other companies or build it in house. I was questioned about SDLC and Testing. Apart from that, I was asked about my interests. The interview ended with me asking him questions.

Till here, the entire process was conducted in 1 day at their office. The selected candidates(6 total - 4 from day 1 and 2 from day 2) were allotted the role Intern, Application Development.

The process was over and I assumed that I had been rejected. But a week later, I received a call from the HR that they wished to conduct additional rounds in my case. At that time, I asked HR clearly if the rounds were for the same role to which she said yes. Later on, I got to know that the additional interviews were for the Automation team.

Technical Interview 3

This round was conducted by Application Development Manager in the Automation Team on Microsoft Teams.

I was asked a leetcode easy question on arrays and a question on joins in SQL. I was asked 4 principles of OOP which I explained with examples. I was asked to write an efficient sorting algorithm that sorts the array till a particular index only. I chose to write the Merge Sort Algorithm. I was asked some CCN questions related to HTTP and Rest APIs which I don't remember now.

Managerial Round

This round was taken by the Head of Automation online a week after the previous interview.

She asked me to introduce myself and share my resume. She asked me the language I was most comfortable in and asked me to rate myself in it. I rated myself 7/10 in C++ and said it was the language I used for DSA and CP. She googled C++ and asked me a very random question related to pointers. I was not able to answer the question. I did not know that keyword but explained pointers in C++ and why they are important. This discussion went on for 15 minutes where we discussed the difference between C++ and Java, use of C++ for building games, etc. As the allotted time was over, I was unable to ask any questions.

A few hours later, I received the mail that I have been selected for the technology intern role.

When I received my offer letter it said 'Intern, Data Automation'. That is when I realised I was interviewing for a different team in my last 2 interviews. So, finally 8 technology interns(of which 5 were from SPIT) were selected with 6 in App Dev and 2 in Automation. There is not much difference in the roles, I guess, as we worked on the same projects and technologies.

I am writing this interview experience 5 months after my interviews. So, I am not able to recall all the questions. But from a preparation perspective for Russell, you need to have a strong hold over CS Fundamentals and know your resume well. Also, practice aptitude if necessary.

Stages: Resume Shortlist → Pen & Paper Test → Technical Interview → Final Interview

Resume Tips:

The shortlisting was relaxed with a 6.0+ CGPA cutoff. I submitted a tech-heavy resume, but in hindsight, adding one or two business case studies or cross-functional experiences would help. Focus on data-driven and machine learning projects.

1. Pen Paper Test :- Candidates Appeared: 102 | Test Duration: 1 hour

● Section 1: Aptitude (8 Questions, +3/-1) Topics included:

○ Coordinate geometry (line/curve equations)

○ Speed-distance

○ Work-time

○ Number systems Time management is key -- solve this in 15-20 mins max.

● Section 2: No Negative Marking (12 Marks Total)

○ Python Pseudo-code (4 Marks):

■ Predict the sum of the series: 0, 2, 6, 12, 20, 30... (1 mark)

→ Pattern: n2+nn^2 + nn2+n

■ Another sequence (3 marks): -1, -1, 5, 19... - slightly tricky and I couldn't fully crack it → Don't panic if one question goes wrong

○ SQL (8 Marks): Tables: Student, House, Test Sample queries:

■ Avg/Max/Min marks per student

■ Second-highest marks

■ Rank houses based on top performer

■ List test types and students who didn't attempt them

Prep Advice:

● SQL: Leetcode Top 50 is enough

● Apti: Practice from IndiaBIX

● Python: Brush up number series logic & patterns

● Tip: Don't freeze. Presence of mind > perfection

Do the SQL top 50 on leetcode that would be enough.

2. 1st Technical Round:- 40 people advanced

● Resume deep-dive (Types of ML Algorithms/Technologies used, and Why)

● ML algorithm intuition: R², RMSE, classification metrics. (Because It was on my resume)

● Career goals and why shift from tech to analyst role Others were asked SQL joins, Pandas basics, API logic -- nothing too difficult if you built your projects yourself.

3. Final Round (Tech + HR + Case Study) : 11 people advanced to this round

A hybrid round testing communication, fitment, and problem-solving. Questions I was asked:

● Tell me about yourself

● Resume walkthrough

● Case Study: Improve profitability of a logistics company with 1000 trucks

○ Ask clarifying questions

○ Segment the problem

○ I brought in AI/ML and compared with operations from airline industry

● Guesstimate: "How many tennis balls can fit inside an airplane?"

○ I wasn't exact, but spoke aloud my approach and kept calm

● Generic HR: 5-year goals, Why InCred?, Why this role?

3 students got placed in InCred

Placement Process:

The information you gather from the pre-placement talk is extremely crucial as it can make the difference between your selection and rejection. I tailored my resume, answered the interview questions and asked my own questions entirely based on what was said during the pre placement talk.

So take screenshots of the PPT, note down what points they talk about, and then try to think of questions to ask or topics to talk about based on your experience and their requirements.
journey.prep:
I am attaching this drive link with the resume I applied with, along with other pdfs that might be relevant to your preparation.

I am also attaching this link where I have discussed my entire placement process, and what is the best way to prepare for Non-tech jobs, including how I made my resume, how to answer the questions - etc.

I have mentioned most of the relevant details above, but some general tips:

1. THE most important thing to remember is that there is always a luck factor involved in these processes - you might have done everything right but sometimes it just is not your day. You can either sulk and waste your time or try to learn from your mistakes, get an outside perspective and keep on learning.

2. Be prepared for the worst, the whole 'placement season' might be just 2 weeks but it might also be 6 months. Do not be anxious about the whole thing - just stay calm and hope for the best.

3. Practice your Interview skills a lot, even if you have excellent communication skills. I probably gave 10 interviews to my brother/ seniors/ roommates. I also probably took 30 odd interviews of friends and roommates. This is the only way to practice giving answers in a professional capacity.

4. The shortlist names are usually revealed just 15/16 hours before the interview or test, so you need to prepare without worrying about the results.

5. Practice generic HR questions - What are your short term and long term plans, plans for further studies (always SAY NO), etc - I will try to give an ideal response and in detailed answer in the doc attached above.

6. People either smile too much or don't smile at all, or avoid eye contact. All of these can negatively affect your chances.

7. Be humble and show curiosity and eagerness to learn. Don't let the interviewer think you are arrogant or a know-it-all.

8. Make a lot of projects - it is the BEST way to learn new concepts and it will allow you to pick and choose appropriate projects for each company to ensure you can put your best foot forward.

9. DO NOT TRY to do everything all at once. Almost all sources of studies/ projects are good enough if you complete them - but if you keep hopping from one source to another, you will end up with nothing done. Set strict deadlines to motivate yourself to finish your work.

10. Talk to your seniors in your target company, talk to people already working in your target industry, and talk to your TPCs, all of them can give you great insights and guidance not just for your placements but for your future career.

11. In case you wish to connect with me, drop me a text on LinkedIn.

Skills and relevant links :

1. Data Analytics: Alex the Analyst - A complete Data Analyst Bootcamp(Python, SQL, Tableau, Power BI, Excel, AWS, etc ), enough to prepare you for most analyst roles. Completely free with a certificate as well!

2. SQL: SQL50 to practice questions

3. Python: For last minute Syntax revision: All Python Syntax in 25 Minutes - Tutorial

4. If you are interested in Finance: The Valuation School is the BEST channel I can recommend, you can also make financial models to add in your portfolio. Other than this, read about terms from Investopedia - Will elaborate more on the doc shared above.

5. Quantitative Aptitude: Read R.S. Agarwal (Shared in the Drive), practice from IndiaBix. For companies like JPMC - you should do CAT level questions.

6. Case Studies: The best way to learn Case studies is by participating in actual competitions, in the last year I participated in a LOT of competitions, all from Unstop. I think I made over 50 PPTs which directly or indirectly prepared me for a lot of questions, even guesstimates. I have also shared a book which helped me make better PPTs for my competitions. You can get other books as well if you just Google - Case study books IIM

7. Guesstimates: I never prepared for guesstimates from any fixed source - but I maintained a book with a lot of information that might help - India's population, Tier wise cities and population, gender ratio, population split by age, unemployment rate, inflation rate, etc. You should read/listen to a few case studies to understand how to approach the problem and how to talk about them. I will also share a very detailed approach to this in the doc.

8. Puzzles: I have been watching riddles/puzzles since my first year from TED-Ed. - There are more riddles other than this playlist, you will find them all in the channel itself. TedEd will help you visualise your problems and help you understand how to approach such problems. Also practice the puzzles in GeeksForGeeks - It is the best website to study anything related to coding or for Job prep.

9. I also did some questions from CodeForces - it will help you develop logical reasoning - not necessary though.

BEST OF LUCK.

DON'T WORRY - IT WILL ALL WORK OUT IN THE END!

journey.howSecured:
The information you gather from the pre-placement talk is extremely crucial as it can make the difference between your selection and rejection. I tailored my resume, answered the interview questions and asked my own questions entirely based on what was said during the pre placement talk.

So take screenshots of the PPT, note down what points they talk about, and then try to think of questions to ask or topics to talk about based on your experience and their requirements.

1. Resume Shortlisting

We were asked to submit our resume on 22nd July, so I made changes based on what my seniors had done and what I felt were appropriate.

Make sure that you tailor your resume every time you apply for a different role. I had applied for 4 companies ( 2 on-campus and 2 off-campus) and I had a different resume for each. They do not have to be big changes, you might just change a project, or add different certifications or change your skills. Make sure that your resume is consistent throughout (Avoid using different date formats, using different bullet types or using Bold or Italics randomly).

After your resume is ready, check your ATS score from 'Resume Worded' : https://resumeworded.com/), anything above 65 is good enough.

The results came out on 23rd July at around 6 pm, so instead of worrying about the results you need to prepare for OA and interviews.

2. Online Assessment (OA) [ 107 students appeared (approx) ]

This was a 60 minute exam with two sections: Quant and Coding. It was a pen and paper test with 8 questions of Quant which had a +3, -1 scheme; 2 questions of Python/pseudo code and 4 questions of SQL.

I felt the quant round was easier as compared to other companies. I have shared all the relevant links in the end to help you prepare. In general the questions are: Find the age, work done and time taken, relative speed, probability and PnC.

The Python part was really just to see your pattern recognition skills. We had to find the sum of n terms of the series given. The first one was easier and of 1 mark : 0, 2, 6, 12, 20, 30……. The second one was of 3 marks with the logic : [ x3 - (x+1)] : -1,-1, 5, 23, 59, 119........... People were either unable to think of the logic or they forgot to find the sum and just wrote the logic. To avoid such mistakes, make sure you read the questions at least twice, once before solving the question and once in between.

The SQL round was of medium difficulty with four questions of 2 marks each. There were questions based on Select, Join (Inner and Right), aggregate functions and Window functions. I practiced SQL using Leetcode's SQL50 and watched a Youtube playlist.

Each section had an individual cutoff so you need to make sure you perform well in each section. I think 18/24 in Quant and 12/24 in Coding was the cutoff but this is just my estimate.

3. Interview Round 1 [ 24 candidates were shortlisted ]

This round lasted 15-20 minutes per candidate with 3 panels of 2 people each: one HR and one technical expert. The questions asked were based completely on the resume, they enquired about each section, projects done, position of responsibilities, certifications and co-curricular activities. They asked a lot of questions on my major project which used Python for data analysis, where they also asked me to write down the formula for single linear regression and multiple linear regression. They also asked me why I chose to do each project and what could be their applications.

They also asked me some concepts based on statistics which I was not sure about - if such a situation arises, be very clear with them that you are not sure of the concept and take a short guess about what it could be. Do not waste their time by pretending to think or give an incorrect answer confidently.

Then they asked me why I was interested in this role, to which I answered by talking about different points throughout my resume. In their pre-placement talk, they mentioned that a Business Analyst needs to know all aspects of a business in order to derive insights for different projects. So, I tried to show them how I have covered all bases due to my committee experience, my projects and my certifications. I also talked about how I liked the JD (Job description) of Incred specifically since it will be high impact work with high ownership. They asked follow up questions on how I know about this and I mentioned that it is one of their values available on the website. In the end, I asked them some questions about their upcoming IPO and how it will impact the day to day working of my job - this was done mostly to show that I had done my study on the company and am aware of their future plans.

The best way to approach such resume based rounds is by taking charge or "breadcrumming", where you end your introduction with a point that they would like to hear more about. For example, at the end of my intro, I told them how I believe I am an ideal candidate for this position because of my Minors in Management from SPJIMR and asked them, "May I elaborate on it?". After each

answer, I tried to add a point in the end that will lead them to ask me a question about something I know the answer to.

Some people were asked questions on writing a simple code for Pandas or Numpy since they mentioned it in their resume, so make sure that you know each and every word of your resume, why it is important and if there are any alternatives.

4. Interview Round 2 [ 11 candidates were shortlisted ]

I was first asked to go through my resume in detail, where I mentioned my Minors in Management from SPJIMR, my projects (the objective, tools I used, industrial application, relevance to the role applied), my committee experience ( along with my learnings and relevance) and my case study competitions ( the problem statement in short and my solution). There were a couple of follow-up questions on the Minors and about the case studies.

This was a guesstimate based round. I was asked how many units of electricity are consumed in India in one year. I was asked to assume that each electrical appliance consumes one unit of electricity in one hour. I started by asking whether I should just consider houses or industries as well. They told me to just consider houses. I then divided the whole problem into smaller parts, India into 4 tiers of cities and the year into three seasons. I also divided the population by 5 assuming that some families have 3 people but some have 6 or more so 5 is a fair guess. Then I made assumptions on how many appliances must be used in each household based on the tier of the city. I also made changes based on the season, for eg, there will be more lightbulbs used during winters since the nights are longer.

I was asked some questions in between, unrelated to the case study, like "Name 10 Tier 1 cities in India". After this they asked me follow-up questions on what could be the potential factors for less electricity in tier 4 cities ( Poor connectivity, cost, and poor infra maintenance), and how I will provide electricity to these cities and what factors I will consider (Coal power plants, nuclear power plants and alternate sources of energy), (Factors : long term environmental impact, cost per unit electricity, set-up cost of each plant, units of electricity required).

After this, I asked a couple of questions on how the use of AI can cause data security concerns and I finished the interview by asking, "If I am selected for this role, what should my roadmap look like to help me be better prepared for when I join?" - This last question shows your excitement for the job and commitment to the company.

A lot of other candidates were asked to take different approaches for their guesstimates, so you must know several common ways to approach any problem. The people who messed up their guesstimates were asked a case study question - for eg. what features would you add in GPay to make it better?

Interviewers care about how you approach any problem and not the exact answer - Just keep talking about why you are making any assumptions and what do you hope to achieve from it. Keep asking questions regarding the things you are not sure about and make sure that you are confident in the approach you are taking. Sometimes they may cross question you to judge your confidence, just justify your approach and make revisions if you think they made a good point.

In the end, 3 candidates were offered a job.

journey.thirdYear:
PPT - 25/07 (online) OA - 28/07 Interviews - 30/07

If you're going through hell, keep going. - Winston Churchill

This is the most relevant quote for your entire placement journey. During your preparation phase before the placement season starts, when giving OAs for companies, before interviews, during interviews, after interviews and when you face rejections after multiple interviews, at each phase you will go through hell but you will come out victorious at the end. The key is to keep going, even if you're facing continuous rejections and feel that there is no hope. The best will come when you least expect it.

Placement Process:
journey.prep:
1. Let's start with the preparation phase before the placement season. The most important part is DSA this will help you clear a lot of Online Assessments for all the major companies. Start as early as possible, the earlier the better. Also what is more important than starting early is maintaining consistency. I was one of the first people to start DSA during the start of 3rd year but then left it

midway for almost the entire Sem 5. Do not make this mistake, once you start make it a habit to do DSA everyday even if it is just one question.

2. You can follow a sheet like Striver's A2Z Sheet or NeetCode or do a combination of both like I did. Start with Striver's SDE Sheet or NeetCode 150 whichever you are comfortable with if you feel confident about Data Structures or go for A2Z Sheet or NeetCode 250 if your basics aren't clear. For Recursion, DP and Graphs make sure to strictly follow Striver and his respective playlists on the topics as it is the best resource on the internet for these topics. The rest you can do from either.

3. Another aspect of DSA is explaining your approach. You may be amazing at DSA but if you cannot explain your approach none of it is any use. When practicing LeetCode, although this might take additional time, but try explaining your approach in your head while you are solving the question

4. Try to do LeetCode contests if you have the time or you complete DSA early enough to practice time management and make sure to practice company style story based questions for OA practice using ChatGPT. You can also experiment with CP if you enjoy doing LeetCode and DSA although I wouldn't recommend it for those of y'all who are doing it for the sake of placements like I was.

5. Next comes SQL, this may seem like an easy topic but this is very crucial as it is asked in almost all interviews. Start with a basic crash course of SQL like Apna College or some other channel to learn basic topics like GROUP BY, ORDER BY, SELECT, JOINS and other basics. Once you have a basic understanding of these jump directly to SQL 50 from LeetCode as the more you practice the better you will be. For each question in SQL 50 if you don't get the solution, go through the solutions of other people or the editorial by LeetCode if given. Do not directly move to ChatGPT that won't help you understand and explore.

6. For OOPS follow Kunal Kuswaha's playlist for OOPs that is the best there is. There is nothing additional required. If you are also working with some other language like C++ or Python refer to OOPs in those languages through ChatGPT and Google. Do preparation for OOPs toward the end of the preparation phase with 2-3 weeks left for the placement season so as to remember the concepts better. After all of this try doing some OS and CCN if time permits.

7. I would recommend doing an internship or two and if you have already done one, make sure to present it well in your resume as this carries a lot of weight. It basically shows the interviewer that other companies also decided to work with you and you have already worked in a professional environment. Even if you do not have an internship, add 3-4 good and diverse projects in your resume so that you can stand out from the crowd. Keep in mind that everyone is going to do normal web dev projects, so to stand you must do different projects that integrate multiple things and try to do a project that includes an AI workflow.

8. Make sure that you know each of your resume projects inside out and you can talk about them for hours with the interviewer. Try to only add projects that you have actually worked on and even if you do add a project right from the internet which I wouldn't recommend but in extreme cases if you do make sure that you put it into ChatGPT or CoPilot and know every aspect of it.

9. Now for the interview part, once you clear the OA try to get a good night's sleep before the interview day but in case it is your first interview and you have a habit and can manage with less sleep, I would recommend that you prepare well the night before if there is something you haven't. Again I would only recommend this if you have done it a lot of times over the years during exams. I did this exact thing and I was a bit sleepy on the D-Day but it was worth it otherwise I wouldn't have been well prepared, so manage your risk accordingly.

10. On the day of the interview, there can be a possibility that your interview might be scheduled later in the day so during this time keep talking to people around you or do some last minute revision but do not overthink and get tensed about your interview. Even if your friends aren't with you, talk to other people so that you get engaged and it takes the edge off.

11. Lastly remember that no matter how much you prepare there will always be situations that work against you like curveball questions you hadn't expected or a stubborn interviewer or any other situation that you did not expect so always be ready for such things. Also be mentally prepared to face ample rejections before you even get an interview or get placed. I got my first interview after facing more than 6-7 OAs and faced 3 interviews before I got placed and for each of these I managed to reach the final round and then got rejected. Keep in mind that this is a part of the placement proces and always be ready to get up and move on.

Resources:

Category Resource/Platform Key Strategy/Notes

OA & Aptitude IndiaBix Good for topics including (percentages, ratios, time-distance).

DSA Striver's A2Z DSA Sheet Understanding patterns is crucial. Always spend 30-45 mins before looking at the solution.I had solved around 75% of the SDE sheet.

Java OOPs Kunal Kushwaha Playlist & If you have time, go through the entire playlist as it is very GFG Notes extensive

DBMS GFG, Code-Help Babbar Supplement lecture notes with these for fast review.

CN GFG CN Notes Supplement lecture notes with these for fast review.

OS GFG OS Notes Supplement lecture notes with these for fast review.

SQL Leetcode 50 questions This should be enough for most of the on campus roles.

Interview ChatGPT Quick and reliable tool to research company background, tech Prep stack, and everything related to your resume or interview answers.

HR Indiabix+ChatGPT Use them to prepare for general HR questions. Use LLMs to tailor your answers according to company values.
