HR Indiabix+ChatGPT Use them to prepare for general HR questions. Use LLMs to tailor your answers according to company values.

General Tips:

A quick backstory about my placement journey -

I began my DSA preparation after the 5th semester but had shifted focus entirely to investment banking for the three months leading up to placement season. Unfortunately, I couldn't clear the Group Discussion round of the J.P.M.C interview, which was a major setback. It was disheartening, as I hadn't ever expected to be eliminated in the very first round.

It was hard for me to switch back to DSA after the long break. But after a lot of practice, I was able to get back on track. After facing 6 rejections, I was able to crack this offer.

Things to keep in mind:

● Your communication skills matter a lot during the interview. Practice thinking out loud while solving DSA problems

● A well crafted resume can help you right from shortlisting to the final HR round. Aim for an ATS score of 70+ on platforms like Resume Worded

● Luck plays a quiet but powerful role during this season.Sometimes, despite giving your all, it slips away; other times, it finds you when you least expect it.

● Gear up for a potential emotional roller coaster, bound by anxiety, fear, hope(lessness), and joy at last. This phase of life will teach you a lot, make sure to learn from every rejection. All you need is one good day. Sooner or later, if you've prepared sincerely, that day will come.

● Make sure to participate in Hackathons (and Case Study Competitions if you are preparing for PM/IB/DA roles). They are a great way of developing good projects and learning new things.

● If you're preparing for a non-tech role, evaluate whether you can also do at least basic DSA preparation in parallel. It proved to be one of the best decisions in my case.

● If you don't get selected, don't be disheartened there's always another company and another chance. Stay focused, stay hopeful, and keep moving forward.

ALL THE BEST FOR YOUR PLACEMENT !!

The Online Assessment was a 90-minute test consisting of 15 questions:

● 13 questions were based on core CS subjects like Java, OOPS, DBMS, CN, and OS.

● 1 SQL question which was very simple, requiring the use of basic WHERE and AND conditions.

● 1 DSA coding question which was repeated from last year: Lexicographically Smallest String After Applying Operations (JobOverflow link).

Tips:

● Make sure to go through previous years' OA questions; the coding question may be repeated.

● Brush up on Java theory and basic DBMS/OOPS concepts.

● SQL basics (especially filtering rows using WHERE and logical operators) should be known.

● Practice DSA regularly using Striver's A-Z sheet to improve speed and accuracy.

2. Technical Interview Round 1 [Number of candidates: 37]

The round began with the interviewer looking at my resume. He asked me to explain any one of my projects. I picked one and walked him through it. He then asked if I had faced any challenges during the project. I mentioned encountering the CORS error, which I had seen in almost every project I built.

He asked how I resolved it. I explained that I used the cors library in the backend to allow the frontend domain to access backend resources. He seemed somewhat satisfied but pointed out that since CORS is a browser-based issue, I should reflect more on why the backend is used to resolve it.

He then asked whether I had used AI/ML in any of my projects. I mentioned that I had completed two college courses : Generative AI and LLMs, but had not integrated them into my projects.

Coding Questions:

He then gave two pattern-printing questions with the condition that I could use only two for loops in total.

Question 1 (n = 5):

*

**

***

**

*

I asked a few clarifying questions (like whether n is always odd) and wrote an example to confirm. I ended up using a while loop externally and nested for loops internally. The interviewer said this was partially correct, as the ideal solution required only two for loops total.

Question 2:

X*X*X

X*X*

X*X

X*

X

This one was easier. I solved it using two for loops and printed X for odd indices and * for even indices using the modulo operator. He was satisfied with my approach.

Java Concepts:

He asked whether Java was my primary language, and I confirmed it. Then he asked multiple Java-related questions:

● HashMaps: How are they implemented? I spoke about hashing techniques like linear probing and explained how linear probing works.

● Time Complexities: I said HashMap provides O(1) average-case and O(N) worst-case complexities. He asked whether search operations can also take O(N), to which I answered yes, due to the linear scan in probing.

● Hashing Properties: I mentioned hashing should be low-cost and reduce collisions. He was looking for additional properties that I couldn't recall.

● Primitive Data Types in HashMap: I said Java does not allow primitive types, only wrapper classes. He asked how primitives are converted into objects, and I correctly answered "autoboxing."

● List vs HashMap Search: I said HashMap has better search performance (O(1) avg) than a List (O(N) worst).

● TreeMap with Objects as Keys: I said it is possible and explained by giving an example of a Person class, which contains name and age as attributed, and using a TreeMap<Person, Integer> with a lambda comparator, e.g., sorting by name using a.name.compareTo(b.name). I also mentioned the need to override hashCode() and equals() methods in such classes.

The interviewer seemed moderately satisfied and selected me for the next round.

3. HR Interview [Number of candidates: 21]

This round was purely HR for me, while many others had a techno-HR round.

● The interviewer started by asking me to introduce myself. I included my internship experience at Triblet SportsTech, where I worked on UI/UX design using Figma.

● He asked what I would do if I didn't have access to Figma, Canva, or any other design tool. I said I would collaborate with my team and sketch designs manually, referring to existing designs from the internet.

● He asked if I had worked in a team. I replied yes and explained that I worked with two other teammates to design desktop and mobile layouts based on the company's theme.

● He inquired if there were any disagreements in the team. I shared a scenario where we had conflicting ideas about a design. I suggested we consult the founder/co-founder and some users to make an informed decision.

● He asked whether I ever took credit for someone else's work during my internship. I said no and gave an example of when I was helped by teammates and gave them full credit during a meeting with the founder.

● He presented a hypothetical: What would I do if I had to deliver a project in a week using C#, which neither I nor my team knew, and my teammates were busy? I responded that I'd learn the basics of C#, implement 2-3 core functionalities, and communicate with the project manager to request a 2-3 week extension while possibly offering extra features to make up for delays.

● Finally, he asked if I had taken undue credit during college. I honestly admitted that I once overstated my contribution to a major project presentation, but I later felt guilty and learned from the experience.

In total, 16 students were selected.

There were a total of 3 rounds: OA, TECHNICAL-1, HR/TECHNO-HR

1. OA Round [135 Candidates Appeared]

The eligibility criteria mentioned was 7+ CGPA, but in reality, only those with 7.5+ were shortlisted.

The OA round [106 marks] had 3 sections:

Section 1: MCQs [46 Marks]

The MCQs were of medium to hard level, and covered topics like Java, OOP, SQL, a few pseudocodes, and C++/C snippets too. Make sure you know OOP, SQL, and Java inside out if you want to crack Barclays. Try to strengthen your core subjects in the 2nd year itself, and practice MCQs in your 6th sem.

Section 2: Coding Question

The coding question was the same as last year, so there's a good chance they'll repeat it next year too.

Link to the question: Leetcode Discuss - String Generation OA Question

The solution on Leetcode is very lengthy and not intuitive (uses DP + KMP).

Here's the greedy solution I used (passes all test cases):

class Solution {

public String generateString(String str1, String str2) { int n = str1.length(), m = str2.length(); int sz = n + m - 1; char[] ans = new char[sz]; boolean[] mod = new boolean[sz]; java.util.Arrays.fill(mod, true);

// 1. Satisfy all 'T' positions for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) { if (str1.charAt(i) == 'T') { for (int j = 0; j < m; ++j) { int pos = i + j; if (ans[pos] != 0 && ans[pos] != str2.charAt(j)) return ""; ans[pos] = str2.charAt(j); mod[pos] = false; } } }

// 2. Fill unassigned positions with 'a' for (int i = 0; i < sz; ++i) { if (ans[i] == 0) ans[i] = 'a'; }

// 3. Enforce 'F' positions for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) { if (str1.charAt(i) == 'F') { if (matches(ans, i, str2)) { int change = -1; for (int j = 0; j < m; ++j) { int pos = i + j; if (pos < sz && mod[pos]) change = pos; } if (change < 0) return ""; ans[change] = 'b'; mod[change] = false; } }

}

return new String(ans); }

private boolean matches(char[] ans, int i, String s2) { if (i + s2.length() > ans.length) return false; for (int j = 0; j < s2.length(); ++j) { if (ans[i + j] != s2.charAt(j)) return false; } return true; } }

If you want to practice or run your own approach, you can try it here: Lexicographically Smallest Generated String - Leetcode

Section 3: SQL Query

I got a very easy SQL query based on basic filtering using WHERE and AND. Some people got slightly trickier ones - for example, extracting a month from a date.

2. Technical Round [37 Candidates Appeared]

This round varied for everyone - some were asked core subject questions, some were asked about their resumes (VERY IMPORTANT: know your resume inside-out), and others were asked system design basics. Barclays focuses more on "WHY" than just "HOW."

For me, I was asked a DSA question, a puzzle, a system design question, and a SQL query.

● Introduction: I introduced myself and mentioned that I enjoy solving DSA on Leetcode and building projects that solve real-world problems. (He wrote this down - probably why he asked me DSA and Design questions).

● DSA Question: He asked me to help sort an array using Merge Sort. I explained the recursion tree, merging logic, why Merge Sort is better than other algorithms, and its time complexity. Then I wrote the code, explained it line by line, and did a dry run with 2-3 examples.

● IDE & Debugging: He asked if I'd used IntelliJ. I said I used to but switched to VSCode since it's better for Dev too. Then he asked how I debug code - I explained all my approaches: using the VSCode debugger, adding print statements, and dry-running edge cases.

● Puzzle Question: Q: Cut a cake into 8 equal parts with 3 cuts. Ans: Two vertical cuts through the center → 4 slices. One horizontal cut across all → 8 slices. (Think 3D!)

● Design Question: Design a Railway Management System. At first, I misunderstood and started with schema design. Then I asked for a hint - he asked questions like: "How to assign platforms?", "How to prevent collisions?", etc. I gave solutions for each.

● SQL Query: Q: Return departments with more than 15 employees. Ans: Simple LEFT JOIN, GROUP BY, and HAVING COUNT(*) > 15.

Tip from this round: Try to think in your head first, structure your answer, and then speak. (I asked for feedback and this is what he told me LOL). But never stay quiet for too long. If you need time, ask for a moment, and speak out your thoughts. Start with what you know and go step-by-step toward optimization.

3. HR / Techno-HR Round [21 Candidates Appeared]

Some had a Techno-HR round, others had just HR. For me, it was purely HR.

● Basic HR questions: Tell me about yourself, why Barclays, etc.

● A lot of behavioral questions - try to align your answers with RISES values of Barclays.

16 Students were offered the job, and 3 were waitlisted.

The placement process can be hectic and stressful, and it's completely normal to feel overwhelmed. I had tests and interviews before this where I didn't make it, and that's okay, not everything will go your way. Just keep showing up, keep preparing, and trust the process. If it's meant to happen, it will. Stay consistent and don't lose hope.

Placement Process:

1. Online Assessment [135 students appeared for this round]
journey.prep:
• It's never too late to start. Whether you're in first year or already into third, what matters is starting today. You'll thank yourself later.

• Choose your primary programming language and stick to it. Be it Java, Python, or C++, master one language thoroughly. But also have a basic understanding of other popular languages, especially if they come up in interviews or MCQs.

• Start DSA preparation seriously. You can follow:

o The A2Z DSA Sheet by Striver (great for structured progress).

o The CSES Problem Set (excellent for logic building and competitive programming).

• Keep 1-2 strong, impactful, and preferably unique projects in your portfolio. Projects that solve real problems, demonstrate initiative, or use newer technologies really help you stand out.

• Don't ignore your core Computer Science subjects like DBMS, OS, CN, OOPs, and SQL. These come up a lot in interviews--both technical and MCQ rounds.

• Participate in extracurriculars! Being active in committees, hackathons, and competitions not only builds your confidence but also shows that you're a team player and proactive.

• It's okay to face rejection. I had tests and interviews where I didn't make it before this offer. But remember: every failure teaches you something, and you only need one "yes."

• Keep your resume updated and tailor it for each company. Highlight relevant projects, achievements, and internships.

• Mock interviews help. Practice with friends or seniors. The more you simulate the pressure, the better you'll perform.

• Always stay consistent -- even if you can only study or code for an hour a day, it adds up.

• And finally, never stop believing in yourself. Confidence and self-belief are game changers.

You've got this! Every small effort counts. The journey might be challenging, but with consistency, smart planning, and the right mindset -- you'll get where you're meant to be.

1. Online Assessment [135 students appeared for this round]

• The online assessment was conducted on HackerEarth and had a 90-minute time limit.

• It consisted of 12 technical MCQs, 1 SQL query, and 1 coding question.

The MCQs were based on CS fundamentals, OOPs, SQL, and code snippet output prediction.

The SQL question was simple and could be solved using a basic WHERE clause with some AND conditions. It required interpreting a table to calculate compensation.

The coding question was string-based, required generating a lexicographically smallest string based on mapping rules from two input strings S1 and S2 (containing only 'T' and 'F').

You had to construct an answer string such that:

o For index i, if S2[i] is 'T', the answer substring starting from i should match S1. o If S2[i] is 'F', then at least one character in that range must differ from S1.

The solution required both brute-force thinking and careful handling of edge cases to ensure the final string was valid and lexicographically smallest.

https://leetcode.com/problems/lexicographically-smallest-generated-string/ https://www.thejoboverflow.com/p/p1926/

Note: The test was exactly the same as the one conducted for the Barclays Summer Internship last year, including the coding and SQL questions. In fact, Barclays has been repeating the same test pattern and questions for the past two years, so going through previ ous year test experiences can give you a strong edge.

2. Technical Round [37 students shortlisted]

The interviews began around 10:30 AM, but I was called only after the lunch break at 3:00 PM. So, if your slot is later in the day, there's no need to worry, delays are normal.

My interview began with a brief introduction round. The interviewer asked me to introduce myself, followed by questions about my family background, CGPA, and whether I was satisfied with my college and academic performance so far.

Next, he asked me about my primary programming language, to which I responded Java. He then asked a simple DSA question on finding duplicates in an array. He handed over his laptop and asked me to code the solution in as many ways as I could.

• I first implemented the solution using a HashSet.

• After that, he asked me to make a few variations in the code, which I successfully implemented.

Following that, the discussion moved to Java concepts and Object-Oriented Programming (OOPs). The interviewer then focused deeply on Exception Handling in Java. He:

• Asked several questions, ranging from basic to advanced level.

• Requested me to code examples using try-catch-finally blocks directly on his laptop.

• Asked about different types of exceptions, their behavior, and expected outputs.

• Also made me predict the output of the code I had written, then verify it by running the program.

While coding and answering, I made a few minor mistakes, but nothing major. The interviewer seemed okay with them, so don't stress too much over small slips.

Lastly, we discussed one of my projects, where I gave an overview and explained the problem statement, tech stack used, and key features.

At the end of the interview, he asked if I had any questions. I asked him about his role at Barclays and the technologies he works with.

That concluded my first technical round.

3. HR Round [21 students shortlisted]

Just 10 minutes after my technical round, I was called in for the HR interview.

The HR round began with the interviewer asking me to introduce myself, followed by questions about the hackathons I had participated in and won.

He then asked me about the company values that were shared during the pre-placement talk (PPT session). He wanted to know:

• What those values meant to me personally

• And how I had implemented any of those values in my daily life

We then had a detailed conversation about the committees I was a part of, and this part of the discussion went on for quite some time.

Towards the end, he asked if I had any questions for him. I took the opportunity to ask about:

• The team he leads at Barclays

• And what kind of work his team is involved in

This brought the HR round to a close.

In total, 16 students, were selected.

Placement Process Overview

The placement process at Barclays involved three rounds, starting with an online assessment and progressing to two interview stages. On July 26th there was an online assessment, followed by interviews on July 29th. Out of 133 participants who appeared for the online assessment, 37 were shortlisted for the first technical interview. Subsequently, 21 individuals advanced to the final Tech + HR round,

Round 1: Online Assessment (90 minutes)

The Barclays online assessment was a three-part test consisting of MCQs, a SQL query, and a coding problem. The MCQs were the key differentiator for shortlisting.

1. Multiple Choice Questions (MCQs)

These questions tested foundational knowledge across various programming languages and concepts.

● Core Language Concepts: Questions involved predicting the output of short code snippets in languages like C++ and Java. Topics included pointers, bitwise operators, control flow (continue), and variable scope.

● Object-Oriented Programming (OOP): This section focused on OOP principles, such as the difference between abstract classes vs. interfaces and method overriding vs. overloading. It also covered topics like the impossibility of overriding private and static methods and the order of class initialization.

● Exception Handling (Java): Questions evaluated an understanding of try-catch-finally blocks. A key point was knowing that a return statement in a finally block overrides any return from try or catch, and that System.exit() prevents the finally block from executing.

2. SQL Questions

This section included both a query and theoretical MCQs.

● Queries: The questions required you to apply your SQL knowledge to real-world scenarios. This involved using multi-table joins to combine data, filtering data by date using functions like EXTRACT(MONTH FROM date), and translating complex business rules into a single SELECT query.

● SQL Theory: MCQs tested your knowledge of commands like DROP vs. TRUNCATE vs. DELETE. A crucial distinction was the difference between an equi join (which uses only =) and an inner join (a broader category of joins).

3. Coding Problem

The coding problem was a single, complex challenge that required careful logical thinking.

● "String Generation": The task was to create the lexicographically smallest string S based on a pattern string (S1) and a rule string (S2) of 'T' (true) and 'F' (false) constraints.

● Solution Logic: The recommended approach was to first satisfy all 'T' constraints. Then, fill the remaining positions with the smallest possible character, 'A'. Finally, iterate through all 'F' constraints and minimally modify the string (e.g., change the rightmost 'A' to a 'B') to break any invalid matches while preserving the lexicographical order. This problem went beyond a simple build-and-check method, demanding a more nuanced strategy to correct violations.

Round 2: Technical Round 1

Following the online assessment, 37 participants were shortlisted for the interview rounds. There were five interview panels, and I happened to be assigned to one of the more challenging ones. My interviewer was highly experienced and went into very detailed questions on every topic. This round lasted for approximately an hour.

The interview began with a standard introduction, after which I was asked to brief him about my projects. He then inquired about the programming languages I was comfortable with. Following this, he asked me to explain the concept of method overloading and to write a Java program demonstrating a real-world example, encouraging me to think beyond common examples like 'Area' or 'Vehicle'. He then moved on to an in-depth discussion about my projects. Noticing my significant frontend projects, he transitioned into detailed questions about React and HTML. He gave a scenario about creating a dropdown within another dropdown using React and asked about the distinction between a textbox and a textarea. Further questions included how to limit the number of words in an input field and how to display the count of letters already entered. While I couldn't recall every specific detail, I explained my approach clearly.

He then asked detailed HTML questions, presenting a scenario where he needed to input seven addresses in a form. He asked how I would extract the second address, impose a limit on the number of addresses, and manage IDs if they were assigned sequentially (e.g., 1 for the first address, 2 for the second). Specifically, he asked what would happen to ID 1 if the first address was deleted--would it be reassigned, or would a new one be created? He also wanted to know how I would track the total number of addresses.

After assessing my Java knowledge, he shifted to SQL. He asked if I knew about Procedures and Triggers, to which I confirmed. He then asked for an explanation and relevant queries. At this point, I honestly confessed that I hadn't practiced writing queries for procedures and triggers, but I explained the underlying concepts. I remained calm and continued to answer all his questions. He then inquired about the partitioning concept in DBMS and what partitioned tables are, asking me to write a query for it. Finally, he asked about different types of indexes in DBMS. The interview concluded with a question about the risks a bank might face and potential solutions.

I left this round feeling devastated and demotivated, convinced it had gone terribly wrong and almost on the verge of tears.

Round 3: Tech + HR Round

To my surprise, I was called for this final round, which shortlisted 21 candidates. This round lasted for about half an hour. The interviewer started by sharing the positive feedback he had received from my first interviewer, which was a huge relief and a pleasant surprise given how I felt after the first technical round.

He then asked me to describe my internship experience and elaborate on my projects, cross-questioning me further to see my understanding and contributions. Following this, he moved on to the HR-specific questions. He asked classic questions like "Why do you want to join Barclays?" and a challenging scenario: "If another company offered you double the salary, would you switch?" He also presented situations involving workplace ethics and problem-solving, such as: "If your manager gives you a task with an unrealistic deadline, how would you approach it?" and "You've completed your work for a strict weekend deadline and left for vacation, but midway, you realize you forgot to push an important update to GitHub. How would you resolve this?" Another thought-provoking question was: "If you were stuck on a project you built from scratch, and a friend helped you resolve a small error that had a big impact, and then you were nominated for an award for that project, would you accept the award or tell your team members about your friend's contribution? Discuss the pros and cons of each decision." He asked many more similar situational questions.

I ensured to be confident and true to myself in my responses, which seemed to satisfy the interviewer. At the end, I took the opportunity to ask him about his role and what Barclays expects from interns, specifically if prior knowledge of finance is required. With these questions, the interview concluded.

Areas for Improvement, Preparation, and General Tips

My selection was largely due to my ability to stay calm under pressure, even when faced with questions I couldn't fully answer. My honesty about my limitations, coupled with explaining my approach or conceptual understanding, showed integrity. My detailed preparation in OOPS, Java, HTML, React, SQL, and DBMS fundamentals was crucial, especially since MCQs were a deciding factor in the initial round. In the HR round, being confident, truthful, and demonstrating problem-solving skills with practical reasoning helped immensely. Engaging the interviewer and asking relevant questions also showed genuine interest and initiative.

Areas for Improvement: My biggest learning from this experience was the need for thorough practical application of concepts, especially in areas like SQL procedures and triggers, beyond just theoretical understanding. It's crucial to not only know what a concept is but also how to implement it with code or queries.

Preparation Strategy:

● Online Assessment: I primarily practiced MCQs from GeeksforGeeks to strengthen my foundational knowledge in OOPS, Java, C++, Objective-C, SQL, and DBMS. For coding, I focused on problems from LeetCode.

● Technical Interview: I focused on preparing OOPS, Java, SQL, and DBMS concepts in depth.

○ Data Structures and Algorithms (DSA): I referred to Striver's SDE Sheet and the Blind 75 LeetCode Java - All Questions Solved for coding practice.

○ SQL: Top SQL 50 on LeetCode was very helpful, along with Lecture 10: Common SQL Queries for Interviews and SQL Bolt for hands-on practice.

○ DBMS: Complete DBMS in 1 Video (With Notes) || For Placement Interviews

○ OOPS & Java: Java OOPs in One Shot | Object Oriented Programming | Java Language | Place… was a key resource. I also practiced Java MCQs from GeeksforGeeks.

○ Frontend (React/HTML): For React, Top 100 React JS Interview Questions and Answers was a valuable resource, and I practiced detailed HTML concepts.

○ Practice SQL, DBMS, Java, OOPS, and React questions from InterviewBit.

● Ensure your resume clearly highlights your projects, particularly showcasing your role and contributions, and the technologies used. Be prepared to discuss every detail mentioned on your resume, as interviewers will cross-question. Don't include anything you're not confident about.

Important Points to Remember on the Day of the Interview:

● Regardless of how challenging the questions get, maintaining your composure is key. A small, calm smile can convey composure and confidence. Don't give up, even if a round feels like it went poorly.

● Always have a pen and paper handy for jotting down thoughts or working through problems.

● Keep your phone screen facing downwards to avoid any distractions.

● Sit straight, maintaining good posture, as it reflects engagement and confidence.

● Strive to make the interview a two-way conversation, engaging with the interviewer. Think out loud while solving problems; it helps the interviewer understand your thought process.

● If you don't know an answer completely, it's better to honestly confess and explain what you do know or how you would approach finding a solution, rather than bluffing.

● At the end, always ask thoughtful questions about the role, team, company culture, or expectations. This shows genuine interest.

By keeping these points in mind, and remembering to stay confident and true to yourself, you can significantly improve your chances during the placement process.

ALL THE BEST!!

You can contact me on LinkedIn anytime you want!!

There was no GPA cutoff this year; however, I would still recommend maintaining a GPA above 8.5 to always be on the safer side. The pre-placement talk took place just before the technical round, unlike the usual PPTs that occur for all candidates before the OA. Barclays conducts its PPT for candidates shortlisted only from the OA. Please be attentive and make sure to note down the points they mention during the PPT, as it helps you prepare well about the company. A company will always prefer a candidate who is well-aware of its mission, values, and objectives.

1. Online Assessment [ 133 students appeared for this round ]

It was conducted on 26th July 2025 at 11am. The OA round lasted 90 minutes and included 15 questions: 13 MCQs on CS fundamentals (specifically OOPS and DBMS), 1 moderate DSA question, and 1 easy SQL question.

In the CS fundamentals part, they particularly focused on Java output-based questions, some of which involved recursion and inheritance. Some MCQs were weighted differently (2, 4, 5, or 6 marks), so it was crucial to get the 6-marker ones correct. One question I remember involved several abstract classes and functions. The main function attempted to instantiate these abstract classes, which would lead to a compilation error, as an abstract class can never be instantiated. This question was lengthy, but if you looked carefully, the answer was obvious at a glance. It was important not to get such questions wrong, especially since they were 6-markers. Another question asked for the default values of instance variables of type boolean and int, the answers being false and 0 respectively. There was also a question on try catch blocks where I had to determine the output. One Java function involved finding the maximum value and its correct output. Additionally, there was a question that provided options for SQL queries, and I had to select the correct one based on a given table schema. It's really important to read each question properly and carefully, without missing any details.

For the SQL question, I was given a single table and had to find customer IDs and calculate a final amount that was 50% more than customer's salary who had a major accident, had a savings account, and an active salary and insurance account . It was an easy question where we were just required to apply multiple AND conditions based on the listed criteria.

The DSA question was similar to : Lexicographical String

Approach: I used a brute-force approach and managed to pass all the test cases. First, I constructed a result string with a length equal to len1+len2-1 (where len1 is the size of str1 and len2 is the size of str2). For every index i in str1 where the value was 'T', I ensured that the substring starting at i in the result exactly matched str2. If any conflict occurred during this placement, I returned an empty string. After placing all 'T'-based substrings, I filled the remaining uninitialized positions with 'a'. Next, for each 'F' position in str1, I checked if the corresponding substring in the result matched str2. If it did (which it shouldn't), I tried to change at least one unfixed character in that range by incrementing it, as long as it wasn't already locked from a 'T' placement. If fixing wasn't possible, I returned an empty string. Finally, the result string was returned after satisfying all 'T' and 'F' constraints.

Most of the students had completed the DSA and SQL questions, so everything boiled down to the MCQ round, which decided who would proceed to the further rounds.

2. Technical Interview Round [ 37 candidates appeared for this round ]

Stay calm, be composed, and trust in what you've studied. The interviewer will ask questions that are important and showcase your problem-solving abilities, not random, vague ones.

My interview began with the interviewer asking for my introduction. It's crucial to prepare your introduction in a way that clearly highlights your strong topics; with a bit of luck, you might only get questions on those areas, but be prepared for everything. The interviewer then asked me to rate my development, DSA, SQL, and database skills. After that, he started by asking me to write a few SQL queries: first, to find the Nth record from a table, and then to find the 7th highest salary from a given set of records. Following this, he asked about the order of execution for any given SQL query. For better clarity, refer to following article Execution Order of SQL Query

Next, he asked several questions about databases, specifically the reasons for choosing a particular database and under what circumstances. Essentially, he wanted to test my capability to implement the appropriate database for a given problem and the reasoning behind that choice. Ensure you provide proper reasons and clarity for your database selection. He also asked how I would optimize a given query search.

After this, he shifted to my resume and asked me to explain my internship project and exactly what I did in it and what were the various challenges I faced in it, which was the most critical bug/error I faced and how did I eliminate it. Always be prepared for questions about your project's goals, objectives, architecture, challenges faced, advantages, disadvantages, the reason for choosing your tech stack, the various alternatives to your tech stacks, possible scalable solutions, and what you learned from it. For every question you're asked, ensure you explain the concept first, followed by an example, and then a real-life application, along with its advantages, disadvantages, and any possible concerns. For one of my projects, I was asked to explain how JWT Tokens works at a core level, followed by a detailed explanation of RBAC . Make sure to explain using a pen and paper, as this demonstrates the clarity of your understanding.

From another project, they asked for the reason behind choosing the IPFS system over Docker, how I would ensure the confidentiality of a user uploading a file to my application, and how I would check if a file had been tampered with. For this, I tried to explain the working of IPFS in detail. As my resume showcased more of my machine learning capabilities, they asked for the reasons behind choosing various algorithms, what would have happened if I had chosen a different algorithm, and how I decide which algorithm is best for a model. What are the various steps involved in deciding which algorithm is best for a given problem. They also asked for the reason behind choosing ROC over accuracy and sensitivity. Always be honest with your answers; if you don't know something, try to relate it to the most relevant concept. They want to

test how you react in such situations, so explain your thought process and how you would tackle the issue. To my surprise, I wasn't asked a single OOPS question throughout my interview. Communicate with your interviewer and ask for hints if you get stuck on a question. The more vocal you are with your thoughts, the better idea the interviewer will get about how confident you are with your answers. There's no need to worry even if you're wrong; just stay calm.

He then asked me, being "more of an ML guy," how I would work on a leader's project with different requirements. In such a situation, you need to showcase your fast learning ability and how well you can adapt to new technologies. I tried to answer by saying that even though I am an ML guy, I have built a few MERN stack-based projects along with projects that use Python with Django, so shifting to a different tech stack would actually help me learn even more new things. I also mentioned that ML is something I am quite familiar with, more inclined towards, and have always loved developing projects around.

At the end, the interviewer asked if I had any questions. I had thoroughly reviewed their PPT, which mentioned that GenAI and ML domains are areas they are currently exploring. So, I asked them about the current stage of Barclays' use of GenAI at a production level and how a new intern could get into such teams and collaborate with everyone.

3. Techno HR round [ 21 appeared for this round ]

The way the first round went for me, I didn't expect to be shortlisted for the next one. I was actually heading home when I found out I was selected for the Techno-HR round and that my interview was in the next 10 minutes. I came running back, calmed myself down, and got ready for it. This round, which was the penultimate one, lasted about 50 minutes. It started with a brief introduction of myself, where I was asked to mention who I am in real life, what qualities set me apart from others, things I like and dislike, the projects I've built with their detailed descriptions, and their social impact. I was asked the following questions:

● Tell me about a situation where you were ashamed of yourself.

● What was a time in your project when your teammates had to suffer because of you?

● Suppose one of your teammates is not willing to work with you; how would you react in that situation?

● Describe a situation in life where you had to make a decision for your team that wasn't welcomed and what was its impact?

● What was that one moment in life when you earned the respect of others?

● Mention a situation where you had to form a cross-dynamic team (people of different ethnicities and age groups), and how did you coordinate with them?

● Suppose you have a conflicting idea that doesn't really work well with your project, but you've worked quite hard on it and want it to be incorporated. However, other teammates aren't willing to accept it; what would you do?

● Describe a moment when you were a liability for the team--basically, you were present but couldn't contribute anything.

● While working in the internship, was there a time when you faced a situation where you got a sudden, revised deadline that was very difficult for you to manage?

● What were some of the major challenges you faced while developing your projects?

● You were given very less time to develop a project by your manager; what would you do in that situation?

Barclays strongly believes in its RISES values: Respect, Integrity, Service, Excellence, and Stewardship.

At the very end, they called 16 people to the Conference Room, where they dramatically announced that these were the individuals who had cheated in the Barclays placement and were therefore "invited to come and join Barclays :) " It turned out to be a small prank on their part, a way to try and scare us. I was honestly filled with so many emotions; tears started rolling down as, after so many rejections and moments of self-doubt, I was finally able to crack Barclays. It really hammered home the idea that fortune favors the brave. People often say that luck contributes a bit to placements, and I do agree with that, but ultimately, you need to put in so much hard work that your efforts clearly shine through, helping you clear each and every round. It's that consistent dedication that truly makes the difference in the end.

OA (26-7-25) PPT & Interview Rounds (29-7-25)

Placement Process:

The whole recruitment process had three main stages. It started with an OA, which turned out to be the toughest part since it filtered out most of the candidates. Those who cleared the OA were invited for the Pre-Placement Talk (PPT), and then had to go through two rounds of interviews. At the end, there was a fun little prank played on the selected candidates--just to lighten the mood after all the seriousness!. Looking back, clearing the OA was the real challenge. It tested everything like aptitude, computer science fundamentals, and coding skills. So, if you're planning to sit for it, my honest advice would be start preparing early, and make sure you're comfortable with all the core concepts.

1. OA Round [ 135 candidates appeared, 37 shortlisted]
journey.prep:
● Master your OOPs concepts -- a majority of the questions came from this area.

● If you know the right answer, be confident. Sometimes interviewers may challenge you on purpose just to test your conviction.

● Know your resume inside out. Don't include anything just to fill space -- if it's on there, be ready to discuss it.

● For coding problems, always start with the brute force approach. Then discuss how you can optimize it.

● Keep talking through your thoughts during the coding part. Don't go silent. The interaction matters as much as the solution.

3. Techno-HR round [19 candidates appeared]

The Techno-HR round began with the usual "Introduce Yourself" question, which helped set a comfortable tone. The interviewer then asked an interesting question: why do you think Java was designed using OOPs? That opened up a deeper conversation about OOP concepts, and he followed up with questions around interfaces, inheritance, and the use of extends and implement keywords.

He then asked me about my internship--what kind of work I did there--and specifically wanted to hear about an incident where I got stuck and how I handled it. It was a good opportunity to share real experience and reflect on problem-solving skills in a work environment. After this, we had a friendly chat about how the software development landscape is evolving. The interviewer casually mentioned how coding nowadays is becoming more about configuring libraries and tools (like in Python) rather than writing every line from scratch. I agreed, and we discussed how that shift is changing the way developers work.

The conversation was very calm and natural. The interviewer was chill and approachable, which made me feel at ease. At one point, he asked me if I preferred being a full-time developer who just codes, or if I'd enjoy a hybrid role like a business analyst--someone who handles tech but also communicates and collaborates with other teams. I appreciated this question because it showed that they were interested in how I see myself professionally, beyond just my tech skills.

After this, he moved to the HR-style situational questions. One of them was quite interesting: he gave me a scenario where I had a deadline the next day, but a teammate was stuck on something. Helping them might mean I'd have to work overnight to finish my own tasks. What would I do? I gave a fairly standard answer--saying that I'd help because it's about the team's success, not just mine. But he challenged me, saying that if I helped, I might lose my own flow and have to restart everything later, which would waste time.

While he was talking, someone served him coffee. He took a sip while reviewing my resume, and I quickly made a connection. I said, "Just like you took a sip of coffee to refresh yourself before continuing, I'd do the same if I were stuck--I'd take a short mental break, help my teammate, and come back even more focused." That spontaneous answer really clicked with him, and I could see he was impressed.

Then came the question: "Why Barclays?" I had already prepared a response that included their core values--RISES--and wove it into a story that reflected my interest in both tech and impact. He seemed satisfied with the answer.

He also asked me if I preferred working in silence or in a collaborative, discussion-heavy environment. After that, there were a few more classic HR questions--strengths and weaknesses, whether I know anything about finance or investment banking, and if I'd be open to learning a completely new tech stack. He specifically asked if I'd be okay moving away from Java and diving fully into Python or something else if the role required it. I assured him I'm open to learning whatever is needed to grow and contribute effectively.

As the interview was coming to an end, he said he was done and asked if I had any questions for him. I said I wasn't aware of his position and would love to know more about his role. We ended up having a nice chat about his responsibilities and how teams work at Barclays. It gave me a deeper insight into the company's structure and culture.

The round lasted for around 40 to 45 minutes, and overall, it felt more like a thoughtful conversation than a strict interview.

I'd say it's really important to be aware of Barclays' RISES values and try to include them naturally in your responses to situation-based questions. Preparing some standard HR questions in advance helps a lot, especially if you can back up your answers with real stories. In my case, I used internship experiences and examples from project collaborations. It's also important to interact with the interviewer--don't just turn it into a Q&A session. Try to make it a discussion. Stay attentive, because small things happening around you can give you the spark for a clever or memorable answer--but make sure you don't get distracted. And lastly, whatever your strengths are, try to reflect them--directly or indirectly--throughout the interview. One more thing that really helped me was paying attention during the PPT (Pre-Placement Talk). Some of the things discussed there--especially around the company's work culture, Barclays' values, and the tech stack they use--came in handy during the HR and project discussion parts. So I'd strongly suggest taking notes during the PPT, because it can give you useful context and even points to connect during the actual interview.

After a long wait, there was a prank where 16 candidates were called and finally we were told that we have been.

Resources:

Aptitude: indiabix DSA striver sheet :LINK Practice questions repeatedly and get familiar with all the common patterns.

SQL : SQL 50 Practice SQL 50 from LeetCode at least 2-3 times before placements, and make sure to cover questions on date and time functions as well. JAVA OOPS: can read GFG along with that aryan mittle's oops playlist is also good.

All the best for your placement!

Prepare well, trust your luck, and enjoy the journey -- it teaches you a lot about handling stress and managing time. Yes, the process can feel hectic, full of stress and overwhelming, but once you're selected, all the effort truly feels worth it.

Feel free to reach out: LinkedIn

1. OA Round [ 135 candidates appeared, 37 shortlisted]

The Online Assessment (OA) round was conducted in college via the HackerEarth platform. It consisted of three sections:

1. MCQs,

2. A DSA coding question, and

3. An SQL query. The MCQ section focused mainly on Java fundamentals, especially OOPs concepts. Many questions included code snippets, where we had to guess the output. The questions were quite tricky and concept-based, so a strong grip on the basics really helped. There was one coding question, which was exactly the same as one asked in a previous Barclays placement drive (here's the link). The SQL part was relatively easy--just a basic query where we had to use a WHERE clause along with an AND condition.

#Tip1: Ensure that you are really clear conceptually with OOPs, as different MCQs had differing weightages attached to them. MCQs turned out to be the deciding factor as most students could solve the DSA question and SQL query fully.

#Tip2: Apart from SQL50 on LeetCode, ensure to familiarize yourself with basic String and Date functions and their syntax in SQL.

2. Tech Round 1 [37 candidates appeared, 19 Shortlisted] (Lasted around 45 Minutes)

The round began with the classic "Introduce Yourself" question. Honestly, this might seem basic, but it's one of the most important parts. A well-planned intro sets the tone for the rest of the interview and can help steer the conversation toward your strengths and areas you're comfortable discussing. In my case, I mentioned that I was confident in Java, OOPs, and SQL queries. The interviewer immediately asked me to rate myself in Java out of 10, and from there, he dived straight into OOPs concepts. OOPs and Java-Focused Questions:

Singleton Class: What it is, when and why to use it.

Inheritance, Abstract Classes, Interfaces: Can an interface extend an abstract class? Can an abstract class implement an interface?

Aggregation , Association: Questions around the class relationships in Java.

Method Overloading vs. Overriding: Why doesn't compile-time throw an error for method overriding?

Constructor Overloading.

Use of super keyword.

Try-Catch-Finally block: In which cases does the finally block not execute?

He then moved to Data Structures. First, he asked me to name the ones I was comfortable with -- I mentioned arrays, stacks, linked lists, hashmaps, and heaps.

He gave me 7 numbers and asked me to sort them using each of the data structures I had mentioned.For arrays, stacks, and linked lists, I explained sorting logic for the arrays, stacks, linked list, heaps. In hashmaps, he asked for the use case explanation. I initially used Bubble Sort, but when asked to optimize, I discussed Merge Sort, along with its time complexity.

Then he started reviewing my resume. Since React was mentioned, he asked:

About React folder structure. Specific project-related questions from my resume.

SQL Questions:

First query: Simple one involving LEFT JOIN and WHERE clause.

Follow-up: Slightly extended version with LEFT JOIN, WHERE, and GROUP BY.

Towards the end, he asked if I had any questions. I asked about: "What frameworks like React are used at Barclays, and who exactly uses them in their workflow?"

The interview lasted for about 40 to 45 minutes.

TIPS:

● Master your OOPs concepts -- a majority of the questions came from this area.

● If you know the right answer, be confident. Sometimes interviewers may challenge you on purpose just to test your conviction.

● Know your resume inside out. Don't include anything just to fill space -- if it's on there, be ready to discuss it.

● For coding problems, always start with the brute force approach. Then discuss how you can optimize it.

● Keep talking through your thoughts during the coding part. Don't go silent. The interaction matters as much as the solution.

3. Techno-HR round [19 candidates appeared]

The Techno-HR round began with the usual "Introduce Yourself" question, which helped set a comfortable tone. The interviewer then asked an interesting question: why do you think Java was designed using OOPs? That opened up a deeper conversation about OOP concepts, and he followed up with questions around interfaces, inheritance, and the use of extends and implement keywords.

He then asked me about my internship--what kind of work I did there--and specifically wanted to hear about an incident where I got stuck and how I handled it. It was a good opportunity to share real experience and reflect on problem-solving skills in a work environment. After this, we had a friendly chat about how the software development landscape is evolving. The interviewer casually mentioned how coding nowadays is becoming more about configuring libraries and tools (like in Python) rather than writing every line from scratch. I agreed, and we discussed how that shift is changing the way developers work.

The conversation was very calm and natural. The interviewer was chill and approachable, which made me feel at ease. At one point, he asked me if I preferred being a full-time developer who just codes, or if I'd enjoy a hybrid role like a business analyst--someone who handles tech but also communicates and collaborates with other teams. I appreciated this question because it showed that they were interested in how I see myself professionally, beyond just my tech skills.

After this, he moved to the HR-style situational questions. One of them was quite interesting: he gave me a scenario where I had a deadline the next day, but a teammate was stuck on something. Helping them might mean I'd have to work overnight to finish my own tasks. What would I do? I gave a fairly standard answer--saying that I'd help because it's about the team's success, not just mine. But he challenged me, saying that if I helped, I might lose my own flow and have to restart everything later, which would waste time.

While he was talking, someone served him coffee. He took a sip while reviewing my resume, and I quickly made a connection. I said, "Just like you took a sip of coffee to refresh yourself before continuing, I'd do the same if I were stuck--I'd take a short mental break, help my teammate, and come back even more focused." That spontaneous answer really clicked with him, and I could see he was impressed.

Then came the question: "Why Barclays?" I had already prepared a response that included their core values--RISES--and wove it into a story that reflected my interest in both tech and impact. He seemed satisfied with the answer.

He also asked me if I preferred working in silence or in a collaborative, discussion-heavy environment. After that, there were a few more classic HR questions--strengths and weaknesses, whether I know anything about finance or investment banking, and if I'd be open to learning a completely new tech stack. He specifically asked if I'd be okay moving away from Java and diving fully into Python or something else if the role required it. I assured him I'm open to learning whatever is needed to grow and contribute effectively.

As the interview was coming to an end, he said he was done and asked if I had any questions for him. I said I wasn't aware of his position and would love to know more about his role. We ended up having a nice chat about his responsibilities and how teams work at Barclays. It gave me a deeper insight into the company's structure and culture.

The round lasted for around 40 to 45 minutes, and overall, it felt more like a thoughtful conversation than a strict interview.

I'd say it's really important to be aware of Barclays' RISES values and try to include them naturally in your responses to situation-based questions. Preparing some standard HR questions in advance helps a lot, especially if you can back up your answers with real stories. In my case, I used internship experiences and examples from project collaborations. It's also important to interact with the interviewer--don't just turn it into a Q&A session. Try to make it a discussion. Stay attentive, because small things happening around you can give you the spark for a clever or memorable answer--but make sure you don't get distracted. And lastly, whatever your strengths are, try to reflect them--directly or indirectly--throughout the interview. One more thing that really helped me was paying attention during the PPT (Pre-Placement Talk). Some of the things discussed there--especially around the company's work culture, Barclays' values, and the tech stack they use--came in handy during the HR and project discussion parts. So I'd strongly suggest taking notes during the PPT, because it can give you useful context and even points to connect during the actual interview.

After a long wait, there was a prank where 16 candidates were called and finally we were told that we have been.

Resources:

Aptitude: indiabix DSA striver sheet :LINK Practice questions repeatedly and get familiar with all the common patterns.

SQL : SQL 50 Practice SQL 50 from LeetCode at least 2-3 times before placements, and make sure to cover questions on date and time functions as well. JAVA OOPS: can read GFG along with that aryan mittle's oops playlist is also good.

All the best for your placement!

Prepare well, trust your luck, and enjoy the journey -- it teaches you a lot about handling stress and managing time. Yes, the process can feel hectic, full of stress and overwhelming, but once you're selected, all the effort truly feels worth it.

Feel free to reach out: LinkedIn

1. OA Round [ 135 candidates appeared, 37 shortlisted]

Eligibility criteria required a CGPA of 7+. There was also some kind of shortlisting based on resumes. The OA round comprised of 3 sections:

Section 1: MCQs mainly covering concepts of OOPs, SQL queries, output based questions based on Java/C++. This was randomized, some people got java based output questions, while others got C++. Most of the questions were OOPs/output related, with a couple of SQL questions.

Section 2: DSA question : String Generation OA question. This question had been repeated by Barclays in previous couple of years, so it was advantageous for students who had practiced the PYQ. Furthermore, test cases were weak, so it was possible to pass all test cases with some simple logic, without a very complex algorithm.

Section 3: SQL query, easy level. Was solvable with some where clauses. Some students got an SQL query that involved extracting the month from a date along with basic logic.

#Tip1: Ensure that you are really clear conceptually with OOPs, as different MCQs had differing weightages attached to them. MCQs turned out to be the deciding factor as most students could solve the DSA question and SQL query fully.

#Tip2: Apart from SQL50 on LeetCode, ensure to familiarize yourself with basic String and Date functions and their syntax in SQL.

2. Tech Round [ 35 candidates appeared, 19 Shortlisted]

We weren't told at what time exactly our individual interviews would be, instead every person was being called and sent to their respective panel. This was a long and drawn out process, and intern and grad interviews were ongoing at the same time. The interviews started at 10am after the PPT, and my interview was finally conducted at 3:30pm. It went on for around 30 mins.

The interviewer started off by testing me on my knowledge of Java & OOPs.

Q. What is inheritance? -> (standard explanation with info about what is inherited from the base class.) Q. In the eg below, how can i call x function in class A in the following cases:

● Inside class B

● By creating an object of B Class A{ void x(){ System.out.println("A"); } } Class B extends A{ void x(){ System.err.println("B"); } }

-> Case 1: Using the super keyword. I then clarified what the super keyword is used for - all parent constructors, variables and functions, except for those which are private and static.

Case 2: Here, I first clarified with the interviewer what the reference type of the object was. This allowed him to further interrogate me about reference type, and what would happen in both cases, where reference type was of A and B. He also asked me if reference type A was even allowed. This in turn allowed me to further elaborate on the difference between references and objects and what each of them are used for. Finally, I answered that we can either make another function in B that calls on the original function in A by using super keyword, or we can make the function in A and B static, and then define the reference type to be A. Since static functions are not inherited, this would call the class in A. This also allowed me to state what run-time polymorphism is, and how the static keyword works.

Q. What is garbage collection in Java? -> Basic answer about cleaning up null objects.

Q. What is memory management in Java? -> I expanded upon what each of heap and stack memory stores.

Q. Which version of Java do you use? -> I stated that I use Java versions 8 and above, highlighting how version 8 onwards, Java introduced flexibility in interfaces and expanded upon how default and static were allowed, and what their use cases were.

#Tip1: At first glance, the questions seem really basic and straightforward. However, how you decide to answer the question and how in depth you go with the explanation lets the interviewer know about your critical thinking skills, how you analyze a problem and how much of the topic depth you are aware of.

#Tip2: Interview rounds really are a test of your mental strength. Try not to worry too much if your interview is happening late, my interview was last on my panel and only lasted 30 mins compared to other interviews which went for an hour and above. I had mentally given up hope since it had been 7 hours of just sitting and waiting, and some students had started with their round 2 while I hadn't even given my round 1. Such situations might be inevitable, so try not to focus on areas that are out of your control. But try not to let it affect your mindset in the interview, just focus on giving your best performance.

The interviewer then moved on to 2 easy level DSA questions.

Q. Sum of digits of a number, till you reach a single digit. Eg. 54312 = (5+4+3+1+2) = 15 = (1 + 5) = 6

Q.Given an array of positive and negative numbers, sort the array into alternating positive and negative elements.

Then we moved on to the projects on my resume, and he asked me questions off of the points I had mentioned in bullets - implementation, why I used a certain thing, etc.

He also asked me if I've worked with cloud deployment, to which I replied honestly with no - but I have deployed my application on render, and explained deployment steps and what CORS is.

I wasn't asked anything regarding SQL, but some other panels did - some things purely depend on your panel and your luck.

#Tip3: Ensure that you really know your projects inside out. It's not necessary to be able to reproduce the code, but you must be aware of the logic and be prepared to justify your design choices. You may ask any LLM to generate relevant questions based on your projects to gain a better understanding of scalability and differing implementation methods.

#Tip4: It's always better to say I don't know over giving a wrong answer.

3. Techno HR round[ 19 candidates appeared]

After 2 hours of anxiously wondering if my name would be called or not, I was called in for the next round. The interview started off with him asking me to introduce myself. I introduced my name, branch, 2 main projects and included a line about the reason I want this job - because I like the satisfaction of debugging something and solving a problem. This led to him starting off with a scenario based problem where he introduced a bug in my project. Thankfully, I had considered all possible edge cases when I was designing my project, so I was able to convince him that my project would not encounter the bug he had explained.

#Tip1: Your introduction really sets the tone for the interview, and allows you to navigate through the topics you want the interviewer to probe you on. I hadn't even planned on including the last line, it was just

something that spontaneously came up in my head and I just said it. I would advise against this - as the interviewer may ask you questions you are unprepared for.

#Tip2: Even if your project is relatively simple, think of making it a complete product. This includes handling edge cases, how your system is designed to scale, and a secure user experience. My main project scope was really simple, but there were enough technical details to discuss with the interviewer because of the extensive tech stack and how I designed the system.

He asked me to design the schema of the project. He then basically gave a scenario where referential integrity of a foreign key was being violated, and asked me if it was possible and why or why not. He then gave a scenario based question based on the project, where a junior disagreed with a certain part of the implementation, and how i would handle it. We then had a discussion on polling vs queuing which was relevant to the logic in my project.

#Tip3: An obvious tip but do keep RISES in mind whenever you're answering any situational questions. Also, prepare scenarios where you demonstrated RISES just in case you're asked about it.

He then asked me if I knew what Binary Search was, its time complexity, and showed me a simple function with a double for loop and asked me for its time complexity (O(n2)).

He then asked me if I was comfortable with python since I had an ML project on my resume. I replied that I wasn't too confident with the language and syntax, as I had mainly used it for its libraries. He then asked what language he could ask questions on, to which I replied with Java.

He then gave me the example:

A one = new A("xx", 1) A two = new A("xx", 1)

Q. Can we do one == two? -> We can, but it will be false as it compares two different objects.

Q. How will you check if the values are equal then? -> By overriding the .equals() method.

He also asked me about PostGreSQL vs MySQL, which I was unable to answer.

Lastly, I was asked another situational question where an important presentation is in my laptop, and if I would give my credentials in such a situation to my friend. I answered no as that would be a security risk.

Some people had this round as a purely HR round, others Techno-HR round.

16 candidates were offered the job.

Hello guys,

The entire placement journey was both challenging and tested my perseverance. Before Barclays, I had cleared all the rounds at PhonePe but was unfortunately rejected in the Hiring Manager round. journey.prep:
● Balance DSA & Development: Don't get stuck in the DSA vs. Development debate. Strive to maintain a healthy balance between both. While DSA and CP build problem-solving skills, in interviews your projects and CS fundamentals often take center stage.

● Maintain a CGPA of 8+: Aim for a CGPA of at least 8.0 to ensure eligibility for most on-campus companies. No matter how skilled you are, missing eligibility criteria due to CGPA can be disheartening.

● Revise CS Fundamentals: Core subjects like OOPs, DBMS, OS, CN, and SQL are crucial. These are frequently asked in interviews and can make or break your performance.

● Basic System Design Knowledge: Get familiar with basic system design concepts. I was asked about this in my PhonePe HM round, so don't ignore it.

● Master One Language: Be fluent in at least one programming language--C++ in my case, but Java or Python are equally good. Depth matters more than breadth here.

● Build Strong Projects: Have at least two solid and unique projects in your resume that you can explain thoroughly and confidently. Your ability to discuss them can drive the interview forward.

● Participate in Coding Contests: Regular participation in CP contests sharpens your thinking under pressure and builds speed--both essential in coding rounds.

● Stay Consistent and Positive: Do your best, be consistent, and give every opportunity your 100%. Remember, luck also plays a role on interview day. Don't get disheartened by rejections--keep going. Opportunities will come; just stay calm, hopeful, and focused.

That setback impacted my confidence and performance in the subsequent companies. However, when Barclays visited our campus, I saw it as a fresh opportunity--and I'm happy to share that I cleared all the rounds successfully.

My key message to all future candidates is: have faith in yourself and in your efforts. If you've worked hard, it will pay off sooner or later. Rejections are part of the process, and luck does play a role. What matters most is giving your best every single time, regardless of the outcome.

1. Online Assessment Round [ 135 students appeared for this round and 37 students shortlisted]

The Online Assessment (OA) round was conducted on 26th July 2025 at 11:00 AM in offline mode at the college campus. The test was hosted on the HackerEarth platform. It consisted of a total of 15 questions, and the duration was 90 minutes.

The 15 questions were divided into the following three sections:

Section 1: MCQs (13 Questions) This section included multiple-choice questions from topics such as OOPs (Java), DBMS (SQL), code

snippet output-based questions, Operating Systems (OS), and Computer Networks (CCN). The MCQs were largely focused on Java OOPs concepts and were conceptual and slightly tricky. It is important to be well-prepared in core CS fundamentals. In my opinion, the MCQ section was the key shortlisting factor, as most students were able to solve the DSA and SQL questions.

Section 2: SQL Question (1 Question) This was a basic SQL query-based question involving date and time functions. The task was to find the names of employees who were working only in the month of October. I solved this using the WHERE clause along with the LIKE operator. Although this question was easy, I have encountered much more difficult SQL questions in assessments for other companies such as MSCI. Therefore, it is important to be well-prepared. I highly recommend practicing the SQL 50 questions sheet available on LeetCode, which I had completed prior to this test.

Section 3: DSA Coding Question (1 Question) Interestingly, this was the exact same question that was asked in the previous year's Barclays placement and summer internship OA. Since I was already aware of it, I was well-prepared.

Question link:

https://leetcode.com/problems/lexicographically-smallest-generated-string/description/

Solution Link:

https://leetcode.com/problems/lexicographically-smallest-generated-string/solutions/7042670/simple-greedy -constructive-approach-c-by-s03n

My Approach: I started with the DSA question and completed it first. Then, I moved on to the SQL question. Both were completed in about 15 to 20 minutes. After that, I carefully attempted the MCQ section, as I knew it would be critical for shortlisting.

Preparation Tips:

#Tip 1: Start preparing for core CS fundamentals and OOPs concepts 2 to 3 months in advance. Even though I code in C++, I prepared OOPs in Java specifically for such assessments.

#Tip 2: Practice the SQL 50 sheet on LeetCode thoroughly. Also, review window functions, as they are commonly asked in interviews.

#Tip 3: Begin DSA preparation at least 6 months before placements. I am more inclined toward DSA and competitive programming, so I maintained a daily streak on LeetCode and participated in contests. It's not mandatory to do competitive programming on platforms like Codeforces, but it definitely helps. You can refer to Striver's SDE Sheet for structured practice. I personally followed Love Babbar's DSA Playlist in C++ during my preparation.

2. Technical Round [ 37 Students Appeared and 21 Students Shortlisted ]

I cleared the OA round, and the interview process was scheduled on 29th July 2025. We were asked to report by 8:30 in the morning. However, since I stay in Kalyan, more precisely in Shahad, and it takes around 1.5 to 2 hours to reach college, unfortunately, I missed my train and reached college a little late. The Barclays Pre-Placement Talk (PPT) had already started, but in a hurry, I submitted one copy of my resume to the TPC and rushed to attend the PPT. Please make sure to come early and be on time. During the PPT, they discussed Barclays' RISES principles. While attending, make sure to note important points like their values, culture, company's Tech Stack, RISES principles, etc.

The first technical interview round began shortly after. I was called to panel number 4. I went there, knocked on the door, and asked for permission to enter. I greeted the interviewer, Mr. Rahul Sir, who was himself an alumnus of SPIT.

He started by asking how my day was and where I stayed. I shared that I commute daily via local trains and the metro, and how I manage my time effectively--solving problems, studying, and listening to music while traveling.

The discussion then moved toward my project section. I have a total of three projects listed on my resume, all of which are Full Stack MERN projects. He began with my third project, Zerodha. He asked me to explain the project. Then he asked how I take user info--does it include personal information like bank details? I answered yes, we take such details and perform encryption and hashing to secure them.

He then asked how the data gets stored in the database and which database I used. I explained that I used MongoDB, a NoSQL database, and also justified why I chose MongoDB.

Next, he moved on to my second project, Job Portal, which is a job application platform. He asked how job seekers' data and their experiences are stored in the database, how I collect the data, and how it gets reflected on the UI. When the recruiter clicks on the user details, how does the page render the information? What are the schemas for the candidates and recruiters?

I explained all of this on pen and paper. I also demonstrated how I implemented the .map() function in JavaScript and React to render user info dynamically. I described how I implemented dynamic search filters in the project.

After this, he came to my first project, StudyNotion, an EdTech platform. He asked why I created this project--what was the inspiration? I told him about my mentoring and teaching experience at Wegyan Institute, and how I wanted to build a platform where students could watch lectures if they missed offline classes. I also discussed features like assignments, DPPs, and other functionalities I implemented.

Later, he asked me some basic Java concepts. Although I am primarily a C++ programmer, I had also learned Java. So if you know Java, it will definitely help in the interview.

Make sure you know your resume thoroughly because they can ask anything and everything from it.

At the end of the interview, he said he was done with his questions and asked if I had any questions for him.

It's always a good idea to ask company-relevant questions to show your interest. I asked:

● What roles and responsibilities would I have if selected, and how can I improve in those areas?

● Can you share your role in the company and the department you work in?

● What is the most fun thing you love about working at Barclays?

He answered all these questions very well, and the interview finally concluded.

This round lasted for around 40 to 45 minutes.

3. Techno + HR Round [ 21 Students Appeared for this round ]

After the first round, I was a little bit confident that I had given my best in the interview and might be called for Round 2. So, I started preparing for standard HR questions using ChatGPT and also revised some questions I had written down in my notes. Meanwhile, I was called in for the second round.

The second round began, and the interviewer asked me how my first interview was. I replied that it went well and was taken by Mr. Rahul Sir, who is our alumnus, and that he shared how he got into Barclays, etc.

For some candidates, this round was a pure HR round, but for me, it was a mix--I was asked both technical and HR-based questions. The interviewer went through my resume and asked about JWT authentication, which I had mentioned in my project. He asked, "What exactly is JWT?" I explained how it contains three sections: payload, header, and signature. He then asked follow-up questions like what does "expiry" mean in JWT, is it set by default or manually, what is the main purpose of JWT, and whether it is stored on the client side or server side. I answered all these questions properly, and we had a discussion around cookies as well.

Later on, he asked how I learned multiple programming languages.

Then he asked, "Have you ever misunderstood anything? If yes, what action did you take, and what was the conclusion?" This was a good question, so I asked him if I could take a minute to think. He said yes. Then I told him about one incident from a past semester: I had misunderstood the exam schedule. I thought the next day was the OS paper, but it was actually the DAA paper. I had prepared for OS, but just 2 hours before the exam, I got to know it was DAA. However, since DAA was my favorite subject and I had solved thousands of problems related to Data Structures and Algorithms, I quickly revised my notes and gave the exam. I ended up scoring well. He seemed impressed with this response.

After that, he asked what contributions I had made in my group projects and about my hackathon experience. I answered everything in detail.

Then he asked, "Have you done anything in your life whose fruits are still being enjoyed by someone?" Since I had already mentioned that I mentored and taught more than 100+ students in offline batches, I told him that some of my students cracked the NEET examination with good marks. He then asked how I got into teaching just after giving my JEE Advanced exam, and also asked what my percentile was.

After all these questions, he said, "Good to know all these things from you," and then told me he was done with his questions. He asked if I had any questions for him.

I asked, "While working at Barclays, if I want to learn new technologies and frameworks, how can I do that and what is the process?"

This round lasted around 30 to 45 minutes.

Finally, 16 students were selected--and I was one of them.

customSections.title: Advice & Tips for Juniors
customSections.content:
● Balance DSA & Development: Don't get stuck in the DSA vs. Development debate. Strive to maintain a healthy balance between both. While DSA and CP build problem-solving skills, in interviews your projects and CS fundamentals often take center stage.

● Maintain a CGPA of 8+: Aim for a CGPA of at least 8.0 to ensure eligibility for most on-campus companies. No matter how skilled you are, missing eligibility criteria due to CGPA can be disheartening.

● Revise CS Fundamentals: Core subjects like OOPs, DBMS, OS, CN, and SQL are crucial. These are frequently asked in interviews and can make or break your performance.

● Basic System Design Knowledge: Get familiar with basic system design concepts. I was asked about this in my PhonePe HM round, so don't ignore it.

● Master One Language: Be fluent in at least one programming language--C++ in my case, but Java or Python are equally good. Depth matters more than breadth here.

● Build Strong Projects: Have at least two solid and unique projects in your resume that you can explain thoroughly and confidently. Your ability to discuss them can drive the interview forward.

● Participate in Coding Contests: Regular participation in CP contests sharpens your thinking under pressure and builds speed--both essential in coding rounds.

● Stay Consistent and Positive: Do your best, be consistent, and give every opportunity your 100%. Remember, luck also plays a role on interview day. Don't get disheartened by rejections--keep going. Opportunities will come; just stay calm, hopeful, and focused.
