1. While explaining my projects, I made a conscious effort to relate them to real-world scenarios--highlighting the actual problems people face and how my project aimed to solve them. This approach helped the interviewer understand the practical impact and relevance of my work.

2. During the explanation of various technical concepts, I used numerous examples to illustrate each point, which helped convey my in-depth understanding clearly. I didn't just explain what I used, but also why I used it, why I chose it over alternatives, and how it benefited the project overall. This demonstrated not only my technical depth, but also my thought process and problem-solving mindset during the development phase. It also reflected my genuine passion for building meaningful projects and thinking through every detail.

3. One of the most important things to remember during interviews is not to get intimidated by the interviewer. They're not there to scare you -- they're there to evaluate you, yes, but also to help you bring out your best. Keeping your mind calm is crucial. When you're relaxed, new ideas, better explanations, and clearer thought processes naturally flow. That's when you're able to think on your feet, connect concepts, and frame your answers effectively.

I would highly recommend adopting a similar approach when discussing your projects--if your interviewer is open to hearing your thought process. In my case, the interviewer was specifically interested in understanding the reasoning behind my decisions.

That said, it's equally important to read the interviewer's expectations. If they prefer direct, to-the-point answers, then align your responses accordingly. Adapting your communication style based on the interviewer's cues can significantly enhance the impact of your responses.

This round lasted approximately 30-40 minutes for me and focused primarily on HR-based questions. While my round didn't involve any technical questions, a few other candidates were asked some basic-level technical queries, so it's best to stay prepared for both.

● The group sizes I've worked with,

● How I handle conflicts or disagreements in a team,

● What I would do in situations requiring leadership, adaptability, or compromise.

The online assessment consisted of a total of 15 questions and had a duration of 1 hour and 30 minutes. Among these, one was a DSA problem of medium to hard difficulty, and another was a relatively easy SQL question. The remaining 13 questions focused on Object-Oriented Programming (OOPs) and SQL concepts. It's important to pay close attention to the weightage of the MCQ questions, as each question carries a different number of points. Make sure to solve the higher-weightage questions carefully, as they can often be the deciding factor in your overall score and selection.

The selection criteria to appear for the test required a minimum CGPA of 7. However, to maximize your chances of being eligible for most companies' online assessments, it is highly recommended to maintain a CGPA of at least 8 or above.

The DSA problem asked in the test has been REPEATED OVER THE PAST 2-3 YEARS!!. It is STRONGLY ADVISED to go through the following question beforehand: 🔗 LeetCode Discuss: String Generation OA Question ➡The first comment contains the complete solution (Peng Cao code) -- please go through it thoroughly.

For the SQL code please go through the Datetime functions in SQL: MySQL Date and Time Functions - GeeksforGeeks

For additional past-year questions, you can also refer to the JobOverflow website.

The OOPs questions, generally asked in either C++ or Java, require a strong foundational understanding of core OOP concepts. I've shared a link below that comprehensively covers all important OOP topics.

As for the SQL MCQ's, although the questions were on the easier side, they still tested your understanding of key concepts like GROUP BY and JOINS. A solid grasp of these basics will be sufficient to tackle them confidently.

I was able to solve all 10 out of 10 test cases in the DSA question, which significantly boosted my chances of selection, as the problem carried a weightage of 50 points. The SQL query question was worth 10 points, but it's important to note that the MCQ section also carried substantial weightage and should not be taken lightly.

In fact, several candidates who solved only 8 out of 10 DSA test cases but performed well in the MCQs were still shortlisted. This clearly shows that a balanced performance across both the coding and aptitude sections is key to maximizing your chances of getting selected.

So, while solving the DSA problem is crucial, make sure to focus equally on the MCQs.

● What problem it solved

● The end-to-end flow of the project

● How I would adapt the project to different real-world scenarios

● How the data was stored in the database

● Whether it was hashed, and if so,

● Which hashing algorithm was used

I believe this question was asked because I had mentioned a cybersecurity internship on my resume.

● Its three sections

● Some basic code snippets to write like jwt.sign() and jwt.verify()

● Where exactly JWT authentication took place in my project flow

Again, these questions were asked because JWT was explicitly mentioned in my resume, reinforcing the fact that the interviewer was closely referring to it.

I was also asked to write several SQL queries, particularly involving:

● GROUP BY,

● HAVING,

● OFFSET, and

● LIMIT clauses

He even gave me a SQL query and asked me to predict its output, testing both my understanding and practical knowledge.

That said, it's equally important to read the interviewer's expectations. If they prefer direct, to-the-point answers, then align your responses accordingly. Adapting your communication style based on the interviewer's cues can significantly enhance the impact of your responses.

The core of my round revolved around team collaboration scenarios. The interviewer asked about:

● The group sizes I've worked with,

● How I handle conflicts or disagreements in a team,

● What I would do in situations requiring leadership, adaptability, or compromise.

It became clear that the objective of this round was not only to assess how well I align with the company's core values, particularly the RISES principles, but also to understand how I approach team collaboration--a critical skill in the corporate environment where working effectively with diverse teams is essential.

OA: (75 minutes) (~240 Candidates appeared)

journey.prep:
In General -

1. Placement is 30% luck, 70% smart work. Focus on what you can control--be well-prepared when the opportunity comes.

2. Give contests and mock interviews even if you feel underprepared. They help you assess your level and improve.

3. Don't fear early failures; better to fail in practice than in interviews.

4. Focus on one company at a time, give your best, and if it doesn't work out--learn, move on, and stay resilient.

These may sound simple, but I struggled to follow them myself at first--don't repeat that mistake.

For MSCI -

1. Research the company thoroughly--memorize key facts & values but also understand their meaning and relevance to your profile.

2. Soft skills are crucial. Even if my answers weren't perfect, I spoke with confidence, used technical terms, and explained with clear, relatable examples.

3. For almost a month, I reviewed past interview experiences and practiced answering questions out loud, refining them for clarity and impact

OA: (75 minutes) (~240 Candidates appeared)

This was an on-campus online assessment conducted on HackerRank, consisting of three questions: two DSA-based and one SQL. The questions were randomly selected from a pool, with most being LeetCode easy to medium level.

● DSA Q1: Slowest Key - LeetCode

Given a list of keypress logs as pairs (key, time), where key is an integer from 1 to 26 representing lowercase letters (1 → 'a', 2 → 'b', ..., 26 → 'z') and time is the cumulative time (in seconds) when the key was released, determine which key took the longest to press. The time taken for the first key is time[0], and for each subsequent key is time[i] - time[i-1]. Return the character that took the maximum time. It is guaranteed that this key is unique.

It's an easy single loop question, give it a try !

● DSA Q2: Distance Between "programmer" Substrings

Given a string containing exactly two non-overlapping occurrences of the word "programmer", possibly separated by arbitrary characters (e.g., "programxxxmerxxxxprogramxxmer"), determine the number of characters strictly between the first full "programmer" from the left and the last full "programmer" from the right.

Characters between may include any letters or symbols.

Example shown below -

I did using unordered_map and two pointers, give it a try !

● SQL Q3: Time and Amount Aggregation with Joins The question involved 2-3 tables and tested a strong understanding of JOINs, GROUP BY, and aggregations. It required summing durations in seconds and converting them to HH:MM:SS format using functions like SEC_TO_TIME, as well as converting cumulative amounts into billions. I chose to skip this question as I wasn't aware of the SEC_TO_TIME function at the time. However, such functions can often be discovered if you forget using IntelliSense by exploring related keywords.

My strategy was to solve DSA quickly, assess the SQL difficulty, and submit if it seemed too complex -- since submission time mattered and very few were able to solve SQL. This approach only works if you're well-prepared; don't skip doable questions.

Offline Technical Round 1: (30 minutes) (~40 Candidates appeared)

The round started with my introduction. I had prepared it well, covering languages I know, brief overviews of my three projects, extracurriculars, and leadership experience.

Tip: A strong intro is important--it sets the tone and flow of the interview. Practice it in front of someone beforehand, to make it smooth and confident.

She then asked about my DDPM ( Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models ) project. Since she wasn't very familiar with it, I explained it clearly using simple terms and a diagram, which she appreciated. Next, we discussed my first project which was an AI-assisted learning platform. I explained the idea, how I identified the problem, and the tech stack I used.

After that, she gave me two SQL questions.

Q.1 Find user IDs of users who have ordered products from more than one category.

I then explained that by grouping the results by user_id, I could use a HAVING clause with a COUNT(DISTINCT category) to filter for users who have ordered from more than one category. After I wrote the complete SQL query based on this approach, the interviewer was satisfied

Q.2 For each category, find the product that was sold the most (by total quantity ordered).

I shared my intuition to first group the orders by product to get the total quantity sold. Then, to use a window function to rank the products within each category based on their total sales. Finally, filter to get the top-ranked product per category. She was satisfied with the approach, and didn't expect to write the entire query.

After the SQL round, she asked two easy DSA questions:

Q1. First Non-Repeating Character - Leetcode I first explained the brute-force approach using two loops, then optimized it using a frequency vector to count frequencies and a second pass to find the first non-repeating character.

Q2. Climbing Stairs - Leetcode I related it to the Fibonacci series. Explained the recursive and DP approaches, but implemented the space-optimized (Thanks to striver) solution using two variables.

She also asked a few theory questions like encapsulation in OOP and indexing in databases, which I answered confidently with examples. At the end, I asked a prepared question related to the Barra product and RiskMetrics, she was working on it so she explained it well, and the interview concluded.

Offline Technical Round 2: (45 minutes) (~15 Candidates appeared)

The second round focused on evaluating my ability to think practically as a developer--beyond just coding skills.

We began with a short introduction, followed by a question about my future plans--whether I intended to pursue a master's degree or launch a startup. Since I had been part of the Entrepreneurship Cell at SPIT for two years. I responded honestly, stating that while I admire both academia and entrepreneurship, my goal is to grow in an industry setting.

Given my background in generative AI, he asked : With AI advancing rapidly, what is the role of a developer today? I highlighted that while AI has made remarkable progress, it still has significant limitations. It lacks genuine reasoning and primarily functions as a predictive model trained on past data. More importantly, AI cannot take accountability. Developers remain crucial for testing, debugging, refining logic, and owning the final product.

We then dove deep into my projects. I presented a generative AI-based application, clearly outlining the problem it solved, the tech stack used, and design decisions. A major discussion point was my use of MongoDB instead of a traditional SQL database. I explained that since LLMs can output structured JSON, it was easier and more efficient to store and manage data in MongoDB. The project didn't require complex joins or strict ACID compliance, and MongoDB's horizontal scalability and high performance made it a practical choice.

He also asked about the vector database I had used--Qdrant. I elaborated on why I chose it, highlighting its ability to perform advanced filtering during semantic search. I gave concrete examples from my project to justify the choice, and the conversation naturally progressed into the architecture, challenges faced, and how I overcame them.

Throughout the discussion, the focus remained on why I made certain technical decisions. We also covered theoretical questions--like the difference between a database and a data warehouse, and what an alternate key is. Rather than just naming types of keys, I walked him through the concept of alternate keys within a hierarchy of super, primary, candidate, and foreign keys.

Toward the end, he asked me about time complexity. Instead of giving definition, I explained it through real-world examples--demonstrating how analyzing time complexity helps identify performance bottlenecks across different hardware and programming languages.

One of the final questions was : Would you choose expensive infrastructure to reduce server load time, or stick to a budget and accept slower performance? I treated it as a real-life scenario. I said that in a perfect world with unlimited resources, we'd all want the best infrastructure--but in reality, we have to balance performance and cost. For instance, if I'm building an app like YouTube, users won't wait 20 seconds for a video to load. In such cases, performance becomes a priority. So I'd first identify the bottlenecks and then decide where to optimize for speed and where to save on budget--always keeping both business constraints and user experience in mind. He seemed satisfied with this practical outlook.

As the interview wrapped up, he asked if I had any questions. I asked about their adoption of generative AI. We had an engaging discussion on how they're exploring AI integration--whether through external APIs or on-premise LLMs. I also raised concerns around data security when relying on third-party APIs, especially for data-sensitive businesses. He acknowledged that the domain is still evolving, and while they're already using AI tools for tasks like code assistance, larger implementation plans are in the works.

Tip: In college or hackathon projects, we often neglect the feasibility and scalability aspects. It's still important to have a basic theoretical understanding of these, even if you don't have practical experience

Online HR Round : (15 minutes) (~8 Candidates appeared)

This was a relaxed and conversational round, primarily focused on understanding my personality and cultural fit. The interviewer began by asking about my family background and hobbies. I had prepared a brief HR-friendly introduction that covered my academic journey, family background, and my passion for playing musical instruments. He then asked what I knew about MSCI, to which I gave a detailed response--covering the company's role in global finance, its significance in investment decision-making, and how MSCI indices provide a global snapshot to help investors make informed choices. I also touched on the technical side of index construction. He expressed curiosity about my specialization in Data Science, and asked whether I'd be open to working in a different domain or department. I explained how my foundation in data science and my keen interest in generative AI have equipped me with strong analytical and adaptable skills. I assured him that I'm quick to learn and flexible enough to contribute effectively, regardless of

the specific domain. Towards the end, I asked a couple of questions--particularly about the scope of learning before the internship begins, since we had a semester gap, and inquired about growth opportunities within the company.

Overall, it was a smooth and engaging conversation that allowed me to present both my technical background and willingness to learn and grow.

Tip: Don't overlook the HR round. Be well-prepared with common HR questions and think through different scenarios in advance. You won't have much time to recollect answers during the conversation, as this round often tests your spontaneity and presence of mind

At the end, 5 students were selected.

journey.thirdYear:
OA on 11th July, Interviews on 15th July 2025

Placement Process:

1. OA: (75 minutes) (~240 Candidates appeared)

This was an online assessment consisting of three questions: 2 DSA based and 1 SQL, on Hackerrank. The DSA questions were randomly selected from a pool of questions.
journey.prep:
● Even if you are not super good at DSA, do practice the standard problems from Striver's SDE sheet, or keep doing LeetCode daily, so that you are able to solve at least medium LeetCode questions comfortably. I also kept giving contests on codeforces and kept a timer on LeetCode problems for timed prep. Hard questions are generally rare beyond the very top companies like PhonePe.

● Also, practicing and completing the LeetCode SQL 50 a week before or even during the placement would give decent experience of SQL.

● For System Design, I referred multiple sources. Piyush Garg (https://www.youtube.com/@piyushgargdev) and Arpit Bhayani (https://www.youtube.com/@AsliEngineering) on Youtube have some top quality content. But do explore other videos as well, some creators may explain niche topics better.

● For core subjects too, I did not have a fixed playlist or resource. I explored different videos or GFG articles for different concepts, even clarified some questions in depth through GPT/Gemini as well. Some good resources include GateSmashers (https://www.youtube.com/@GateSmashers), and again Arpit Bhayani. Make sure you know what things are asked commonly, focus on understanding maximum concepts, through any videos or articles or questioning GPT on the same.

● Prepare your introduction and some general HR questions or description about your projects/internships/committee roles if asked in detail and have it down in written word for word. You can use AI tools to enhance this. You may not be able to speak it exactly how you've written, but it helps you maintain a proper flow each time you encounter a particular question which you've prepared and increases confidence while answering. Confidence and clarity was an important factor they checked other than technical knowledge as I mentioned above.

● Read all the interview experiences of that particular company before interviews, not just 1 or 2. Questions asked are mostly on similar lines, or you get an idea that what variety of questions are asked. For example, LC easy to medium level DSA questions were asked to people in other panels,. Few I could remember are Next Permutation (DP based) and Left Hand View of a Tree, as well as Buy and sell stock questions on LeetCode.

● I would agree that luck did play some part as I did not get asked any DSA question, which made the process relatively easier for me. But at the same time, I did mention one-liners about all my projects in my general intro in all rounds, which perhaps helped steer all interviews towards the resume/dev side. You can also prepare intros pointing towards your strengths, may it be DSA, dev or whatever,

● .During these interviews, there were also EDS OAs going on to which I hadn't applied, but some of my friends did, and some of them had to reschedule his interview

slot to a later timing during the OA, which (maybe not by itself) played a role in them not getting selected despite a good first-round interview. Do not juggle yourselves between two companies, stay focused for one and prepare for it.

● Do not be demotivated if you're rejected. Even I was rejected right at the HR round during my interviews at WorkIndia as only 2 people were hired. I was sad for a day, but then moved on soon, and began my further preps. Companies come till October, that offer decent packages, some even more than this, move on as soon, and start the grind forward, If you consider yourself to be at least average level throughout college, You will get placed sooner or later, with a decent package. Hence do not give up. ALL THE BEST for your placements!

● Feel Free to connect on LinkedIn if you need any help https://www.linkedin.com/in/aroosh-joshi-59601524b/

1. OA: (75 minutes) (~240 Candidates appeared)

This was an online assessment consisting of three questions: 2 DSA based and 1 SQL, on Hackerrank. The DSA questions were randomly selected from a pool of questions.

● DSAQ1: (https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/dsa/python-program-to-find-uncommon-words-from- two-strings/ ) The first question was to find uncommon words from two strings, given the full sentence string separately. This was an easy question using split() and a two-pointer approach.

● DSA Q2: (https://leetcode.com/problems/maximum-or/description/) The second question involved maximizing the OR value (OR of all elements) in an array, given you can multiply any element by 2, at most k number of times. I did manage to pass all test cases for this one, although not with an optimal solution.

● SQL Q3: This was a SQL question involving two tables related to voter information.

The goal was to return a summary of each state, showing the names of voters who voted in that state along

with the number of times each voter voted.

Given Tables:

Voters: Votes:

voter_id | name voter_id | state

---------|-------- ---------|-------

1 | Tanvi 1 | California

2 | Gaurang 2 | California

3 | Drishya 2 | California

4 | Rahul 1 | California

4 | Texas

Expected Output :

state | voters_summary

--------------|---------------------------

California | Tanvi x 2, Gaurang x 2

Texas | Rahul x 1

I wasnt able to solve this question, as it involved use of CTEs and Group_Concat, etc..

Solving 2 DSA questions fully was enough to qualify for the next round, which I did. Around 41 students were shortlisted for Tech Round 1.

2. Offline Technical Round 1: (30-45 minutes)

I was firstly asked to introduce myself. Then, the interviewer delved into my resume, particularly focusing on a GenAI project, which I described to him in detail. He further questioned me about how vector databases work in LangChain, and what cosine similarity is. I was well aware of these topics and answered them appropriately.

He also asked me about static and dynamic components in React. Since I'm not primarily a frontend person, I mentioned the single basic React project I made in my first year, how I used components as reusable entities, and what I could make out by the name dynamic components, while clearly mentioning that it had been a while for me working with React and frontend in general.

He also asked me what I knew about MSCI - I had researched the website beforehand and gave the appropriate answer.

Then, I was asked a simple question of reversing a string, using OOP. I just created a class with a string as an attribute, and a method for string reversal. And the interviewer was satisfied with that.

A SQL query was presented, based on INNER, LEFT, and RIGHT JOIN where tables contained equal entries (These were two different tables with only 'id' as the attribute). This was more of a trick question as all these joins would result in the same table with 6 rows where a.id = 1 and b.id = 1. I too found it tricky first and described the theory about these joins, stating that, according to my knowledge, all the tables should be the same, as mentioned above. To which the interviewer replied that yes, this is the right answer.

Another SQL problem involved: Given a table Products (pid , ..) and Orders (pid, oid), find the products that are unsold. The key here was to consider that orders are only logged for products that are sold (as there is no 'status' column). This could then be solved by simply LEFT JOINING Products and Orders and selecting where oid = NULL.

A puzzle was given: 6 balls of different weights and a weighing machine. Find the heaviest ball while using the weighing machine the minimum number of times. Here I was unable to arrive at a number less than 6 with various combinations. So he gave me a hint that we can also put multiple balls on the scale at once. Then I realized we can split the balls into groups of 3 and pick the heavier group and repeat a similar process with the heavy group.

Then he opened for questions. First, I asked him about himself. Then I asked a question about MSCI particularly, that given they manage such huge amounts of indexes, there must be a large amount of data to be processed, and that too in real time, so how is all this managed. His answers to both the questions were very detailed and he seemed happy.

A proper shortlist wasn't announced in this round, as after the first round itself, people who were selected were called for the second, while those who were rejected were informed so. Around 20-22 students may have been selected in total.

3. Offline Technical Round 2: (45-60 minutes)

"How does your typical day go?" - This was a question that I wasn't expecting or prepared for as the first question. I answered covering my college routine, assignments, LeetCode practice, and working on projects/hacks.

"What have you done in your college life overall?" - I answered this honestly, explaining that I explored React in my first year but realized it wasn't my cup of tea, then started with Django and also learning ML since last one year, also mentioning my elective "build LLM from scratch" which I had taken last sem as a PE.

"What are your hobbies?" - I play chess as a hobby, my rating is 1000 rapid on chess.com and around 700 in blitz and bullet. Apart from that I also play keyboard as a hobby, again not professionally, but as a hobby.

"Write down an algorithm to teach someone new to the keyboard." - The question was ambiguous, so I asked for clarification. To which he said, "just describe how you would teach keyboard to a beginner." So I explained the entire process from basic keys, chords, and once they reach a certain level (which can be determined by tests), teaching them basic songs, and advanced songs once they advance tests.

"Design an ER diagram based on whatever I explained" - .I started with a users table, a courses table, a courseTaken table (with FK to user_id and course_id) which can be joined, then a table for lessons (FK to course_id), and tests (FK to lessons). The key here is not to describe each and every table or attribute, but to describe the core tables and keep them normalized, avoiding any redundant tables, etc. Since I have designed SQL schemas for a lot of my Django projects, I was fairly confident in designing and explaining this and also ready to explain further.

Then I was asked about my projects which I started to describe.The interviewer interrupted and asked about a particular project, which was the Alumni-Connect App I made during the SIH finals. I described all the features correctly. He then asked how the alumni would benefit from this, to which I replied we also had a job portal where alumni can list referrals they have, which would then also benefit them. Also, our college has a business incubation system where student-startups can be incubated and they can also hire students from the college through this portal. Then he asked about the role of AI in this project as my resume and intro pointed towards that. I said that in this project there was a very small role of AI, in the FAISS based recommendation system to recommend alumni/student profiles based on a user's own profile/resume. I explained the working in detail.

Then he asked about my profile, being focused towards AI and Python, what I would do If I knew there was remotely no use of AI and Python in my role. I answered that, given enough time, I would learn whatever technology is offered, while also making suggestions from my side that maybe AI can make this particular part of the application better, and maybe we can integrate an AI part externally through APIs, while not moving away from the main tech stack of the applications, may it not be Python.

Puzzle: "Split or Steal" - Two people play a game, each time: if they both split, they get equal reward; if one splits and one steals, the stealer gets all of the reward; if both steal, no one gets the reward. This is repeated for n turns (n=20,100). What strategy would you use to maximize your reward? This is more to check the thought process rather than a right answer. I too started with the simpler strategy to always steal, so we at least win the game, even with minimal reward, but then the interviewer told me, "why do you think the other will also always steal?" To which I gave the better solution: to start by splitting, and if the other person steals repeatedly, we too start to steal a couple of times, to indicate that "We're not giving steals for free" and the other person would also not earn anything if they kept stealing.

He then asked me about GROUP BY and HAVING in SQL. I did answer that it is used to filter after the use of GROUP BY ,within the groups, but I think I could have maintained more clarity in that answer. He then asked me the difference between data warehouses and

relational databases. I didn't have much idea of warehouses other than the fact that they're used to store large amounts of structured data, while relational databases are used in order to describe relations and whenever there are joins. He did grill me that joins can also be done in warehouses, to which I agreed that I didn't have much idea about warehouses. I told that relational databases are particularly useful to show relations like foreign keys, example: posts, comments, etc.

Then he opened for questions, and I asked him about himself (because MSCI interviewers generally don't introduce themselves at the start and the HR may ask who you interviewed with to check you). He was an SPIT alum himself, and worked at MSCI on the data engineering side. Then I asked about what he expected from freshers at MSCI to which he replied smilingly that "I don't expect much from freshers except basic logical and problem-solving skills and decent projects, and once they join in they can be groomed according to the role if the basic requirements are considered."

Around 10 students were selected for this round.

4. Offline HR Round: (30 minutes)

The HR Round was very chill and I was asked very basic questions:

"Introduce yourself professionally," based on my projects and as a person, and where I live. My branch is Data Science, but my projects were ML-based, so I was asked about the difference between ML and Data Science and what I was actually interested in, to which I replied that ML and Data Science are dependent upon each other, and that I'm trying to explore the entire pipeline, and ML is just a part which helps overall.

She asked about my family background. She too asked, "Do you know about MSCI?" and "How do you know about it?" - I told her whatever I researched and that I knew about MSCI since it has been coming to college for placements for the last few years. She asked if I invest or plan to invest - I don't invest currently, as I am less into the finance side, but I plan to invest.

"Are you planning on any further education like masters/MBA?" - If I were to opt, I would choose MS over an MBA because of my interest in tech. But still, I find many courses from top institutions online itself, which makes me question whether doing a masters is worth it. Hence, I want to first work in the industry and while focusing on upskilling myself through such online courses and then take a call on it. She also asked whether I would be able to relocate / which location I would prefer.

She opened for questions. I asked a couple of questions, starting with what was being expected from me, to which the HR replied that the main thing they expect is clarity of thought regarding future goals. (She mentioned that people who are considering masters straightaway may lack focus in the organization and must at least try to stay 3-4 years before taking a call). My previous answers were very well aligned to her expectations. Secondly, I just asked for general feedback (you can also ask this from tech interviewers). To which she

replied that I was moving my chair throughout, which showcases my nervousness, but that she understood that this may happen during an interview and advised not to do it generally.

5 students were selected.

But at the same time, I did mention one-liners about all my projects in my general intro in all rounds, which perhaps helped steer all interviews towards the resume/dev side. You can also prepare intros pointing towards your strengths, may it be DSA, dev or whatever,

● .During these interviews, there were also EDS OAs going on to which I hadn't applied, but some of my friends did, and some of them had to reschedule his interview

slot to a later timing during the OA, which (maybe not by itself) played a role in them not getting selected despite a good first-round interview. Do not juggle yourselves between two companies, stay focused for one and prepare for it.

● Do not be demotivated if you're rejected. Even I was rejected right at the HR round during my interviews at WorkIndia as only 2 people were hired. Companies come till October, that offer decent packages, some even more than this, move on as soon, and start the grind forward, If you consider yourself to be at least average level throughout college, You will get placed sooner or later, with a decent package. journey.howSecured:
1. OA [No CGPA criteria AFAIK so everyone was eligible to sit for the OA]

The OA was a coding test, 75 minutes in duration. There were 2 coding/DSA problems and an SQL problem. The coding problems were both pretty basic and brute force would usually pass for all. I used Python. And I'd recommend using it if you haven't started with any language yet, because I think it's faster to type out :)

○ Problem 1: There's a keypad. Each key takes a certain amount of time to press every time you press it. Input is a list of integer pairs like [[0,2], [1,6], [3,8], [2, 4], …]. Here, [0,2] means 'a' took 2 seconds to be pressed and so on. So all letters (keys) are 0 indexed starting from 'a'. The output should be the letter of the key that had the maximum pressing time. I just created a pair ret = [-inf, -inf], and traversed the input, let's call the current pair cur, and whenever cur[1] > ret[1], set ret = cur. In the end just return the character associated with ret[0].

○ Problem 2: Input is a string. This string's various substrings contain multiple permutations of the word "programmer" as subsequences. The task is to find the number of letters between the first and last such substring. For example:

"rgtscmpxmrreoqwiqwrgmttpmrreoa"

Here, the highlights are the first and last such substrings in the given string and answer is 6. (oqwiqw).

Many ways to solve this.

- Brute Force: Create a frequency map of the string "programmer". Now traverse the input string, and starting from each index, traverse ahead while building a temporary frequency map of this traversal. The first time this temp map becomes equal to our og freq map, store the final index of the current traversal. The last time that happens, store the first index of the final traversal. Then subtract both and add 1 and return.

- That's O(n^2) but coding it up took like 10 minutes. Rather I could have just done the above starting from the first index first, then reverse the input string and do it from the

first index again, and store the final index of both, fix the reversed index, subtract, add 1.

○ Problem 3: Given 2 tables, States, and Votes. The Votes table has the votername, state voted for. Return, for each state, a comma separated concatenated string of name of voter, and number of votes given, in the same cell. Example output:

state votes

Texas John Doe x 2, Jane Doe x 8, …

California Tyler Durden x 6, Jack x 9, …

Simple problem, but you have to remember the aggregate function's name that concatenates strings over the table. Logically it should be called something like agg_str() or str_agg() as it is in Postgres, but it is GROUP_CONCAT() in MySQL. This was given in the previous experiences but I guess I'd missed it. Don't make that mistake. Go through each and every single previous year experience from '24, '25 and this year's. They're the most efficient revision you'll get.

41 people were shortlisted. All solved at least the 2 coding problems. I'm guessing there was a time cut-off of 40-50 minutes max.

2. Technical Interview L1 [ 41 people ]

This round, for me, was just DSA questions with a few introductory questions about my projects and internships. As I entered, the first thing I was asked was the full form of MSCI. I got the last word wrong. He said "It's International! You should at least know this much bro!" and we laughed about it. Then he asked me what problems were there in the OA. I briefed him on shorter versions of the questions and explained how I solved them. He then apologized for jumping directly to questions and we introduced ourselves to each other. He was excited for the process and ended up taking a good 5 minutes introducing himself. I'd recommend developing the skill of ad libbing answers to these questions. Preparing "scripts" for intros, personal questions, even project questions kills your flow and the interview's vibe. It's meant to be a fun conversation. Don't make it boring or dull for the interviewer or yourself. I took my time, introduced myself, my internships and projects in depth for about 5-10 minutes.

He started asking DSA questions. The first one was how to check if there are cycles in an undirected graph. I know. Simple af. I didn't understand at first and misunderstood that it was directed and started explaining a topo sort approach (Kahn). He then said "it could be directed or undirected". And then my brain froze up. I got really confused and just could not think at all anymore. If that happens, drink some water or something to give your brain time to get back to normal. He saw me being confused af and he was like aight let's move on. He then asked how to get the top view of a binary tree (horizontal difference). Then right/left view (bfs). Then a matrix problem, a spin on the "number of ways to get from top left to bottom right cell of a matrix" problem (simple 2d dp). So all the dsa problems were very basic. When you get something wrong, be graceful about it. I was very surprised that I got selected for the next round.

He then asked me a little about my projects, and how I handled authentication in them, and how to do it without using a third party service. I replied "using JWT" and that building a middleware that verifies the JWT header was a viable solution. He inquired a bit about my knowledge of JWT. I told him whatever I knew about it.

He asked me whether I know what flexbox is. I described its usecase, and compared it to css grids which came later but are much cleaner for 2d layouts. I added that flex animates while grid doesn't. But I now think that wasn't completely true. He asked me whether I've ever written pure CSS. I said even while using bootstrap (which I did in an internship), we have to write pure CSS to style low level bootstrap components, so yes I have.

He then asked me why I want to pursue a career in software when I am from the EXTC branch. I just explained to him how I'd found the EXTC syllabus more interesting and why, before I took admission. But actually studying something and building projects based on that knowledge is very different from what its syllabus looks like on a table of contents. I frequently built IOT projects in my first year and worked with various microcontrollers like the ESP and STM32; Over time, I found myself more drawn to the coding side -- not just programming the microcontrollers, but also building client-facing software for those systems. That naturally pulled me deeper into core CS subjects, which I studied alongside my coursework. It wasn't an easy switch but I'm glad I made it, and now I have knowledge on both ends of the technology spectrum.

My interview went like a very interesting conversation you have with a friend. A lot of it was just him talking about his work at MSCI and me asking questions, or me talking about my internships and projects, both of which he found interesting. I'd frozen up on one question and still I was called for the next interview. Some people had answered all of theirs right and still weren't. It's a combination of the panel and your conversation skills. To be safe, get every question right. But if you don't, be graceful about your wrong answers. Make a joke about it. Keep the interview light and always keep a classy, genuine smile up throughout.

People were being called for the next round one by one as their reviews were coming in. I don't know the exact figure but I don't think more than 30 people got through.

3. Technical Interview L2 [ I think around 25-30 people probably got through]

Always walk in with a bright smile and a "how are you". Don't be a drag and just walk in and sit. Shake their hand. Lighten up the environment. Ask them about their day. The first thing I was asked this time was again the full form of MSCI. I said Morgan Stanley Capital International and was promptly shut down. "We don't have a full form". "Always the trick questions", I lamented jokingly and we laughed about it. He asked about my day and who my previous interviewer was. Then he opened his laptop and on it, my resume. (By the way, this round's interviews were taken by the Executive Directors of MSCI.)

He began by asking me to introduce myself. Then he asked me which project I would like to start with. I went with the first real-world project I'd ever built: Techrace. He opened the github repo. I'd drafted a nice ReadMe which he read through while I described it. I told him how I'd been part of the backend team of 2, and that Techrace is a location based treasure hunt, where clues are provided to players and they've to reach the locations, and there are powercards yada yada (I'm sure y'all know what it is). He

asked me what db we used. We used Firebase RTDB for real time streaming, and Firestore for static data. He asked me to describe the schema and the whole architecture. I took my time, about 5 minutes. He asked me why RTDB. I explained that team state, powercard timestamps, and location data are better stored in the RTDB. He asked me why. That data requires real time sync and it's a real time game, it needs lower latency; also rtdb has some offline support so I plugged that in. "So the client side application would read directly from the rtdb for some features?". Yep. "Isn't that unsafe?". It seems like there would be data inconsistencies, but the client was not allowed to write to the db, only read from it; and the reads would only be on non-critical data.

"Suppose I apply the freeze on a team, and at the approximately same time someone else applies the freeze on the same team. What happens?". I covered a piece of paper in the JSON schema of the application, the model of the powercard states, and the controller for powercard usage. I explained that using the async-mutex npm module, we create mutex states of each team stored in a js object in-memory. When the request to freeze team 007 comes from team 069, and it reaches the controller, Mutex.acquire() is called on the state of that team. When the request to freeze 007 then comes from team 420, if the lock is not released yet, the respective error object is thrown for the later request. He asked me to write the full code and I obliged. He asked which other tech on my resume has the mutex functionality. After a bit of thought, and mentioning Java for its semaphore functionality, I realized he was talking about golang.

"Very good. Now, what happens if there is a loading error and I click a powercard twice? How much of my balance will be deducted?". I explained that we couldn't handle concurrent requests in-game because of our lack of knowledge back then. "How would you do it?". I said I could create a similar object of lock states for the requestor. He found that to be smart but asked me to think further for a better solution. I said I could apply high precision rate limiting, or enforce time gaps between requests. "Gaps for erroneous requests can also vary". DB-level transaction control is offered by firebase. He questioned its thoroughness. I conceded I didn't know any more solutions. He revealed assigning UUIDs for each request from each user is the best way. Requests with the same UUID are erroneous.

He asked a few questions about the stack and what exactly my part was in the backend. I said I was doing the C of the MVC, aside from the error handling and frontend interfacing. We moved on to my next project, which was a pure Java based low latency stock exchange engine core, with a spring boot wrapper for the communication layer.

I explained to him the full architecture of the entire system. He asked me to jot down the db schema. I did. He asked me some questions about the schema. I answered them, but while I did I realized he was going deep into the database side of this project which was not the purpose of the project at all. I explained to him the purpose of the project was to replicate the structure and architecture of a real stock market engine core and use an object oriented approach for the prototype while also keeping it as low latency as possible. He then started asking me questions about the business logic once he realized the persistence layer mustn't be as well thought out whereby.

So no persistence? How do you process this very important data? In-memory. Using relevant data structures. So all the DSA knowledge doesn't go to waste. What data structures did you use?

So there will be 2 order books for each company, buy and sell. For price-time priority, each limit price will be stored in a sorted hashmap, specifically a TreeMap. And the orders at each price will be stored in a doubly linked list. Why TreeMap? What's a TreeMap? And he asked about its abstracted implementation. I explained the whole Map, Hashmap, SortedMap, TreeMap hierarchy, and it's built on Red-Black trees.

Why a doubly linked list for orders? Couldn't you use a- Yes I initially used a queue for it, but when I benchmarked the engine, order cancellation was a bottleneck. DLLs have faster removal. Sketch the OOP model I wrote down a summarizing code of how the whole system worked. While answering all of the above questions too, I'd been sketching detailed figures while explaining everything so he is on the same page the whole time.

Then, based on the rough ER diagram I'd drawn prior, he asked me a few questions. To simplify the only sorta challenging one: Tables: User (uId, uname, balance, holdings), Trades (tradeId, sellerId, buyerId, volume, price). Return the number of times I have sold and bought a set of stocks. I first misunderstood it such that I have to return that for every user. So I wrote a subquery that left joins User with Trades on uid = sellerid, and returns uname, count(tradeid) as sells. And I explained that a parent query can return the name, sells and buys. He explained he only wanted it for one user, which I said would just be a join and where clause for both buy and sell and he agreed. He said there's a much easier way to do this and that there's no time now but I should think about it. I said every time I've ever used a subquery, there's turned out to be much easier ways to do that task that made me facepalm. That made him laugh.

He then asked me about my internships, and asked me why I've only done ones in front-end roles. I said I got them based on the level of skills and knowledge I already had at the time, and I was much better at frontend technologies at the time of beginning them. He asked what the biggest obstacles had been for me on the technical and the professional side of my projects or internships, and how I'd overcome them.

He asked me if I had any questions for him. I asked him how long he's been with the company and how his experience has been. He didn't seem very interested in answering questions like these so I switched it up and asked him what type of work could I expect to be assigned if I were in his team. He said he has no idea what type of work is even assigned to immediate interns and we laughed a bit about that. The whole interview went perfectly. I think it could be the longest L2 interview of the day - it lasted for about 1.5 hours.

Around 9 candidates were selected for the HR round. I was probably the 4th. I was called in as soon as I came out of the interview.

3. HR Interview [9 candidates]

I was asked about my day till then, and how the rest of my interviews had been. I'll just list all the questions then a bit about my approach for answering them.

- About yourself and your family. Your hobbies.

- About yourself professionally.

- So many technologies in your project, why not stick to one.

- Have you worked in a team?

- Prefer working in a team or solo.

- Why xyz internship

- Extra curricular activities in college life?

- Our work hours can be off putting to some. Can you handle them?

- Prefer Mumbai or Pune?

- You trade, so will you be ok with the company telling you to stop because of our rules?

- What have been your biggest strengths and weaknesses throughout your professional life.

Be genuine, and explain with thorough examples. Your aim is to convince them of your answer's sincerity, not just tell them your answer.

Again, I can't stress this enough, smile.

5 people were offered the internship in the end.

journey.prep:
1. DSA Preparation Start DSA preparation early on. Try to consistently practice at least 1-2 questions every day. I personally followed Striver's SDE Sheet, which is very well-structured and covers most interview-relevant topics.

https://takeuforward.org/strivers-a2z-dsa-course/strivers-a2z-dsa-course-sheet-2

Always try to solve questions yourself first. If you're stuck, watch the video explanation but make sure to code it yourself afterwards. Keep revising important questions and try to identify and remember common problem patterns across topics.

2. Core Subjects - Java and OOPs I started with the basics of Java. Here's a link I referred to: https://youtu.be/eIrMbAQSU34?si=_Vq7MalRpZaXJsO9

For OOPs concepts, I followed Kunal Kushwaha's playlist, which explains everything in a beginner-friendly manner. Additionally, I read articles on GeeksforGeeks, which helped reinforce key concepts like encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism, and abstraction.

https://youtu.be/BSVKUk58K6U?si=NQVHOYRXLAgVkir6

https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/java/object-oriented-programming-oops-concept-in-java/

3. DBMS (RDBMS) For RDBMS, I watched CodeHelp by Love Babbar's one-shot video. It covers almost all the concepts required for interviews.

https://youtu.be/dl00fOOYLOM?si=IE8ak_4YztXdYTOf

4. SQL I learned the basics from W3Schools and practiced extensively on LeetCode. I completed all 50 questions from the SQL 50 list and also solved 10-15 additional medium/hard-level questions to get more comfortable

https://www.w3schools.com/sql/default.asp

https://youtu.be/OT1RErkfLNQ?si=1Ctjw2Ud6hQRm-X-

https://leetcode.com/studyplan/top-sql-50/

5. Operating Systems & CN For OS and Computer Networks, basic articles from GeeksforGeeks are more than enough. Focus on understanding concepts like process/thread, scheduling, memory management, TCP/IP, and HTTP. I wasn't asked this in interviews but some of my friends were asked about these subjects.

6. System Design in OOPs In some interviews, you're asked to design systems like a Library Management System, Parking Lot, or ATM Machine using OOPs concepts. So, be prepared to design small-scale systems applying classes, objects, inheritance, and design principles. Practice dry-running a few systems beforehand.

7. Final Interview Tips Before every interview, research the company, their culture, products, and latest updates. This not only helps you frame better answers but also helps you ask relevant questions at the end of the interview, which leaves a strong impression. Prepare an introduction which basically summarizes your resume. Know your projects and your resume very thoroughly.

If you have any questions, I'll be more than happy to help. You can reach out to me directly on WhatsApp or Linkedin.

All the best

Interviews:

1. Technical Round 1

2. Technical Round 2

3. HR Round

1. Online Assessment [Around 240 candidates appeared for this round]

There were 2 DSA questions and 1 SQL question in the online assessment and the time duration was 75 mins.

Q1 : Given an array of integers, find the sum of elements of all possible subarrays of the array. For example, if the input array is [1, 2, 3], then the sum of all possible subarrays is 20. The subarrays are: [1], [2], [3], [1, 2], [2, 3], [1, 2, 3] Sum = 1 + 2 + 3 + 3 + 5 + 6 = 20 Here, I followed a brute-force approach by calculating all possible subarrays and maintaining the sum of all the subarrays. I was able to pass 14 out of 15 test cases.

Q2 : Given an array of integers, the task was to reach the end of the array while maximizing the score based on allowed jumps. There were two jump conditions:

1. I could take one step to the immediate right, i.e., i → i+1

2. I could take a jump of length p such that p is a prime number ending with 3 (e.g., 3, 13, 23, etc.).

The goal was to reach the end of the array while collecting the maximum possible score (i.e., sum of visited elements). I followed a dynamic programming (DP) approach and used memoization to avoid recomputation. At each index, I considered both the one-step jump and all valid p jumps. I recursively computed the maximum score possible from that point onward, and memoised the results.

Q3: This was a SQL question involving two tables related to voter information. The goal was to return a summary of each state, showing the names of voters who voted in that state along with the number of times each voter voted. Given Tables: Voters: Votes: voter_id | name voter_id | state ---------|-------- ---------|------- 1 | Tanvi 1 | California 2 | Gaurang 2 | California 3 | Drishya 2 | California 4 | Rahul 1 | California 4 | Texas

Expected Output : state | voters_summary --------------|--------------------------- California | Tanvi x 2, Gaurang x 2 Texas | Rahul x 1

The question was supposed to be solved using GROUP_CONCAT() I couldn't fully solve the question during the interview due to time constraints. Try to solve the DSA questions fully first as they have the most weightage to get selected for interviews.

2. Technical Interview 1 [ 39 candidates were shortlisted for this round. ]

The round lasted for approximately 50 minutes. The interviewer began by introducing himself, and then asked me to give a brief introduction. After that, I was asked two DSA questions.

Q1: Vertical Sum of a Binary Tree : The question was based on binary trees. I was asked to compute the sum of all elements in the tree that lie along the same vertical line, and return an array of sums for each vertical line.

For example, the output was expected to look something like: [4, 2, 12, 3, 7].

I suggested using a hash map to store the sum of nodes at each horizontal distance (HD). I used HD = 0 for the root, HD - 1 for the left child, and HD + 1 for the right child. As we traverse the tree, we keep adding values to the same horizontal distance key in the hash map. I mentioned that since Python dictionaries are unordered, we'd need to sort the keys before generating the final output array and coded up the entire solution on paper. I was asked to perform a dry run and the interviewer was satisfied with my solution and moved on to the next question.

Q2 : The second question was a standard problem on detecting a cycle in a directed graph. I approached the problem using a Depth First Search (DFS) technique. To handle the detection, I used two boolean arrays: one to keep track of all the nodes that had been visited globally, and another to track the nodes in the current DFS recursion path. I explained this logic clearly and proceeded to code the solution during the interview. I was asked to perform a dry run and the interviewer was satisfied with my approach.

After the DSA questions, the interviewer shifted the focus to my projects and began going through my resume. He asked me to briefly explain the projects I had worked on and the technologies I used. Following that, he delved deeper into the topic of authentication, asking both conceptual and implementation-related questions. He wanted to understand how I had implemented authentication in my projects and how the flow works in a typical web application. Specifically, he asked about JWT (JSON Web Tokens) and its structure. The questions included:

Q1 : What is present in the JWT header structure?

Q2 : What is the complete authentication flow, how the token is generated, returned to the client, stored, sent in subsequent requests, and how token expiry (token window) is handled?

Q3 : How can we implement role-based access control? Here I answered that we can use wrappers or decorators to restrict access to api endpoints and maintain security and role based access. Then there were several questions on databases.

The interview concluded with the interviewer asking me if I had any questions for him. I took this opportunity to ask about the advancements in AI and how they are being leveraged in the finance domain, where both high volumes of data and data integrity are critically important. The interviewer answered the question briefly and the interview ended.

3. Technical Interview 2 [ Around 20 candidates were shortlisted for this round. ]

The second interview lasted for about an hour. The interviewer began by introducing himself and then asked me to introduce myself. I gave a brief overview of my background, skills, and projects. He then asked me which topics in DSA I was most comfortable with. I mentioned that I enjoy working with graphs and heaps. Following that, he asked me to explain real-life applications of graphs, which I answered with relevant examples like in maps for determining shortest paths.

He proceeded to ask a DSA question, which was a variation of Dijkstra's algorithm. I was asked to code the solution on paper. I wrote the code and explained the entire logic. During the explanation, he asked several detailed questions about each part of my code--why I used heaps, how I handled initialization, and the overall structure of the solution.

He then asked me to think through potential edge cases and confirm whether my code handled them. After that, he asked me to do a dry run of the code. I walked him through the step-by-step execution, and he was satisfied with my explanation and approach. After the DSA question, the interviewer briefly moved on to my resume. He asked about my participation in hackathons and what I had implemented in one of them. He then asked about the projects listed in my resume, including their purpose and technical implementation.

Since I had mentioned LangChain in my resume, he asked several questions related to it. These included: what is LangChain, why is it used, what is LangGraph, why not build directly without LangChain, and what advantages it offers. I answered these questions based on my project experience. Next, he asked me to explain another project I had worked on, including the technologies I used. He then shifted focus to OOP concepts and asked questions about the static keyword, implementation of singleton classes, encapsulation, and interfaces.

After that, he asked me two SQL questions. He initially provided two tables: student and subject, and asked a medium-level SQL query involving joins, which I solved successfully. Then he added a third table called department and asked a follow-up query. I was able to solve all three queries completely, and the interviewer seemed satisfied.

Then he asked a few questions related to React like to explain the component structure, then explain the two hooks usestate and useffect. Then he asked about Virtual DOM and working of virtual DOM and how it improved efficiency. Then he asked some general topics like MongoDB and databases. He asked me to explain the differences between SQL and NoSQL databases, and in what scenarios I would choose one over the other. He also asked me to give two real-world examples where I would use both types, which I was able to answer.

Finally, he asked me about different types of NoSQL databases beyond key-value stores. I admitted I wasn't aware of all the types. He then asked about indexing in DBMS and whether indexing can be done in NoSQL databases as well.

The interview concluded after this discussion and I asked about how AI is leveraged in finance. He answered briefly and the interview concluded.

4. HR Round [ 8 candidates were shortlisted for this round. ]

The HR round was very relaxed and conversational. The interviewer was warm and made me feel comfortable from the beginning. It felt more like a discussion than a formal interview and lasted around 15 minutes.

1. Introduce yourself

2. Mention something interesting that is not in your resume

3. What do you like to do besides tech?

4. Explain two of your projects

5. Describe a time you worked in a team

6. Do you prefer working individually or in a team?

7. Where do you see yourself in 5 years?

8. Are you planning for higher studies?

For the question about higher studies, I responded that I'm not planning to pursue them. I shared that I believe gaining hands-on industry experience is the right path for me.

At the end of the interview, she asked if I had any questions for her. I asked about MSCI's commitment to ESG and climate initiatives, and how those values are integrated into the company's work culture. She appreciated the question and gave a thoughtful response before concluding the interview.

[ 5 students were offered the job ]

1. Resume Shortlisting [ Everybody above 6 CGPA applied ]

Applications opened on Superset on 1st September with a minimum eligibility criteria of 6 CGPA. However, during the shortlisting stage, only students with 7.5 CGPA and above were considered. Resume shortlisting was done based on keywords in the resume, required skills, or possibly relevant internships and projects. After this round, 13 students were shortlisted, and the list was announced on 8th September.

Pre-Placement Talk -

The PPT was conducted just before the interviews on 10th September by TransBnk's CTO and HR. They explained about the company--how they started, what motivated them, their current situation, and the type of candidates they were looking for. They also gave us an overview of the company's complete workflow.

I am specifically mentioning this round because attending PPTs and interacting with the presenters can really help during interviews. This worked for me too--I asked a few questions during the PPT based on the homework I had done about the company beforehand. This showed my genuine interest, and they answered my questions in detail. Then we were introduced to the two panelists who would conduct the technical interviews--both were senior developers at the company.

2. Technical Interview [ 13 students appeared ]

The first panelist started the interview by asking me for my introduction. He then went into detail about my internships and asked me to explain my projects. I explained all my projects thoroughly. After that, he went through the skills section of my resume and asked whether I had learned those skills through my college curriculum. I clarified that I had self-studied most of them.

He then noticed the extracurricular skills mentioned in my resume and seemed curious, so we had a short discussion about them for about a minute. After this, he began asking technical questions based on my resume and projects. He asked me about JWT, its working, and format, which I explained in detail. He also asked the difference between JWT and Session, along with some follow-up questions. Later, he moved on to questions about Java, including multithreading, its types, and working. Since one of my projects involved AWS, he asked me to explain AWS, its services, use cases, and overall working. Finally, he said, "That's all from my side," and handed it over to the second panelist.

The second panelist gave me a problem on paper: Missing and Repeating Number I directly explained my optimal approach based on equations and then wrote pseudo code on paper. He was satisfied with my explanation.

Next, he gave me a slightly tricky problem: "How would you sort a file containing numbers of size 8GB when you only have 6GB RAM?" He asked me to sit in another cabin and solve it while he interviewed the next candidate. I wrote down multiple approaches (not code, just logic) and then went back to explain them. My approaches included swap memory, virtual memory, and an external merge sort-based approach. They seemed satisfied with my answers.

This round lasted for about 25-30 minutes.

3. HR Interview [ 6 students appeared ]

After almost 2 hours of waiting and the lunch break, I was called for the HR interview. There was one panelist, the same person who had presented the PPT and was the HR representative of the company.

The interview began with my introduction, followed by an overview of my projects and internships. He then asked about my internships in detail. The discussion moved on to my interests, future goals, 5-year and 10-year plans, and whether I had any plans for pursuing a master's degree. I explained my reasons clearly.

He then grilled me for a while on one question: "Would you start your own venture if you had the right resources and people?" After that, he asked why I chose engineering and why I pursued a diploma instead of HSC. He also asked me to share something that wasn't mentioned on my resume.

Towards the end, he said, "That's all from my side," and asked if I had any questions. I asked him a couple of questions about the company, which he answered in detail. I also gave some inputs in between, showing that I had done my homework about the company. He even recalled the question I had asked during the PPT. The interview concluded after about 20 minutes.

The results were announced after all interviews were completed. They played a small prank on us by calling four of us into a cabin and saying they had only three vacancies, asking who would back off. After a tense moment, they revealed they were just kidding and offered jobs to all four of us. 🎊

journey.prep:
1. Aptitude Preparation:

○ Don't take aptitude lightly. I initially thought only a few companies would ask for it, but almost every company includes aptitude in their selection process.

○ In some of the companies, I was able to solve the coding questions, but I couldn't solve the aptitude questions correctly, so I wasn't shortlisted for the next round.

○ Start preparing at least one month before placements to build confidence and speed.

○ Resources for Aptitude: IndiaBix & FreshCareers

○ Tricks and Shortcuts for Aptitude: Imran Sir Maths & Last Moment Tuitions

2. DSA Preparation:

● Follow Resources:

○ Striver DSA Sheet (A to Z) - Covers all important DSA topics systematically. Striver's A2Z DSA Sheet

○ Aditya Verma's YouTube Channel: Offers detailed explanations and tutorials on various DSA concepts. Aditya Verma

● Daily Practice:

○ Solve problems on LeetCode daily. Starting just one month before placements is usually not enough. Regular practice builds speed, accuracy, and problem-solving intuition.

● Contests and Challenges:

○ Participate in daily/weekly coding contests. This helps improve problem-solving under time pressure and exposes you to a variety of question types.

3. SQL / Database Preparation:

○ Practice Queries: Solve at least 50 SQL problems on LeetCode covering different concepts like SELECT, JOIN, GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY, subqueries, and aggregation functions.

○ Understand Concepts: Be clear about SQL vs NoSQL, normalization, relationships, and indexing.

○ Practical Application: Try to write queries on sample databases to understand how tables relate and how data can be extracted efficiently.

○ Understand ER Diagram to SQL Conversion.

○ Resources: GeeksforGeeks: Mapping from ER Model to Relational Model & CodeChef: ER Diagrams to Tables Practice Problems

○ DBMS One shot: DBMS Concept (For Concept Revision)

4. Javascript: Javascript

5. Java: Complete Java Programming Course

6. Output Guess Questions: Geeks for Geeks

7. Communication Skills / Soft Skills

Clarity and Confidence: Speak clearly and confidently during interviews. Avoid filler words and maintain a steady pace.

Think Aloud:

○ While solving coding or technical problems, explain your thought process aloud.

○ This helps the interviewer understand your approach, reasoning, and problem-solving skills, even if the final answer isn't correct.

Active Listening: Pay attention to the interviewer's questions and respond accordingly. Don't interrupt; it shows respect and good listening skills.

8. Believe in God's Plan / Stay Positive:

○ Trust that everything happens for a reason. Stay calm and positive throughout the preparation and interview process.

○ A strong mindset and faith can help you stay motivated even during challenges or setbacks.

BEST OF LUCKKK!!

If you need any help or want to know more feel free to reach out .

1. Resume Shortlisting [Everyone above 6 CGPA applied ]

Applications opened on Superset on 1st September with a minimum eligibility criterion of 6 CGPA. However, during shortlisting, only students with 7.5 CGPA and above were considered. Shortlisting was done based on keywords in the resume, required skills, and relevant internships or projects. A total of 18 students were shortlisted, and the list was announced on 8th September.

Pre-Placement Talk -

The PPT was conducted just before the interviews on 10th September by TransBnk's CTO and HR. They explained about the company--how they started, what motivated them, their current status, and the kind of candidates they were looking for. I carefully noted down key points from the presentation that later came up in my technical interview. I made sure to connect what the presenters shared with the homework I had done about the company. This gave me clarity and confidence when interacting with the interviewers.

2. Technical Interview [ 18 candidates appeared for this round ]

The first round was taken by a panel consisting of two interviewers and lasted around 45 minutes to 1 hour. It began with a simple "Introduce yourself," after which they focused on my projects. They asked me to explain the workflow of my projects in detail. After discussing the projects, the interviewers shifted their attention to my technical skills and asked questions on RabbitMQ, OOP concepts, whether Java is single-threaded or multi-threaded, the difference between method overloading and method overriding, and the difference between SQL and NoSQL databases. They also asked about the internship I had done and

what work I had completed during it. At one point, they asked why I chose the SDE profile when my course is AIML.

They also asked questions on Spring Boot and React hooks. On the DSA side, I was given a coding problem to solve live on their laptop, which was the LeetCode problem Set Matrix Zeroes.

Tips & Takeaways:

For project-related discussions, it's really helpful to use the STAR method--first explain the situation your project was solving, then your role or task, the actions you took (technologies, code, concepts used), and finally the result or outcome. Make sure to be thorough with your resume and the skills you have mentioned, because interviewers often dive deep into whatever is listed. When discussing projects, including details about the code and how it works can make your explanation more clear and convincing.

3. HR Interview [ 6 candidates appeared for this round ]

The HR round began with a simple "Introduce yourself" question. After that, he asked me to explain my projects, but not in too much detail--just enough to understand my role and the technologies I worked with. He also asked about my strengths and weaknesses to get a sense of my personal and professional qualities. One of the key questions was why I chose to start my career at TransBnk instead of joining a bigger MNC. Towards the end of the round, he asked if I had any questions, and I asked, "How does TransBnk support fresh graduates in their career growth and learning?" This showed my interest in learning and developing within the company. The HR round lasted around 15 to 20 minutes and mainly focused on understanding my personality, motivation, and alignment with the company culture.

Tips & Takeaways:

● Be well-prepared with common HR questions, as most companies ask similar questions.

● Always ask a question at the end of the interview--it shows that you are genuinely interested in learning more about the company and its culture.

● Be confident while answering; do not appear hesitant or unsure.

● Maintain a positive attitude and always have a smile on your face throughout the interview.

4. Prank Round [ 4 candidates appeared for this round ]

After the HR round, there was a funny prank round. They called four people and said that only three seats were available, so someone would have to back out. Naturally, it created a little tension, but then they revealed that it was a prank and that all of us were actually selected for TransBnk. It was a light-hearted way to end the process and made the announcement memorable.

4 students were offered the job and I am one of them.
