journey.prep:
1. Prepare for Quantitative Analysis and Aptitude: For companies like KPMG, aptitude and quantitative analysis play an important role. Practice regularly on platforms like GeeksforGeeks, IndiaBix, or other competitive aptitude sites. Time management is crucial, so focus on both accuracy and speed.

2. Resume: o Use a clean and professional format, such as a LaTeX template. o Keep your resume ATS-friendly to increase the chances of being shortlisted. o Be precise and impactful: describe your projects in 2-3 points each, and quantify your achievements wherever possible. Numbers and results stand out. o Prepare your resume thoroughly from start to finish: Make sure you are familiar with every detail, description, and word mentioned in it, so you can confidently discuss any aspect during the interview. Being well-versed with your own resume shows professionalism and

helps you answer questions accurately and convincingly. Parnika Das Resume

3. Internship and Work Experience: From my observation, candidates with some form of internship experience tend to have an advantage, especially in technical rounds. Even part-time internships or summer projects provide real-world exposure and talking points for interviews. This is not a strict rule, but it definitely helps strengthen your profile. (It helped me a lot to stand out)

4. Strengthen CS Fundamentals and DSA: Prepare both the theory and coding aspects of computer science. This includes: o Data Structures & Algorithms (DSA) o Computer Science fundamentals like Operating Systems, DBMS, Networking, etc. o Solve as many coding questions as you can. Do the questions on your own, and if you are not able to do it, learn it from any explanation video and do it by yourself. Follow the Strivers' sheet or Leetcode Top Interview 150. And for SQL, you can solve LeetCode SQL 50. o Practising coding problems regularly will build confidence for technical interviews.

5. Communication is Key: Your ability to communicate effectively is often the first impression you make. Clear and confident communication can give you a significant edge over other candidates. Practice introducing yourself, explaining your projects, and discussing your experiences concisely and engagingly.

6. Maintain Confidence and Positivity: o Keep a smile on your face during interviews. o Show confidence without arrogance. (Most Important) o Put in the effort to make a strong impression on the interviewer.

7. Academic Performance Helps: A good academic record (preferably 7.5 GPA or above) adds weight to your profile. However, academics alone are not enough - balance it with projects, internships, and skills.

8. Early and Consistent Preparation: o Start placement preparation as early as possible. o Maintain a healthy balance between studies, skill-building, and personal life. o Consistent effort beats last-minute cramming. o

9. Resilience and Patience: Placement journeys are rarely smooth: o At first, you may struggle with clearing online assessments. o Even after clearing OA rounds, you might get rejected in interviews. o Sometimes, rejection happens even after the HR round, which can be heartbreaking. Key: Don't lose hope. Hard days are part of the journey, and persistence is what separates success from failure. Give your 100% in every attempt, but also accept that luck plays a great role.

10. Believe in Yourself: o Put in your best effort. o Keep improving, learning, and refining your skills. o Stay motivated, even when facing setbacks.

My Overall Placement Experience

I started my journey by attempting several Online Assessments (OA), which were initially challenging. Gradually, as I improved my speed and accuracy, I began clearing OAs after 5 tests or something, but then faced rejections in interview rounds. In one process, I was even rejected after the HR round, which was very disheartening. During my interviews, I focused on presenting my projects, internships, and experiences clearly, highlighting the technologies I worked with, challenges I faced, and how I resolved them. I made sure to stay confident, smile, and communicate effectively, which helped me leave a positive impression. I practised quantitative aptitude, DSA, and CS fundamentals rigorously and maintained a decent academic record alongside internships and projects. I also asked thoughtful questions about the role and career growth, which left a strong impression on the interviewers. Despite the ups and downs, I learned to stay persistent, balance preparation with personal life, and give my best in every attempt . Receiving the Letter of Intent from KPMG was the culmination of all the hard work, and the experience was truly unique compared to my peers. I believe the key takeaways were patience , consistency, preparation, and belief in oneself.

All the Best!!!

The selection process for the Analyst - Tech Enablement Role (KPMG 2nd Role) was officially announced on 3rd September 2025. Initially, it was mentioned that the process would include an Online Assessment (OA), followed by a Group Discussion, two Technical Rounds, and one HR Round. However, the Group Discussion round was later cancelled, and the process moved directly to the Technical Interviews after the Pre-Placement Talk. Our process took place online from college.

1. [Online Assessment Test] [ About 20 candidates for second role only]

The Online Assessment (OA) was held on 8th September 2025 and was of easy to medium difficulty. It mainly focused on Quantitative Analysis, along with other aptitude -based questions. It consisted of 55 questions with 3 sections being Aptitude, Quantitative Analysis and Verbal Ability. The test was for 40 minutes only. It was proctored with camera access and full -screen mode enabled, ensuring a monitored and fair evaluation environment. Each question required proper calculations, logical thinking, and step -by-step solving; there were no simple one-word or direct MCQ-type questions. It required quick problem -solving skills as the time limit was quite tight. Both speed and accuracy played a crucial role in performing well in the assessment. It was conveyed that those who applied for the first role and cleared the test of the first role were allowed to sit for the second round directly if they applied.

2. [Technical round 1] [ 14 candidates]

After the announcement, the process began with a brief online Pre -Placement Talk (PPT) conducted jointly with SPCE students (their offer and role were different). The session was quite informative, covering details about KPMG as an organisation, what the firm does, its service lines, work culture, and the type of work we would be involved in. They also explained that the role would include client interactions, analytical work,

and frequent travelling as part of on-site engagements. Following the PPT, the Group Discussion round was skipped, and the process moved directly to the Technical Interviews. A total of 14 candidates were shortlisted and divided into two panels, with 7 candidates in each. The interviews were conducted online through Microsoft Teams, with each slot spaced approximately 20 minutes apart. The overall process was well-organised and smooth, giving candidates ample time to prepare between rounds. I was the first candidate to be interviewed in my panel. The interviewer began the conversation in a friendly manner by asking how I was doing, which helped ease the initial nervousness. He then asked me to introduce myself, following which he requested me to give a brief overview of my work experiences. Since I had three prior work experiences, including one at Amazon India, he showed particular interest in understanding the kind of projects I had worked on. He went in-depth about my responsibilities, the technologies I was introduced to, and how I managed and contributed to each project. We discussed the challenges I faced, the problem-solving approaches I used, and the overall learning outcomes from each role. My interview didn't follow the typical question-answer format; instead, it felt more like an engaging discussion about my experiences and professional journey. The interviewer seemed genuinely interested in understanding how I applied my knowledge in real-world scenarios, which made the interaction quite comfortable.

After discussing my work experiences, the interviewer moved on to ask about my academic background. He asked me what subjects I had learned during my computer engineering course and what I was currently exploring. I mentioned that I was learning about emerging technologies like Cloud Computing and Blockchain, which naturally led to a deeper conversation about new advancements in technology. He seemed interested and asked me which of the latest technologies fascinated me the most and why, along with a few related follow-up questions. After that, he shifted the focus toward Computer Science fundamentals. He asked me about the different sorting algorithms I had explored and specifically questioned me on the difference between Bubble Sort and Merge Sort, discussing their time complexities and use cases. He also asked me to tell him the pseudo-code of the merge sort algorithm briefly. He then moved to Data Structures and Algorithms (DSA) , asking me to explain the fundamentals , such as stacks and queues, along with their real-life applications. For instance, he gave examples like the undo-redo functionality in applications and how it relates to stack operations. He also asked me some OOPs fundamentals as well but not so much in depth. The discussion was quite interactive, as he appreciated the logical reasoning behind my answers and encouraged me to explain concepts in my own words.

Towards the end of the interview, he asked me if I had any questions for him. I took the opportunity to ask about the key responsibilities I would have as an Analyst at KPMG and also inquired about the career growth opportunities within the organization. He seemed particularly impressed by the second question, appreciating my curiosity about long-term development. He then explained both aspects in great detail , describing the nature of the work, the kind of projects analysts are involved in, and the structured growth path within KPMG. It was an insightful conclusion to the interview and gave me a clearer understanding of the role and the organization's work culture. He then ended the interview. The interview was around 45 minutes, so he didn't get to ask much about my other skills. He didn't ask about my projects and all. Other candidates were asked some other basic CS fundamental questions, hobbies, projects and basic DSA.

3. [Technical round 2] [ 6 candidates]

6 candidates were divided into 2 panels again.

In the second round, the interviewer in my panel focused primarily on my projects rather than my internship experiences. He began by asking me to introduce myself, and then I briefly mentioned my internships. After that, he delved deeper into my latest projects, asking me about how I implemented them, the tech stacks I used, the challenges I faced, and how I resolved them. I had four projects in total, and he specifically asked about my final year project as well as my first two projects -- one based on Kubernetes and the other on Machine Learning. He was keen to understand which projects were group projects and which were individual, and for the group projects, he wanted to know my specific contributions and how I coordinated with my team. The interview was relatively brief, lasting around 25 minutes, but it went well. Towards the end, he again asked if I had any questions. I asked about the kind of work an Analyst does and the typical career progression from Analyst to Associate Consultant, which he explained in detail. Unlike some other candidates, I was not asked about location preferences. Everything was going smoothly, and the interaction felt positive and engaging. Unfortunately, despite a good technical discussion, I did not get selected for the HR round.

4. [HR round]

The HR round was a brief 10-minute online meet that mainly covered basic HR questions. I was asked about my hobbies, strengths and weaknesses, and why they should hire me. The conversation felt largely formal in nature, serving more as a procedural step rather than a detailed interview. Shortly after this call, I received my Letter of Intent from KPMG. Overall, this experience was quite different from what my peers and friends went through, making it a unique and memorable process.

Out of these 4 candidates from the HR round, 3 were sent a Letter of Intent and 1 candidate from the technical round 2 (that was me) was also sent a letter of intent.

1. Online Assessment (MCQ Round)

2. Machine Coding Round (Don't be afraid after reading "Machine Coding Round"; see below for what I've written)

3. Interview

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

1. Online Assessment (MCQ Round) [ 92 candidates appeared for this round ]

Platform : HackerEarth Eligibility: CE and CSE (For the 2025 passout batch, EXTC was also eligible, so for 2027, anything could happen.) There was a 7.5+ CGPA criteria to apply. (Just telling in case you don't know -- the college considers CGPA of only 5 semesters till the 6th sem result is out. In our case, from August 8th, they began considering the 6th semester CGPA as well)

There were 21 technical MCQs and 50 mins were given, but 15-20 mins were more than enough to complete everything. Since there was a lot of time, I noted down a few points and some less-known theory questions:

1. In VB-style, -1 is true and 0 is false

2. Output-based question on recursion

3. What is Anonymous FTP

4. What is CORS

5. What is lazy loading

6. How to select an HTML tag using ID

7. Questions based on HTTP status codes - so study all status codes

8. DHCP is an application-level protocol

9. One question was on operator precedence - had to evaluate an expression

10. There was a question asking for the order from bottom to top for elements (terms like relative, absolute, z-index were mentioned)

11. Again, a question on order of console.log() means asking for output which involved Promises and setTimeout - basically question on event loop (Study the event loop in JS - one of the favorite interview questions when it comes to JS)

12. Ping does not use port

13. Valid ping command - remember all octets must be numbers between 0 to 255, other options had URLs so were invalid

14. One SQL question on joins - options had actual SQL queries

A key point: They evaluate not just your MCQ score but also shortlist based on your resume, so ensure it highlights solid development skills.

11 candidates were shortlisted for the next round, but out of those, 2 got oﬀers from Barclays and 2 from IDFC. So ﬁnally only 7 candidates appeared for the next round.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

2. Machine Coding Round [ 7 candidates appeared for this round ] [Oﬄine] [ 2hrs ]

As I mentioned, don't be afraid after reading "Machine Coding Round." It's just a problem statement, and you need to provide a solution. BrowserStack has been using the same problem statement for the last 3-4 years. The problem involves implementing Socket.IO for real-time updates, so make sure you're comfortable with it.

We were called to BrowserStack's oﬃce in Goregaon for the machine coding round and interview.

HR called every selected candidate 2 days before the interview to invite us to their Goregaon oﬃce. On the call, she mentioned there would be 2 rounds: machine coding and then an interview. She also said the machine coding problem statement requires knowledge of Socket.IO and suggested practicing for the machine coding round.

Candidates were divided into batches, with 5 candidates per batch and one mentor per batch. On the same day, there were candidates from other colleges too. I think there were about 12 batches in total. I was in Batch 1 with 5 candidates, all from our college. The other 2 candidates from our college were in Batch 2 with 3 candidates from a diﬀer ent college.

Instructions Provided to Us:

What to bring:

● Personal laptop

● Hard copy of resume

● Government-issued photo ID

Ensure the following setup on your laptop before the interview:

● Compiler/interpreter of your preferred programming language

● IDE/code editor of your choice

● Root/admin access to the system

● Latest version of Chrome, Firefox, Safari, or Edge

We were allowed to use our personal laptops, and Google and GPT were permitted.

Problem Statement:

(You'll ﬁnd it in a GitHub repo too - my solution is linked at the end of this section.)

This problem requires you to implement a log-watching solution (similar to the tail -f command in UNIX). However, the log ﬁle is hosted on a remote machine (same machine as your server code). The log ﬁle is in append-only mode.

You need to implement the following:

● A server-side program to monitor the given log ﬁle and stream updates as they happen using Socket.IO for real-time communication. This will run on the same machine as the log ﬁle. You can use any programming language for the server.

● A web-based client (accessible via a URL like http://localhost/log) that displays updates in the ﬁle in real-time, without requiring a page refresh. The page should load once and keep updating. On initial load, the user should see the last 10 lines of the ﬁle.

Problem Constraints:

● The server must push updates to clients in real-time using Socket.IO.

● The log ﬁle could be several GBs. How do you optimize retrieving the last 10 lines?

● The server should not retransmit the entire ﬁle every time; it should only send updates.

● The server must handle multiple clients simultaneously.

● The web page should not stay in a loading state after the ﬁrst load and should not reload thereafter.

● You may not use oﬀ-the-shelf external libraries or tools to read the ﬁle or provide tail-like functionalities (except Socket.IO for real-time updates).

You'll be evaluated on code quality, testability, modularity, and handling of corner cases.

In this round, you can ask the mentor any doubts. At the end, the mentor will review your solution and test it thoroughly. For me, the mentor asked me to open the URL in two browsers, perform a hard refresh, and test edge cases. He also used a bash script to simulate automatic updates in the text ﬁle, adding \n, \t, and \r characters to check if everything worked correctly.

Tip: Know every single line of your code and why you wrote it, as the mentor will ask about your logic and the reasoning behind speciﬁc lines, especially how you implemented Socket.IO for real-time updates.

After this round, we had lunch at their oﬃce through their catering service. Then, after lunch, they announced the results, and only 3 candidates were selected for the next round.

Sometimes they also ask this PS:

Browser automation without using automation frameworks.pdf

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

3. Interview Round [ 3 candidates appeared for this round ] [ 50-55 min in my case]

The interviewer was the Director of Engineering. He kicked things off by introducing himself and then asked about my CET, SSC, and HSC scores, and why I chose SPIT. After that, he asked me to give a quick introduction about myself. Then, he asked about my internship experience, specifically what I did during it and what kind of work I handled. I shared details about my role, the tasks I contributed to, and the impact I made, like leading development or solving specific challenges. Once I was done, he explained the interview flow: first, we'd dive into my projects, and then he'd test my problem-solving skills.

He started with, "Tell me about a project where you faced a lot of difficulties and challenges." So, I began explaining one of my projects, and while I was talking, he jumped in with questions. He asked about specific situations where I hit technical roadblocks, how I resolved them, and how I tackled things overall.

Then came the "why" questions:

● Why did I pick Next.js over React.js for my project? (I used Next.js, so I explained my reasoning--stuff like server-side rendering and better SEO.)

● Why SQL over NoSQL? Then, in SQL, why PostgreSQL over MySQL? What was the reason behind these choices?

● What if I had used a NoSQL database for the same project? How would it have impacted things?

After the "why" questions, he dug deeper into scaling and deployment:

● How would I scale up my existing project?

● What factors did I consider when deploying my project?

● How was I monitoring things post-deployment, and why did I choose Vercel for deployment?

● Since I used NeonDB (PostgreSQL), what features did NeonDB provide that helped throughout my project?

After the project discussion, we moved to a DSA question: Daily Temperatures. It's a classic Monotonic Stack problem. He asked me to write proper code on paper and do a dry run with the example he gave. I walked through the solution, explaining the stack logic and how it tracks indices to compute the result.

All three of us landed the offer! 🏆🏎

Most asked questions at BrowserStack : (Questions in Red were asked in my interview)

1. Web and Networking Basics:

○ How does the internet work?

○ How does an image get downloaded in a browser?

○ What happens behind the scenes when you enter a URL in a browser?

○ If you type google.com and the page doesn't load, how would you debug it?

○ How does google.com work?

○ Describe the journey of a request.

○ HTTP vs HTTPS.

○ TCP vs UDP.

○ Study all HTTP status codes.

○ Headers in HTTP requests and responses.

2. Database and System Design:

○ HAVING vs WHERE in SQL.

○ What is a REST API?

○ What is SOAP?

○ All types of logs used while building a system.

○ Huge file handling: You have a 1TB file and need to count word occurrences with only 8GB of RAM. How would you process it? (MapReduce)

○ What are messaging queues?

3. Concurrency and Processes:

○ Process vs Thread.

○ Difference between async, concurrency, and parallelism.

4. Testing and Deployment:

○ Testing before deployment.

○ How would you design the onboarding flow for your favorite product?

5. DSA Questions:

○ Daily Temperatures (Monotonic Stack)

○ Move Zeroes

○ Add Two Numbers

○ Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters

○ 3Sum

The questions were easy to medium level. If you have built projects using JS it would be a piece of cake and the entire test could be completed in 30 mins max. Accuracy matters over here for clearing the cutoff.

2. Machine Coding Round [ 11 shortlisted 7 appeared ]

It was conducted in Batches offline in the BrowserStack office in Oberoi Commerz 2. Due to the limited number of students they had confined a single batch for SPIT. The PS for the machine coding round is shared below:

This problem requires you to implement a log-watching solution (similar to the tail -f command in UNIX). However, the log file is hosted on a remote machine (same machine as your server code). The log file is in append-only mode. You need to implement the following:

● A server-side program to monitor the given log file and stream updates as they happen using Socket.IO for real-time communication. This will run on the same machine as the log file. You can use any programming language for the server.

● A web-based client (accessible via a URL like http://localhost/log) that displays updates in the file in real-time, without requiring a page refresh. The page should load once and keep updating. On initial load, the user should see the last 10 lines of the file. Problem Constraints:

● The server must push updates to clients in real-time using Socket.IO.

● The log file could be several GBs. How do you optimize retrieving the last 10 lines?

● The server should not retransmit the entire file every time; it should only send updates.

● The server must handle multiple clients simultaneously.

● The web page should not stay in a loading state after the first load and should not reload thereafter.

● You may not use off-the-shelf external libraries or tools to read the file or provide tail-like functionalities (except Socket.IO for real-time updates). You'll be evaluated on code quality, testability, modularity, and handling of corner cases.

The Machine coding round began at 10:30 AM and we were given roughly 2 hrs to build the backend server. You may find the solutions online, but an optimal solution that caters to the edge cases of the invigilator is preferred. You are not allowed to use any AI agents or LLMs or medium articles during this round, our invigilator was right beside us. You may refer to the documentation for development. You can interact with the invigilator during the round. Primary goal is to develop the solution using Socket.IO , I preferred NODE for the backend and socket implementation to display logs realtime with a confined Buffer to prevent parsing the logs. The invigilator would test it on multiple edge cases, like real time parsing, multiple browser compatibility with realtime logs and order in which they appear or cases where '\n' appears while parsing logs. If it passes all the cases and you are able to explain your code really well then you would be moved forward to the next round.

3. Director Of Engineering Round [ 3 shortlisted ]

For preparation you may go through medium or GFG articles. Mine was an interesting one, I was the only one who had an online interview with the Senior Director in the office for 30 mins. He read my resume and given that I had worked with a corporation with exposure to multiple hacks and techstacks, was exempted from basic questions. I was asked about one of my favourite projects and what role did I play in that project. Then moved on to internship experiences, what tasks did I perform in Russell Investments as Summer Intern, what project did I work on. He asked if I had exposure to Prod and deployment which I explained pretty well. I was quickly moved to behavioral questions like how will I tackle Deadlines, How will I deal with my teammate who differs in an opinion. It was the most fun director round.

All the 3 received the offer.

1. Online MCQ Test (23/07/2025) - HackerEarth

• Number of Candidates Appeared: 92

• This round was conducted on HackerEarth and consisted of 20 multiple-choice questions to be solved in 90 minutes.

• Topics included: HTML, CSS, JavaScript, DBMS, Computer Networks.

• The questions were fairly easy and mostly based on fundamentals.

• Shortlisted Candidates: 11 (Note: 4 candidates had offers from Barclays and IDFC, so they did not appear for further rounds.)

2. Machine Coding Round (30/07/2 025) - BrowserStack Mumbai Office

• Number of Candidates Appeared: 7

This problem requires you to implement a log watching solution (similar to the tail -f command in UNIX). However, in this case, the log file is hosted on a remote machine (same machine as your server code). The log file is in append-only mode. You may implement the server in any programming language.

You have to implement the following:

1. A server side program to monitor the given log file and capable of streaming updates that happen in it. This will run on the same machine as the log file.

2. A web based client (accessible via URL like http://localhost/log ) that prints the updates in the file as and when they happen and NOT upon page refresh. The page should be loaded once and it should keep getting updated in real -time.

3. The user sees the last 10 lines in the file when they visit the page for the first time.

Problem Constraints Please read these thoroughly

 The server should push updates to the clients as we have to be as real time as possible. Do this by Websokets in node you can use socket.io

 Be aware that the log file may be several GB, how to optimise for retrieving the last 10 lines - Use list of last 10 lines and updates it when file changes and read file in reverse and load small chunk in buffer instead of loading complete file.

 The server should not retransmit the entire file every time. It should only send the updates. - Create event update (to get new lines) init (to get last 10 lines)

 The server should be able to handle multiple clients at the same time.

 They will be evaluating you for working solution, code efficiency, corner cases, etc

 For more info visit this - Log Watcher Solution

• After this round, a lunch break was given, and then results were announced.

• Shortlisted candidate - 3

Instead of selected, they call out the names of those who are not selected. If your name isn't called, you've made it to the next round.

3. Technical + HR Interview (30/07/2025) - BrowserStack Mumbai Office

• Number of Candidates Appeared: 3

• The interview began with a short introduction from both sides.

• Then we had an in-depth discussion about my project--why I built it, the tech stack used, and the reasoning behind the choices and features of project lasted about 20 minutes.

Technical Questions Asked:

1. Next Greater Element - Using monotonic stack .

2. SQL vs NoSQL - Differences and use cases with real life example.

3. Process vs Thread - Why processes are needed if threads exist .

4. Troubleshooting - What to do if a website doesn't open or internet isn't working tell me all options for troubleshoot.

5. 10 TB File Problem -

o Problem: Find the word "programmer" in a 10 TB file

o My approach:

 Initially said I'd read the file and search line by line

 Interviewer pointed out memory limitations

 Then I proposed dividing the file into blocks

 They raised a concern: the word may split across blocks (e.g., 'prog' and 'rammer')

 I suggested using buffer overlap between blocks

 Also mentioned using multiple threads for parallel processing

At the end, they asked if I had any questions. I asked, "If I get selected, what would a typical day at BrowserStack look like?"

Result: The next day, HR informed me and another one that I had been selected. Next week they added one more to shortlisted list. Total Candidates Offered: 3

Placement Preparation Tips

1. Start Early with Core Subjects

Begin your placement preparation as early as possible. Focus on fundamental computer science subjects such as DBMS, Operating Systems, Computer Networks, and Object-Oriented Programming (OOPs). Make concise, revision-friendly notes for these subjects to help during the last-minute prep. Also, research frequently asked interview questions to become familiar with recurring patterns and concepts.

2. Resume

Your resume should reflect your actual knowledge and experience. Avoid adding skills or technologies that you cannot explain if asked in the interview it may come off as dishonest and create a negative impression. At the very least, ensure you understand the basic concepts of everything mentioned. Tailor your resume slightly depending on the specific role you're applying for.

3. Pay Attention to the Company Presentation

The first step in most placement processes is usually a company presentation. Be attentive and note important details about the company's history, products, services, and culture. If you have doubts about the roles and responsibilities, clarify them early. This will help you make an informed decision and also position yourself as someone who is genuinely interested in the company.

4. Practice is Key for Online Assessments

For Online Assessments (OAs), consistent practice can make a big difference. Participate in coding contests and take timed tests to improve your problem solving speed and accuracy. This will also help you identify your weak areas and improve over time.

5. Approach Interviews Calmly and Confidently

In interviews, focus on explaining your approach clearly rather than jumping to give the right answer immediately. Interviewers are more interested in your thought process and problem- solving skills. Staying calm and confident shows that you can perform under pressure, which is an essential trait for any role.

6. Stay Positive and Keep Improving

Finally, don't lose hope if things don't go as planned. Focus on how you can improve your chances of getting selected. Understand your strengths and weaknesses, and keep refining them throughout the placement season. Persistence and continuous improvement are key.

 You should give 60% time for DSA and 40% for Projects building.  You can't do only dsa or projects you need to do both.  Try to give leetcode or codeforces weekly contest so you will learn time management.  This was my 3rd Inteview I saw my friends gave more interviews than and not selected so be patient so keep grinding you will definitely get results.  It is not too late or early start hardwork from as soon as possible.  Please don't cheat in placement process it will affect whole college due to you.  In placements, luck plays a major role. General Imp Question:

If you have AI in your resume learn about RAG, as interviewers generally know that in AI (asked in all 3 companies for me).

HashMap, HashSet, ArrayList internal implementation in java, JRE/JDK/JVM/JIT in java.

All types of questions on Palindrome(easy to hard), and sorting algos.

Indexing in dbms, have strong hold on sql mostly joins and subqueries are asked.

My Journey:

I completed an internship and a Data Analysis course after second year. Won a few DA competitions in November, but still in December I was really not confident of having a chance at getting a good placement, I did not have great dsa knowledge either. I effectively began my journey in first week of January. Earlier I used to practice very few dsa problems and that too in python. But my seniors told me about how important java is for companies so I switched to java. ( I did it because I was not too advanced in dsa then and was anyways going to start from scratch.) If you are solving in python/c++ pls continue, just do oops and java workings well theoretically.

January: began with java, close to 80 dsa problems, 1 hack participation

February: Gen AI course,close to 50-60 dsa problems

March: Gen AI course, 100 dsa problems, began trying lc contests

April: 150 dsa problems, completed the course, finalist in hackathon(first time)

May : 50-60 dsa, won here technologies hack(first time)

June: Did not focus on solving new problems, rather kept revising topics and solved problems, began with theory topics - java,oops,dbms,os,ccn

Resume: Do not lie about anything, first interview rounds are completely based on your resume. If you dont know about anything that is written it gives a bad impression. Know about every project in detail. Its ok to not know a lot of things, just know whatever you have written. My resume was completely AI/ML/DA/LLM/GENAI based, absolutely nothing about development as I did not know much about it.Also mention those things at the top which you want the interviewer to see, there is no specific order. 3-4 projects are enough, some skills. Pls do mention about any sports you would have played in your life. My MSCI and IDFC first round interviewers were very interested in my cricket skills and that really helped me. Just add one line but do add.

Projects:You dont need to have the best projects, you can have okish projects but need to know everything you did. You can take them from github, but again, know everything. If you can deploy them somewhere, that can be good as you can show it live to interviewer. But that is absolutely not necessary.

Interview: If you are asked something you dont know about, there are 2 ways,either you have absolutely now idea about it- just say sir i am not aware about it. Or you can relate it to some other topic. In that case mention that i dont know exactly, but i feel this is similar to the other thing i have worked on. First round is just resume based, no need to worry much. Also just to impress the interviewer dont speak fancy words which you are not aware of or have good knowledge about. It happened with me at MSCI, where I mentioned an advanced topic too early, so then he went a bit deeper into it and I was not able to answer all of it. The interviewers are mostly chill so they will calm you down.

DSA: DSA is necessary, but 500-700 problems are not, you can crack the best of companies even with less problems solved. But the more you solve, the more confidence you will have of solving unseen problems in oa or interview. Confidence is really important in dsa as in the pressure if you cant think of the right approach, it can get difficult. Codeforces, CP is absolutely not needed for any company other than PHONE PE. I still havent solved any problem on codeforces. If you like solving thats great but please ensure you are working on other aspects also. Also do ensure that you can take input in your language, as leetcode does not prepare us for that. Leetcode contests solving can be helpful, to get practice but dont panic if you can solve only 1 or two problems or even if you cant solve any problem in a contest. You can directly skip HARD problems on LC. Follow strivers A2Z Sheet. MSCI, Barclays and UBS had medium problems but idfc had easy problems. In interview mostly easy -medium are asked or they may not even ask. Even if you have not solved many problems, in june try to read through all easy-medium problems in strivers sheet. Having an idea can help you atleast come up with an approach in interviews.

OS/CCN/JAVA OOPS/DBMS/Aptitude/puzzles: I began with all this in June, You can start in May ideally. Java oops are extremely important, dbms comes next, along with sql, os is slightly important, while ccn mostly wont be asked, although its good to know basics.

Hackathon: Please participate in hacks. If you dont have the confidence, or no one is taking you in their team, find 3 others like you and participate. Because A- it gives you some impactful projects and B- if you sincerely give your best for 24 hours, for 4-5 hacks you will eventually win one for sure. It is helpful in interviews as it validates your skills for the interviewer. Also winning hacks dont require extraordinary skills these days. Just you need to be able to use open source tools well and present well. Please participate in company hackathons, if you win or even reach finale , they will select you for placement. Although if you are not able to win, that is not the end of the road, its not at all necessary.

Role: If you have certain preferences its ok to let go of some roles. But please be realistic, if you have confidence in your preparation, only then leave companies. Because it may happen that good companies might go away. Also please dont be too dependent on one role/company. MANY PEOPLE WERE WAITING FOR WORKINDIA DA, BUT IT DID NOT COME. At the same time it is important to have a few target companies and give it your all for it.

I wont say that placement is very much dependent on LUCK, It plays some part, but if you have not prepared well you have very little chance that luck would get you placed. But if you are well prepared luck can take you that extra mile. Overall if you have prepared well, You will do well eventually.

If you have given your best effort right from the time you decided to be serious (6/5/4/3/2 months) something good will happen, just keep going, Rejections can be tough, but eventually it will help you get something better. In my case I did not get MSCI, but rather got my preferred role,location and pay.

ALL THE BEST!!

Dont hesitate to reach out, 9372138292

Nomura visited for 3 roles:

ITD

CDO: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1ntYAHYcKOkuCpI2mwIhOWmvhz4NgVfL2YF2yuLjhwWU/edit?us p=drive_link

GM

Criteria for ITD was OA Aptitude while for others it was just resume shortlisting. We were asked to select 2 role preferences. But I think that OA score was also considered for other 2 as I got shortlisted for all 3 roles.

1. [OA] [200 ]

This was a complete Aptitude test, consisting of 3 sections: Verbal, Logical Reasoning, Quants Aptitude. For all three I had practiced from IndiaBix. Since I had given almost 10 OA's by now, I was confident (this really matters). The day before I gave practice tests for each of these sections on IndiaBix and realised that I was scoring maximum in Quants apti, followed by logical and then verbal. So in OA I began with Quants then logical then verbal, although the sections were in opposite ordering. Many students followed the given

(verbal-logcal-quant) order and thus had almost no time for many quants questions. So identify your strong area and begin with that. I practiced only from IndiaBix for this, I began practicing for Aptitude probably in July itself, focused more on Aptitude after MSCI.

Interview Day: I was in all the 3 shortlists, while this gave me more chances, there was a possibility of me losing focus, so ensure that you cut out all the noise and stay focused on the day of the interview. Now first the GM GD happened, topic- Is AI making us smarter or dependent, this did not go well for me and I did not go further. Then for ITD something unexpected happened, Due to suspicion of copying, all 28 candidates were asked to give another pen-paper OA, where they just shortlisted 7 for further rounds(no one knows what criteria was followed as most of us had solved all the questions correctly). So I did not get through in ITD as well. By the time my CDO Interview began I was already out of the other two.

2. [Tech Interview] [8-CDO, 28-ITD, 19-GM ]

So the interview began with them asking me to skip introduction and just give one line description of my projects and my role in them. I had 4 projects mentioned, all related to Data Analysis, ML and LLM, GEN AI. So my resume was highly aligned with the role. I had done an internship, so I also explained about my role in that and spoke about a few of my skills. There were 2 interviewers. One of them started questioning about one of my (Gen AI powered tool, that converts wikipedia topics into easy to understand comic strips) project.She first asked who is your target audience for this project. I answered that the younger students in age 12-20 who are inquisitive to learn about new things. Then she asked how will you control younger students from generating images of vulgar content. I tried explaining that firstly, wikipedia wont have much vulgar content, and secondly we were taking user's age as one of the user preferences and were passing it through prompts for our model. So we can ensure via structured prompting that the user does not get any vulgar images. She honestly was not convinced. The other interviewer then began by giving a problem. I have 1000 resumes, and want to perform searching in this, how can I do it(similar question was asked in IDFC as well), I explained the entire RAG framework and how it would make the searching very easy. Then he gave me another problem that, every morning he has to get up at 4 and mark a set of tasks as 0 or 1 based on the result, how would I solve it. Now just when he began writing 0 and 1 Logistic regression clicked in my mind. I explained to him the entire flow and working of logistic regression. He was satisfied with both my answers. Then he asked more about what I had done in internship. I spoke about flight price prediction (regression) model. I had mentioned R2 score as an accuracy metric in the resume. He questioned that we dont use R2 score to measure accuracy, I told him that since it was a regression model we cant use accuracy/precision, etc and rather we use mse/rmse/r2 score. He then asked me to explain what R2 score is. I knew about it and explained him with a short example. He then asked me to explain precision and recall. I answered that correctly as well. Then he asked me to give one line explanation about Encoder and Decoder and their examples. I gave a satisfactory answer to that as well. Now in the meantime, the other interviewer had left the room to take a call, this can be a bit distracting, but just try to focus on your answers. Also whenever interviewer asks u about a question, try to question him back, to get complete understanding of his question if you did not understand something. He then asked me to mention all ML algos I know about. I mentioned linear reg, logistic reg, random forest, decision trees,etc. He asked whether I knew about XGBoost. I told him that I had idea about its working but did not have experience working with it. He gave a remark that, did you just move to learning LLMS without completing all ML algos? I mentioned that I knew about them but had not worked with all the ML algos. He then asked me, how good am I in

python, I said 8 on 10. He then asked a DSA question, given an array of numbers find the minimum elements you need to choose to reach the target value. I thought for about 2-3 minutes,( greedy, dp,etc) but could not get an ans, then i just thought of using the brute force and told him for each element we will choose it and then check how many more we need to reach target and maintain a minimum count. So accepted the brute force (since this role did not require much dsa knowledge). Then they asked 2 sql questions 1 was a group by and count query (given document id and curr_status, count the no. of days that document is in the curr_status, each row denotes a day). Then next she gave 2 columns and asked me to explain all types of joins. They then asked if I had any questions for them. I did ask one about gen ai applications in nomura. And then about the diff in culture that nomura has as compared to other companies. They answered these for almost 5 mins. Overall, the interview went well, I was expecting to be called for next round.

3. [HR] [2- CDO ]

Only 2 candidates gave this round for CDO. It was a casual round. Interviewer asked me to give an intro, then asked me about the field I want to work in. Then she said that since I was shortlisted for all 3 roles, give me an explanation about all 3 roles. Then family background and higher studies preference(definitely no). And then I asked her 3 questions about what do u look for in a person not tech skills but general skills, one good thing about nomura and one not so good thing. She answered well for 5-10 mins. But then she left the room with me and when we reached the tpc standing outside tpo, she just said he is done for the day, he can go home. I was like what?? Nothing went alarmingly wrong in the interview, why am I being asked 2 go home, the tpc also said that you are not selected so you can go home now. I felt, I will have to start preparing for companies again from tomorrow. So both the hr round candidates were asked to go home. Then message came that every cdo candidate can go home and results will come later. So then there was some hope, given that only 2 gave the hr round. And finally the result came. 2 were shortlisted for CDO, 1 FOR GM, 3 FOR ITD.

1. [OA] [ 200 ]

The first round was an Online Assessment, which consisted of three sections:

● Analytical Reasoning

● Quantitative Aptitude

● Verbal Ability Total Duration: 60 minutes

Verbal Section

This section included reading comprehension passages and sentence correction/fill-in-the-blank type questions. The questions were pretty straightforward and easy to handle with a decent understanding of grammar and reading speed.

Quantitative Section

The quants questions were moderately easy -- covering basic math concepts. However, the Data Interpretation (DI) problems required more time and could become time-consuming if not planned properly. A good strategy is key to managing this section effectively.

Preparation Note:

I hadn't done a lot of dedicated practice before this round, but I found that IndiaBix was a really good platform to brush up on Aptitude and Verbal topics. If you're preparing for such rounds, I'd recommend giving it a go.

SHORTLISTING FOR CDO WAS BASED ON OA AND RESUME

2. [Tech Interview] [8-CDO, 28-ITD, 19-GM ]

I was interviewed for the Chief Data Officer (CDO) role, and there were two interviewers taking the interview simultaneously. The conversation began with a simple "Introduce yourself" question.

As they went through my resume, they noticed that I had done a lot of hackathons and development-focused projects. Since the role was related more to data analysis, they asked me about my interest in the role and whether I'd be comfortable switching gears from development.

I answered honestly. I mentioned that while my journey started from the development side and I naturally feel inclined toward it, I've also worked on projects that align with data roles and would be comfortable and interested in this direction as well.

Project Discussion

They asked me to explain two ML-related projects:

1. Rapid Compliance Checker (RAG-based)

I explained the RAG (Retrieval Augmented Generation) architecture used in this project. They asked a follow-up: "RAG gives k results. What if only 1 is relevant and the rest are not?"

I answered by talking about an optimized approach using Graph RAG, which helps improve contextual relevance and filter better responses using semantic relationships.

2. Voice Automation Platform

This project included a smart suggestion engine which detects tasks and offers to perform them. The suggestions were based on Gemini. They grilled me a bit here -- especially about how Gemini handles sensitive or inappropriate language.

For example, they asked what would happen if someone asked Gemini to send a bad word/abusive message. I replied that Gemini won't acknowledge such prompts, but in case it does, we can fine-tune the model or even build a custom LLM to avoid that. They mentioned the cost of fine-tuning, so I proposed a lighter solution -- prompt-level checks to prevent such actions rather than acknowledge them.

DSA Question

They asked me if I was comfortable with Python, to which I said yes.

Question:

Group the anagrams from the list: ["abc", "cba", "tea", "eat", "pig", "gpi", "pay"]

I was able to solve it immediately -- and instead of using a dictionary (map), I used a 26-sized array for each word. When asked why, I explained that it avoids extra space overhead, while maintaining the same time complexity.

System Design: ATS Scanner

Next, I was asked to design an ATS (Applicant Tracking System) Scanner that could fetch the 5 most relevant resumes for an SDE role.

I drew the RAG-based architecture again, explaining each step:

● Document Retrieval

● Chunking resumes

● Vector embedding and storing

● Extracting keywords from the job description (like expected technologies and tools)

They asked how I would extract these keywords. I gave an example using Nomura's JD, which had a "Technologies we expect" section. I mentioned we can automate the extraction using LLMs.

SQL Questions

They gave me a complex SQL query involving DENSE_RANK. I was able to understand and write the query within 2 minutes. They seemed quite impressed and also appreciated that I clarified the question properly before answering.

https://leetcode.com/problems/department-top-three-salaries/description/?envType=study-plan-v2&envId=to p-sql-50 (SIMILAR TO THIS)

They then asked about joins. They gave me two tables and asked to find the output for each type of join.

Table 1: Table 2:

id id

1 1

1 2

1 3

1 4

5 5

Though it was a bit tricky, I managed to answer all join variations correctly.

Closing Conversation

By now, the atmosphere was quite friendly. They asked me about where I stay, how I commute to college, and we had a light conversation about the company.

At the end, they asked if I had any questions. I asked: "How do you ensure the authenticity of data when it's coming from multiple sources?"

We had a small discussion on that, and then the interview was wrapped up.

Overall, it was a friendly and engaging experience where I got to talk about both my development and data-related work. I appreciated the depth of their questions and the interest they showed in my answers.

3. [HR] [2- CDO ]

I was the first one to be called for the HR round. The conversation was very casual and felt more like a normal chat than a formal interview.

The HR asked me about:

● My family background

● Where I stay

● My personal goals and aspirations

It lasted around 10-15 minutes, and nothing too technical or intense came up.

But here's where things took an unexpected turn.

A Twist After the HR Round

After the round ended, the HR simply told me, "Your process for today is over, you can go home now."

I was shocked and confused. Usually, candidates are asked to wait or are given further instructions. So, I went to the placement coordinator and asked what this meant.

They quietly told me, "This usually means you're not selected."

I was genuinely sad and disappointed and left the campus thinking I hadn't made it.

But then -- after some time -- the final HR result list came out, and my name was in it!

Turns out, it was a bit of a prank or a surprise moment -- and I was actually selected.

2 STUDENTS WERE OFFERED THE ROLE I WAS ONE OF THEM

The interview experience is slightly longer than usual, but I've tried to cover any questions anyone can have. I hope this 5 minute read can really help you out in your preparation.

Placement Process:

The company came with 3 roles - GM, ITD and CDO. We were required to fill in 2 of our preferences. The ITD role had an aptitude test and shortlisting for GM and CDO roles were done on the basis of our resumes. I had applied for ITD and GM.
journey.prep:
1) It's very very important to not lose hope or give up. Right till the start of my 3rd year, I was planning to do Non Tech and not even sit for tech companies. But my internship changed my perspective. I started DSA, more dev, and things started falling into place. So even if you haven't started yet, it's never too late. Just work hard and give it your all.

2) Luck is a major major factor in placements. Do not underestimate it, but also do not let it affect you as well.

3) Resume building is very crucial. Know the format well, ONLY INCLUDE WHAT YOU ARE CONFIDENT ABOUT, learn the concepts if you have lied on your resume.

My Resume - Aman_Kanojia_Resume.pdf

4) Pick a programming language to master. I chose Python. Companies prefer Java a lot, almost all of them. So maybe go for that or C++, and practice Python every now and then.

5) Giving contests on Leetcode or Codeforces (again, Competitive Programming can help a lot, it's not required though). This will help you learn to code under time constraints.

6) Build your communication skills, very important for interviews. Maybe help each other by taking each other's interviews. I had been good at it, so I didn't prepare much. But one can rehearse, get some tips from youtube and participate in competitions for it.

It is very important to know how to answer your interviewers be it Tech or HR. Always greet when you enter, wait for their offer to take a seat, greet when leaving. These minor things leave an impact. Know how to build stories around your answers from past experiences, or maybe even lie a little, elaborate on your answers, give some extra information to what you're asked to show how you stand out. These things specifically help in HR rounds a lot.

Prepare a good introduction about yourself. It should include the following points:

● First greet and thank for the opportunity

● Name, degree, college and year. Where you've been born and brought up (cover this in like 2 short sentences max)

● A brief about your skills (like good fundamentals in Full Stack Development or Machine Learning, built scalable projects)

● Mention your internship experience if you have any in 2-3 lines, what you did there and how it was for you

● Give an overview of 1 or 2 of your projects, what they are and what they solve. Unless asked for, don't explain more projects.

● Then cover any extracurricular activities apart from Tech, like I was the Head of Marketing for Oculus. Your experience in it and what you did.

● Move on to any achievements, competitions, hobbies (all of this in one line)

● And lastly, but most importantly, briefly explain why you are a good fit for the role by matching with JD and covering your skills.

Any introduction anywhere between 30 seconds to 1.5 minutes is good enough.

7) DSA is not only going to get you better at Data Structures and Algorithms, but also build your logical thinking and fluency with the language you code in.

Resource - https://takeuforward.org/strivers-a2z-dsa-course/strivers-a2z-dsa-course-sheet-2/

This right here is your Bible for DSA, and I'd personally recommend Striver's videos. You can also take a look at Neetcode 150. Striver's SDE sheet is when you're well versed with DSA.

8) Prepare for OOPS, preferably in Java, and the language you are confident about.

Resource- OOP 1 | Introduction & Concepts - Classes, Objects, Constructors, Keywords

CheatSheet- https://whimsical.com/object-oriented-programming-cheatsheet-by-love-babbar-YbSgLatbWQ4R5paV7Egq Fw

For Java - https://www.tpointtech.com/java-tutorial

9) Prepare for DBMS and SQL from Love Babbar's videos.

DBMS - Introduction to DBMS Placements Course 2022

SQL - Leetcode SQL 50 is more than enough https://leetcode.com/studyplan/top-sql-50/

10) Prepare for Puzzles and Guestimmates as well.

Puzzles - https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/aptitude/top-100-puzzles-asked-in-interviews/

Guesstimates - Videos on youtube Cheatsheet - https://180dcsrcc.in/guesstimate-cheat-sheet-2024/

11) You can prepare for System Design as well, which I have done. Even if it's not asked directly, it improves your understanding of concepts very well. Although you can easily skip this.

12) GFG is great for questions on Core Concepts (OS, CCN, Language specific)

13) Prepare Aptitude questions from IndiaBix - http://indiabix.com/aptitude/questions-and-answers/

14) Have at least 3 projects ready. They shouldn't be too simple, having some impact is always appreciated. Projects on Development or Machine Learning are the most common.

15) Actively participate in Hackathons, maybe even Case Study Competitions (it will give you more confidence)

journey.howSecured:
The company came with 3 roles - GM, ITD and CDO. We were required to fill in 2 of our preferences. The ITD role had an aptitude test and shortlisting for GM and CDO roles were done on the basis of our resumes. I had applied for ITD and GM.

1. Pre-placement Talk - 28th July

2. Aptitude Test (for ITD, not GM, but the year prior, there was an aptitude test for GM as well) - 31st July

3. Group Discussion Round - 1st August (up to the HR round)

4. Technical Round-1

5. Technical Round-2

6. HR Round

Now the further rounds were conducted for just me and another student after we cleared HR (no clear reason was given as to why)

7. Virtual Techno HR Round 1 - 4th August

8. Virtual Techno HR Round 2 - 4th August

I'll cover details of the OA (Aptitude Test) very briefly. Around 180+ students applied for the OA. It was a 60 minute exam with 20 questions on Analytical, Verbal and Quantitative Sections each (thus total 60 questions), conducted on MeritTrac's Platform - Pariksha. The questions were easy to medium. What mattered most was speed. I was able to complete around 55 questions by the end, and tried smart guesses for the rest, as there were no negative marking. So solve the easier questions first, as you can switch between questions and sections.

The OA results came at around 7 in the evening. Shortly after the shortlists for GM and CDO also came out. I was shortlisted for ITD and GM roles. Generally all shortlists come a day prior to the interviews. So if one is selected for interviews, for that day they should go through their Resume very well first and foremost. BE VERY THOROUGH ON WHAT YOU ADD ON YOUR RESUMES, otherwise it's better to skip that skill. Then quickly try revising basic concepts, DSA notes if you have any, and skim through the interview experiences of that particular company, as it gives you a fair idea of the process. These are the things that I did.

The below part is only going to be focused for the GM role. For ITD, there are other interview experiences in the drive which you can check out.

GM Role JD - GM SPIT Tech focused Intern role_JD - 2025.pdf

Some people have misconceptions that the role is Non Tech, but it's not the case. It's a Tech Role which you can see in the JD.

1. Group Discussion [ 19 students appeared for this round ]

The 19 students were split into two panels. There were around 9 students in my panel. The topic was given to us directly during the GD (no prior indication), and no phones allowed, pure brainstorming. The topic was relatively easy to prepare on - 'Is AI making us Smarter or Dependent'. I had gathered my panel members prior to the round and advised them that we should do the GD collaboratively, allowing everyone to keep their points, and avoid opposing and conflicts as much as possible, which would give everyone a fair chance. This worked, and the GD went very smooth, and lasted for around 30 minutes. I made around 3-4 valid points. Make sure to actively participate in the discussion, but not dominate it as well. The key is to be confident, be active and try to maintain fluency. The motive of the GD is just to see how well and actively a student participates, contributes and presents their ideas in a discussion. Take a pen and paper to jot down points. Examples of GDs on youtube, are more than enough to prepare.

2. Technical Round-1 [ 10 students appeared for this round ]

The round began with the interviewer asking me to introduce myself.. I introduced myself, told him about my internship and my contribution to it. Then I talked about my projects, giving him some overview about them, to which he would ask some questions in between regarding them. Then he began asking some basic questions, such as defining data structures like Hashmap, Stack, Queue, LinkedList, etc. This was pretty easy, so I even explained some extra info for each, such as what is collision in hashmap, struct of LinkedList,etc and gave examples for each. Then he proceeded to ask two easy level DSA questions:

1) Implement Queue using Stack - Simple implementation using 2 stacks

2) Remove duplicates from an array (order should be maintained) - Using a Hashmap to maintain order and remove duplicates. I solved both of them very quickly, and the interviewer only needed the logic, no code or pseudocode. Then he asked me briefly about my experience with Flask, React, etc (they were mentioned in the JD), but didn't ask any questions about them. He then asked me if I knew Python, to which I replied that it was my primary language. Then he proceeded with asking multiple questions on Python. Some of them were:

1) Simple questions like the difference between List and Tuple. Which of them can be used as a key in a dictionary, which cannot, and why not.

2) What is List Comprehension and what's the syntax

3) How dictionaries work in Python, how to sort them by keys and by values.

4) OOPs questions in python and how is it implemented in Python, what are abstract methods, and access modifiers in python.

5) What are Decorator Functions in Python (he asked me to write a decorator function)

6) What is args and kwargs

7) Write a function to convert a Flattened Dictionary into an Unflattened Dictionary. E.g) Flattened Dictionary : table= {'a.b.c':1, 'd.e':2, 'f':3} as input should give Output: table={a:{b:{c:1}}, d:{e:2},f:3} I wrote a recursive function explaining each step while writing the function, and was able to solve it in some time. He wanted to check how efficiently I write codes in python.

I was able to answer all questions except the syntax of the decorator wrapper function. I asked him a question about the role and his experience at the end. The interview lasted for around 35 minutes.

3. Technical Round-2 [ 6 students appeared for this round ]

The interviewer looked through my resume and asked me a question on what Apache Kafka is and how it works (it was mentioned on my resume). I explained all the concepts related to Kafka, how they work, gave examples of their use-case and real life scenarios, and how I implemented it into my project. Then he gave me two tables, and asked me to first tell him what I can infer from it, and then write the SQL query for it.

The question was as follows: Given a table, lets say Table, for every Note, print the entire row with the max Tranche Transactions Note Pipeline Tranche

T1 N1 P2 2

T2 N1 P1 1

T4 N2 P1 2

T1 N2 P1 1

T2 N3 P2 1

Output: Transactions Note Pipeline Max_Tranche

T1 N1 P2 2

T4 N2 P1 2

T2 N3 P2 1

I had messed up a bit initially, to which the interviewer gave me a hint, after which I was able to solve the query. The query included Sub Query, Aggregation, Grouping and Join concepts. It was as follows:-

SELECT t2.Transactions, t2.Note, t2.Pipeline, t2.Max_Tranche FROM ( SELECT MAX(Tranche), Note AS Max_Tranche FROM Table GROUP BY Note) AS t1 JOIN Table AS t2 ON t1.Note=t2.Note

After this he began asking me questions on core DBMS. Some of the questions were:

1) What is RDBMS? Why is it used?

2) What is Normalisation and what is its purpose? What are the pros and cons of an overly normalized table and a completely unnormalised table

3) What is Indexing, how does it work? Why is it beneficial? Which data structure is used for it, and how does it work? When is it a good option and when is it not?

4) What is Partitioning and Sharding. What's the difference?

5) What is Data Replication? Why is it important?

6) What is a Composite Key? How is it different from the Primary Key

7) What is a Foreign Key and what happens when you delete a row with a primary key as the foreign key to another table. How do you resolve the error? There were a few more basic questions, I don't remember clearly. I was able to answer all the questions asked to me, and I tried to always give some extra info related to the solution. The interviewer seemed content with all my answers. After this he was about to ask me a DSA question, but asked to just explain Collision in hashmaps, that's it. At the end I asked him how the transition from college to corporate is, and what was his experience. The interview lasted for around 25-30 minutes.

4. HR Round [ 4 students appeared for this round ]

The interview began with the interviewer asking me a brief intro about myself, what I've done and what are my skills, and my experience as the Head of Marketing at Oculus. He then asked me about my understanding of the JD. I replied according to what I had researched about it. Then he asked me for the top 3 qualities about myself, and a little about my internship. He then asked me what drives me to do more. Looking at my CGPA, he asked me if I was in the top 30% of my class, and why I was not higher. Then he asked me a tricky question, which was "When should one do MBA" (he wanted to check if i had any plans for it). I turned it around by stating that the correct question should be "Why MBA", and started building around it. He proceeded to ask me questions about my family background and where I live. He also mentioned that my travel from Colaba to Powai won't be so joyous, to which I said I'm accustomed to it, and might consider shifting. He asked me to rate myself in coding, what would be my actions if someone is better at it, at work, and what ratio would I draw between tech and finance market during my work. Lastly, I made comments on how I'm a good fit for the role, as the role serves both verticals of Tech and Finance, and I have the appropriate technical, communication skills and the business acumen required.

So the key to clearing HR is being honest, confident and not lying. You do need to build stories around your answer, give examples from your experiences and never give single statement answers. Apart from that they want to see how you present yourself, your expressions, and how you handle pressure. They don't want robots who just know how to work.

Note - After this round, only one student was immediately selected, and me and another candidate were scheduled for more Virtual Interviews on 4th August (1st was a Friday, and offices are closed on weekends, hence Monday). However we did figure out that we were being considered for different roles, as

the other candidate had a completely Non Technical and Financial Background, and his process was different as well.

No clear reason was given as to why this was being done. But I need to admit, I was a bit confused and slightly disappointed. The next 2 days were very stressful, somewhat torturous, as no information was given regarding what will be the next rounds, how they will go about and why they were scheduled.

But it's very important to keep your composure, not lose hope. I kept talking to two of my friends who really supported me during the process, to keep my mind off these things. I didn't exactly prepare anything extra in those 2 days, as I believe there's no point to it, and it's just gonna add more pressure. I did prepare for some common HR questions though.

On Sunday night, the TPC instructed me to keep my phone on the entire time the next day, as even they didn't know when the interviews would be scheduled. So I was ready in formals and my laptop from 8 in the morning. Later I was informed that my interview is at 2:30 pm.

5. Virtual Techno HR Round-1

It began with the interviewer asking me to introduce myself and talk a bit about my internship and projects, and how I did them. She then said she'll be asking me questions on Python, to which I thought it would be like the last round, but it wasn't the case. She began by asking me what's the difference between loc and iloc. I thought she meant about the 'Lock' in threading in python, to which i explained everything. She then told me she means loc and iloc in Pandas. I was taken aback at that time as i had never done pandas specifically, which i told her as well. Regardless, she went to ask me questions on Pandas, like:

1) loc and iloc

2) How to drop null values

3) How to fill in rows with null values

4) How to merge two dataframes

5) What's the difference between Left merge and Right merge

I explained approaches for all of them, but did not know the syntax for them, which I honestly told the interviewer.

She then asked me some behavioral questions. She asked me how I would proceed if I had worked on something, which was later discarded because the manager feels there's a more optimal approach. I replied honestly that I would try to understand the situation and adapt to the better solution, as we always go through that in DSA. Then she asked me what I do if I'm stuck somewhere and not able to solve a certain problem or write some code. I explained that I tend to read documentations first, then try sites like StackOverflow, maybe ask my peers or seniors, and then lastly try some AI tools like ChatGPT or Claude. She asked me in what ratio, which approach I would use. Then she asked me what I would do if a member in my team is slacking in terms of work or not performing. I gave an appropriate answer, saying I would discuss with that member first, try to understand the problem, if it still doesn't solve it, i'd probably escalate to the manager. I gave example scenarios or past experiences for each answer as well.

At the end, I made a statement that although the interview started on the wrong note, as I wasn't able to give the syntax for Pandas, I'm a quick learner and can adapt well to new technologies, instances of which I have proved earlier. To this she said it's alright.

The interview lasted for around 45 minutes.

In all honesty I had almost given up hopes as I was not able to give good responses to the technical questions. Also the other candidate had given a good interview, and another round was already scheduled for him at 6:30 (not for me till then). Just as I gave up, I received a call from the TPC that we both have been called to the office the next day at Powai. However, I had been shortlisted for the OA of another company for the next day, so he asked me to make a decision, to which I said I want to proceed with Nomura (obviously). Later the people at Nomura themselves said that they don't want me to miss my OA for another company, and that they're ready to immediately take the next round at 7:30 PM. So I rushed back to my laptop in formals.

6. Virtual Techno HR Round-2

The interviewer (she was taking the interview from her home as well, as it was too late) began by asking me to give an introduction about myself, my projects, my experiences and so on. Then asked me to explain in detail about one of my mentioned projects, and what state it is in now. I gave a complete explanation of the architecture, high level design, working, flow, use of the project, and how it was used in a real competition. She then asked me what challenges I faced during that project, and how I solved them. She asked if I had ever worked with something that was new to me in a short period of time. She then asked me about my internship experience and what was my most important learning there. She also asked me what I did as the Head of Marketing at Oculus.

She then asked a few python questions. She told me that there's a lot of electronic data coming in continuously, and we only have limited memory resources. So how would I process the data? I told her that I would use Pagination to split the incoming data into chunks, then use multithreading to parallelly process the data, with each thread responsible for some chunk of data, and finally use the garbage collector to discard threads not in use. She was satisfied with the answer. She then asked me what are lambda functions and asked me multiple implementations of it. The other questions were very easy.

Then she asked me about my hobbies and if I had any questions. By the end the interview almost became a bit casual, we were almost just conversing at that point. The interview lasted for around 35 minutes.

Later I was told the results will be announced the next morning. At that point I completely stopped thinking about what could happen. I reached college for the next OA, at my desk in the designated classroom, and with just a few minutes to the OA, Sparsh Ma'am from the TPO came and informed me that I have been selected, and I do not need to give the OA. I reconfirmed it with her, as I was not expecting the results to come so randomly. Alas, I took a sigh of relief.

At the end I was selected from the 2 candidates giving the extra interviews, and one was initially selected on the first day itself. So 2 people for the GM role.

A Small Overview of my Placement Process Experience:

So the entire placement process was a complete rollercoaster ride in itself, and there were a lot of ups and downs. About some other companies I applied for, I reached the JPMC interviews but couldn't appear for them due to a family emergency. This taught me that there are some things which are beyond our control. I reached the HR round for Work India but was one of the 2 students out of 4 who weren't selected. So you never know what requirements the companies have, and you may get rejected even at the last minute.

Other times either I couldn't clear the OA, and for one of the companies I couldn't sit for the OA because the CG criteria for it was 8, and I had a CG of 7.9. (Try to keep your CG above 8)

So yeah, there's a lot going on, and a lot of luck (trust me, a lot !!) involved in the process. But I think overall, if you've worked hard, and if you have the skill sets, you'll end up in one of the good companies regardless. Just remember to not give up, have faith in yourself and keep trying. Everything happens for a reason.

customSections.title: Advice & Tips for Juniors
customSections.content:
1) It's very very important to not lose hope or give up. Right till the start of my 3rd year, I was planning to do Non Tech and not even sit for tech companies. But my internship changed my perspective. I started DSA, more dev, and things started falling into place. So even if you haven't started yet, it's never too late. Just work hard and give it your all.

2) Luck is a major major factor in placements. Do not underestimate it, but also do not let it affect you as well.

3) Resume building is very crucial. Know the format well, ONLY INCLUDE WHAT YOU ARE CONFIDENT ABOUT, learn the concepts if you have lied on your resume.

My Resume - Aman_Kanojia_Resume.pdf

4) Pick a programming language to master. I chose Python. Companies prefer Java a lot, almost all of them. So maybe go for that or C++, and practice Python every now and then.

5) Giving contests on Leetcode or Codeforces (again, Competitive Programming can help a lot, it's not required though). This will help you learn to code under time constraints.

6) Build your communication skills, very important for interviews. Maybe help each other by taking each other's interviews. I had been good at it, so I didn't prepare much. But one can rehearse, get some tips from youtube and participate in competitions for it.

It is very important to know how to answer your interviewers be it Tech or HR. Always greet when you enter, wait for their offer to take a seat, greet when leaving. These minor things leave an impact. Know how to build stories around your answers from past experiences, or maybe even lie a little, elaborate on your answers, give some extra information to what you're asked to show how you stand out. These things specifically help in HR rounds a lot.

Prepare a good introduction about yourself. It should include the following points:

● First greet and thank for the opportunity

● Name, degree, college and year. Where you've been born and brought up (cover this in like 2 short sentences max)

● A brief about your skills (like good fundamentals in Full Stack Development or Machine Learning, built scalable projects)

● Mention your internship experience if you have any in 2-3 lines, what you did there and how it was for you

● Give an overview of 1 or 2 of your projects, what they are and what they solve. Unless asked for, don't explain more projects.

● Then cover any extracurricular activities apart from Tech, like I was the Head of Marketing for Oculus. Your experience in it and what you did.
