Luck is a very important factor in this placement process but that too will only work if you keep working hard.

About GM Role :

On 31st July, at around 8p.m. I found out that my resume had been shortlisted for the GM role. I did not know anything about the role and called up a senior to find out about the role. Even though the JD says Global Markets Analyst(which sounds non-tech) the role is completely a tech based role which closely works with the Global Markets division of Nomura. The title of the JD even said tech focused intern. The senior told me that all the work he was doing there was tech related along with exposure to finance(something that I was looking for). He also guided me how to approach the interviews and how to prepare for GD which was going to be the first round.

GM JD - https://drive.google.com/file/d/1ZnsTaifPX5qplLdzshR0_k1uR72aqFyr/view?usp=sharing

1. Group Discussion [18 Students appeared for this round]

The first round for GM is a Group Discussion round. This round lasted for around 30 minutes. We had a group of 8 students. The topic was pretty easy on is AI making us smarter or dependent. Before the GD we as a group had decided that we would not cut each other mid sentence(can disagree though). This ensured that our GD went smoothly without screaming or any fighting. The key in this round is to be confident in what you are speaking. Take a paper or a small notebook and note what your peers are saying as well so you can add to their points or disagree with them. Any youtube video showing how to act in a GD should suffice.

2. Technical Round-1 [ 10 students were shortlisted ]

After 10 minutes of finishing the GD, I was called for my interview.(So if you are the first one called up you might not get time to prepare so be ready beforehand). This round lasted for around 40 minutes. Firstly he asked me to introduce myself and walk through my resume. Simple DSA questions were asked like sort the array(I gave 4 approaches). I offered to write pseudocode for merge sort as well but the interviewer was

happy with my explanation. I was also asked to implement a linked list using a stack(simple 2 stack approach(a FIFO data structure using LIFO)). I was asked a few questions on linked list as well such as finding the middle of the linked list and checking if the linked list has a cycle or not(easy, slow and fast pointer approaches). He asked if I knew python but I told him I only used python for api calls to Gemini. He said it's fine and moved on. Then he asked on my projects and told me to draw the architecture of one of my projects.(a simple drawing of frontend, backend, load balancer and how the request is serviced). Middle of Linked List Linked list has a cycle or not Merge Sort

A few tips for this round:

1. Prepare a solid Introduction covering everything in your resume and focusing on stuff you are confident at.

2. Whenever given a question, walk through the entire solution from start to finish with the interviewer. They are more interested in how you are approaching the problem. If you don't know something, ask for a hint but don't go silent.

3. Practice DSA so that even if a simple question is asked you are able to confidently answer it.

3. Technical Round 2 [ 6 students were shortlisted]

I read the interview experience of my senior before this round and they said that Nomura asks puzzles. So I went through the first 10-15 puzzles of GFG top 100 puzzles. To my luck, I was asked one puzzle from there itself and I went through the solution of the puzzle in detail with the interviewer. After this I was given a medium level SQL query to solve.Given a table lets say Data, for every Note, print the entire row with the max transactions

Notes Pipeline Transactions

N1 P1 400

N1 P2 500

N1 P3 200

N2 P1 400

N2 P2 300

N3 P1 100

Output

Notes Pipeline Transactions

N1 P2 500

N2 P1 400

N3 P1 100

Normal GROUP BY notes would not work as then you wouldn't be able to print pipeline or else you would have to include pipeline in your GROUP BY as well but that would not give correct output.

ANSWER

Select d.notes, d.pipeline, d.transactions From Data as d INNER JOIN ( SELECT Notes, max(transactions) as maxtrn From data GROUP BY Notes) as t ON d.notes = t.notes AND d.transactions = t.maxtrn

Another way is to use WHERE (notes, transactions) IN and the same subquery as above

After this I was asked a DSA questions Merge Intervals.Again pretty standard. After this I was asked to walk through my resume projects and was asked some React questions related to Virtual DOM, hooks and callback questions. I was not very confident in all my answers but tried to answer as much as I knew. After this he also told me to explain the system of one of my projects and the use of RabbitMQ(which I had used). I was able to answer it. In the end I asked him a few questions about Nomura and if there was anything he would like me to explain again.

Puzzles

A few tips for this round:

1. Prepare all your Projects in your resume thoroughly. From tech stack to why did you use that tech stack. Whatever you use in your projects, lets say MERN, read top interview questions for it.

2. The JD mentioned python and React. I didn't know Python in detail so I honestly said I don't know and they were fine with it. Dont try to force something that u dont know because if they ask questions and you are not able to answer it leaves a bad impression.

3. Practice SQL top 50 on leetcode.

4. HR Round [ 4 students were shortlisted]

This was actually my longest round. The interviewer asked me a lot of questions. It started with my understanding of the role. Then he told me what I would have to learn for this role and I answered honestly that I didn't know half of the stuff mentioned in the JD. Then I was asked 3 words to describe myself. Then he asked me about my hobbies. He told me how my friends would describe me and 3 of my bad qualities as well. Then he asked me what gets me motivated and how to motivate me as well. He asked me about my family background. The key point for HR is to answer everything honestly. Don't prepare a lot before this round. Read a bit about the company and JD . They don't want someone who is mechanical.

2 students were offered the job for this role.I was one of them :)

3. Technical Interview 1

4. Technical Interview 2

5. HR Round

1. Online Aptitude Test [ 180+ students appeared]

This was an online aptitude test conducted on MeritTrac's Online Assessment Engine - PARIKSHA, The test consisted of 60 questions, divided equally into Analytical, Quantitative, and Verbal sections, with no negative marking. The total time was 60 minutes, so time management was crucial.

The level of difficulty was easy to medium, but the Analytical section had around 8-9 Data Interpretation

(DI) questions which were quite lengthy. A key point -- check in advance if a calculator is allowed. In my case, it was allowed, but we were not informed clearly, which made solving DI questions more time-consuming. If calculators aren't allowed, I suggest using the round-off method to reach the closest answer faster.

Tip: Start with the Verbal section -- passages and sentence-based questions were straightforward. Quants was easy too, but DI can eat up time if you don't plan ahead.

Resources I used:

● IndiaBix: Pick a topic, then practice multiple pages, not just the first set -- the site has commonly asked questions with clear solutions.

● YouTube: CareerRide Aptitude is a good channel for learning tricks of aptitude. https://youtube.com/playlist?list=PLpyc33gOcbVA4qXMoQ5vmhefTruk5t9lt&si=GM_wTZqebs-y0 zAF

Insider tip: If Nomura is visiting other colleges a day or two before, try to connect with students from those campuses -- the topics and question patterns are often similar. 😉

2. Technical Interview I [ 28 candidates were selected ]

The list of selected candidates from the aptitude test was declared on 31st July at 7 PM, and my Technical Interview Round 1 was scheduled the very next morning , so there were hardly a few hours to prepare!

How I prepared: I quickly revised my Java OOPs concepts, core SQL queries including window functions, self joins and cross joins. I also went through my projects thoroughly -- focusing on questions like "Why did I choose this tech stack?" and "What could have been an alternative approach?"

The interview: I entered the room, greeted the interviewer and asked permission to sit. He was very polite and friendly. The very first question he asked was, "What's the meaning of your name?" Then he asked me to introduce myself , he specifically suggested covering my bachelor's degree, any internships, and the tech stack I worked on.

Tip: While introducing yourself, explain a basic overview of your best-known project -- this helps you lead the interview in a direction you're comfortable with.

After the introduction, he asked me to explain all my projects briefly, and my specific role if it was a group project. Next, he asked about my subjects during Bachelors and Masters , which ones I liked and disliked. He moved on to, "Why should we select you? What skills do you have?" here I highlighted my strong academic background, and connected it to my previous answers for example, mentioning that although I didn't like a particular subject, I still managed a good CGPA.

Then came the practical task: He asked me to convert my e-commerce project (originally in MERN) to Java -- and gave me some time to think and explain.

Tip: Always think aloud -- even if the interviewer pretends to be busy, they are paying attention to how you approach a problem, not just the final solution.

Unexpected twist: Midway through, the interview was paused and all candidates were called to give the aptitude test again the panel suspected some unfair practices in the earlier round.

This surprise test had 3 questions:

1. Aptitude: A tap can fill a tank in 10 hrs, B in 8 hrs, and C can empty it in 12 hrs. If all three are open, how long will it take to fill the tank?

2. DSA: Maximum Subarray Sum , I wrote the brute force approach, but explained the optimized Kadane's Algorithm logic too.

3. SQL: Find the employee(s) with the highest salary under each manager. I didn't remember the exact syntax but mentioned how it could be solved using GROUP BY and window functions (PARTITION BY).

Tip: They don't expect perfect answers they value your approach, logic and thought process more. Write down whatever valid, strong ideas you have.

In any round, explain your thoughts well , clarity and confidence matters!

After the retest, the results were declared out of 28 students, only 7 were selected, out of which 2 were directly promoted to Round 2 , I was one of them. The exact criteria were not disclosed.

3. Technical Interview II [ 7 candidates were selected out of 28 ]

This round was much more technical and intense , they really grilled me for almost an hour. There were two panelists in the room. I handed over my resumes and the interview began.

Again, I was asked to introduce myself , Tip: Always use words you're confident about, and never fake your resume ,they read every single line carefully.

The first panelist asked which project I was most comfortable with. I chose my AI Interviewer System and explained that I had actually deployed it. She asked me to explain the entire architecture, what tech stacks were used, and why I chose them.

Since the project included session analytics, she gave me a situation: "How would you get the analytics for how many people answered a particular question and analyze it based on their scores?" I suggested storing each question separately instead of an entire session and comparing strings but she wasn't convinced. I then proposed a DB design change using foreign keys. I asked for hints but realized they were more interested in seeing how I think, so I kept explaining my thoughts in all directions.

Then the second panelist shifted the focus to Data Structures. I honestly said I only had a basic idea. He asked about HashMaps, for example: "Can a key in a HashMap be a class?" I answered yes, but with constraints, although I couldn't recall all the details. He also asked me about Stack and Heap memory, Object and reference , where are they stored etc. He asked about sorting algorithms how Quick Sort, Merge Sort work, their time complexities, best & worst cases, Bubble Sort, BST etc. He also asked me to write short code snippets showing different time complexities as well as the sorting algorithms. I initially mixed up Bubble Sort with Insertion Sort, but when he cross-questioned, I immediately spotted my mistake and corrected it.

They switched back to another project of mine and asked deep questions about it. One tricky yet simple question was: "What happens if you keep pressing the submit button repeatedly but the data hasn't been stored yet?" I gave multiple approaches but she wasn't satisfied and kept grilling me, which led to a chain of questions about REST APIs the difference between GET, POST, PUT methods, when to use which, how to handle listing all products vs. a single product, and whether parameters can be accessed from the URL in a GET request. I could answer some parts confidently. She then asked me to explain the entire e-commerce

application workflow, cart, wishlist, order, everything as well as authentication and authorization techniques I implemented.

The other panelist asked about my comfort level in Java. I said I knew the basics. He mentioned some advanced concepts I didn't know, and I honestly admitted it. So he switched to OOPs concepts. I explained encapsulation, inheritance, and also mentioned that multiple inheritance is possible through interfaces. However, since I had just revised Java a day before, I wasn't fully clear on how interfaces enable multiple inheritance internally, so they grilled me on this too. I still shared what I thought could be the reason, showing my thought process.

He then asked, "How would you design any project?" I said I'd start with gathering requirements, spend good time finalizing the database design (and I admitted that in my past project, I had picked MongoDB mostly because it's easy to use and scalable, but this interview made me realize there are many more factors to consider).

Suddenly, they shifted to HR questions:

● "What if your project partner is not working?" I said I'd first try the approach-discuss method, but she wasn't fully convinced, so I added that I'd take necessary steps to inform the reporting manager if required.

● "What would you do if you want to prove your point and reject another idea?" -- she grilled me here too, testing my approach to conflict resolution.

At the end, I asked for feedback -- she said I should expand my thought process more!

Tips:

● Be confident about whatever you say -- but also make sure it's logically sound.

● Don't bluff -- honesty stands out more than pretending to know everything.

● They test how you think, not just how much you know.

4. HR Round [ 3 candidates were selected out of 7 ]

The HR round was quite relaxed and straightforward. The HR asked me about where I live, and why I chose SPIT despite being rank 1 in the entrance. We spoke about my hobbies, my strong academic background, and why I wanted to work at Nomura. He also asked about my plans for further studies just to understand my long-term goals.

Overall, it was a friendly conversation and a positive way to wrap up the entire process!

All 3 candidates were selected for the ITD role.

Process involved:

1. Pre-placement talk

2. Aptitude test

3. Technical Interview 1

4. Technical Interview 2

1. Preplacement Talk:

This was an online round. We were briefed about the company, its values and the roles they offered. There were 3 roles available for us in 3 different divisions, ITD, GM and CDO. It is recommended to have your webcam on and ask questions during the pre-placement talk.

2. Online Aptitude Test [181 Students appeared for the test] This was an online aptitude test conducted on MeritTrac's Online Assessment Engine - PARIKSHA. The test consisted of 60 questions, with 20 questions each in the verbal, analytical,

and quantitative sections, with no negative marking. The time limit was 60 minutes so timing is the key here. The questions were of easy-medium difficulty. Mostly, people use IndiaBix which is sufficient for practicing. I'd recommend solving the verbal and analytical questions first and then moving on to the quants as this section is time consuming. Some questions are purely in the test to waste your time. Try and identify these types of questions and keep them for the end. I split the test into 10 minutes for verbal, 15-20 for logical and 30-35 minutes for the quantitative section.

Somebody had mailed the TPO about a cheating scandal in the OA test which prompted the TPO to inform the company about the same. Things like these tarnish the reputation of the college and further discouraged the company from hiring more students.

Due to the allegations, Nomura decided to take another written OA which consisted of 1 DSA question, 1 quant and 1 sql query within 20 minutes.

The dsa question was pretty easy where we basically had to return the largest sum of a contiguous part of an array. Since the entire array was given to be positive you can just sum up all numbers and return the total sum. In case the array contains negative numbers, Kadane's Algorithm can be used to solve this problem. I had written both approaches in my solution describing the cases.

Again the quant and query were pretty easy.

They used this test to eliminate 20 of the 27 students from interviews directly.

I had given my 1st Technical Interview before this test.

2. Technical Interview - 1 [ Remaining 7 students from the written OA were shortlisted for this]

This round started at around 10 am. I was asked to introduce myself. It happened before the written OA test. Most of the early questions were based on my resume. I had mentioned a Spring Boot project and told him that Java is my primary programming language. So the next 80% of our discussion revolved around Spring Framework, Java and OOPS (I was very happy that he went towards this :) . He asked me about inheritance and polymorphism and gave me different scenarios. Also I was asked about binary search tree, quick sort algo and time complexity in general. Then I was asked about the actual implementation of HashMap in Java and how the internal methods are implemented (also asked about hashing function, collisions and how they are handled). Next I was given a simple SQL query and asked some HR type questions. Then we just talked casually about the entire placement process and asked me about my experience throughout the journey. At this point we were having just a normal conversation about stuff and he asked if I had any questions for him to which I asked a couple and the interview ended. This was a pretty chill experience for me since all the topics we discussed we my favs.

3. Technical Interview - 2 [6 students were shortlisted for this round]

This round started at around 2:30 pm post lunch. There were 2 interviewers in each panel for this round. He asked me to give my introduction but nothing from my resume lol. We started by discussing Spring Framework (yet again yess) and how it differs from MERN, its benefits and widespread use cases. We talked about JUnit testing and how unit testing works further delving into different types of testing methodologies. They went through my resume and asked me detailed questions about the technical skills that I had mentioned in the resume. I was asked questions about MERN stack and databases used in my projects. We had a discussion about JWT and how it works. I was also asked about Hadoop and how it works (I had mentioned hadoop on my resume). We also talked about how Spring Security works and how it is different from some other ways to secure web applications.

We discussed about Stripe (used in a project) payment gateway which is similar to razorpay and how it works. This was a relatively shorter round than the first one (1st was 75 minutes long ) which lasted around 40 minutes.

4. HR Round [ Total 3 candidates appeared for this round ] This was a pretty chill round as the HR and I were just having a fun conversation about my hobbies, Music, movies & series recommendations for him to which I recommended Chernobyl and The Green Book. Then he asked me how my usual day looks compared to the one we were having and I told him it had been unexpectedly smooth. I had mentioned a CFI course and he asked me about and I said it was purely out of curiosity about accounting. We talked about some things I had not mentioned on my resume and he wrapped things up from his side.

All 3 students (2 B.Tech + 1 MCA) were finally offered the role :)

Have 4-5 good projects covering important domains and use them appropriately for the JD you're applying for. Interviewers often ask 2-3 niche questions to try and shake your confidence. In such times, try and steer the discussion to the nearest relatable topic/case you can think of instead of saying idk.

For vague questions or scenarios be upfront and ask them the details before assuming especially for puzzles and dsa questions.

I had done 90% of the Striver's A2Z DSA course and solved LeetCode Daily problems, maintained a streak of 300+ which covered most of the DSA areas. This was certainly a bit overkill but I enjoyed solving it. Solving even about 150 varied and good quality problems are enough.

For SQL, leetcode-sql-50 will suffice (I personally did the first 30 only lol).

I didn't really practice for OAs specifically but Indiabix and Interviewbit are helpful.

I had made sure to do some web development in Spring Framework, since Java was my primary programming language.

Make sure every single thing mentioned on your resume is relevant and you have sufficient knowledge about the topics and projects mentioned.

Questions related to tech stack used, not used, why, how, are litmus tests for interviewers to test your technical knowledge and skills so be prepared for them.

The first few interviews might feel a bit overwhelming, but once you get the hang of it things get pretty easy. Keep a smile and just be yourself.

Some backstory up until this interview: Sometimes interview rounds are quite tough. I was asked 5 DSA questions in the MSCI process, one of which was to implement heapify process and I couldn't recall and that was the only thing which I couldn't answer which got me out. So sometimes even though you try your best, destiny wants you somewhere else :) I got shortlisted for interview rounds for JPMC, UBS, MSCI, IDFC before Nomura. IDFC was just a day before the Nomura OA and I had reached the final 4th round which was online which was taken by their IT Lead and welp I couldn't make it. I was pretty devastated with the result and my mental health took a hit since I was pretty confident on getting a positive result. I gathered all the courage for the Nomura OA the very next day and my friends & family helped immensely getting through that. The 15-20 days of placement season were no doubt some of the most tense days of my life. The uncertainty, series of negative results plays tricks on your psyche. There's a very good quote by Rick and Morty that sums up the process 'Everything will be fine in the end, Morty ; And if it isn't, it's not the end yet' eventually everything will fall into place that's for sure. It's ok to be anxious, there's no way not to be. Try and compose yourself and use the experience from negative results to iteratively work on weaknesses and better yourself.

Just know that some time in the future you will look back at this time and have a chuckle :)

Things might feel out of control or unlucky at times but have trust in your abilities and Keep giving your best cuz you only need luck to be on your side just once.

To everyone reading this, Best of Luck for your future escapades and know that you deserve the best!!

For any questions, you can find me here : LinkedIn : Shardul
